heading: Introduction
text:
## **Introduction**

There is a moment every squirrel rehabilitator knows. The phone rings. Or you open your door to a neighbor standing on the porch holding a shoebox. Inside is something small, still, and impossibly fragile — a baby squirrel, a juvenile in shock, or an adult with wounds that speak to an encounter they barely survived. And the question that follows is always the same: *What do I do now?*

This book was written to answer that question.

**What this book is.** The Comprehensive Squirrel Bible is both a field guide and a clinical reference. Its narrative chapters are written for the rehabber on the ground — the person who has just received an animal and needs clear, practical guidance fast. Its embedded veterinary protocol blocks, marked throughout with ⚕, are written for the licensed veterinarian or permitted wildlife rehabilitator who needs mg/kg dosing, differential diagnosis, and structured treatment pathways. Neither audience needs to read the other’s material. Both share the same page.

**Who wrote it and why.** This guide was developed by Tye Lombardi and published by Mad Ferret Press. It grew out of a single observation: the gap between “internet forum advice” and a formal wildlife medicine textbook was costing squirrels their lives. This book is not a replacement for a veterinarian — it is a bridge to one. It is what you reach for at 2 a.m. when your vet’s office is closed and the animal cannot wait.

**National scope.** This edition covers practices applicable across the United States and, where laws permit, broadly in North America. State-specific regulations — wildlife rehabilitation permits, euthanasia authority, and reportable disease lists — vary by jurisdiction. Readers must contact their state fish and wildlife agency for local compliance requirements. Any references to specific state agencies in this text should be read as examples only; your state agency is the authority for your location.

**The ethics of intervention.** We rehabilitate because release is possible. Reunification with the mother is always preferred over human intervention. Imprinting — the loss of the squirrel’s natural fear of humans — is the enemy of a successful release. The goal of every action in this book is a squirrel back in the canopy, wild and wary, surviving without us.

**The limits of this book.** This is not a substitute for veterinary care, a licensed permit, or hands-on training. Readers practicing without a permit should contact their state fish and wildlife agency. A sick squirrel always benefits from a veterinarian’s assessment — use this guide to prepare, not to replace that relationship.

**How to navigate this book.** Part I covers your safety and zoonotic risks. Part II covers baby squirrels from intake through independence. Part III covers emergency triage. Part IV is an A–Z clinical conditions reference. Part V covers medications and dosing. Parts VI and VII cover release and long-term care. Part VIII addresses the rehabber’s own wellbeing and sustainability. Appendix A contains the full Veterinary Formulary for licensed use.

**A word to the veterinary clinician.** The vet-protocol blocks throughout this book (marked ⚕ and structured with QUICK IDENTIFIER / MEDICAL TREATMENT headers) are written for the clinical reader and can be read independently of the surrounding narrative. Drug dosing is expressed in mg/kg where known. The full formulary is in Appendix A.

The squirrel in the shoebox is waiting. Let’s begin.

heading: The Squirrel Care Ethics
text:
## **The Squirrel Care Ethics**

Rehabilitating wildlife is not a hobby; it is a profound responsibility. To provide care for a squirrel is to enter into a silent contract to return a wild being to its rightful place in the canopy. These principles are the soul of this book and the foundation of our work, regardless of your geography.

1. The Goal of Rehabilitation Is Release

The measure of your success is not how much a squirrel trusts you, but how well it can survive without you. Every action—from the way you feed to the way you house—must be filtered through a single question: “Does this move the squirrel closer to life in the wild?” If an animal cannot be released, our goal shifts from rehabilitation to a dignified end of life.

2. Reunification Is Always Preferred

A plastic syringe is no match for a mother squirrel. Before we intake, we must exhaust every effort to reunite a healthy infant with its mother. Human intervention should be the last resort, born of necessity, not the first impulse, born of a desire to “help.”

3. Avoid Imprinting: Respect the “Wild”

A squirrel that loses its fear of humans is a squirrel with a diminished chance of survival. We are not their friends; we are their temporary guardians. Minimize unnecessary handling, avoid “baby talk,” and ensure they remain wary of the species that poses their greatest threat: us.

4. Wildlife Are Not Pets

A squirrel is a wild animal in a temporary state of crisis. Treating them like pets is a disservice to their biology and an insult to their nature. They do not belong in your bed, on your shoulder, or in a permanent cage. We provide a bridge back to the woods, not a destination in a living room.

5. Know Your Capacity: Avoid Hoarding

Compassion without boundaries leads to “Rescue Burnout” and, more dangerously, a decline in the standard of care. Quality of care must always take precedence over the quantity of animals. Know your limit, honor it, and refer to another rehabber when you are at capacity.

6. The Ethical Responsibility of Care

Once you take an animal into your care, you are responsible for its pain, its hunger, and its dignity. This means following proven medical protocols, seeking veterinary partnership for prescriptions and surgery, and having the courage to provide a “good death” through euthanasia when recovery is impossible.

heading: Ch. 1 — Keeping Yourself Safe — Zoonotic Diseases & Volunteer Safety
text:
## **1\. Keeping Yourself Safe — Zoonotic Diseases & Volunteer Safety**

A Zoonotic Disease is any infection that can be transmitted from animals to humans. While squirrels are generally “clean” compared to other wildlife, a rehabber must maintain a “Bio-Secure” mindset to protect themselves, their families, and their domestic pets.

1. The “Rabies” Myth

The Reality: According to the CDC, small rodents like squirrels are almost never found to be infected with Rabies and have not been known to transmit Rabies to humans.

The Risk: In Idaho, the primary Rabies vector is bats. If a squirrel was attacked by a rabid bat or skunk, it would likely die from the trauma before becoming infectious.

Protocol: If you are bitten, wash the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes. Contact your local health department for peace of mind, but do not panic.

2. Sarcoptic Mange (The “Itch”)

What it is: Microscopic mites (Sarcoptes scabiei) that burrow under the skin.

Transmission: Direct contact with an infested squirrel or their bedding.

In Humans: It causes “Scabies”—intensely itchy, red bumps, usually on the wrists, webbing of fingers, or waistline.

Prevention: Always wear gloves when handling a balding or crusty squirrel. Bag and wash all “mange-room” fleece in hot water with bleach.

3. Baylisascaris procyonis (Raccoon Roundworm)

The Danger: This is the most serious zoonotic threat. Squirrels can carry the larvae, but the eggs come from Raccoon feces. If you use outdoor branches or “play structures” that were exposed to raccoon latrines, you are at risk.

In Humans: If ingested, the larvae can migrate to the brain or eyes (Neural Larva Migrans), which is often fatal or causes permanent blindness.

Prevention: Never use dirt or branches from the wild without disinfecting them. Scrub everything. Wash hands religiously.

4. Leptospirosis

What it is: A bacterial disease spread through the urine of infected animals.

Transmission: Contact with urine-soaked bedding or if urine gets into an open cut on your hand.

Symptoms: Flu-like symptoms, fever, and in severe cases, kidney or liver failure.

Prevention: Wear gloves\! If a squirrel “pees on you” (a common occurrence), wash the area immediately with antibacterial soap.

5. Giardia & Coccidia

What they are: Intestinal parasites.

Transmission: Fecal-oral route (getting microscopic amounts of feces in your mouth—usually from touching your face after cleaning a cage).

Symptoms: Severe diarrhea and cramping.

Prevention: Designate “Squirrel-Only” cleaning tools. Never wash squirrel syringes in the same sink where you wash your dinner dishes.

### **Other Animals in Your Home**

Most of us rehab with dogs, cats, and other pets in the house. Some products that are safe for squirrels are dangerous to them, and the reverse.

| Product | The risk | Who's at risk |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Permethrin** (common in dog flea treatments and yard sprays) | Fatal to cats, even in small exposures. We don't use it on squirrels at all (see the Never-Use list). | Cats |
| **Ivermectin** (including Mange Balls left outside) | Neurotoxic at very low doses to dogs carrying the MDR1 gene. | Collies, Australian Shepherds, Shetland Sheepdogs, German Shepherds, and other herding breeds |
| **Chlorhexidine** | Keep it out of ears (can damage hearing and balance if it reaches the middle ear) and eyes (corneal injury). Use only diluted. | Cats especially |
| **Essential oils, including tea tree** | Toxic when applied or diffused. Also toxic to squirrels. | Cats |
| **Xylitol** (some peanut butters, sugar-free products, flavored powders) | Deadly. Read every label. | Dogs and squirrels |
| **Frontline (fipronil)** | Fine for your dogs and cats, deadly to squirrels. Never use it on a squirrel, and keep freshly treated pets away from your babies. | Squirrels |

heading: Ch. 2 — Bite Prevention & Human Protocol
text:
## **2\. Bite Prevention & Human Protocol**

A squirrel’s jaw is designed to exert several thousand pounds of pressure per square inch. Their incisors are razor-sharp and can easily penetrate through fingernails and down to the bone. Respect the teeth.

1. Smart Handling: The Defensive Layer

The Glove Rule: For adult squirrels or “high-strung” juveniles, gloves are non-negotiable. \* Welding Gloves: Provide the best puncture protection for aggressive adults.

Double-Gloving: For less aggressive but “nippy” squirrels, wear a pair of thick nitrile gloves under a pair of leather gardening gloves.

The “Burrito” Method: Always use a thick fleece or towel to “scoop” a squirrel. This creates a visual and physical barrier between your hands and the teeth.

No “Face Time”: Never hold a squirrel near your face. A sudden noise can cause a “fear-bite” to your nose, lips, or eyes.

2. Body Language: The Warning Layer

The Flag: If the squirrel is “flagging” (violently waving its tail), it is agitated. Do not reach in.

The Chatter: If you hear teeth chattering or clicking, the squirrel is telling you it is prepared to bite.

The “Lunging Poke”: If a squirrel lunges and hits you with its nose without biting, it is a “final warning.” Withdraw immediately.

3. The Bite Protocol: What to do if bitten

If a squirrel latches on, DO NOT JERK AWAY. This causes the recurved teeth to tear through your flesh like a hook. Wait for the squirrel to release, or gently blow in its face to startle it into letting go.

Bleed It Out: Do not immediately stop the bleeding. Squeeze the wound to encourage blood flow for 60 seconds; this helps “flush” bacteria out of the deep puncture.

The 15-Minute Scrub: Wash the wound with antibacterial soap and warm running water for a full 15 minutes. Scrubbing is the most effective way to prevent infection.

Disinfect: Apply Betadine or Hydrogen Peroxide, followed by an antibiotic ointment (Neosporin).

Medical Follow-up:

Tetanus: Ensure your Tetanus booster is up to date (within the last 5–10 years).

Antibiotics: Watch for “Red Tracking” (lines moving up the arm), extreme heat, or throbbing. Squirrel bites often carry Pasteurella or Bartonella (Cat Scratch Fever). If the bite is on a joint or a finger, see a doctor—infections in the hand spread rapidly through the tendon sheaths.

Rabies: Remind medical staff that squirrels are not known to transmit Rabies to humans.

heading: Ch. 2 — Bite Prevention & Human Protocol › 2A. The Rescuer Starter Kit
text:
## **2A. The Rescuer Starter Kit**

These are the things I keep on hand at all times. The Must Haves are non-negotiable. The Nice to Haves are the little things I've found over the years that make the job easier — they are optional.

### **Must Haves — Babies**

- **Formula:** Esbilac Puppy Milk Replacer, powder in a can (NOT Goat's Milk Esbilac, and NOT the pre-mixed liquid), plus Fox Valley 20/50 and heavy whipping cream. See Ch. 5.
- **Miracle Nipple Mini for Pets and Wildlife.** Don't buy the cheap knock-offs. The real ones give a slow, controlled flow; the knock-offs flow too fast and make it easy to aspirate a baby.
- **Syringes, 1 cc and 3 cc.** Use only a 1 cc O-ring syringe for babies under 100 g (see Ch. 15). Replace syringes often — old plungers stick and then "jump," flooding the throat.
- **Unflavored Pedialyte** for the first 24 hours of rehydration only (see Ch. 5).
- **A heating pad with an "always on" setting.** Most heating pads shut themselves off after about two hours, which means a baby goes cold in the middle of the night. I use a Milliard pad: always-on, a removable washable cover, and a low setting that won't overheat babies. Put it under only half the container.
- **Soft fleece blankets.** The more the better, so laundry day never leaves you without. No terry cloth — claws snag.
- **Unscented baby wipes.** Their noses are sensitive.
- **A bulb nasal aspirator ("snot sucker").** I use the Briggs Baby Nasal Aspirator. This can be the difference between life and death when formula comes out the nose (see Ch. 15).
- **A carrier for transport.** A simple pet carrier that lives in your car for pickups and emergencies.
- **Honey and calcium tablets for emergencies:** Spring Valley Calcium 600 mg + Vitamin D 20 mcg, and Calcium Carbonate 600 mg. Used in Honey Calcium Water (Ch. 5, 11A).
- **L-Glutamine:** NOW Foods L-Glutamine 500 mg capsules. An amino acid added to formula; we've noticed a real difference in development in babies who get it.

### **Must Haves — Bigger Kids**

- **Rodent block:** Henry's Healthy Blocks / Henry's Wild Bites (or Mazuri Rodent Block). Any Henry's squirrel variety is fine — let your baby pick a favorite.
- **A cage to contain them** so they don't run all over. I use a 4-tier ferret/chinchilla cage on casters: room to climb, space for a branch or two, a pull-out tray, and you can hose the whole thing off at the end of the season.

### **Nice to Haves**

- **Mug warmer:** keeps a mug of hot water warm so your formula-filled syringes stay at temperature while you feed.
- **Handheld milk frother:** mixes formula smooth and fast.
- **Bene-Bac Plus probiotic gel:** a probiotic (not a vitamin). I give it to babies as they wean onto fresh foods. See Formulary: Prebiotics and Probiotics.
- **Silicone multi-nipple self-feeder ("the pumpkin"):** brilliant for feeding several older babies at once. Set it on an upside-down cereal bowl to raise the nipples to a comfortable height. **Never use it with babies under 6 weeks — they can aspirate.**

## **3\. Intake & Reunification Protocols**

The most sophisticated piece of squirrel-care equipment ever invented is a mother squirrel. Before we commit to months of human intervention, our first duty is to determine if nature can still do the job.

### **7A: The Reunification Decision: Reunite or Raise?**

Reunification is the goal for any healthy, uninjured baby. A mother squirrel will almost always take her baby back if she is able, even if it has been handled by humans. (The “human scent” myth is just that—a myth.)

#### *When NOT to Reunite (Immediate Intake Required):*

If any of the following are present, the window for reunification is closed:

Cat Contact: Even if no wounds are visible, cat saliva contains Pasteurella bacteria, which is fatal to squirrels within 48-72 hours. These babies need immediate antibiotics.

Fly Strike: If you see “rice grains” (fly eggs) or maggots, the baby is compromised and needs medical debridement.

Hypothermia: A cold baby is a dying baby. You cannot leave a cold baby out for a mother; she will likely sense the lack of vitality and abandon it.

Obvious Injury: Head trauma (blood from nose/ears), broken limbs, or puncture wounds.

The 24-Hour Rule: If the baby has been on the ground for a full night, it is likely too dehydrated and stressed for a successful reunite without first being stabilized.

The Reunification Protocol: How to Do It Safely

Warmth is Mandatory: A mother will not pick up a cold baby. Activate a hand warmer or rice sock, wrap it in a fleece, and place it under the baby in a small box or basket.

Containment: Use a shallow box or a “reunite basket” tied securely to the nesting tree (or the closest safe tree). Ensure the baby cannot crawl out, but the mother can easily reach in.

Timing: Mothers move babies during daylight hours. If the sun goes down, the baby comes inside.

The “Call for Help”: Use a phone to play “Squirrel Distress Calls” (available on YouTube or your app) at a moderate volume to alert the mother to the baby’s location.

The “Mom Is Watching” Myth vs. Reality

The Myth: “I’ve been watching for two hours and I haven’t seen her, so she’s gone.” The Reality: Mother squirrels are wary. If a human, a dog, or a noisy neighbor is within 50 feet, she will stay hidden. She is likely watching you, waiting for you to leave.

The Fix: Tell the finder they must go inside and watch through a window. Total silence and zero visibility are required for her to feel safe enough to retrieve her young.

### **What to Tell the Finder (So They Don’t Sabotage It)**

“Don’t Feed It”: Feeding a baby improper milk or cow’s milk causes bloat and diarrhea, making it less likely the mom can successfully transition it back.

“Hands Off”: Once the baby is in the warm basket, leave it alone. Constant “checking” by the finder is the \#1 reason reunites fail.

“The Clock is Ticking”: Remind them that we have a window of roughly 2-4 hours before the baby’s hydration levels drop too low.

Reuniting Older Juveniles vs. Pinkies

Pinkies: These are easy to contain but have zero ability to regulate heat. They require constant monitoring of the heat source.

Older Juveniles: These “teenage” squirrels may try to bolt from the basket. They often don’t need a “reunite” as much as they need a “soft nudge” back toward their nest if they are just exploring—but if they are approaching humans (the “statue” behavior), they are likely dehydrated and need rescue.

### **Decoding Squirrel Language & The “Help Me” Statue**

To the untrained eye, a squirrel sitting still is just “resting.” To a rehabber, the posture and the sound tell the whole story.

1. The “Statue” Behavior: Juvenile Help-Seeking

When a juvenile (6–10 weeks) is orphaned or in trouble, they often exhibit a specific behavior known as “Statue-ing.”

The Look: The squirrel sits perfectly still, often in a high-traffic area (middle of a lawn, on a porch, or at the base of a tree). They do not run when you approach.

The “Approach”: Unlike a healthy wild squirrel that “spirals” up a tree, a help-seeking juvenile may actually walk toward a human or stay put even if a dog is nearby.

The “Puff”: Check the fur. A healthy squirrel has sleek fur. A squirrel in distress often looks “puffed up” or “spiky,” a sign of dehydration or cold.

The Verdict: If a juvenile allows you to get within 3 feet without fleeing, they are likely compromised and need intake.

2. Identifying Distress Calls

If you don’t hear a mother, you can sometimes “summon” her using a baby’s distress call.

The Sound: It is a high-pitched, rhythmic “peep” or “chirp” that sounds almost like a bird but with a raspy, crying quality.

The Search: Tell finders to search YouTube or a search engine for “Baby Squirrel Distress Call” and play it at full volume on their phone near the tree.

The Response: A healthy mother will often come charging down the tree within minutes of hearing this sound. If she doesn’t appear after 30 minutes of playback, the baby is officially orphaned.

3. The “Bungee & Basket” Trick (Tree Placement)

Getting the reunion basket high enough to be safe from cats but low enough for the mom to find is an art form.

The Basket: Use a wicker basket or a plastic container with drainage holes drilled in the bottom. Line it with the original nesting material or a piece of fleece (never towels—claws get snagged).

The Bungee Hook: Do not use nails (which damage the tree). Use a bungee cord or a long piece of twine.

Height: Hang the basket 6 to 8 feet up the trunk. This is the “sweet spot”—it’s out of reach for most roaming cats and dogs, but the mother will easily smell the baby and hear the distress calls from that height.

Placement: Place it on the shady side of the tree. Direct Idaho sun can overheat a baby in minutes.

text:
## **4\. Age and Development Milestones**

Determining the age of a squirrel is the first step in creating a care plan. Feeding frequency, formula concentration, and the “Wilding-Up” process all depend on where the squirrel sits on this timeline.

Weight vs. Features WARNING: “Never age a squirrel by weight alone.” An emaciated 6-week-old can weigh the same as a healthy 3-week-old, but their medical needs are vastly different.

### **1\. Pinkies (0–1 Weeks)**

Appearance: Completely hairless, pink/red skin, eyes and ears sealed shut.

Behavior: Entirely dependent on external heat; cannot thermo-regulate.

Care Focus: Critical warmth (100°F–102°F) and feeding every 2–3 hours. Hydration is the biggest risk here.

### **2\. Grays/Young Fuzzies (1-2 Weeks)**

Appearance: A fine “shadow” of dark fuzz appears on the back/head. The underside is still pink.

Behavior: Start to wiggle and “root” for the nipple.

Milestone: Bottom front teeth (incisors) may begin to erupt.

### **3\. Fuzzies / Full Grays (2-3 Weeks)**

Appearance: Fully covered in short, sleek fur.

### **4\. Infants (3–4 Weeks)**

The Big Shift: This is a major developmental leap. Once eyes open, the squirrel’s curiosity explodes.

Behavior: More active wiggling.

### **5\. Babies (4–5 Weeks)**

Appearance: Fur coming in. Still blind and while they can hear a bit, ears are still tight against head. Tail is still long and rat like but now fully covered in fur.

### **5\. Toddlers (5–6 Weeks)**

Major Milestone: Eyes open\! Hello world\!

Appearance: Proportionally “top-heavy” with large feet and a fluffier tail. Upper incisors erupt.

Behavior: Sitting up to groom; shaky “popcorning” (play jumping). They begin to investigate solid foods seriously.

### **6\. Toddlers (6–8 Weeks)**

Appearance: Miniature versions of adults. Tail is filling out significantly.

Behavior: Climbing and hanging from the top of the cage.

Milestone: They should be eating solids well. Formula feedings drop to 2–3 times per day.

### **7\. Juveniles/Pre-Release (8–10 Weeks)**

Appearance: High muscle tone; sleek and fast.

Behavior: “Wilding up.” They should begin to show wariness toward humans and become aggressive about their space.

Milestone: Transition to the outdoor pre-release cage for acclimation.

### **8\. Teens (10–12 Weeks)**

Appearance: Nearly full size, but “lanky.”

Behavior: High-energy caching (hiding food). They are learning the sounds and sights of the outdoor world from the safety of the release cage.

### **9\. Release (12–14+ Weeks)**

Criteria: Fully weaned, weather-acclimated, and showing appropriate fear of predators.

The Goal: Soft release. The door is opened, but the “home base” remains available for food and safety as they explore.

### **10\. Adults**

Identification: Fully filled-out frame, thickened tail, and (in males) prominent scrotal development. Adults are typically only in care for injury/illness, not development.

text:
## **5\. The Squirrel Diet & Formula Guide**

Nutrition is medicine. A squirrel’s metabolic rate is incredibly high, and their requirement for a specific Calcium-to-Phosphorus ratio is non-negotiable.

### **11A: Feeding Babies / Formula Guide**

**The Formula.** We use Esbilac Puppy Milk Replacer (powder) mixed equally with Fox Valley 20/50, plus heavy whipping cream. **Why:** this blend is the closest we've found to mother's milk. Fox Valley 20/50's high fat supports a neonate's rapid growth, and the cream adds more of the fat that wild milk is rich in.

**We do not use Fox Valley 32/40.** If you have some, save it and add it to homemade treats for older kids only (see Boo Balls, 11D).

**Recipe**

- 1/4 cup Esbilac Puppy Milk Replacer powder (NOT Goat's Milk Esbilac and NOT the pre-mixed liquid — the liquid often causes diarrhea)
- 1/4 cup Fox Valley 20/50
- 1 cup hot water (120–125°F)
- 2 Tbsp heavy whipping cream
- Optional: 1/4 tsp probiotics and 1/8 tsp L-Glutamine (one 500 mg capsule). We've found these help digestion, and our babies come out fatter and healthier.

1. Add the powder to the water — not water to powder. Let it wet and sink for 5 minutes.
2. Whisk well with a wire whisk. Let it cool to room temperature.
3. Once cool, add the cream, probiotics, and L-Glutamine together. (Heat kills probiotics.)
4. Refrigerate. Make fresh every 3 days. Heat only what you need and discard any warmed formula you don't use — reheating destroys nutrients.

**No Fox Valley?** It happens with supply problems. Double the Esbilac and follow the rest of the recipe.

**Water.** Mix formula with bottled spring water or tap water. **Never use distilled water.**

**The Ratio.** Always start a new baby on a diluted mix (1 part powder to 3 parts water) for the first 24 hours to prevent bloat, then move to the standard recipe above (1:2).

**Temperature.** Formula must be fed at 100°F–105°F — about a squirrel's own body temperature. Cold formula will not be digested and will sit in the gut and ferment.

### **Pedialyte Is for the First 24 Hours Only**

**Never mix Pedialyte — or any electrolyte solution — into formula once a baby has transitioned.** It changes the formula's nutrient and mineral balance and can cause serious digestive problems or death. Too much sodium can also damage the kidneys.

1. **Hydration first.** Rehydrate a dehydrated baby with warm, unflavored Pedialyte for up to the first 24 hours.
2. **The transition is the only exception.** While moving from Pedialyte to formula, the step-down mixes in Ch. 14 and Ch. 33 (for example 50/50, then 75% formula / 25% Pedialyte) are appropriate. Once the baby is on full formula, Pedialyte stops.
3. **After that, use Honey Calcium Water** (below) for extra hydration between feedings.

### **Honey Calcium Water (Between-Feeding Hydration)**

This is our miracle liquid. We use it in place of Pedialyte for babies who are on full formula, and it is truly lifesaving.

**Large batch**

- 3.5 cups water
- 6 Tbsp honey
- 2 calcium carbonate tablets (600 mg)
- 2 Spring Valley Calcium 600 mg + Vitamin D 20 mcg tablets

Crush the tablets fine and mix well. Calcium carbonate settles — **shake before every use.** Refrigerate and make a fresh batch every 5 days.

**When to use it:** between feedings, as needed, for supplemental hydration — especially with diarrhea (Ch. 33) or heavy urination such as Bordetella cases (Ch. 21). **Never mix it into formula.**

**No honey on hand?** The same ratio works with light Karo syrup: 3.5 cups water to 6 Tbsp light Karo.

*Delicious in tea, too — but make your own jar. Syringes that have been in a sick baby's mouth go back into the babies' batch.*

### **11B: Weaning**

Weaning is a process, not an event — and **the squirrel leads it.** Never force a baby to wean on your schedule.

**When.** Most squirrels start self-weaning around 10 weeks. Some start as early as 8; others would ask for formula every day until the end of time. Realistically, stop formula at 16 weeks. That's tough love.

**Starting solids (about 6 weeks).** Let your baby get to know what solids are with soft fruit: grapes and blueberries cut in half with the skins peeled off (they can choke on skins at this age). I let them gnaw on pieces while I prepare formula or feed siblings. From the start, also offer rodent blocks (Henry's Healthy Blocks or Mazuri). Later add kale, broccoli, apple, sweet potato, and small chunks of walnut.

**Keep the blocks in the picture.** Offer blocks alongside the fruit from day one, and once they're eating well, keep fruit and nuts a small part of the diet (see 11C). That's what prevents MBD.

**Help them self-feed.** Tear potato bread into small chunks in a shallow dish and pour warm formula over it so they can pick up pieces. Thicken formula with rice baby cereal into a gruel. Over time, add chopped veggies and softened rodent blocks to this "gruel bread stew."

**Cutting back.** Keep offering formula throughout. Drop a feeding only when they're eating solids well **and** still gaining weight — then wait a few days before dropping another.

**Done.** Around 11–12 weeks most squirrels are eating independently and ready to move toward soft release (Ch. 83).

### **11C: Feeding Adults / Non-Releasable Squirrels**

For adults in recovery or those who cannot be released, the “Healthy Squirrel Diet” is a pyramid:

Base (80%): Rodent Blocks.

Mid (15%): Fresh leafy greens (Kale, Bok Choy, Dandelion greens).

Top (5%): Treats (1 almond or 1 piece of apple per day). Never feed corn or peanuts; they are “calcium killers.”

### **11D: The Squirrel Bible Recipes**

#### *1\. Hydration & Crisis Care*

Karo Syrup Water (The Energy Boost):

1 cup warm water \+ 1 tbsp Karo Syrup.

Use: Immediate energy for hypoglycemic “Boing” squirrels.

Homemade Pedialyte (The 24-Hour Emergency Only):

1 tsp salt \+ 3 tsp sugar \+ 1 quart warm water.

Note: Use only for 24 hours. Prolonged use causes salt toxicity.

#### *2\. Specialized Support*

The BRAT Diet (For Diarrhea):

Bananas, Rice cereal, Applesauce, Toast crumbs.

Mix small amounts into formula to bind the stool.

Constipation Recipe (The “Move-It” Mix):

1 drop of olive oil or a small dollop of canned pumpkin (plain, not pie mix) added to formula.

#### *3\. Homemade Blocks (The Maintenance Mix)*

See Recipes 1–5 in 11D for full ingredients and bake times.

Karo Syrup Water (The Energy Boost):

1 cup warm water + 1 tbsp Karo Syrup.

Use: Immediate energy for hypoglycemic “Boing” squirrels.

Homemade Pedialyte (The 24-Hour Emergency Only):

1 tsp salt + 3 tsp sugar + 1 quart warm water.

Note: Use only for 24 hours. Prolonged use causes salt toxicity.

#### *2. Specialized Support*

The BRAT Diet (For Diarrhea):

Bananas, Rice cereal, Applesauce, Toast crumbs.

Mix small amounts into formula to bind the stool.

Constipation Recipe (The “Move-It” Mix):

1 drop of olive oil or a small dollop of canned pumpkin (plain, not pie mix) added to formula.

#### *3. Homemade Blocks (The Maintenance Mix)*

See Recipes 1–5 in 11D for full ingredients and bake times.

text:
### **Recipes 1–5: Treats**

**These are treats, not a diet.** They're for weaned juveniles, pre-release kids, and backyard squirrels. Treats stay about 5% of what a squirrel eats (see 11C). If a recipe uses peanut butter, use a **xylitol-free** brand — almond butter works great too.

#### **Recipe 1: Baked Treat Balls**

*Makes 50+ one-inch balls.*

- 1 cup almond butter
- 1/2 cup finely chopped walnuts
- 1/2 cup raw, unsalted pumpkin seeds
- 2/3 cup plain rolled oats
- 1/2 tsp calcium supplement (Squirrel-Cal)
- 4 tsp almond flour
- 2 Tbsp water, plus a little more as needed

1. Preheat the oven to **180°F** (170°F is fine if that's your oven's lowest setting).
2. Mix everything, adding water a little at a time until it rolls. A 1-Tbsp scoop makes a perfect 1-inch ball.
3. Bake on a foil-lined tray for 3 hours to dry and harden.
4. Leave out on the counter overnight. Store in a zip-top bag in the fridge.

Birds love these too if they're put out in a feeder.

#### **Recipe 2: Quick No-Bake Almond Cookies**

- 2 Tbsp almond butter (crunchy or creamy)
- 2 Tbsp uncooked oats
- 2 Tbsp chopped walnuts
- 1 Tbsp finely ground almonds

1. Microwave the almond butter for 20 seconds.
2. Stir in the oats, walnuts, and almonds until well mixed.
3. Scoop 1/4-tsp portions onto wax paper and let cool.
4. Serve on a platform feeder.

#### **Recipe 3: Boo Balls (Raw and Baked)**

*Weaned juveniles and older. This is the best use for leftover Fox Valley 32/40.*

- 50 g rodent block, ground to a fine powder
- 50 g Fox Valley powder (leftover 32/40, or 20/50)
- 50 g walnuts, pecans, or hazelnuts, ground fine (stop before it turns into nut butter)
- 20 g coconut oil, melted
- About 100 g (one small jar) fruit baby food such as apple or plum, warmed
- Probiotic: 3 capsules multi-strain acidophilus, or 1 capsule acidophilus

**Raw:** Mix the dry ingredients and the probiotic, then work in the warm baby food and coconut oil. Cover and chill at least 5 hours or overnight, until it's like cookie dough. Roll 1/2-tsp (5 g) balls. Serve 3–4 a day, or as many as get eaten. Keeps 1 week in the fridge. Vary the nut to keep them interested.

**Baked (crunchy):** Make the dough without the probiotic and chill overnight. Roll 1/4–1/3 inch thick with a lightly greased rolling pin and bake at **250°F for 1 hour**. Cool 10 minutes, cut into small squares, and let cool completely. Then dust with the probiotic (heat kills live cultures). Keeps 2 weeks in the fridge, longer frozen.

*Adapted from Squirrel Refuge (squirrelrefuge.org).*

#### **Recipe 4: Immune Booster Balls (and the Mange Ball Variation)**

*Recipe courtesy of Letetia Linette Day.* Easy to make and safe for healthy squirrels.

- 1 cup oatmeal
- 4 Tbsp coconut oil
- 2 Tbsp xylitol-free peanut butter (almond butter works great too)
- 15 drops small-animal vitamin drops (the rat/hamster kind from the pet store)
- Optional but recommended: 10 drops CBD oil, 1 tsp flaxseed oil, 1/4 banana, 1 tsp nutritional yeast flakes, 2 Tbsp crushed shelled peanuts, 2 Tbsp crushed shelled walnuts (or any shelled nuts you have)

Mix and form 1/2-inch balls. Freeze and pull out as needed. One or two a day is plenty.

**Mange Ball variation — ADULTS ONLY.** For a free-roaming adult squirrel with mange, add ivermectin paste (from a farm supply store): squeeze a rice-grain-sized bit onto a slightly thawed ball.

- **Dose three times:** day 1, day 10, and day 20. Plain booster balls are fine on the days in between.
- **Not for babies, juveniles, or squirrels in care.** Paste can't be dosed by weight; for animals in care use the measured 1 mg/mL ivermectin protocol in the Formulary.
- **Why peanut butter is OK here:** it's a small amount over a short dosing schedule. The everyday "no peanuts" rule in 11C still stands.
- **Dog warning:** if the balls go outside, dogs can find them. Ivermectin can poison dogs that carry the MDR1 gene at very low doses — collies, Australian Shepherds, Shetland Sheepdogs, German Shepherds, and other herding breeds. See "Other Animals in Your Home," Ch. 1.

#### **Recipe 5: Baked Protein Blocks**

*A rehab-community favorite.*

- 80 g whey protein isolate (unflavored, or unsweetened vanilla — **check the label for xylitol**)
- 130 g ground walnuts or pecans
- 1/3 cup whole wheat flour
- 1 tsp aluminum-free baking powder
- 45 g Henry's Healthy Vitamins (about half a package)
- 1 egg
- 1 tsp vanilla
- 2 Tbsp coconut oil
- 1 small jar baby food (banana is a favorite) or canned pumpkin
- 2 Tbsp almond butter

1. Mix together, adding a little water only if needed.
2. Pat into a layer about 1/2 inch thick.
3. Bake at **205°F for 90 minutes.**
4. Cool, cut into blocks, and store in the freezer.

### **AT-A-GLANCE: Feeding by Age Chart**

| Age | Frequency | Volume (5-7% of Body Weight) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 0-2 Weeks | Every 2-3 Hours | 0.5cc \- 1.5cc |
| 2-4 Weeks | Every 3-4 Hours | 2cc \- 5cc |
| 4-6 Weeks | Every 4-5 Hours | 6cc \- 10cc |
| 6-8 Weeks | 3 Times Daily | 12cc \- 18cc \+ Solids |
| 8-12 Weeks | 1-2 Times Daily | Offer until they self-wean |

### **AT-A-GLANCE: Formula Mixing Quick Chart**

Standard Mix: 1 Scoop Powder \+ 2 Scoops Very Warm Water.

Pro-Tip: Mix formula at least 2 hours before feeding (or even the night before) to allow the powder to fully dissolve and the air bubbles to dissipate. This drastically reduces “gas bloat.”

### **Squirrel Doc Notes:**

The “5-7% Rule”: I included the weight-based volume because it’s the safest way to prevent overfeeding/aspiration.

Peanuts/Corn: I made sure to flag these as “calcium killers” since that’s a common mistake finders make.

Homemade Blocks: Since you have three versions, I framed them as being selected based on the squirrel’s specific health status (Growth vs. Recovery).

heading: Ch. 6 — The Veterinary Partnership
text:
## **6\. The Veterinary Partnership**

Finding a vet who will see a squirrel is only half the battle. The second half is ensuring that the appointment is productive, professional, and respectful of the vet’s license.

### **1\. How to Find a Squirrel-Friendly Vet**

Look for “Exotics” or “Pocket Pets”: Search for clinics that treat rats, guinea pigs, or rabbits. These vets are already comfortable with small-mammal anesthesia and micro-dosing.

The “Invasive” Check: In states like Idaho, remind the clinic that the squirrel is a “non-protected/invasive species,” meaning they don’t need a special federal wildlife permit to provide treatment.

Ask the Right Question: Don’t ask “Do you treat squirrels?” Ask: “Do you have a vet on staff comfortable with small-mammal surgery and rodent pharmacology?”

### **2\. How to Advocate (Without Being an “Expert”)**

Vets are highly trained professionals. If you walk in and say, “The Squirrel Bible says you should do X,” they may shut down. Instead, use “The Collaborative Approach”:

The Script: “I work with a specialist who has 35 years of experience with this species. I have their peer-reviewed clinical protocols and weight-based dosing charts with me. Would you like to review them to see if they fit your treatment plan?”

The Goal: You are offering them a resource, not an instruction manual. You are making their job easier.

### **3\. What to Say (and What NOT to Say)**

| SAY THIS | DON’T SAY THIS |
| :---: | :---: |
| “I have weight-based protocols from a specialist.” | “I read on a Facebook group that…” |
| “I am prepared to handle all post-op rehab.” | “Can I just leave him here with you?” |
| “What are your thoughts on using \[Drug Name\] for this?” | “You have to give him \[Drug Name\].” |
| “He was found in \[Specific Location/Context\].” | “I’ve been trying to treat him at home for a week.” |

### **4\. How to Photograph Injuries for Consultations**

If you are doing a remote consult or sending photos ahead to a clinic:

Scale is Vital: Always place a common object (like a coin or a pen) next to the wound so the vet can judge the size.

Lighting: Use natural, indirect light. Flash often “washes out” the detail of a wound.

Multiple Angles: Take one “Body Map” shot (the whole squirrel) and three “Macro” shots (close-ups of the injury).

Clear the Fur: If possible, gently move fur away from the wound so the margins are visible.

### **5\. Building a Long-Term Vet Relationship**

Be the “Easy” Client: Have your intake form filled out and the squirrel already “burritoed” or in a clear container for easy viewing.

Follow Up: Send a “Success Photo” once the squirrel is released. Vets usually only see the “broken” animals; seeing a successful release reminds them why they helped you.

Respect the Techs: The technicians are the gatekeepers. If you make their lives easier with your handling guides and clear notes, they will advocate for your squirrels to the vet.

### **The “Emergency Call” Script**

Keep this by your phone or saved in your notes.

Step 1: The Introduction “Hi, my name is \[Name\], and I am a wildlife rescuer. I have a \[Pinky / Juvenile / Adult\] Red Fox Squirrel in critical condition, and I am looking for a clinician who can provide \[Emergency Stabilization / Exam / Surgery\].”

Step 2: Addressing the “Invasive/Legal” Hurdle (Crucial for Idaho) “I understand this species is considered invasive/unprotected in Idaho, so I can confirm there are no special permit requirements for your clinic to see this animal. I am prepared to pay for the exam and take full responsibility for all post-op rehabilitation.”

Step 3: The “Specialist” Value-Add “I am working with a Subject Matter Expert with 35 years of experience. I have weight-based dosing charts and surgical protocols ready for the vet’s review to make this as quick and easy as possible for your team.”

Step 4: The Triage Brief (Choose the one that fits)

If Aspiration: “The squirrel has aspirated and has a rhythmic lung click. He needs an immediate antibiotic protocol.”

If Trauma: “The squirrel has \[Head Trauma / A Broken Limb\] and needs an X-ray and pain management.”

If MBD: “The squirrel is showing signs of Metabolic Bone Disease with seizures and needs immediate calcium stabilization.”

Step 5: The “Close” “Can you check if Dr. \[Name\] has a 15-minute window to see this patient today?”

### **What NOT to Say on the Phone**

“Is it free?” Clinics are businesses. Asking for free work immediately puts the receptionist on the defensive.

“I’ve been treating it at home.” While honest, it can sometimes flag “practicing without a license” to a vet. Frame it as: “I have performed basic stabilization (heat/hydration) but he now requires veterinary-level intervention.”

“It’s my pet.” Never say this. In many states, keeping a squirrel as a pet is illegal. Always refer to yourself as a “Rescuer” or “Guardian.”

### **Squirrel Doc Strategy: The “Golden Rule” of Calling**

Remind your volunteers: If the first five vets say no, call the sixth. Vet receptionists are trained to say “no” to things they don’t recognize. By using the script above, you are speaking the language of a professional, which makes it much harder for them to turn you away.

heading: Ch. 7 — Shock Triage — Emergency Protocol › 7A. 6-Checkpoint Rapid Assessment Table
text:
### **7A. 6-Checkpoint Rapid Assessment Table**

Shock is not a single event — it is a spectrum. Identify where the animal is on that spectrum before reaching for a syringe.

| Checkpoint | STABLE | CRISIS |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Gum Color | Bubblegum Pink | White, Grey, or Blue |
| Capillary Refill Time | \< 1 second | \> 2 seconds |
| Toe Temperature | Warm | Cold / Icy |
| Mobility | The “Hungry Wiggle” | Flat / Non-responsive |
| Skin Hydration | Snaps back immediately | “Tents” — stays up |
| Eyes | Bright, tracking | Glassy, fixed, or closed |

**Critical Note:** A squirrel can look deceptively “okay” in the first 30–60 minutes after a traumatic event. Compliance in a wild squirrel means the body no longer has the energy to fight. That is not calm — that is a crash in progress.

**The Golden Rule:** You cannot hydrate a stalled engine. You must restart it first.

| 🔴 SHOCK TRIAGELIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCYSystemic circulatory and metabolic collapse. Time-sensitive staging is everything. |
| :---: |

QUICK IDENTIFIER — WHAT YOU’LL SEE

Shock is not a single event. It is a spectrum. Identify where the animal is on that spectrum before reaching for a syringe.

| Checkpoint | STABLE | CRISIS |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Gum Color | Bubblegum Pink | White, Grey, or Blue |
| Capillary Refill Time | \< 1 second | \> 2 seconds |
| Toe Temperature | Warm | Cold / Icy |
| Mobility | The “Hungry Wiggle” | Flat / Non-responsive |
| Skin Hydration | Snaps back immediately | “Tents” — stays up |
| Eyes | Bright, tracking | Glassy, fixed, or closed |

| Critical Note: A squirrel can look deceptively “okay” in the first 30–60 minutes after a traumatic event. This is Phase 1 — the body is compensating. Do not mistake stillness and compliance for stability. Compliance in a wild squirrel means the body no longer has the energy to fight. That is not calm. That is a crash in progress. |
| :---: |

WHY IT MATTERS — CONSEQUENCES IF UNTREATED

In neonatal squirrel rehabilitation, shock is a metabolic “drain.” The cardiovascular system is failing to deliver oxygen and glucose to the organs. Each phase represents a deeper failure state, and the window between Phase 1 and Phase 3 can close in a matter of hours — sometimes minutes.

The critical error most rehabbers make is reaching for fluids or food before heat. Pushing Sub-Q fluids into a cold, vasoconstricted body creates a fluid pocket under the skin that cannot be absorbed, further chills the animal, and can cause tissue sloughing.

| Golden Rule: You cannot hydrate a stalled engine. You must restart it first. |
| :---: |

There is a second, less understood killer hiding inside shock: Capture Myopathy — the systemic collapse triggered by extreme overexposure to adrenaline and cortisol. A squirrel can survive the initial trauma, appear to stabilize, and then drop dead an hour later because the handling and stress of “being helped” chemically destroyed the heart muscle. This is not rare. It is one of the most common causes of preventable death in a rehab setting, and it is covered in full below.

THE THREE PHASES OF SHOCK

Use the phases to calibrate your response — not to decide whether to intervene.

| PHASE 1 — COMPENSATORY SHOCK (The “Warning” Phase)Visual Cues: Eyes open and bright but may appear frantic or “over-reactive.” Animal may be restless or flinch at touch.Clinical Markers: Gums bright pink or brick red (hyperemic). CRT under 1 second. Extremities still warm.Triage Protocol: Aggressive intervention using the full 4-step hierarchy. The gut is still functioning — antibiotic and antiprotozoal coverage is indicated. Do not wait to see if they improve on their own.Prognosis: Good to Guarded with immediate, appropriate intervention. |
| :---: |

| PHASE 2 — DECOMPENSATORY SHOCK (The “Crash” Phase)Visual Cues: Animal is “flat.” Poor muscle tone. Head-holding absent. Minimal or no response to handling.Clinical Markers: Gums pale, muddy, or greyish-pink. CRT over 2 seconds. Toes, ears, and tail cold to the touch. Respiratory clicking or open-mouth gasping may begin.Triage Protocol: Stabilize before medicating. No oral fluids — swallow reflex is suppressed and aspiration risk is critical. Mucosal dextrose only. Sub-Q fluids once warm. Quiet and dark are not optional at this stage — they are medicine.Prognosis: Poor. Requires 24–48 hours of intensive stabilization before prognosis can be reassessed. |
| :---: |

| PHASE 3 — IRREVERSIBLE SHOCK (The “Terminal” Phase)Visual Cues: Total lack of response to stimuli. Body appears fully relaxed or limp. Agonal breathing (the gasping brainstem reflex) may be present — do not mistake this for breathing.Clinical Markers: Gums white or blue (cyanotic). Bradycardia — severe slowing of the heart rate.Triage Protocol: Comfort care only. Invasive procedures cause more distress than benefit. Provide warmth, darkness, and quiet. Contact a vet immediately for humane euthanasia assessment.Prognosis: Grave. Focus shifts to dignity. |
| :---: |

IMMEDIATE ACTION — THE 4-STEP TRIAGE HIERARCHY

Non-negotiable order of operations. Do not skip steps. Do not rearrange steps. The sequence is the protocol.

| STEP 1: HEAT — Restart the EngineApply a heating pad on LOW under half the enclosure so the animal can self-regulate. Target 96–99°F for neonates. A cold cardiovascular system cannot pump effectively, cannot absorb fluids, and cannot metabolize glucose. Every other intervention is wasted until core temperature rises.Do not use High heat — see Flash Heating under Prevention. |
| :---: |

| STEP 2: QUIET AND DARK — Stop the Adrenaline DumpThis is the Capture Myopathy prevention step. MEDICAL TREATMENT — VET PROTOCOL

Sub-Q Fluids: Lactated Ringer’s Solution (LRS). Warm to body temperature before administration. Volume: 5–10% of body weight in ml, divided across 2–3 doses over 24 hours. Administer in scruff or flank tent. Cold LRS is contraindicated.

Dextrose: 5% Dextrose solution or Honey Water (1:3). Mucosal application to gum line. Do not force oral administration in Phase 2 or 3 — aspiration risk is critical when swallow reflex is suppressed.

Antibiotics: Baytril (Enrofloxacin) indicated in Phase 1 with suspected infectious cause. Withhold until animal is stabilized and warm in Phase 2 or 3\.

Oxygen: Flow-by oxygen indicated in Phase 2 with respiratory distress. Reduces cardiovascular workload during active decompensation.

Warming Protocol: Slow and steady. Target a 1–2°F increase per 15 minutes. Rapid rewarming causes peripheral vasodilation — see “Flash Frozen Paradox” below.

CAPTURE MYOPATHY — THE “DROP DEAD” PHENOMENON

Capture Myopathy is why a perfectly healthy-looking squirrel suddenly dies. It is the systemic collapse triggered by extreme overexposure to adrenaline and cortisol — the animal literally “scares itself to death” at a cellular level. In this context, we define it as Metabolic Insult from Fear, and it is intimately connected to the shock triage decision tree.

The “Chemical Burn” — Lactic Acidosis

When a squirrel is in extreme stress — during capture, in a loud environment, or during over-handling in Phase 1 or 2 shock — the muscles run on anaerobic emergency fuel. This process dumps massive amounts of lactic acid into the bloodstream. The blood pH drops (acidosis), which damages the heart muscle and kidneys.

The animal may appear completely fine for 30–60 minutes — then collapse and die as the acid load overwhelms the cardiovascular system. This most often occurs after a high-speed chase, intense handling, or prolonged exposure to stressors during intake.

The “Flash Frozen” Paradox

When hypothermia and Capture Myopathy occur together, they create a lethal stalemate:

The cold slows the heart (Shock).

The stress creates the acid (Myopathy).

Because the heart is too slow to flush toxins from the muscles, the lactic acid sits and continues damaging tissue.

The moment you warm the animal and circulation restores, that “toxic slug” of accumulated acid hits the heart all at once.

| This is why a hypothermic squirrel that was also stressed during capture can appear to be “turning the corner” after rewarming — and then crash suddenly. The rewarming itself triggers the delivery of the accumulated poison. The prevention is not to avoid warming — it is to combine warming with the Quiet/Dark protocol from the moment of intake, minimizing the acid load before circulation is restored. |
| :---: |

PREVENTION — THE PREVENTABLE SINS

Most shock begins with the initial trauma. But a significant number of deaths are caused by the human trying to help too quickly, too aggressively, or in the wrong order.

A. Rehabber-Induced Secondary Shock

The “Rehydration Rush” — Osmotic Shock

Administering a full concentration of formula or a large bolus of electrolytes too fast causes a dangerous fluid shift — water is pulled out of the cells and into the blood too quickly, which can cause the brain to swell or the heart to fail.

Prevention: Slow, incremental rehydration over 4–6 hours. Start dilute. Increase concentration as the animal stabilizes.

The “Cold Feed” — Metabolic Shutdown

Feeding a baby whose gut is cold. Without adequate core temperature, the body cannot produce the digestive enzymes needed to process formula. The formula sits, ferments, and triggers bloat, toxic shock, or both.

Prevention: The Warm to the Touch Rule. No formula until the baby is active, alert, and warm. No exceptions.

The “Aspiration Spike”

Attempting oral hydration of a Phase 2 (Decompensated) baby. The swallow reflex is suppressed during decompensatory shock. The baby aspirates the fluid. The resulting respiratory distress triggers a massive cortisol spike that accelerates progression from Phase 2 to Phase 3\.

Prevention: If they are flat, no oral fluids. Sub-Q or nothing.

Improper Rewarming — Flash Heating

Placing a hypothermic baby directly on a heating pad set to High. Rapid rewarming causes immediate peripheral vasodilation — all the blood rushes to the skin, dropping blood pressure at the heart and brain simultaneously.

Prevention: Low and Slow. It should take 30–60 minutes to restore core temperature. Always set the pad to Low and cover only half the enclosure.

B. Capture Myopathy Prevention

The “Look at the Baby” Syndrome

Allowing family members, pets, children, or multiple volunteers to view or touch a new intake. To a squirrel in shock, every face is a predator. Every “cute” interaction is a cortisol spike that pushes them closer to metabolic collapse.

Prevention: New intakes go directly into a quiet, dark, covered space. No exceptions during the first stabilization period. One handler only.

Over-Manipulation During Triage

The instinct to clean every wound, remove every flea, and assess every toe in the first ten minutes. Most of this can wait. A perfect wound assessment is useless on a dead squirrel.

Prevention — The Rule: Stabilize first, assess second. Triage for immediate life threats (arterial bleeding, airway obstruction) and leave everything else until the animal has had at least 30–60 minutes of quiet warmth.

The “Hero” Feeding

Forcing a syringe into a terrified baby’s mouth. The physical fight to resist the syringe can trigger the final adrenaline dump that causes fatal cardiac arrest.

Prevention: If they are fighting you, they are not ready. A squirrel that needs to be forced to eat is a squirrel that needs heat and quiet first.

PROGNOSIS & RECOVERY

Recovery depends entirely on which phase intervention begins, and how closely the 4-step hierarchy is followed.

Phase 1 animals caught immediately with correct sequencing have good survival rates. Phase 2 animals require 24–48 hours of intensive stabilization before any prognosis can be offered. Phase 3 is rarely survivable, and the ethical priority shifts from intervention to comfort and dignity.

Warning Signs — Recovery is Failing:

Gums remain pale or worsen after rewarming.

No urine output after 12 hours.

Respiratory clicking that develops or worsens after stabilization.

“Rebound Crash” 6–12 hours after apparent stabilization — this is the Flash Frozen Paradox delivering its delayed acid load. Any animal that crashes after appearing to stabilize should be taken to a vet immediately.

| The Golden Rule of Shock Triage:Heat before fluids. Quiet before assessment. Sequence before speed. |
| :---: |

heading: Ch. 7 — Shock Triage — Emergency Protocol › 7B. The Baby Squirrel Tree Fall
text:
## **7B. The Baby Squirrel Tree Fall**

**A bloody nose isn't the end.** A baby found under a tree after a storm — not moving, blood at the nose — looks hopeless. Most of the time it isn't. Give warmth before you give up.

**Squirrel physics.** A squirrel falling from the canopy hits the ground at only about 13–15 mph. A furred juvenile is light and its tail works like a parachute, so these falls are often survivable. **Pinkies and grays don't have that fluffy tail yet**, so the youngest fallers are more fragile.

**The bloody nose (epistaxis).** Often it's a burst vessel in the nose — like a boxer taking a punch. Stillness is usually shock, not death. But a bloody nose after a fall means **watch for head trauma (Ch. 43) even if the baby bounces back**, and nose or mouth bleeding can also mean rodenticide poisoning rather than the fall (Ch. 60).

### **The 20-Minute Reboot**

1. **Box:** a shoebox lined with soft fleece or an old T-shirt.
2. **Heat — warm, not hot:** a heating pad on low or a sock filled with warm rice, under only half the box. Overheating hurts an injured brain too (Ch. 43).
3. **Darkness:** close the lid. Keep it quiet.
4. **Wait 20–30 minutes.** Do not feed or give water.

Most of the time, when you open that box, the baby will be awake and looking at you.

### **Reunite, or Rehabber?**

- **Fully alert, steady, no further bleeding:** try reunion with mom (Ch. 3). The "scent myth" is false — she wants her baby back.
- **Wobbly, uneven pupils, still bleeding, or not fully alert:** rehabber, not reunion.
- **Dragging a leg or visible bone:** rehabber or vet — but warm first. Shock kills faster than a broken leg.
- **Open-mouth breathing or gasping:** emergency — likely chest trauma or pneumonia. Nothing by mouth; get to a rehabber now.

heading: Ch. 8 — Abscesses & Localized Infections
text:
## **8\. Abscesses & Localized Infections**

An abscess is a localized collection of pus, typically resulting from a bite wound (conspecific or predator), puncture, or infected skin injury. In squirrels, these can become walled off and severe if not managed promptly.

Warning Signs

Physical: A firm or fluctuant (squishy) swelling under the skin. It may be hot to the touch, red, or actively draining foul-smelling pus.

Behavioral: Pain when touched, lethargy, or decreased appetite.

The “Head Emergency”: Abscesses on the face, jaw, or neck are high-risk. They can quickly obstruct the airway or press on the eyes. Because squirrels are obligate nasal breathers, facial swelling is a medical emergency.

Immediate Treatment Protocol

Systemic Antibiotics: Start a broad-spectrum antibiotic immediately (Clavamox or Baytril) to treat the infection from the inside out.

Manage Drainage:

If Open/Draining: Apply warm, moist compresses for 5–10 minutes 3–4 times daily. This encourages the pocket to stay open and continue draining.

The “Heal from Inside Out” Rule: Never let an abscess scab over until the swelling is completely gone. If it closes too early, the infection will simply build up again.

Flush: If the hole is large enough, gently flush with a diluted Chlorhexidine or Betadine solution using a syringe (no needle).

If Closed/Firm: Do not attempt to “squeeze” a closed abscess. This can push the infection deeper into the bloodstream (sepsis). A veterinarian may need to professionally lance, debride, and flush the cavity.

Post-Care & Prevention

Topical Support: Once the wound is draining and clean, a thin layer of Silver Sulfadiazine (SSD) Cream or Neosporin can be applied to the surrounding skin, but do not plug the drainage hole with thick ointment.

Separate Animals: If the abscess was caused by a cage mate, separate the squirrels immediately to prevent further injury and allow for stress-free healing.

Monitor for Sepsis: If the squirrel becomes cold, extremely pale, or unresponsive, the infection may have gone systemic. This requires immediate veterinary intervention and aggressive fluid therapy (LRS).

Ch. 8 — Abscesses & Localized Infections

## 8. Abscesses & Localized Infections

An abscess is a localized collection of pus, typically resulting from a bite wound (conspecific or predator), puncture, or infected skin injury. In squirrels, these can become walled off and severe if not managed promptly.

Warning Signs

Physical: A firm or fluctuant (squishy) swelling under the skin. It may be hot to the touch, red, or actively draining foul-smelling pus.

Behavioral: Pain when touched, lethargy, or decreased appetite.

The “Head Emergency”: Abscesses on the face, jaw, or neck are high-risk. They can quickly obstruct the airway or press on the eyes. Because squirrels are obligate nasal breathers, facial swelling is a medical emergency.

Immediate Treatment Protocol

Systemic Antibiotics: Start a broad-spectrum antibiotic immediately (Clavamox or Baytril) to treat the infection from the inside out.

Manage Drainage:

If Open/Draining: Apply warm, moist compresses for 5–10 minutes 3–4 times daily. This encourages the pocket to stay open and continue draining.

The “Heal from Inside Out” Rule: Never let an abscess scab over until the swelling is completely gone. If it closes too early, the infection will simply build up again.

Flush: If the hole is large enough, gently flush with a diluted Chlorhexidine or Betadine solution using a syringe (no needle).

If Closed/Firm: Do not attempt to “squeeze” a closed abscess. This can push the infection deeper into the bloodstream (sepsis). A veterinarian may need to professionally lance, debride, and flush the cavity.

Post-Care & Prevention

Topical Support: Once the wound is draining and clean, a thin layer of Silver Sulfadiazine (SSD) Cream or Neosporin can be applied to the surrounding skin, but do not plug the drainage hole with thick ointment.

Separate Animals: If the abscess was caused by a cage mate, separate the squirrels immediately to prevent further injury and allow for stress-free healing.

Monitor for Sepsis: If the squirrel becomes cold, extremely pale, or unresponsive, the infection may have gone systemic. This requires immediate veterinary intervention and aggressive fluid therapy (LRS).

heading: Ch. 9 — Agonal Breathing
text:
## **9\. Agonal Breathing**

Agonal breathing in a squirrel is a critical sign of impending death or severe brain oxygen deprivation, characterized by involuntary, sporadic gasping or snorting noises rather than functional breathing. It is a brainstem reflex often mistaken for recovery, but it usually indicates cardiac arrest or terminal distress.

Appearance: Deep, infrequent, and irregular gasps, often with long pauses between breaths.

Sounds: Snorting, gurgling, or wheezing noises.

Context: It occurs when the brain is severely deprived of oxygen or the animal is passing away.

Action: It is not a sign of recovery; it indicates the animal is likely unconscious and in its final moments.

If you are dealing with a wild squirrel exhibiting this behavior, it is in extreme distress, and professional intervention is usually not successful at this stage.

Keep the squirrel calm, quiet and in a dark place and allow nature to take its course. While losing any squirrel is not easy, you are doing a great kindness by allowing it to pass in peace, dignity and safety.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

Palliative Care: If the squirrel is at a vet clinic, heavy sedation (Midazolam or Alfaxalone) can be given to ensure the transition is peaceful.

Euthanasia: Usually indicated to prevent the “panic” of the gasping reflex.

heading: Ch. 10 — Amputation Care & Management
text:
## **10\. Amputation Care & Management**

🔴 HIGH MONITORING – The Critical 72-Hour Window.

THIS SECTION COVERS MEDICALLY AMPUTATED LIMBS.

IN THE EVENT YOU ENCOUNTER A SQUIRREL WHO HAS LOST A LIMB DUE TO AN ACCIDENT, AN INJURY OR ANY OTHER SITUATION, THAT SQUIRREL REQUIRES IMMEDIATE VET CARE AND SHOULD BE SEEN BY A TRAINED MEDICAL PROFESSIONAL.

DO NOT TREAT ON YOUR OWN.

Amputations are a heavy reality in squirrel rehab. While a vet must perform the surgery, the rehabber’s job is the high-stakes “aftercare”—managing the balance between healing and the squirrel’s relentless urge to “fix” (chew) the surgical site.

A squirrel can live a full, wild life with three legs (especially a missing hind limb), but the success of the surgery depends entirely on the first few days of recovery.

Post-Surgical Triage

Incision Watch: Check for “gapping,” oozing, or a foul odor.

Color Check: The skin around the sutures should be pink, not purple or black (necrosis).

The “Nibble” Factor: Watch for any obsessive grooming. A squirrel can remove its own stitches in seconds.

The First 72 Hours: Critical Stabilization

Strict Confinement: Use a small, solid-walled “hospital” tub with no climbing elements. Movement should be restricted to allow the internal sutures to begin knitting.

Heat Support: Post-surgical patients struggle to regulate their temperature. Provide a [heating pad](https://wildlifewelfare.org/injured-wildlife) on low under half of the bin to allow the squirrel to self-regulate.

The “Zero-Snag” Rule: Use only flat, anti-pill fleece. Loop-textured towels can snag on sutures, leading to catastrophic wound reopening.

Nursing Care & Complication Watch

Incision Monitoring: Check the site twice daily. Normal healing is pink and dry. Seek help if you see:

Dehiscence: The wound edges pulling apart.

Seroma: A soft, fluid-filled bulge under the skin (liquid accumulation).

Necrosis: Skin turning dark purple, black, or feeling cold.

Pain Management: Follow your vet’s schedule for Meloxicam or Gabapentin. If the squirrel stops eating or begins to chew the site, their pain is not controlled.

Infection Control: Ensure the full course of [antibiotics](https://pacificwildlifecare.org/rehabilitation-process/) (e.g., Clavamox or Baytril) is finished to prevent bone infection (osteomyelitis).

Deterring Self-Mutilation (The “Hardware” Guide)

The “Neck Pillow”: If the squirrel obsesses over the stitches, a soft fleece “donut” collar can be more effective and less stressful than a hard plastic cone.

Bitter Deterrents: Apply Bitter Apple spray to a bandage or around (never on) the wound.

Sedation: If behavioral chewing persists, discuss a [Trazodone](https://www.facebook.com/groups/841345960725845/posts/1162745435252561/) protocol with your vet to keep the squirrel calm during the “itchy” phase of healing.

Release Prospects

Hind Limb: High success rate. Squirrels balance primarily with their tail and remaining hind leg; they can often climb and jump effectively enough for release.

Front Limb: Moderate success. Front paws are vital for handling food and precise climbing.

Tail: Loss of the full tail significantly impairs balance and predator evasion; these cases are often evaluated for non-releasable placement.

Recovery from amputation is a significant challenge in squirrel rehabilitation, requiring careful management to ensure the animal’s well-being and successful healing. The period immediately following surgery is critical for preventing complications and allowing the squirrel to adapt.

Ongoing Post-Amputation Care and Management

Intensive monitoring is essential during the initial recovery period. This includes closely observing the surgical site for any signs of infection, such as redness, swelling, discharge, or foul odor. Ensuring the incision remains clean and intact is paramount. Squirrels have a strong natural instinct to groom and may attempt to interfere with the surgical site, which can lead to complications like dehiscence (wound reopening) or infection.

Managing the squirrel’s environment plays a crucial role in recovery. Providing a safe and comfortable space that minimizes the risk of re-injury is important. This may involve adjusting the enclosure to prevent excessive climbing or activities that could strain the surgical area. Using appropriate bedding that is clean and does not pose a entanglement risk to sutures is also necessary.

Addressing pain is a key component of post-amputation care. Working closely with a veterinarian to establish a pain management plan is vital for the squirrel’s comfort and to prevent self-mutilation driven by discomfort or phantom limb sensations.

Adapting to Amputation

A squirrel’s ability to adapt after an amputation depends on various factors, including the specific limb lost and the individual animal’s resilience.

Hind Limb Loss: Many squirrels can adapt well to losing a hind limb, often maintaining a good level of mobility and climbing ability. Their tail plays a significant role in balance, aiding in their adaptation.

Front Limb Loss: Losing a front limb can be more challenging for a squirrel, as front limbs are essential for tasks like handling food and climbing. Adaptation is still possible, but may require a longer period of support and observation to ensure the squirrel can forage and navigate effectively in its environment.

Tail Amputation: The tail is crucial for balance and agility, particularly for avoiding predators and moving through trees. The extent of a tail amputation can significantly impact a squirrel’s ability to thrive in the wild. While some can adapt to partial tail loss, complete tail loss can make it very difficult for a squirrel to survive in a natural setting.

Successful rehabilitation and potential release of an amputee squirrel require careful assessment of its ability to cope with its environment and perform essential survival tasks. Collaboration with experienced wildlife veterinarians is essential throughout the process.

heading: Ch. 11 — Anaphylaxis (Systemic Allergic Shock)
text:
## **11\. Anaphylaxis (Systemic Allergic Shock)**

Anaphylaxis is a severe, multi-system allergic reaction. In squirrels, the “shock organ” is often the lungs and the gastrointestinal tract. This means the squirrel isn’t just “itchy”—they are unable to breathe and their circulatory system is collapsing.

### **1\. Common Triggers**

Insect Venoms: Multiple stings (bees/wasps) or fire ant attacks.

Medication Reactions: Occasionally seen with specific antibiotics or vaccinations (if administered).

Environmental Allergens: Rare, but can occur with certain bedding or cleaning chemicals.

### **2\. Clinical Signs (The “Red Alerts”)**

Immediate Onset: Symptoms usually appear within seconds to minutes of exposure.

Facial Swelling (Angioedema): The “puffy” face, especially around the eyes and snout.

Respiratory Distress: Gasping, “honking” sounds, or blue/purple tinged gums (cyanosis).

Extreme Itching/Agitation: The squirrel may frantically claw at its face or ears.

Sudden Gastrointestinal Distress: Projectile vomiting or explosive diarrhea (often bloody).

Collapse: The squirrel goes limp and the heart rate drops (Bradycardia).

### **3\. The Emergency Protocol**

CRITICAL: Anaphylaxis is a veterinary emergency. If you see these signs, do not “wait and see.” Injectable intervention is required.

#### *Phase 1: Immediate Stabilization*

Oxygen: If you have an O2 concentrator or tank, get the squirrel into 100% oxygen immediately.

Epinephrine (The Gold Standard): If a vet is available, they will administer Epinephrine @ 0.01 mg/kg. This reverses the airway constriction and raises blood pressure.

#### *Phase 2: Secondary Support*

Steroids (Dexamethasone): Used to reduce the systemic inflammatory “storm.”

Antihistamines (Diphenhydramine/Benadryl): \* Dose: 2 mg/kg (Oral or Injectable).

Note: Benadryl is a “follow-up” drug; it is too slow to stop an active anaphylactic collapse on its own.

#### *Phase 3: Environmental Flush*

If the trigger was an ant attack, once the squirrel is stable and breathing, bathe the animal in cool water with Dawn dish soap to remove any residual formic acid/venom from the fur.

### **4\. Recovery & Observation**

A squirrel that survives anaphylaxis is at high risk for a “Biphasic Reaction”—a second wave of shock that occurs 4–12 hours after the initial event.

Protocol: Strict observation for 24 hours. Keep the squirrel in a quiet, climate-controlled environment.

Hydration: Maintain Sub-Q fluids as the blood pressure may remain low for several hours.

### **The “Anaphylaxis/Ant Bite” Emergency Script**

The Setup: Tell the volunteer to put the phone on speaker while they keep the squirrel in an oxygen-rich environment (or near an open window for fresh air).

The Script: “This is \[Name\] with \[Rescue Name\]. I have a Type 1 Anaphylactic Emergency with a squirrel patient. The trigger was \[Fire Ant Attack / Medication Reaction\].

The squirrel is currently \[Gasping / Projectile Vomiting / Showing Facial Edema\] and is in Decompensated Shock.

I am 5 minutes away. I need to know if you have Epinephrine and Dexamethasone ready, and if a tech can meet me at the door with Oxygen.

heading: Ch. 12 — Anemia (The Pale Patient)
text:
## **12\. Anemia (The Pale Patient)**

A squirrel’s metabolic rate requires a high volume of oxygen-carrying red blood cells. When those cells are depleted—either by “blood-sucking” parasites or internal hemorrhaging—the squirrel will crash, often appearing “lethargic” when they are actually suffocating at a cellular level.

1. Clinical Signs of Anemia

The Gum Check: Press your finger against the gums or tongue. They should be bubblegum pink. If they are white, porcelain, or a faint “muddy” grey, the squirrel is severely anemic.

Cold Extremities: The body pulls blood away from the paws and tail to protect the heart and brain.

Lethargy & Lack of “Spunk”: An anemic squirrel is too weak to struggle.

The Parasite Load: If the squirrel is covered in fleas or has more than 2–3 ticks, assume anemia. (A single squirrel flea can consume a significant percentage of a neonate’s blood volume in 24 hours).

2. The “Flea Triage” Trap

CRITICAL WARNING: Do not immediately bathe a severely anemic, flea-ridden baby in Dawn dish soap. The stress of the bath and the sudden temperature shift can cause a “shock crash.”

The Alternative: Use a flea comb or tweezers to remove the bulk of the parasites manually. Once the squirrel is warm and hydrated (Stage 1 Stabilization), you can use a dilute Capstar or a vet-approved topical, but only when the squirrel is stable.

3. Staging the Anemic Squirrel

Stage 1: Mild (Pinkish-Grey Gums)

Cause: Minor flea load or slight dehydration.

Protocol: Remove parasites. Provide iron-rich support. If weaning, introduce dark leafy greens (kale/spinach) and high-quality blocks.

Stage 2: Moderate (White/Porcelain Gums)

Cause: Heavy parasite load or internal bruising (falls).

Protocol: \* Warmth & Oxygen: Anemic squirrels have less oxygen in their blood; a quiet, oxygen-rich environment helps.

Iron Support: A tiny drop of Beef Gerbers Baby Food (which contains heme-iron) or a microscopic amount of Pet-Tinic (vitamin/mineral supplement) can be added to the formula.

Stage 3: Severe/Critical (Ghost-White Gums & Gasping)

Cause: Massive blood loss or chronic starvation.

Protocol: This is a veterinary emergency.

The “Hail Mary”: Vets may need to provide a Vitamin K1 injection (if poisoning/clotting is suspected) or Sub-Q fluids with added B12.

Note: Blood transfusions are generally not a reality for squirrels, so we must rely on stopping the loss and supporting the “factory” (bone marrow) to make more cells.

4. Internal Hemorrhaging (The “Invisible” Anemia)

If a squirrel has no fleas but has white gums and was found after a fall or cat attack:

**Check for:**  Bruising on the abdomen or blood in the urine/stool.

Protocol: Strict cage rest. Do not move or palpate the squirrel unnecessarily, as this can dislodge internal clots and restart the bleeding.

heading: Ch. 13 — Ant Bites (see also Wasp Bites; see also Anaphylaxis)
text:
## **13\. Ant Bites (see also Wasp Bites; see also Anaphylaxis)**

An injured baby squirrel, particularly one attacked by ants or wasps, needs immediate warmth and professional, specialized care, as these bites can be fatal in just a few hours.

Immediate Emergency Actions

Keep it Warm: Baby squirrels cannot regulate their own temperature. Place the squirrel in a box with a soft, clean cloth (no loose strings) and a heat source, such as a sock filled with rice and microwaved for 30–60 seconds, or a heating pad on the lowest setting. Make sure the baby can move away from the heat.

Remove Ants/Stingers: Gently remove any remaining ants. If stung by a wasp, try to gently scrape the stinger off using a hard surface like a credit card.

Do Not Feed: Do not give the baby any formula, milk, or water. Feeding a cold or stressed squirrel can cause aspiration and death.

Find a Rehabilitator: Contact a local wildlife rehabilitator or veterinarian immediately. Ant bites can cause rapid infection.

Temporary Care

Clean the Wounds: Gently clean the bite areas with warm water and a very mild, non-scented soap. A tiny amount of antibiotic ointment (like Neosporin) can be applied, but the priority is professional care.

Keep it Quiet: Keep the box in a dark, quiet, and secure place away from pets and children.

When to Seek Immediate Help

If the squirrel is cold, lethargic, has bleeding wounds, or is covered in ants/eggs.

If you see small white spots on the skin (pustules) 8-24 hours after an ant attack.

If the squirrel starts showing any signs of anaphylaxis.

In wildlife rehabilitation, the development of white pustules after a fire ant attack indicates a necrotic reaction to the venom. While these pustules are initially sterile, they represent significant skin damage and a high risk for secondary bacterial infection.

BugGuide.Net \+2

Clinical Management of Pustules

Do Not Pop: Avoid squeezing or lancing the pustules, as this can introduce bacteria and lead to cellulitis. They should be allowed to dry up and flake off naturally, usually within 4–10 days.

Topical Treatment:

Gentle Cleansing: Clean the affected area once or twice daily with a damp cloth or a [diluted 1% Betadine](https://www.squirrel-rehab.org/rehabinfo/stabilization.html) or chlorhexidine solution (diluted to the color of weak tea).

Antibiotic/Steroid Ointments: Apply ointments containing corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and [antibacterial agents](https://research.entomology.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/28/2014/03/ENTO_004.pdf) like Neosporin or Silver Sulfadiazine (SSD) cream to prevent secondary infection.

Systemic Support:

Pain & Inflammation: Administer nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as Metacam (Meloxicam) to manage pain and reduce systemic swelling.

Antihistamines: If itching is severe, Children’s Benadryl (Diphenhydramine) can be used to prevent the animal from scratching and further damaging the skin.

Antibiotics: For severe cases or if the pustules break, start oral antibiotics such as Clavamox or Baytril (Enrofloxacin) to prevent or treat secondary bacterial infections.

Wildlife Rehabilitators of North Carolina \+10

Monitoring for Complications

Secondary Infection: Watch for spreading redness, increased heat in the limbs, or foul-smelling discharge, which may indicate [cellulitis or abscess formation](https://ncwildliferehab.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Squirrel-2021-Bergman.pdf).

Hydration: Ensure the baby remains well-hydrated, as the stress of the attack and subsequent healing can lead to dehydration.

If the baby is not injured severely and you are waiting for a rehabilitator, you can try to keep it warm and comfortable in a quiet, dark place until they arrive.
