## 13. Ant Bites (see also Wasp Bites; see also Anaphylaxis)

An injured baby squirrel, particularly one attacked by ants or wasps, needs immediate warmth and professional, specialized care, as these bites can be fatal in just a few hours.

Immediate Emergency Actions

Keep it Warm: Baby squirrels cannot regulate their own temperature. Place the squirrel in a box with a soft, clean cloth (no loose strings) and a heat source, such as a sock filled with rice and microwaved for 30–60 seconds, or a heating pad on the lowest setting. Make sure the baby can move away from the heat.

Remove Ants/Stingers: Gently remove any remaining ants. If stung by a wasp, try to gently scrape the stinger off using a hard surface like a credit card.

Do Not Feed: Do not give the baby any formula, milk, or water. Feeding a cold or stressed squirrel can cause aspiration and death.

Find a Rehabilitator: Contact a local wildlife rehabilitator or veterinarian immediately. Ant bites can cause rapid infection.

Temporary Care

Clean the Wounds: Gently clean the bite areas with warm water and a very mild, non-scented soap. A tiny amount of antibiotic ointment (like Neosporin) can be applied, but the priority is professional care.

Keep it Quiet: Keep the box in a dark, quiet, and secure place away from pets and children.

When to Seek Immediate Help

If the squirrel is cold, lethargic, has bleeding wounds, or is covered in ants/eggs.

If you see small white spots on the skin (pustules) 8-24 hours after an ant attack.

If the squirrel starts showing any signs of anaphylaxis.

In wildlife rehabilitation, the development of white pustules after a fire ant attack indicates a necrotic reaction to the venom. While these pustules are initially sterile, they represent significant skin damage and a high risk for secondary bacterial infection.

BugGuide.Net +2

Clinical Management of Pustules

Do Not Pop: Avoid squeezing or lancing the pustules, as this can introduce bacteria and lead to cellulitis. They should be allowed to dry up and flake off naturally, usually within 4–10 days.

Topical Treatment:

Gentle Cleansing: Clean the affected area once or twice daily with a damp cloth or a diluted 1% Betadine or chlorhexidine solution (diluted to the color of weak tea).

Antibiotic/Steroid Ointments: Apply ointments containing corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and antibacterial agents like Neosporin or Silver Sulfadiazine (SSD) cream to prevent secondary infection.

Systemic Support:

Pain & Inflammation: Administer nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as Metacam (Meloxicam) to manage pain and reduce systemic swelling.

Antihistamines: If itching is severe, Children’s Benadryl (Diphenhydramine) can be used to prevent the animal from scratching and further damaging the skin.

Antibiotics: For severe cases or if the pustules break, start oral antibiotics such as Clavamox or Baytril (Enrofloxacin) to prevent or treat secondary bacterial infections.

Monitoring for Complications

Secondary Infection: Watch for spreading redness, increased heat in the limbs, or foul-smelling discharge, which may indicate cellulitis or abscess formation.

Hydration: Ensure the baby remains well-hydrated, as the stress of the attack and subsequent healing can lead to dehydration.

If the baby is not injured severely and you are waiting for a rehabilitator, you can try to keep it warm and comfortable in a quiet, dark place until they arrive.

text:
## **14\. Anorexia (Refusing to Eat) — Baby Squirrels**

Anorexia, especially in a baby squirrel, is not normal.

Baby squirrels love to eat, so if you suddenly have a baby who is refusing the nipple, you need to figure out why…and you need to figure it out fast.

Baby squirrels have an extremely high metabolism. Too many missed meals can quickly lead to hypoglycemia, dehydration, and rapid decline.

In other words…

Figuring out why your baby isn’t eating is a race against the clock.

Common Reasons a Baby Squirrel May Refuse to Eat

1) Transition (The only “normal” reason)

This is the one time reluctance to eat can truly be blamed on…reluctance to eat.

A baby who is transitioning onto formula…especially one who has spent more than a few days with mom…is naturally going to be hesitant when faced with a silicone nipple full of formula.

In this case, a missed meal isn’t automatically a crisis. It’s often a waiting game.

Be patient. The baby has to figure out:

you are offering a meal

the formula is food

the delivery system is completely different than what they’re used to

2) Nasal Blockage (Congestion / Bloody Nose / Facial Trauma)

A baby may refuse to eat simply because they can’t breathe through their nose.

This can be caused by:

facial trauma

a bloody nose

congestion / upper respiratory infection

Figuring out which of the three it is will help you treat the underlying cause and get your baby munching again.

Check the nose for signs of obstruction.  
Squirrels are nose breathers, so a baby who can’t inhale through their nose is far less likely to latch on.

They are also more likely to try to breathe through their mouth while simultaneously eating…

…and that is a recipe for aspiration disaster.

If facial trauma or a bloody nose is suspected:  
A baby with facial trauma or a bloody nose will understandably have difficulty breathing due to swelling or blood blocking the nasal passage.

If possible, gently clear the airway using:

steam (to loosen congestion or clots)

a warm, damp cloth (gentle wipe only)

careful removal with tweezers only if there is visible debris or a fully dried clot at the opening

⚠️ Do not dig into the nostrils. Only remove what is clearly loose and accessible.

If the nose is actively bleeding:  
A drop or two of Afrin can help stop the bleeding.

⚠️ Important:  
You can pick your squirrels.  
You can pick your nose.  
But please…don’t pick your squirrel’s nose…unless you can clearly see an easily accessible clot or debris that would benefit the squirrel when removed.

3) Bloat / GI Distress (Common \+ Dangerous)

A bloated baby squirrel may refuse to eat, latch briefly and then stop, or fight the nipple completely.

This is not “being picky.”  
This is often pain, pressure, and digestive shutdown.

Bloat is common in babies who:

were fed the wrong formula

were overfed

were fed too fast

were fed while cold

were fed while dehydrated

have poor gut motility due to illness or stress

Signs of Bloat / GI Trouble

A belly that looks tight, round, or distended

Baby seems uncomfortable, squirmy, or stiff

Little or no stool output

Diarrhea (yes…bloat and diarrhea can happen together)

Clicking, squeaking, or “complaining” during feeding

Baby refuses the nipple or repeatedly pulls off

Why This Matters

A bloated baby is at increased risk for:

aspiration (especially if they fight you)

dehydration (GI issues drain fluids fast)

rapid decline

A baby who is bloated and refusing to eat is not a “wait and see” situation.

What to Do

Pause formula until you identify what’s going on

Warm the baby and ensure proper heat support

Hydrate first if dehydration is suspected

Check for constipation and stimulate appropriately

Reduce feeding volume and slow down feeding speed once feeding resumes

Consult an experienced rehabber/vet quickly if the baby is worsening

Critical Note

If the baby is struggling to breathe, lethargic, or rapidly declining, treat it as an emergency.  
Bloat can spiral quickly in tiny babies.

Overfeeding vs. True Bloat (Quick Difference)

A baby can look “milk drunk” and round after a good meal…that’s normal.

Overfeeding usually looks like:

belly is full but still soft

baby settles and sleeps

normal warmth and normal behavior

stool/pee still happening normally

True bloat usually looks like:

belly feels tight, hard, or distended

baby is fussy, uncomfortable, or refusing to eat

poor stool output or sudden diarrhea

baby may fight feeding or seem weaker than normal

symptoms worsen instead of improving with time

When in doubt, assume bloat is serious and slow down. It’s always better to miss a little formula than to push a baby into aspiration or GI collapse.

---

### **Constipation Relief**

Not eating because he's backed up? See Ch. 41 — the toothbrush technique and the full constipation ladder.

---

4) Dehydration (The \#1 “Silent” Cause of Refusing to Eat)

A dehydrated baby squirrel often won’t eat…or will latch briefly and then stop.

This is because dehydration affects:

energy levels

digestion

body temperature

and the baby’s ability to safely process formula

A dehydrated baby is also at higher risk for:

hypoglycemia

aspiration

and rapid decline

If a baby is refusing food, always consider dehydration early.

Common Signs of Dehydration

Dry or tacky gums

Sticky saliva

Dark urine or very little urine

Lethargy / weak suck

Poor skin elasticity (tent test may be unreliable in very young babies)

Constipation (often paired with dehydration)

Important Rule

Do not push formula into a dehydrated baby.  
If the baby is dehydrated, formula can be harder to digest and may worsen GI issues.

What to Do

Warm the baby first (if needed)

A cold baby will not digest properly and may refuse to eat.

Rehydrate before feeding formula

Use warmed unflavored Pedialyte or appropriate rehydration fluids per your protocol.

Offer small amounts slowly

Hydration is a slow correction…not a one-shot fix.

Once hydration improves, reintroduce formula gradually

Appetite often returns quickly once hydration and body temp stabilize.

When to Escalate

If the baby is refusing all fluids, extremely lethargic, cold, or declining quickly…treat it as an emergency and consult a vet or experienced rehabber immediately.

5) Congestion Due to Illness (Most Critical \+ Fastest Intervention)

This is by far the most critical reason a baby squirrel isn’t eating…and often the one that requires the fastest intervention.

Baby squirrels can get sick fast, and infections don’t need long to wreak havoc on those tiny systems.

If a baby is congested due to illness, they may:

struggle to breathe

refuse to latch

fight the syringe/nipple

or repeatedly pull off and panic during feeding

Congestion Issues to Watch For (Very Closely)

Two of the biggest, fastest-moving culprits include:

Pneumonia

Bordetella

Both strike quickly.  
Both can present with similar symptoms.  
And both can leave a baby struggling to breathe…actively fighting you when it’s time for a meal.

Important Reality Check

Baby squirrels will often still eat even if they’re in pain.  
I wasn’t kidding when I said they live to eat.

So when a baby suddenly refuses food, assume there is a serious underlying issue (breathing, dehydration, illness, temperature, or GI)…and investigate immediately.

When to Stop Feeding Immediately

Stop the feeding attempt right away if you see any of the following:

Clicking, wheezing, or wet breathing

Bubbles at the nose

Formula coming from the nose

Baby is gagging, choking, or coughing

Baby is thrashing, fighting hard, or panic-breathing

Baby suddenly becomes weak, limp, or unusually sleepy

Belly becomes tight/hard during the feeding

Baby cannot breathe comfortably through the nose

Baby is cold to the touch or not fully warmed

Feeding a baby who is struggling to breathe, cold, or fighting hard increases the risk of aspiration, and aspiration can become fatal quickly.

Final Reminder

A baby squirrel doesn’t skip meals for no reason.

If a baby is refusing the nipple, something is wrong…even if it isn’t obvious yet.  
Don’t assume “picky.” Assume cause, and work the problem fast.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

FOR FORMULA TRANSITION REFUSAL

Gradual Transition Protocol: Mix old and new formula in increasing ratios over 3-5 days:

Days 1-2: 75% old formula, 25% new formula

Days 3-4: 50% old formula, 50% new formula

Days 5-6: 25% old formula, 75% new formula

Day 7: 100% new formula

Flavor Enhancement: Add 1-2 drops vanilla extract per 10cc formula to mask taste differences

Patience: Some babies take 7-10 days to fully accept new formula; maintain gradual approach

FOR NASAL CONGESTION-RELATED ANOREXIA

Steam Therapy: Provide steam treatments 2-3 times daily before feedings to clear nasal passages

Saline Drops: Use sterile saline nose drops to loosen mucus before wiping clean

Decongestant (if severe): Pediatric decongestant 1 drop per 100g body weight 30 minutes before feeding (use cautiously, short-term only)

Treat Underlying URI: If colored nasal discharge present, start antibiotics (see URI protocol)

FOR BLOAT/GI DISTRESS-RELATED ANOREXIA

DO NOT FEED until bloat is resolved \- feeding a bloated baby can cause rupture or aspiration

Simethicone: 0.3cc per 100g body weight orally every 4 hours to break up gas

Abdominal Massage: Gentle clockwise circular massage to stimulate gut motility

Hydration Only: Offer Pedialyte in small amounts until abdomen softens

Resume Feeding: Once abdomen is soft and baby is passing stool/gas normally, start with diluted formula

FOR DEHYDRATION-RELATED ANOREXIA

Rehydration Protocol: Offer unflavored Pedialyte every 30-60 minutes until hydration restored

Subcutaneous Fluids (if severe): Warmed LRS or saline 5-10% of body weight once or twice daily

Gradual Formula Reintroduction: Once hydrated, offer 50% Pedialyte/50% formula mixture for first 2-3 feedings, then transition to full-strength formula

Monitor Urine Output: Should see urination within 2-4 hours of rehydration; if not, repeat fluids

FOR ILLNESS-RELATED ANOREXIA

Identify and Treat Underlying Condition: URI, pneumonia, parasites, injury \- address primary illness

Appetite Stimulant (if needed): Nutri-Cal or similar high-calorie supplement 0.5-1cc orally 2-3 times daily to maintain blood sugar

Syringe Feeding (if necessary): If baby is too weak to nurse but has swallow reflex, carefully syringe-feed small amounts (0.5-1cc) every 1-2 hours

Veterinary Consultation: If anorexia persists beyond 24 hours despite treatment, seek professional evaluation

SUPPORTIVE CARE

Frequent Small Feedings: Offer food every 1-2 hours in small amounts rather than large feedings 3-4 times daily

Maintain Warmth: Keep baby consistently warm (90-95°F for pinkies, 85-90°F for furred babies)

Reduce Stress: Minimize handling, provide dark/quiet environment, avoid overcrowding

Weight Monitoring: Weigh baby daily at same time; weight loss of more than 5-10% indicates critical situation

Hydration Maintenance: Continue offering Pedialyte between formula feedings if baby is eating poorly

heading: Ch. 15 — Aspiration & Feeding Safety
text:
## **15\. Aspiration & Feeding Safety**

🔴 CRITICAL – The leading cause of death in hand-reared squirrels.

Aspiration occurs when formula is inhaled into the lungs instead of swallowed into the stomach. This can lead to rapid-onset bacterial pneumonia.

Warning Signs:

During Feeding: Formula “bubbles” from the nose, choking, gasping, or formula leaking from the mouth.

Post-Feeding: Sudden breathing difficulty, lethargy, or “clicking” sounds with every breath (heard by holding the squirrel’s chest to your ear).

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

STOP FEEDING IMMEDIATELY. Do not attempt to “finish the syringe.”

Clear the Airway:

Hold the baby head-down at a 45° angle to let gravity assist drainage.

Gently pat the back to encourage the clearing of the trachea.

Use a nasal bulb or electric aspirator to quickly suction both nostrils and the mouth.

Positioning: Keep the baby upright for at least 30+ minutes after the incident.

Assess Vital Signs:

Check gum color: Pink is normal; Pale or Blue indicates a lack of oxygen (emergency).

Listen for “clicking” or “crackling” sounds in the lungs.

The Safe Feeding Protocol (Prevention)

To prevent aspiration and choking, you must mimic the natural nursing position used by the mother squirrel.

1. Proper Posture (Sternal Recumbency)

Tummy Down: Never feed a squirrel on its back like a human baby.

Upright/Forward: For neonates (unfurred), hold them vertically. For older babies (furred), place them on a flat, stable surface like a table or your lap.

The “U-Grip”: Support the head by placing your thumb and forefinger in a “U” shape under the jaw to keep it steady.

2. Equipment & Control

Syringe Size: Use only a 1cc O-ring syringe for babies under 100g. Larger syringes (3cc+) have plungers that can “slip,” flooding the throat with too much formula at once.

The “Push-Pause” Method: Deliver one tiny drop at a time. Wait for the squirrel to swallow and breathe before offering the next drop.

Nipple Length: Only the [tip of the nipple](https://www.ewildagain.org/feeding-nipple-for-rehab-squirrels) should be in the mouth (approx. 1/4 to 1/3 inch). Pushing it deeper blocks the airway.

3. Immediate Response to “Milk Nose”

If you see formula bubbles come out of the nose:

STOP immediately.

Tilt Down: Hold the squirrel head-down for a few seconds to let gravity drain the fluid.

Wipe: Clean the nose and mouth.

Pause: Do not resume feeding for at least 15–30 minutes until breathing is completely clear.

Medical Treatment for Aspiration Pneumonia

If you hear clicking or the squirrel shows respiratory distress, the aspiration has likely moved into the lungs.

Immediate Antibiotics: Start a broad-spectrum antibiotic immediately (Baytril or Clavamox) to prevent or treat pneumonia. See Medication Chart for dosing.

Nebulization: If available, nebulize with Gentamycin or sterile saline to help clear the lungs.

Supportive Care: Keep the baby warm and quiet. Monitor breathing continuously for 48 hours.

Consult a Vet: If there is no improvement or if the clicking persists after 48 hours of antibiotics.

Prevention Protocols

Never feed a squirrel on its back. They must be upright or leaning slightly forward.

Control the Flow: Use Miracle Nipples and never “push” the plunger; let the squirrel control the suckle.

Pre-Feeding Check: If a baby is congested, clear the nasal passages before starting the feed.

Ch. 15 — Aspiration & Feeding Safety

## 15. Aspiration & Feeding Safety

🔴 CRITICAL – The leading cause of death in hand-reared squirrels.

Aspiration occurs when formula is inhaled into the lungs instead of swallowed into the stomach. This can lead to rapid-onset bacterial pneumonia.

Warning Signs:

During Feeding: Formula “bubbles” from the nose, choking, gasping, or formula leaking from the mouth.

Post-Feeding: Sudden breathing difficulty, lethargy, or “clicking” sounds with every breath (heard by holding the squirrel’s chest to your ear).

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

STOP FEEDING IMMEDIATELY. Do not attempt to “finish the syringe.”

Clear the Airway:

Hold the baby head-down at a 45° angle to let gravity assist drainage.

Gently pat the back to encourage the clearing of the trachea.

Use a nasal bulb or electric aspirator to quickly suction both nostrils and the mouth.

Positioning: Keep the baby upright for at least 30+ minutes after the incident.

Assess Vital Signs:

Check gum color: Pink is normal; Pale or Blue indicates a lack of oxygen (emergency).

Listen for “clicking” or “crackling” sounds in the lungs.

The Safe Feeding Protocol (Prevention)

To prevent aspiration and choking, you must mimic the natural nursing position used by the mother squirrel.

1. Proper Posture (Sternal Recumbency)

Tummy Down: Never feed a squirrel on its back like a human baby.

Upright/Forward: For neonates (unfurred), hold them vertically. For older babies (furred), place them on a flat, stable surface like a table or your lap.

The “U-Grip”: Support the head by placing your thumb and forefinger in a “U” shape under the jaw to keep it steady.

2. Equipment & Control

Syringe Size: Use only a 1cc O-ring syringe for babies under 100g. Larger syringes (3cc+) have plungers that can “slip,” flooding the throat with too much formula at once.

The “Push-Pause” Method: Deliver one tiny drop at a time. Wait for the squirrel to swallow and breathe before offering the next drop.

Nipple Length: Only the tip of the nipple should be in the mouth (approx. 1/4 to 1/3 inch). Pushing it deeper blocks the airway.

3. Immediate Response to “Milk Nose”

If you see formula bubbles come out of the nose:

STOP immediately.

Tilt Down: Hold the squirrel head-down for a few seconds to let gravity drain the fluid.

Wipe: Clean the nose and mouth.

Pause: Do not resume feeding for at least 15–30 minutes until breathing is completely clear.

Medical Treatment for Aspiration Pneumonia

If you hear clicking or the squirrel shows respiratory distress, the aspiration has likely moved into the lungs.

Immediate Antibiotics: Start a broad-spectrum antibiotic immediately (Baytril or Clavamox) to prevent or treat pneumonia. See Medication Chart for dosing.

Nebulization: If available, nebulize with Gentamycin or sterile saline to help clear the lungs.

Supportive Care: Keep the baby warm and quiet. Monitor breathing continuously for 48 hours.

Consult a Vet: If there is no improvement or if the clicking persists after 48 hours of antibiotics.

Prevention Protocols

Never feed a squirrel on its back. They must be upright or leaning slightly forward.

Control the Flow: Use Miracle Nipples and never “push” the plunger; let the squirrel control the suckle.

Pre-Feeding Check: If a baby is congested, clear the nasal passages before starting the feed.

Listen: Develop the habit of listening to the lungs before every feeding.

3. Immediate Response to “Milk Nose”

If you see formula bubbles come out of the nose:

STOP immediately.

Tilt Down: Hold the squirrel head-down for a few seconds to let gravity drain the fluid.

Wipe: Clean the nose and mouth.

Pause: Do not resume feeding for at least 15–30 minutes until breathing is completely clear.

Emergency Treatment

If you hear the “click,” the squirrel needs immediate Veterinary Care for antibiotics (such as Baytril or Clavamox).

Do not wait: By the time you hear clicking, the infection is already in the lungs.

Warmth & Oxygen: Keep the squirrel [extra warm](https://henryspets.com/pages/baby-squirrel) and avoid any stress until they can be seen by a pro.

heading: Ch. 17 — Ataxia (Loss of Coordination)
text:
## **17\. Ataxia (Loss of Coordination)**

Ataxia is not a disease; it is a clinical sign that the neurological system is misfiring. A squirrel with ataxia may stumble, tilt its head, circle incessantly, or “star-gaze” (look straight up for no reason).

### **1\. The Three Common Causes of Ataxia**

| Cause | Key Indicators | Recovery Outlook |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Head Trauma (The Fall) | Rapid onset, bleeding from nose/ears, unequal pupil size (anisocoria). | High (if inflammation is controlled early). |
| MBD (Metabolic Bone Disease) | Twitching, “bunny hopping,” seizures, history of poor diet. | High (if calcium is stabilized immediately). |
| Raccoon Roundworm (Baylisascaris) | Progressive “drunk” walking, rolling, head tilt, loss of fear. | Poor/Terminal (zoonotic risk—extreme caution). |

### **2\. Clinical Staging of Neurological Distress**

#### *Stage 1: Mild (The “Drunk” Squirrel)*

Signs: Slight wobble, overstepping with paws, able to eat but messy.

Protocol: Low-Stimulation Zone. The brain needs “sensory deprivation” to heal. Use a solid-sided tub (not a wire cage), dim lights, and zero noise.

Medication: The vet may prescribe Meloxicam (Metacam) to reduce brain swelling.

#### *Stage 2: Moderate (The “Circler”)*

Signs: The squirrel can only walk in circles, has a permanent head tilt, or “popcorns” uncontrollably.

Protocol: Soft-sided bedding only (fleece “nest” to prevent injury during tumbles).

Medication: The vet may escalate to Dexamethasone or Mannitol if they suspect high intracranial pressure.

#### *Stage 3: Severe (The “Roller” or “Star-Gazer”)*

Signs: Continuous rolling (cannot stay upright), star-gazing (neck hyperextended), or non-responsive pupils.

Protocol: VET IMMEDIATELY. This level of ataxia often indicates permanent brainstem damage or advanced Roundworm.

Safety Note: If Roundworm is suspected, use gloves and bleach all bedding. This parasite is dangerous to humans.

### **3\. The “Head Tilt” Distinction**

Inner Ear Infection: If the squirrel is alert and eating but has a head tilt, it may be a simple ear infection.

Neurological: If the head tilt is accompanied by “nystagmus” (eyes flickering back and forth like a ping-pong ball), the issue is in the brain.

### **4\. “The Wait and See” Rule**

Brain injuries take time. A squirrel that looks “terminal” on Day 1 may be 90% recovered by Day 14 if kept in a dark, quiet environment.

Do Not Euthanize for simple ataxia until you have provided 72 hours of anti-inflammatory treatment and sensory deprivation, unless the animal is in respiratory distress.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

FOR HEAD TRAUMA-RELATED ATAXIA

Anti-inflammatory: Dexamethasone 0.5-2 mg/kg subcutaneously or intramuscularly once, then 0.1-0.5 mg/kg orally once daily for 3-5 days to reduce brain swelling

Alternative Anti-inflammatory: Meloxicam 0.2 mg/kg orally once daily if dexamethasone unavailable (less potent for brain inflammation but safer for long-term use)

Supportive Care: Keep baby quiet in dark, padded environment; minimize handling and stress

Monitoring: Improvement should be visible within 24-48 hours if trauma-related; if no improvement or worsening, reassess diagnosis

FOR MBD-RELATED ATAXIA

Emergency Calcium: Liquid calcium gluconate 100 mg/kg orally three times daily for first 48 hours, then twice daily for 7-10 days

Vitamin D3 Supplementation: 100-200 IU per kg body weight daily to improve calcium absorption

Dietary Correction: Switch immediately to proper formula (Fox Valley or Esbilac puppy formula) with correct calcium:phosphorus ratio

Monitoring: Neurological symptoms should improve within 3-7 days as calcium levels normalize; bone changes take weeks to months

FOR SUSPECTED BAYLISASCARIS (RACCOON ROUNDWORM)

Antiparasitic: Fenbendazole 50 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days, OR Ivermectin 0.2-0.4 mg/kg subcutaneously once, repeat in 14 days

Anti-inflammatory: Dexamethasone 0.5 mg/kg orally once daily to reduce brain inflammation from dying parasites

heading: Ch. 18 — Bladder Expression & Urinary Stasis
text:
## **18\. Bladder Expression & Urinary Stasis**

🔴 CRITICAL NURSING SKILL – Prevent Bladder Rupture & Infection.

In both[Suckling Trauma](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/nursing-on-genitals?authuser=0) and [Spinal Injury](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/spinal-traumahind-end-paralysis?authuser=0)cases, the inability to urinate is a silent killer. If the bladder overfills, it can rupture, or the back-pressure can cause permanent kidney failure. For a seasoned rehabber, mastering the “gentle squeeze” is the difference between life and death.

When a squirrel cannot pee on its own—whether due to Genital Nursing (swelling/scabs) or Spinal Trauma (nerve damage)—you must become their bladder.

Identifying the “Full” Bladder

The “Peach” Feel: A full bladder feels like a firm, round marble or a small peach in the very low abdomen (just above the pelvis).

Dribbling: “Overflow incontinence” occurs when the bladder is so full it leaks a few drops, but the squirrel isn’t actually emptying. This is not a successful pee.

Pain: The squirrel may grunt, click, or show abdominal tension when the area is touched.

The Manual Expression Protocol

STEP 1: Softening the “Plug”

Warm Soak: Before pressing, use a warm, wet cotton ball to soak the genital area for 60 seconds. This softens any dried formula, urine crystals, or scabs that are physically blocking the opening.

Chlorhexidine/Betadine: Use your diluted Chlorhexidine from your list to clean away any “crusties” that could trap bacteria.

STEP 2: The “C-Crip” Technique

Positioning: Hold the squirrel upright or on its back (if it’s a spinal patient).

Placement: Place your thumb and forefinger on either side of the lower abdomen, just above the pelvic bone. You should feel the “marble.”

The Squeeze: Apply a steady, very gentle squeezing pressure backward toward the tail.

Warning: Never use sharp or forceful pressure. If you push too hard against a total blockage (like a hard scab), you can rupture the bladder.

STEP 3: The “Finish”

Empty Completely: Continue until the “marble” is gone and the lower belly feels soft and flat.

Frequency: For spinal patients, express 3–4 times daily. For suckling trauma, express before every feeding.

Secondary Complications (From Your List)

Urine Scald: Chronic dampness causes the skin to peel and burn. After expressing, dry the area thoroughly and apply a thin layer of SSD Cream (Silver Sulfadiazine) or A\&D Ointment.

UTI (Urinary Tract Infection): Stagnant urine grows bacteria fast. If the urine is cloudy, bloody, or has a strong “ammonia” smell, start Amoxicillin/Clavamox or Baytril immediately.

Bladder Atony: If the bladder stays overstretched for too long, the muscles lose their “snap” and will never work again. Constant expression is the only way to prevent this.

Rehabber Insight: The “Spinal Reflex”

Sometimes, just stimulating the area with a warm cotton ball (as you would for a neonate) can trigger a reflex pee in spinal patients. Always try this first before resorting to manual expression.

heading: Ch. 19 — Bladder Stones & Sludge (Urolithiasis)
text:
## **19\. Bladder Stones & Sludge (Urolithiasis)**

🔴 URGENT – Can cause a total urinary blockage.

Bladder stones (uroliths) are considered uncommon to rare in squirrels. While highly prevalent in domestic pets like dogs, cats, and even guinea pigs, squirrels rarely develop them unless there is a significant underlying issue, such as a chronic untreated UTI, severe dietary imbalance, or a congenital defect.

Natural Diet: Wild squirrels naturally maintain a balanced Calcium:Phosphorus ratio by chewing on bones, bark, and roots.

Short Lifespan in the Wild: Stones often take time to form; wild squirrels may not live long enough for them to become symptomatic.

Metabolism: Their high metabolic rate and frequent urination help “flush” the system before crystals can coalesce into stones.

That being said, bladder stones are a real risk for sanctuary squirrels. “Sludge” is a thick, toothpaste-like collection of calcium crystals that settles at the bottom of the bladder. If these crystals clump together, they form hard stones (uroliths) that can tear the bladder lining or plug the urethra.

When You Might See Them (Sanctuary Residents)

In a sanctuary setting, stones become more of a risk due to age and controlled diets.

The “Tums” Overdose: Chronic over-supplementation of [Calcium/Tums](https://henryspets.com/pages/baby-squirrel) for MBD can lead to excess calcium in the urine (Hypercalciuria), which is a primary building block for stones.

Chronic Stasis: For spinal patients like those you manage, urine that sits in the bladder too long allows minerals to settle and form “sludge,” which eventually hardens into stones.

Dietary Imbalance: Diets high in Oxalates (like spinach, certain berries, or too many nuts) can trigger [Calcium Oxalate stones](https://www.lodivet.com/calcium-oxalate-uroliths/).

Signs of a Stone (Urolith)

Because squirrels can’t tell you they have a “kidney stone” cramp, look for:

The “Sandy” Fleece: After the squirrel pees, the urine dries and leaves behind a gritty, white, or beige “sand” on the bedding.

Persistent Blood: You see blood in the urine (Hematuria), but it doesn’t resolve after a full course of antibiotics for a UTI.

Stutter-Streaming: The squirrel starts to pee, stops suddenly in pain, then starts again (as a stone rolls over the exit).

The “Hard” Marble: During manual expression, the bladder feels “crunchy” or you feel a hard, distinct “stone” inside the soft tissue.

Loud Teeth Grinding (Bruxism): A sign of intense abdominal or renal pain.

The “Flush & Adjust” Protocol

STEP 1: Immediate Internal Irrigation

Aggressive Hydration: Increase Lactated Ringers (LRS) or water intake. The goal is to “water down” the mineral concentration in the bladder so the crystals can’t clump.

Sub-Q Fluids: If the squirrel is “gritty,” a vet-approved course of subcutaneous fluids can help flush the kidneys and bladder more effectively than oral water alone.

STEP 2: Dietary Correction

Balance the Calcium: If you are treating for MBD, ensure you aren’t over-dosing. Use Squirrel Blocks as the primary source rather than excessive Tums.

Oxalate Audit: Eliminate high-oxalate “treats” like spinach, chard, or excessive berries, which bind with calcium to form stones.

STEP 3: Pharmaceutical Management (From Your List)

Meloxicam: Essential for managing the intense inflammation caused by a stone “scraping” the bladder wall.

Antibiotics: Stones often go hand-in-hand with UTIs because the bacteria “hide” in the stone’s crevices. Use Baytril or Clavamox if the urine is foul-smelling.

The “Seasoned” Warning: Total Blockage

If a stone moves into the urethra and plugs it, the squirrel will hunch, scream, and be unable to pass a single drop. This is a surgical emergency. You cannot “squeeze” a stone out during manual expression; attempting to do so can rupture the bladder.

Prevention for Spinal Patients

Frequent Expression: Don’t let urine sit. Expressing 4 times a day prevents the minerals from having time to settle and “sludge” at the bottom of the bladder.

The “Tilt” Method: Occasionally tilt the squirrel head-up during expression to ensure the “heavy” sediment at the bottom of the bladder is flushed out.

Management for Rehabbers

If you suspect a stone, Radiographs (X-rays) are the only definitive way to see it. Unlike a UTI, you cannot “cure” a stone with antibiotics from your list; they typically require [surgical removal](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8569880/) by a vet.

Bloat & Gastrointestinal Stasis

Bloat is a critical medical emergency in squirrels. A distended, hard abdomen indicates trapped gas or a dangerous buildup of undigested formula that can lead to organ failure or death if not resolved immediately.

Warning Signs

Physical: The belly feels tight/hard like a marble or drum; the abdomen looks visibly swollen or “stretched.”

Behavioral: The baby is restless, crying, refusing to eat, or stretching its body out in discomfort.

Output: A lack of bowel movements or very hard, dry stool.

The “Red Belly” Warning: An angry, dark red, or purple-tinted abdomen is a sign of sepsis or gut necrosis. This is nearly always fatal and requires an immediate veterinary emergency visit.

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

STOP ALL FORMULA IMMEDIATELY. Do not put more food into a stalled digestive system.

Administer Gas Relief: Consider administering a product containing simethicone. There are infant gas drops available for this purpose.

Hydrate Only: Switch to oral rehydration (warm water with a small amount of Karo syrup). Using solutions with high salt content for long-term bloat may exacerbate dehydration in a stalled gut.

Warmth: Ensure the baby is thoroughly warm. A cold squirrel cannot digest food; feeding a cold baby is a primary cause of bloat.

Treatment Protocols

For General Constipation:

Warm Water Soak: Place the baby’s lower half in comfortably warm water.

Massage: While in the water, perform a gentle, clockwise circular massage on the abdomen. This follows the natural path of the colon.

Repeat: You may need to repeat the soak/massage until the baby passes stool.

Re-introduction: Once the belly is soft, resume feeding with a diluted formula mixture for a period before returning to full strength.

The “Water Flush” Protocol (For Wrong Formula/Toxic Ingestion):

Ch. 19 — Bladder Stones & Sludge (Urolithiasis)

## 19. Bladder Stones & Sludge (Urolithiasis)

🔴 URGENT – Can cause a total urinary blockage.

Bladder stones (uroliths) are considered uncommon to rare in squirrels. While highly prevalent in domestic pets like dogs, cats, and even guinea pigs, squirrels rarely develop them unless there is a significant underlying issue, such as a chronic untreated UTI, severe dietary imbalance, or a congenital defect.

Natural Diet: Wild squirrels naturally maintain a balanced Calcium:Phosphorus ratio by chewing on bones, bark, and roots.

Short Lifespan in the Wild: Stones often take time to form; wild squirrels may not live long enough for them to become symptomatic.

Metabolism: Their high metabolic rate and frequent urination help “flush” the system before crystals can coalesce into stones.

That being said, bladder stones are a real risk for sanctuary squirrels. “Sludge” is a thick, toothpaste-like collection of calcium crystals that settles at the bottom of the bladder. If these crystals clump together, they form hard stones (uroliths) that can tear the bladder lining or plug the urethra.

When You Might See Them (Sanctuary Residents)

In a sanctuary setting, stones become more of a risk due to age and controlled diets.

The “Tums” Overdose: Chronic over-supplementation of Calcium/Tums for MBD can lead to excess calcium in the urine (Hypercalciuria), which is a primary building block for stones.

Chronic Stasis: For spinal patients like those you manage, urine that sits in the bladder too long allows minerals to settle and form “sludge,” which eventually hardens into stones.

Dietary Imbalance: Diets high in Oxalates (like spinach, certain berries, or too many nuts) can trigger Calcium Oxalate stones.

Signs of a Stone (Urolith)

Because squirrels can’t tell you they have a “kidney stone” cramp, look for:

The “Sandy” Fleece: After the squirrel pees, the urine dries and leaves behind a gritty, white, or beige “sand” on the bedding.

Persistent Blood: You see blood in the urine (Hematuria), but it doesn’t resolve after a full course of antibiotics for a UTI.

Stutter-Streaming: The squirrel starts to pee, stops suddenly in pain, then starts again (as a stone rolls over the exit).

The “Hard” Marble: During manual expression, the bladder feels “crunchy” or you feel a hard, distinct “stone” inside the soft tissue.

Loud Teeth Grinding (Bruxism): A sign of intense abdominal or renal pain.

The “Flush & Adjust” Protocol

STEP 1: Immediate Internal Irrigation

Aggressive Hydration: Increase Lactated Ringers (LRS) or water intake. The goal is to “water down” the mineral concentration in the bladder so the crystals can’t clump.

Sub-Q Fluids: If the squirrel is “gritty,” a vet-approved course of subcutaneous fluids can help flush the kidneys and bladder more effectively than oral water alone.

STEP 2: Dietary Correction

Balance the Calcium: If you are treating for MBD, ensure you aren’t over-dosing. Use Squirrel Blocks as the primary source rather than excessive Tums.

Oxalate Audit: Eliminate high-oxalate “treats” like spinach, chard, or excessive berries, which bind with calcium to form stones.

STEP 3: Pharmaceutical Management (From Your List)

Meloxicam: Essential for managing the intense inflammation caused by a stone “scraping” the bladder wall.

Antibiotics: Stones often go hand-in-hand with UTIs because the bacteria “hide” in the stone’s crevices. Use Baytril or Clavamox if the urine is foul-smelling.

The “Seasoned” Warning: Total Blockage

If a stone moves into the urethra and plugs it, the squirrel will hunch, scream, and be unable to pass a single drop. This is a surgical emergency. You cannot “squeeze” a stone out during manual expression; attempting to do so can rupture the bladder.

Prevention for Spinal Patients

Frequent Expression: Don’t let urine sit. Expressing 4 times a day prevents the minerals from having time to settle and “sludge” at the bottom of the bladder.

The “Tilt” Method: Occasionally tilt the squirrel head-up during expression to ensure the “heavy” sediment at the bottom of the bladder is flushed out.

Management for Rehabbers

If you suspect a stone, Radiographs (X-rays) are the only definitive way to see it. Unlike a UTI, you cannot “cure” a stone with antibiotics from your list; they typically require surgical removal by a vet.

Bloat & Gastrointestinal Stasis

Bloat is a critical medical emergency in squirrels. A distended, hard abdomen indicates trapped gas or a dangerous buildup of undigested formula that can lead to organ failure or death if not resolved immediately.

Warning Signs

Physical: The belly feels tight/hard like a marble or drum; the abdomen looks visibly swollen or “stretched.”

Behavioral: The baby is restless, crying, refusing to eat, or stretching its body out in discomfort.

Output: A lack of bowel movements or very hard, dry stool.

The “Red Belly” Warning: An angry, dark red, or purple-tinted abdomen is a sign of sepsis or gut necrosis. This is nearly always fatal and requires an immediate veterinary emergency visit.

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

STOP ALL FORMULA IMMEDIATELY. Do not put more food into a stalled digestive system.

Administer Gas Relief: Consider administering a product containing simethicone. There are infant gas drops available for this purpose.

Hydrate Only: Switch to oral rehydration (warm water with a small amount of Karo syrup). Using solutions with high salt content for long-term bloat may exacerbate dehydration in a stalled gut.

Warmth: Ensure the baby is thoroughly warm. A cold squirrel cannot digest food; feeding a cold baby is a primary cause of bloat.

Warm Water Soak: Place the baby’s lower half in comfortably warm water.

Massage: While in the water, perform a gentle, clockwise circular massage on the abdomen. This follows the natural path of the colon.

Repeat: You may need to repeat the soak/massage until the baby passes stool.

If the bloat is caused by inappropriate milk (KMR, Cow’s Milk, etc.), flushing may be necessary.

Flush: Administer plain warm water at intervals.

STIMULATE: You must stimulate for urination after each flush. The bladder fills rapidly and can rupture if the baby isn’t stimulated.

heading: Ch. 21 — Bordetella Bronchiseptica in Baby Squirrels
text:
## **21\. Bordetella Bronchiseptica in Baby Squirrels**

Identification • Quarantine • Supportive Survival Protocol

Applies to: Pinkies, fuzzies, eyes-open babies, toddlers  
Risk level: 🔥 HIGH  
Contagion risk: 🦠 VERY HIGH  
Outcome without fast intervention: Often fatal

■ AT-A-GLANCE: “Is This Bordetella?”

If you see both of the following…

⭐ Crispy Fur

Fur becomes dull, clumped, matted, stuck to the body.

⭐ Ring Tail

Visible tail rings and rapid tail thinning as fat stores collapse.

🚨 Treat it as Bordetella until proven otherwise.

■ Why This Chapter Exists

Bordetella is one of the most lethal, fast-moving killers of baby squirrels in rehab care.

It is:

contagious

often misdiagnosed

capable of killing before classic respiratory signs appear

frequently accompanied by secondary infections

This chapter is designed for the reality of rehab:

You don’t have 3 days to “watch and see.”

You have hours.

1) What Bordetella Is (Rehab Version)

Bordetella bronchiseptica is a gram-negative bacterium commonly associated with dogs (kennel cough) and other mammals.

In baby squirrels, Bordetella often presents as:

systemic illness

dehydration collapse

fever

respiratory distress (sometimes late)

GI symptoms / secondary infections

2) Why Bordetella Is So Dangerous in Babies

Baby squirrels are uniquely vulnerable because most arrive already compromised:

orphaned/abandoned

hypothermic

dehydrated

underfed

stressed

lacking maternal antibodies

Bordetella exploits that weakness aggressively.

In many cases:

The baby does not “slowly get sick.”  
They crash.

3) How Bordetella Spreads

Bordetella spreads through:

airborne droplets

direct contact

contaminated hands and clothing

shared feeding tools

bedding, cages, incubators

dog/cat exposure (including saliva)

Rehab reality:

One case can become a facility-wide outbreak fast.

4) Hallmark Signs (The “Oh Shit” Moment)

Many symptoms can occur with Bordetella… but two signs show up again and again in real rehab cases as the “this is it” moment:

⭐ Hallmark \#1: Crispy Fur

The fur becomes:

matted

dull

clumped

stuck down to the body

This is often the visible sign of severe systemic dehydration \+ fever.

⭐ Hallmark \#2: Ring Tail

The tail shows:

visible rings

rapid thinning

loss of fat reserves

Together, these signs are a major red flag.

5) Full Symptom List (Common Patterns)

General / Systemic

lethargy and weakness

sudden refusal to eat

fighting feeding attempts

rapid weight loss

fever (“sticky” baby, damp or hot to the touch)

“raisin” wrinkling and skin tenting

Wetness / Urination

profuse urination

wet belly and hind end

bedding constantly soaked

baby feels damp despite a dry environment

Respiratory

sneezing

nasal discharge

audible breathing

gagging/coughing

labored or oppressed breathing

GI / Secondary

diarrhea (sometimes severe)

stool changes that mimic coccidia

dehydration worsened by GI symptoms

■ Differential Diagnosis: What Bordetella Mimics

Bordetella is frequently mistaken for:

coccidia

aspiration pneumonia

URI

stress diarrhea

dehydration from feeding errors

failure to thrive

Key rehab pattern:

If a baby looks like coccidia but does not improve with appropriate care…

Bordetella should move to the top of your list.

6) Incubation and Timing

Bordetella incubation is often cited as 2–15 days, but rehab exposure timing is rarely clear.

What matters is this:

Once symptoms begin, progression can be rapid.

■ EMERGENCY ACTION: FIRST 15 MINUTES

This section is intentionally medication-free.

Your job is:

stabilize \+ isolate \+ prevent spread

Step 1: Assume contagion

Stop handling other squirrels

Wash hands immediately

Change shirt/gown if possible

Treat the baby as infectious

Step 2: Isolate immediately

Separate cage/bin

Separate bedding

Separate feeding tools

Separate trash and laundry

Step 3: Stabilize

Priorities:

heat

hydration

humidity

low stress

■ RED FLAG: “This Is Vet Time”

Bordetella is not a home-remedy illness.

If you suspect Bordetella:

Contact a veterinarian immediately.

Even experienced rehabbers treat Bordetella as a vet-guided case.

7) Vet Communication Script (Copy/Paste)

Use language that is clear, pattern-based, and medically grounded:

“I have a juvenile/nestling squirrel with rapid onset dehydration, fever, and systemic decline. Fur is becoming matted/crispy, tail rings are visible, and there is profuse urination. Respiratory symptoms may be present or emerging. This pattern matches Bordetella bronchiseptica cases we’ve seen in rehab settings. I need guidance on antibiotic therapy and supportive care for a neonate.”

This communicates:

urgency

credibility

and the suspected organism

8) Treatment Framework (Published Version)

This book does not publish mg/kg dosing for prescription medications.

However, rehabbers still need to understand the logic of Bordetella treatment.

Bordetella treatment is typically:

antibiotic-driven

time-sensitive

often requires combination therapy

heavily dependent on supportive care

■ Why Combo Antibiotics Are Common in Rehab

Neonates present a unique challenge:

they feed frequently

they are prone to dehydration collapse

they cannot tolerate GI disruption well

medication absorption is less predictable

Many veterinary protocols rely on:

a strong first-line antibiotic early

or a combination approach if resistance is suspected

■ CRITICAL WARNING: DOXYCYCLINE \+ FORMULA

Many Bordetella protocols include doxycycline.

Doxycycline absorption is reduced by minerals including:

calcium

magnesium

iron

zinc

aluminum

Baby squirrels consume calcium constantly through milk replacer.

🚫 DO NOT mix doxycycline into formula.

This is a common hidden treatment failure.

Rehab reality:

Neonates feed so frequently that perfect spacing is not always possible.

This does not mean doxy is useless…  
It means absorption can be inconsistent, and your vet may adjust the plan.

9) Supportive Care That Saves Lives

Antibiotics matter… but Bordetella babies often die from dehydration collapse before antibiotics can fully work.

Supportive care is not optional.

Heat

Keep stable warmth

Avoid overheating

Sick babies cannot thermoregulate well

Humidity

Helps reduce dehydration

Can improve breathing comfort

Especially important with congestion

Hydration

Monitor weight frequently

Sick babies may require hydration support between feeds

Dehydration can become severe rapidly

Low Stress

Stress worsens outcomes.  
Limit handling to medical necessity.

Feeding Strategy

Sick babies may:

refuse to eat

fight feeding

aspirate more easily due to respiratory distress

Slow down. Prioritize safe technique.

10) Quarantine Rules (Non-Negotiable)

Bordetella is highly contagious.

Minimum quarantine:

14 days

Gold standard:

21 days

Best-practice quarantine includes:

separate housing

separate feeding tools

separate bedding and laundry

strict handwashing

disinfect after every contact

order-of-care rule: healthy first, sick last

■ OUTBREAK CONTROL CHECKLIST

If you suspect Bordetella in one baby, assume exposure has already occurred.

Immediately:

quarantine the symptomatic baby

stop shared play areas

separate age groups

disinfect feeding stations

switch to strict PPE workflow

monitor all squirrels twice daily

11) When to Escalate Immediately

Seek urgent veterinary escalation if you see:

labored breathing

open-mouth breathing

blue/gray gums

inability to feed safely

rapid weight loss

dehydration that won’t stabilize

seizures

collapse

suspected aspiration pneumonia layered on top

12) What NOT To Do

This section saves lives.

🚫 Do not wait for “more obvious” symptoms.

Bordetella can kill before classic respiratory signs fully develop.

🚫 Do not treat this as “just diarrhea.”

Bordetella is systemic.

🚫 Do not assume it’s “just coccidia.”

Bordetella can mimic it and can coexist with it.

🚫 Do not skip quarantine.

This is how outbreaks happen.

🚫 Do not mix doxycycline into formula.

This is one of the most common hidden failures in rehab.

13) The Hard Truth

Even with excellent care, Bordetella can kill baby squirrels.

But rapid identification… especially when you catch the hallmark signs early…

⭐ Crispy fur \+ ring tail

…can mean the difference between:

losing the baby overnight  
and

saving them with timely intervention

■ OPTIONAL SIDEBAR: Zoonotic Risk

Bordetella is not typically considered a major zoonotic threat, but infections in humans have been documented, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

Best practice:

wash hands

avoid face contact

wear gloves in outbreak situations

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

Primary Antibiotic: Baytril (Enrofloxacin) 20–30 mg/kg (High-end dose) twice daily.

Secondary Antibiotic (Combo Therapy): Doxycycline 5–10 mg/kg once daily is often added for dual-pathogen coverage.

🚫 THE DOXY WARNING: Never mix Doxycycline into formula. Calcium/minerals in the milk bind to the drug and prevent absorption. Space Doxy at least 1-2 hours away from feeding.

Supportive Care: Sub-Q fluids (LRS) at 5–10% of body weight twice daily to combat the massive fluid loss from profuse urination.

Duration: Minimum 14–21 days. Bordetella relapses are common if treatment is stopped at 7 or 10 days.

heading: Ch. 22 — Bot Flies (Cuterebra / “Warbles”)
text:
## **22\. Bot Flies (Cuterebra / “Warbles”)**

MODERATE – Distressing appearance, but generally treatable.

Bot flies are parasitic larvae that develop just beneath a squirrel’s skin. While they create unsightly, fluid-draining lumps (called “warbles”), a healthy squirrel can typically tolerate several at once without long-term harm.

Identifying the Signs

Visible Lumps: Hard, boil-like swellings, often around the shoulders, chest, or neck.

The “Breathing Hole”: A small, distinct opening at the center of the lump where the larva’s dark spiracle (breathing tube) may be visible.

Irritation: Redness, local fur loss, or the squirrel over-grooming the site.

Movement: You may occasionally see the larva shifting or pulsing within the swelling.

Treatment Protocol

CRITICAL WARNING: Never squeeze or force a larva out. If the larva ruptures under the skin, it can release toxins that cause [Anaphylactic Shock](https://gsvs.org/blog/botfly-in-dogs-emergency-care/) or deadly sepsis in the squirrel.

STEP 1: Coaxing the Larva

Suffocation Method: Coat the breathing hole thickly with [White Petroleum Jelly](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/integumentary-system/cuterebra-infestation-in-small-animals/cuterebra-infestation-in-small-animals) (Vaseline). This blocks the larva’s air supply, forcing it to surface.

Wait: Leave the jelly for 10–15 minutes. The larva will often back out of the hole on its own to find air.

STEP 2: Gentle Extraction

Tweezers/Forceps: Once the larva’s rear end is poking out, use sterilized tweezers to grasp it firmly (but gently) and pull it out in one smooth motion.

Check the Site: Ensure the entire larva has been removed. If it breaks, seek [Veterinary Assistance](https://www.nwrawildlife.org/page/Rehabilitator_Resources) immediately.

STEP 3: Aftercare

## 22. Bot Flies (Cuterebra / “Warbles”)

MODERATE – Distressing appearance, but generally treatable.

Bot flies are parasitic larvae that develop just beneath a squirrel’s skin. While they create unsightly, fluid-draining lumps (called “warbles”), a healthy squirrel can typically tolerate several at once without long-term harm.

Identifying the Signs

Visible Lumps: Hard, boil-like swellings, often around the shoulders, chest, or neck.

The “Breathing Hole”: A small, distinct opening at the center of the lump where the larva’s dark spiracle (breathing tube) may be visible.

Irritation: Redness, local fur loss, or the squirrel over-grooming the site.

Movement: You may occasionally see the larva shifting or pulsing within the swelling.

Treatment Protocol

CRITICAL WARNING: Never squeeze or force a larva out. If the larva ruptures under the skin, it can release toxins that cause Anaphylactic Shock or deadly sepsis in the squirrel.

STEP 1: Coaxing the Larva

Suffocation Method: Coat the breathing hole thickly with White Petroleum Jelly (Vaseline). This blocks the larva’s air supply, forcing it to surface.

Wait: Leave the jelly for 10–15 minutes. The larva will often back out of the hole on its own to find air.

STEP 2: Gentle Extraction

Tweezers/Forceps: Once the larva’s rear end is poking out, use sterilized tweezers to grasp it firmly (but gently) and pull it out in one smooth motion.

Check the Site: Ensure the entire larva has been removed. If it breaks, seek Veterinary Assistance immediately.

STEP 3: Aftercare

Disinfect: Flush the empty cavity with a mild antiseptic like diluted Betadine or Saline Solution.

heading: Ch. 23 — Broken Bones & Fractures
text:
## **23\. Broken Bones & Fractures**

A squirrel with a broken bone is in immense pain and is at high risk for shock. Your primary goal is stabilization and pain management.

1. Types of Fractures

Closed Fracture: The bone is broken, but the skin is intact. You will see swelling, bruising, or a limb held at an unnatural angle.

Greenstick Fracture: Common in young squirrels. The bone “bends” and cracks but doesn’t snap fully. It is stable but very painful.

Compound (OPEN) Fracture: The bone has pierced the skin. This is a surgical emergency. The risk of bone infection (osteomyelitis) is nearly 100% without immediate internal antibiotics.

Comminuted Fracture: The bone is shattered into multiple pieces (often seen in BB/Pellet injuries or Car Strikes).

2. The “No-Touch” Triage

If you suspect a break (limping, dragging a leg, or an obvious “bend”):

Do Not Palpate: Do not “feel around” to find the break. You can sever a nerve or artery with the sharp bone ends.

Confined Movement: Place the squirrel in a small, padded carrier. Remove all climbing toys, hammocks, or high perches. The squirrel must stay flat to prevent the break from shifting.

Pain Relief: Administer Meloxicam immediately (refer to the dosage chart in Ch. 80). Inflammation causes as much pain as the break itself.

3. To Splint or Not to Splint?

The General Rule: DO NOT splint unless you are a trained professional or the squirrel is extremely calm. A struggling squirrel will fight a splint, often turning a simple closed break into a compound fracture.

Exceptions: If the vet is 24+ hours away and the limb is flopping dangerously, you can create a “soft splint” by wrapping the limb in a thick layer of cotton padding (cast padding or gauze) and securing it with cohesive wrap (VetWrap). Never wrap tight—check for swelling/cold toes every hour.

4. Compound Fracture Emergency Care

If bone is visible:

Flush: Gently drip sterile saline over the bone and wound to keep the tissue moist.

Protect: Cover with a sterile gauze pad soaked in saline.

Antibiotics: Start Baytril or Clavamox immediately. Open bone is a direct highway for bacteria into the bloodstream (sepsis).

5. The Prognosis

Simple Breaks: Squirrels are incredible healers. A simple leg break often knits back together in 3–4 weeks with strict cage rest.

Spinal/Pelvic Breaks: If the squirrel has no “Deep Pain Sensation” (no reaction when you pinch the toes hard), the spine may be severed. (See Ch. 69: Spinal Trauma & Hind-Limb Paralysis).

The “Wild” Factor: A squirrel with a “badly set” leg that heals crooked may be non-releasable, as they cannot navigate the canopy safely.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

INITIAL ASSESSMENT

Physical Examination: Assess fracture type, location, and severity; check for additional injuries

Radiographs (X-rays): Required to determine exact fracture pattern, number of fragments, and alignment

Pain Assessment: Evaluate pain level and provide appropriate analgesia

Shock Assessment: Check for signs of shock (pale gums, cold extremities, rapid heart rate); treat if present

PAIN MANAGEMENT

Meloxicam (NSAID): 0.2 mg/kg orally once daily for 5-7 days \- reduces pain and inflammation

Buprenorphine (opioid, for severe pain): 0.01-0.05 mg/kg subcutaneously or orally every 8-12 hours for first 48-72 hours

Tramadol (alternative opioid): 5-10 mg/kg orally twice daily for moderate to severe pain

Note: Adequate pain control is essential for healing \- pain causes stress, suppresses immune system, and delays recovery

FRACTURE REPAIR OPTIONS (BASED ON TYPE AND LOCATION)

CLOSED FRACTURES \- CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT

Splinting/Casting:

Used for stable, minimally displaced fractures of lower leg (tibia/fibula) or forearm (radius/ulna)

Splint must immobilize joint above and below fracture

Padding is critical to prevent pressure sores

Change splint every 5-7 days to check healing and adjust for swelling changes

Duration: 3-4 weeks for young squirrels, 4-6 weeks for adults

Cage Rest (No Splint):

Used for stable fractures of upper leg (femur) or upper arm (humerus) where splinting is impractical

Baby confined to small, padded container (no climbing structures) for 3-4 weeks

Natural muscle support provides stabilization

Works well for greenstick fractures

COMPOUND FRACTURES \- SURGICAL MANAGEMENT

Wound Debridement (CRITICAL FIRST STEP):

Surgical cleaning of wound to remove contaminated tissue, dirt, and bacteria

Flush with copious sterile saline

Remove any devitalized (dead) tissue

heading: Ch. 24 — Burns (Fire & Chemical)
text:
## **24\. Burns (Fire & Chemical)**

🔴 CRITICAL EMERGENCY – High Risk of Shock and Sepsis.

Triage: Assessing the “Burn Grade”

1st Degree: Red, painful skin; singed fur. (Painful, but high recovery rate).

2nd Degree: Blistering, “wet” looking skin, and extreme pain.

3rd Degree: “Leather-like,” charred, or white/waxy skin. Crucial: These are often painless because the nerve endings are destroyed, but they are the most life-threatening.

Emergency Stabilization Protocol

STEP 1: Stop the “After-Burn”

Cooling: If the burn is fresh (within 30 mins), apply lukewarm (never ice-cold) sterile saline or water for 10 minutes.

Do NOT Peel: If fur or debris is stuck in the burn, leave it for the vet. Peeling it can tear away viable underlying tissue.

STEP 2: Massive Rehydration (The “Parkland” Reality)

Burned squirrels “leak” plasma and fluids through their wounds. They will die of hypovolemic shock and kidney failure if not flushed.

Aggressive Fluids: Administer warm Lactated Ringers (LRS) subcutaneously immediately. Burn patients often require 1.5x to 2x their normal daily fluid maintenance.

STEP 3: Wound Management (From Your List)

SSD Cream (Silver Sulfadiazine): This is your \#1 tool. It is soothing, creates a bacterial barrier, and prevents the wound from drying out (which causes more tissue death).

Avoid “Grease”: Do not use butter, heavy oils, or thick Neosporin on fresh burns; these trap the heat and “cook” the tissue further. Use SSD or [Betadine](https://henryspets.com/pages/baby-squirrel) diluted to “weak tea” color.

STEP 4: Pharmaceutical Support (From Your List)

Pain Management: Burns are agonizing. Start Meloxicam immediately. For severe cases, discuss Gabapentin with your vet to help with the “nerve fire” pain.

Antibiotics: Burned skin is a magnet for Pseudomonas and Staph. Start Baytril or Clavamox as a “loading dose” to prevent systemic sepsis.

The “Rehabber’s Watch”

Sloughing: Between Days 3 and 7, dead skin will begin to “slough” off. This looks disgusting but is part of the healing process. Keep the area clean with Chlorhexidine.

High-Protein Diet: Healing skin requires massive amounts of energy. Boost their diet with High-Protein Blocks and extra hydration.

Contracture: As burns heal, the skin shrinks and tightens. If a burn is over a joint (like an elbow or knee), the squirrel may lose the ability to extend the limb, making them non-releasable.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

FLUID THERAPY (PARKLAND FORMULA FOR BURNS \\\>10% BSA)

Parkland Formula: 4 mL × body weight (kg) × % body surface area burned \\= total fluid volume needed in first 24 hours

Administration Schedule:

Give 50% of calculated volume in first 8 hours

Give remaining 50% over next 16 hours

Use warmed Lactated Ringer’s Solution (LRS)

Route: Subcutaneous fluids for small burns; IV fluids for severe burns if available

Monitoring: Check hydration status every 4-6 hours; adjust fluid rate based on urine output and skin tent

Example: 100g squirrel with 15% BSA burn:

4 mL × 0.1 kg × 15 \\= 6 mL total in 24 hours

Give 3 mL in first 8 hours, then 3 mL over next 16 hours

TOPICAL BURN TREATMENT

Silver Sulfadiazine Cream (SSD) \- GOLD STANDARD:

Apply thin layer to all second and third-degree burns twice daily

Why SSD: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial; prevents infection in burn wounds

Application: Clean wound gently with saline, pat dry, apply cream, cover with non-stick gauze

Duration: Continue until wound is fully healed or ready for skin grafting

heading: Ch. 25 — Cancer: Tumors & Neoplasia
text:
## **25\. Cancer: Tumors & Neoplasia**

🟡 MONITORING – Differentiating the Dangerous from the Benign

Not every lump is an abscess or a bot fly. If a mass is solid, slow-growing, and does not “drain” when lanced, it may be a tumor. In squirrels, these are often aggressive and can metastasize quickly due to their high metabolic rate.

Identifying a Potential Tumor

Texture: Firm, “woody,” or fixed to the underlying muscle or bone (it doesn’t “slide” under the skin).

Growth: Unlike an abscess, which appears overnight, a tumor typically grows steadily over weeks.

Appearance:

Melanoma: Often appears as a dark, pigmented, or blackened mass. It can be flat or raised and may ulcerate (bleed) as it grows.

Fibroma/Sarcoma: Generally skin-colored but can become massive, impeding the squirrel’s ability to move or climb.

Location: Common on the digits, limbs, or jawline.

[Odontoma:](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/odontomas?authuser=0)a benign but invasive tumor-like mass of dental tissue at the root of the upper incisors. See Odontoma for full information.

The Diagnostic Roadmap

The “Poke” Test (FNA): A vet can perform a Fine Needle Aspirate to see if the lump is full of pus (infection) or solid cells (potential cancer).

Biopsy: For a definitive diagnosis, a small tissue sample must be sent to a Pathology Lab. This determines if the mass is benign (non-spreading) or malignant (cancerous).

Management & Ethics

Surgical Removal: If the tumor is small and localized (like on a toe or the tip of the tail), Surgical Excision by a vet can be curative.

Palliative Care: If the cancer is systemic or inoperable, the focus shifts to quality of life. Use your permitted Meloxicam or Gabapentin to manage inflammation and discomfort.

Release vs. Euthanasia: A squirrel with active cancer is not a candidate for release. They cannot survive the physical demands of the wild while battling a malignancy. If the tumor impacts their ability to eat, climb, or groom, humane euthanasia is the most compassionate path.

A Note on “Squirrel Pox” Mimicry

In areas where [Squirrel Fibromatosis (Pox)](https://www.nwrawildlife.org/page/Rehabilitator_Resources) is present, viral skin tumors can look identical to cancer. However, Pox usually presents as multiple smaller nodes across the body, whereas cancer is more often a single, primary mass.

heading: Ch. 26 — Capture Myopathy (Stress Myopathy)
text:
## **26\. Capture Myopathy (Stress Myopathy)**

LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY – IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED

Capture Myopathy is a fatal condition triggered by extreme fear or physical overexertion. It causes massive muscle breakdown, flooding the body with lactic acid and toxins that lead to organ failure. It is most commonly seen in juvenile squirrels (7–12 weeks) following a high-stress rescue or “chase”.

Critical Symptoms

Physical: Trembling, weakness (especially in hind legs), or a “stiff” gait.

Behavioral: A wide-eyed “freeze” response or total lack of responsiveness.

Vital Signs: Hyperventilation (rapid breathing) and a body that feels hot to the touch.

Advanced Signs: Inability to grip, stumbling, drooling, or dark/reddish-brown urine (a sign of kidney damage).

Emergency Treatment Protocol

STEP 1: Eliminate All Stimulation

Environment: Immediately place the squirrel in a dark, quiet, well-ventilated box.

Handling: Stop all physical contact. Every touch increases the metabolic “burn.”

Isolation: Move away from all other animals (dogs/cats/other squirrels).

STEP 2: Manage Temperature & Hydration

Cooling: If the squirrel is hot to the touch, do not add heat. Allow them to cool naturally in a room-temperature environment.

Hydration: Offer oral electrolytes only if the squirrel is fully alert and able to swallow. Never force fluids into a compromised animal.

Professional Care: Consult a [Wildlife Veterinarian](https://www.nwrawildlife.org/page/Rehabilitator_Resources) regarding Sub-Q fluids; these should only be administered under expert guidance to avoid further stress.

STEP 3: Enforce Absolute Rest

Safety: Use a flat, padded surface with no climbing elements to prevent injury from falls or stumbles.

Zero Stress: Ensure no sudden noises or visual triggers for at least 24 hours.

STEP 4: Monitor Closely

Check the squirrel hourly for the first 6 hours.

Note: Many “mysterious deaths” are actually unrecognized Capture Myopathy. Because it is often fatal despite treatment, prevention is your most powerful tool.

Prevention (The Golden Rules)

NEVER Chase: Use traps or nets; never engage in a prolonged physical chase.

Quiet Intake: Keep the initial rescue and examination fast, dark, and silent.

Minimize Restraint: Avoid prolonged holding or “cuddling” during the first 24 hours.

Predator Gap: Ensure the squirrel cannot see or smell domestic pets during the intake process.

*See also §7 Shock Triage, §7D Capture Myopathy — The “Drop Dead” Phenomenon.*

heading: Ch. 27 — Cat & Dog Attacks (Pasteurella / Capnocytophaga)
text:
## **27\. Cat & Dog Attacks (Pasteurella / Capnocytophaga)**

An attack by a cat or dog is an extreme medical emergency for a squirrel. Even if no visible wounds are found, a single “micro-puncture” from a tooth or claw can introduce deadly bacteria into the bloodstream, causing fatal septicemia (blood poisoning) within 24–48 hours.

Why It’s Critical

Rationale: Metronidazole covers anaerobic bacteria and has anti-inflammatory effects

DO NOT SUTURE BITE WOUNDS:

Bite wounds must heal by secondary intention (from inside out)

Suturing seals bacteria inside and causes abscess formation

Exception: Large gaping wounds may need loose sutures after 3-5 days of antibiotic treatment and wound cleaning

Open Wound Care:

Flush wounds twice daily with sterile saline or diluted chlorhexidine

Apply topical antibiotic ointment (triple antibiotic or silver sulfadiazine) after cleaning

Cover with non-stick gauze pad; change bandage twice daily

Monitor for abscess formation (swelling, heat, discharge)

Abscess Management (if develops):

Requires surgical lancing and drainage by veterinarian

Flush abscess cavity with sterile saline

Pack with antibiotic-impregnated gauze; remove and replace daily

Continue systemic antibiotics for full course

Debridement (if tissue necrosis occurs):

Dead tissue must be surgically removed to allow healing

May require multiple debridement procedures as infection progresses

Extensive tissue loss may require skin grafting or flap surgery

Meloxicam: 0.2 mg/kg orally once daily for 5-7 days \- reduces pain and inflammation

Buprenorphine (for severe pain): 0.01-0.05 mg/kg subcutaneously or orally every 8-12 hours for first 48-72 hours

Tramadol: 5-10 mg/kg orally twice daily for moderate to severe pain

Subcutaneous Fluids: Warmed LRS or saline 5-10% of body weight twice daily if baby is dehydrated or in shock

heading: Ch. 28 — Choking & Airway Obstruction
text:
## **28\. Choking & Airway Obstruction**

*For chest-cavity air trauma, see §29 Collapsed Lung (Pneumothorax).*

🔴 IMMEDIATE LIFE THREAT – Every Second Counts

Choking occurs when food, a foreign object, or aspirated formula blocks the airway. Because squirrels are obligate nose breathers, a blockage in the throat or nasal passage can lead to rapid respiratory failure.

Signs of Choking

The “Silent Panic”: The squirrel is wide-eyed and gasping but making no sound.

Pawing: Frantic scratching at the mouth or throat.

Color Change: Gums and tongue turning pale, grey, or blue (cyanosis).

Limpness: Sudden loss of muscle tone as oxygen levels drop.

Emergency Resuscitation Steps

STEP 1: Clear the Oral Cavity

Visualize: Open the mouth gently but quickly.

Manual Clear: If you see the obstruction (food, fleece fiber, etc.), use your pinky finger or a pair of Hemostats to sweep it out. Do not push deeper if you cannot see the object.

STEP 2: Gravity & Back Blows

Positioning: Hold the squirrel face-down at a 45-degree angle, supporting the head and neck securely.

The Pat: Use the palm of your hand to deliver 3–5 firm, quick “thumps” between the shoulder blades. Gravity helps the object slide forward.

STEP 3: Modified Heimlich (For Small Mammals)

Chest Thrusts: If the airway is still blocked, lay the squirrel on a firm surface.

Technique: Place two fingers on the center of the chest (just below the nipple line). Give 3–5 quick, sharp downward compressions. This uses the air left in the lungs to “pop” the obstruction out like a cork.

STEP 4: Post-Choke Recovery

Mouth-to-Nose: If the squirrel is not breathing once the object is cleared, seal your lips around the squirrel’s nose and mouth and deliver tiny, gentle puffs of air (the volume of a “breath” in your cheeks) until the chest rises.

Aspiration Watch: Any choking incident involving liquids or food carries a high risk of Aspiration Pneumonia. Monitor for clicking sounds or labored breathing for the next 48 hours.

Crucial Warning

NEVER shake a squirrel. This can cause fatal brain hemorrhaging or spinal cord injury. Use firm pats, not swinging motions.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

Dexamethasone: A one-time dose may be given by a vet to reduce throat swelling after a traumatic choking incident.

Observation: Monitor for Aspiration Pneumonia for 48 hours.

heading: Ch. 29 — Collapsed Lung (Pneumothorax)
text:
## **29\. Collapsed Lung (Pneumothorax)**

A collapsed lung is one of the most urgent respiratory emergencies in squirrel rehabilitation. It occurs when air escapes from the lung into the chest cavity, causing the lung to partially or fully collapse. This can follow a shooting, a fall from height, a crushing injury, or any trauma to the chest wall. Unlike airway obstruction — where the problem is a blockage — pneumothorax involves the structural integrity of the breathing apparatus itself.

*See also §28 Choking & Airway Obstruction for airway-blockage emergencies. See also §68 Shootings for penetrating chest wounds.*

**COLLAPSED LUNG (PNEUMOTHORAX)**

🔴 LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY — Air trapped in the chest cavity.

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

The “Fish Gape”: Persistent open-mouth gasping that does not improve with rest.

Barrel Chest: The chest looks unnaturally “puffed” or rounded, but breathing is shallow.

Subcutaneous Emphysema: A “crunchy” or “bubble-wrap” feel under the skin around the neck or shoulders (air escaping the chest).

Context: Usually follows a cat attack, dog shake, or being stepped on.

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

When the lung is punctured (by a rib or tooth), air fills the space *around* the lung. This pressure prevents the lung from expanding. The squirrel is essentially suffocating even though their airway is clear. Without a vet to remove the trapped air, the squirrel will eventually die of respiratory failure.

#### *Immediate Action*

Positioning: Keep the squirrel upright. Do not lay them on their back or side, which increases pressure on the functioning lung.

Occlusive Dressing: If you see a “sucking” chest wound (a hole that whistles), immediately cover it with a gloved finger or plastic wrap with Vaseline to seal it.

Oxygen: If you have an oxygen concentrator, place the squirrel in an O2 chamber immediately.

Transport: This is a surgical emergency. Get to a vet for “thoracentesis” (needle aspiration of the air).

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

Thoracentesis: A needle is inserted into the chest cavity to draw out the trapped air.

Pain Management: Buprenorphine for the intense pain associated with chest trauma.

Antibiotics: Mandatory if the collapse was caused by a bite.

#### *Prognosis & Recovery*

Timeline: If air is removed and the leak heals, recovery can be quick; however, many cases relapse.

Success Rate: Poor without veterinary surgical intervention.

#### *Prevention*

Predator Safety: Ensure all outdoor pre-release cages are double-screened.

Handler Awareness: Walk carefully in areas where “loose” squirrels are running.

heading: Ch. 30 — Coma: The Comatose or Semi-Comatose Squirrel
text:
## **30\. Coma: The Comatose or Semi-Comatose Squirrel**

A squirrel in a coma is unresponsive to sound, touch, or pain. Their breathing may be very slow, and their body temperature will drop rapidly.

1. The “Life Check”

Before assuming the squirrel is gone:

Heartbeat: Feel deep under the left “armpit.” A comatose squirrel may have a heartbeat as slow as 40–60 bpm (normal is 150+).

Corneal Reflex: Gently touch the corner of the eye. If the eyelid flinches, there is still brain activity.

Toe Pinch: Squeeze the webbing between the toes hard. A deep-coma squirrel will not react; a semi-comatose squirrel may pull back slightly.

2. The “Triple-D” Protocol (Immediate Triage)

If the squirrel is alive but unresponsive:

Darkness: Light is a stimulus that a bruised brain cannot handle. Keep the eyes covered.

Dexamethasone (The Steroid): This is one of the few times a steroid is vital. A vet must administer it to stop the brain from swelling against the skull. Do not use Meloxicam and Steroids together (this causes fatal stomach ulcers).

Downward Angle: Lay the squirrel on a flat surface with the head slightly lower than the tail (about a 15-degree angle). This helps prevent fluid from pooling in the brain and keeps the airway clear if they regurgitate.

3. Support Measures

Heat (Critical but Careful): A comatose squirrel cannot move away from a heat source. Use a heating pad on LOW and place several layers of fleece between the squirrel and the pad.

Hydration: NEVER give oral fluids to a comatose squirrel; they will aspirate and die instantly. All hydration must be Sub-Q (Subcutaneous) (Ch. 32).

Turning: Every 2 hours, gently flip the squirrel to the other side to prevent lung congestion and “bedsores.”

4. The “Waking Up” Phase

If the squirrel begins to twitch, “paddle” their legs, or make small noises:

Do Not Restrain: They may go through a “manic” phase as the brain re-boots. Keep them in a heavily padded, small box so they don’t hurt themselves.

Sugar Boost: Rub a tiny bit of Karo syrup or honey on their gums (not in the mouth) to provide a quick glucose spike to the brain.

5. Prognosis: When to Call It

The 48-Hour Rule: If there is zero improvement or “menace reflex” (blinking) after 48 hours of steroid treatment and Sub-Q fluids, the brain damage is likely permanent.

The “Quality of Life” Check: If the squirrel wakes up but is blind, cannot swallow, or has permanent “circling,” they are non-releasable and may need humane euthanasia if their distress cannot be managed.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

EMERGENCY ANTI-INFLAMMATORY

Dexamethasone: 1-2 mg/kg subcutaneously or intramuscularly immediately, then 0.5-1 mg/kg every 12 hours for first 48 hours

High-Dose Rationale: Coma indicates severe brain swelling; aggressive steroid dosing is necessary to reduce intracranial pressure

Route: Injectable preferred over oral since comatose baby cannot swallow safely

Duration: Continue high-dose protocol for 48 hours, then taper if improvement occurs

SUPPORTIVE CARE

Fluid Therapy: Subcutaneous LRS or saline 5-10% of body weight every 6-8 hours; avoid overhydration (worsens brain swelling)

Oxygen Support (if available): Provide supplemental oxygen via flow-by or oxygen cage; brain needs maximum oxygen to recover

Nutritional Support: Do NOT feed orally while comatose; if baby survives past 24 hours without regaining swallow reflex, consult vet about tube feeding or IV nutrition

Bladder Expression: Gently express bladder every 4-6 hours if baby is not urinating spontaneously (comatose animals lose bladder control)
