## 30. Coma: The Comatose or Semi-Comatose Squirrel

A squirrel in a coma is unresponsive to sound, touch, or pain. Their breathing may be very slow, and their body temperature will drop rapidly.

1. The “Life Check”

Before assuming the squirrel is gone:

Heartbeat: Feel deep under the left “armpit.” A comatose squirrel may have a heartbeat as slow as 40–60 bpm (normal is 150+).

Corneal Reflex: Gently touch the corner of the eye. If the eyelid flinches, there is still brain activity.

Toe Pinch: Squeeze the webbing between the toes hard. A deep-coma squirrel will not react; a semi-comatose squirrel may pull back slightly.

2. The “Triple-D” Protocol (Immediate Triage)

If the squirrel is alive but unresponsive:

Darkness: Light is a stimulus that a bruised brain cannot handle. Keep the eyes covered.

Dexamethasone (The Steroid): This is one of the few times a steroid is vital. A vet must administer it to stop the brain from swelling against the skull. Do not use Meloxicam and Steroids together (this causes fatal stomach ulcers).

Downward Angle: Lay the squirrel on a flat surface with the head slightly lower than the tail (about a 15-degree angle). This helps prevent fluid from pooling in the brain and keeps the airway clear if they regurgitate.

3. Support Measures

Heat (Critical but Careful): A comatose squirrel cannot move away from a heat source. Use a heating pad on LOW and place several layers of fleece between the squirrel and the pad.

Hydration: NEVER give oral fluids to a comatose squirrel; they will aspirate and die instantly. All hydration must be Sub-Q (Subcutaneous) (Ch. 32).

Turning: Every 2 hours, gently flip the squirrel to the other side to prevent lung congestion and “bedsores.”

4. The “Waking Up” Phase

If the squirrel begins to twitch, “paddle” their legs, or make small noises:

Do Not Restrain: They may go through a “manic” phase as the brain re-boots. Keep them in a heavily padded, small box so they don’t hurt themselves.

Sugar Boost: Rub a tiny bit of Karo syrup or honey on their gums (not in the mouth) to provide a quick glucose spike to the brain.

5. Prognosis: When to Call It

The 48-Hour Rule: If there is zero improvement or “menace reflex” (blinking) after 48 hours of steroid treatment and Sub-Q fluids, the brain damage is likely permanent.

The “Quality of Life” Check: If the squirrel wakes up but is blind, cannot swallow, or has permanent “circling,” they are non-releasable and may need humane euthanasia if their distress cannot be managed.

Route: Injectable preferred over oral since comatose baby cannot swallow safely

Fluid Therapy: Subcutaneous LRS or saline 5-10% of body weight every 6-8 hours; avoid overhydration (worsens brain swelling)

heading: Ch. 31 — Congestion: The “Snuffles” & Stuffy Nose / Upper Respiratory Infection (URI)
text:
## **31\. Congestion: The “Snuffles” & Stuffy Nose / Upper Respiratory Infection (URI)**

### **31A. Congestion / “Snuffles”**

🟡 MODERATE – Annoying, but can lead to Aspiration if not managed.

In the rehab world, a runny nose is usually one of three things: environmental allergies, a mild Upper Respiratory Infection (URI), or “Milk Nose” from a messy feeding session.

NOTE: The “Feeding Trap” NEVER feed a squirrel that is actively congested. They will inhale the formula trying to catch their breath. Clear the nose first, wait 15 minutes, and then feed slowly.

Signs of Congestion

The “Click”: A wet, bubbly sound from the nose (distinct from the deep chest click of Pneumonia).

Face Rubbing: Obsessively wiping their nose on their paws or bedding.

Nasal Discharge: Clear (allergies/irritation) vs. Yellow/Green (infection).

Open-Mouth Breathing: A red-flag sign that the nasal passages are 100% blocked.

The “Snuffle” Guide: Identifying Nasal Issues

Know the difference between a “wet nose” and a “deadly lung.”

If a squirrel is making noise or has discharge, use this triage to decide which protocol to follow.

The “Click” Test: Nose vs. Lungs

Nose Click: If you hear a click, wipe the nose and use a Decongestant Spray (Afrin) dabbed on the outside. If the click disappears, it was just nasal congestion.

Lung Click: If the click is rhythmic, metallic, and persists even after the nose is wiped and cleared, it is Aspiration Pneumonia. Go to the Pneumonia Protocol immediately.

1. “Milk Nose” (Immediate Post-Feeding Issue) \- aka ASPIRATION

This is a mechanical error where formula has entered the nasal passages during a feeding session and is known as Aspiration. This is a potential EMERGENCY.

The Signs: White, milky bubbles coming out of the nose immediately during or after a feeding. Sneezing and “pawing” at the face.

The Sound: A “wet,” bubbly sneezing sound.

The Action: Stop feeding. Tilt the squirrel head-down at a 45-degree angle for 10 seconds to drain. Use a tissue to “wick” the liquid away. Skip the rest of the meal to allow the nasal passages to clear.

Risk: High risk of transitioning into [Aspiration Pneumonia](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/aspiration-pneumonia?authuser=0) if the squirrel is “forced” to finish the bottle. Stop reading this page and go to [Aspiration](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/aspiration-formula-in-lungs?authuser=0) NOW\!

2. Upper Respiratory Infection / URI (The Bacterial Issue)

This is a “head cold” that, left untreated, can travel down into the chest.

The Signs: Thick, sticky, or “colored” (yellow/green) nasal discharge. Dried “crusties” around the nostrils.

The Sound: A persistent, “stuffy” snuffling or whistling sound as they breathe.

Risk: Moderate. Can quickly turn into Pneumonia if the bacteria migrates. Stop reading this page and go to [Upper Respiratory Infection](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/upper-respiratory-infection?authuser=0) NOW\!

3. Environmental Allergies (The Irritation Issue)

Just like humans, squirrels react to dust, strong scents, or improper bedding.

The Signs: Clear, watery nasal discharge. Repeated “dry” sneezing. Red or watery eyes.

The Sound: Frequent, sharp “achoo” sounds but clear breathing between sneezes.

The Action: Switch bedding to Anti-Pill Fleece immediately. Avoid cedar or pine shavings. If it persists, use a dose of Benadryl from your list to dry up the histamine response.

Risk: Low, but chronic irritation can weaken the immune system.

The “Clear the Air” Protocol

STEP 1: Mechanical Clearing

The Nose Tweezer: Use a sterile cotton swab or a tiny corner of a tissue to “wick” away visible moisture.

Saline Flush: Use a single drop of Saline Solution in each nostril to loosen dried crusts.

Decongestant: A tiny drop of Afrin (Decongestant Spray) on a Q-tip, gently dabbed outside the nostril, can help shrink swollen nasal tissues. Caution: Do not use for more than 3 days to avoid “rebound” congestion.

STEP 2: Humidity Control

The “Steam Room”: Bring the squirrel (in its carrier) into a bathroom while you run a hot shower. The steam helps thin out mucus so they can sneeze it out.

Nebulizer: If you have one, nebulizing with Saline or Albuterol (per vet guidance) is the gold standard for stubborn congestion.

STEP 3: Pharmaceutical Support

Benadryl: If the discharge is clear and the squirrel is sneezing, it’s likely an allergy to bedding (cedar/pine) or dust. Use your Benadryl to dry up the secretions.

Antibiotics: If the snot turns “colored” or the squirrel becomes lethargic, start Baytril or Doxycycline to prevent the URI from traveling down into the lungs.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol — Congestion**

Saline Drops: Usually all that is needed to clear the irritant.

Benadryl: In rare cases of confirmed allergies, a vet may prescribe a tiny dose of diphenhydramine (1 mg/kg).

Primary Antibiotic: Baytril (Enrofloxacin) 10 mg/kg twice daily for 7–10 days.

Saline Drops: One drop of sterile saline in each nostril to help the squirrel sneeze out the blockage.

Nebulization: Highly effective for clearing deep sinus congestion.

### **31B. Upper Respiratory Infection (URI)**

🟡 MODERATE TO HIGH URGENCY – Stop the downward migration.

In squirrel rehabilitation, an Upper Respiratory Infection (URI) is often the precursor to fatal pneumonia. For a seasoned rehabber, the goal is to stop the infection in the “head” (sinuses and throat) before it migrates to the “chest” (lungs).

Advanced Signs of URI

The “Gunk”: Thick, sticky, or discolored (yellow/green) nasal discharge that may dry and “seal” the nostrils shut.

Ocular Involvement: Runny, squinty, or “crusty” eyes (conjunctivitis) often accompany a URI.

Mouth Breathing: If the nose is blocked, the squirrel will tilt its head back and gasp through its mouth.

Lethargy & Anorexia: A squirrel that can’t smell its food won’t eat. They become dull and “puffed up”.

The “Seasoned” Treatment Protocol

STEP 1: Aggressive Nasal Hygiene

Wick and Flush: Use a warm, damp cotton ball to soften and remove crusts. If nostrils are blocked, use one drop of Saline Solution in each nostril to loosen deep mucus.

Mechanical Suction: A [Baby Nose Aspirator](https://www.wildlifecenterflorida.org/wp-content/uploads/Rehabilitation-of-Eastern-Gray-Squirrels-2020Formatted-for-PDF-file-1.pdf) can be used very gently to clear the primary airway.

Spa Day: Use the “Steam Room” method to loosen mucus. Clean nostrils with Saline. If the discharge is colored or the squirrel is lethargic, start Baytril or Doxycycline to stop the infection from reaching the lungs.

STEP 2: Nebulization (The Gold Standard)

If the squirrel is “rattly” but not yet clicking in the chest, nebulizing is your most powerful tool.

Setup: Place the squirrel in a small, sealed plastic bin with a hole for the [Nebulizer Tube](https://respiratory-therapy.com/department-management/clinical/guidance-to-reduce-infection-risk-nebulizers/).

The Solution: Use 3–5ml of 0.9% sterile saline. Nebulize for 10–15 minutes twice daily.

The Add-In: Vets may prescribe adding [Gentamicin or Baytril](https://www.vin.com/apputil/content/defaultadv1.aspx?pId=25844&catId=150705&id=9768917) directly into the nebulizer cup to deliver antibiotics directly to the airway lining.

STEP 3: Pharmaceutical Intervention (From Your List)

The “Big Guns”: [Baytril (Enrofloxacin)](https://www.squirrelrefuge.org/infections-in-squirrels) is the preferred choice for primary bacterial URIs.

The “Deep Tissue” Choice: If the infection is stubborn or involves the sinuses, Doxycycline is often added as it penetrates respiratory tissue exceptionally well.

The “Broad Spectrum” Load: [Amoxicillin/Clavamox](https://fwra.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Basic-Medicine-for-Wildlife-Rehabilitators-final.pdf) is effective but must be used with caution in rodents; ensure the squirrel is also receiving Probiotics (like Bene-Bac) 2 hours apart from doses.

Crucial Rehabber Warning: The “Contagion” Factor

URIs are extraordinarily contagious in a rehab setting.

Isolation: A URI squirrel should be in a separate room from healthy litters.

Fomite Control: Do not share syringes, bedding, or even “nests” between squirrels until they have been symptom-free for 7 days.

Handwashing: [Pasteurella and Bordetella](https://www.ewildagain.org/_files/ugd/276f2e_f52232d55a44439fa140ed32a464104a.pdf?index=true) can hitchhike on your skin and clothes.

heading: Ch. 32 — Dehydration & Fluid Therapy
text:
## **32\. Dehydration & Fluid Therapy**

Dehydration in squirrels is a life-threatening condition that must be corrected before any food or formula is administered. A dehydrated squirrel cannot digest formula; feeding them while in this state can lead to fatal bloat or gut stasis.

Warning Signs

The Skin Tent Test: When you gently pinch the skin on the back of the neck or shoulders, it “tents” (stays up) instead of snapping back instantly.

Physical: Sunken eyes, a dry/sticky mouth, and lethargy.

Severe Signs: White spots in the eyes (a sign of advanced dehydration) and cool extremities.

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

WARM THE SQUIRREL FIRST: Never give fluids to a cold squirrel. Ensure the body temperature is stable before starting rehydration.

Stop All Formula: Formula is too thick for a dehydrated gut to process.

Offer Electrolyte Solution: Use an unflavored electrolyte solution (like Pedialyte) or a homemade oral rehydration solution (ORS).

Frequent Dosing: Offer small amounts frequently until hydration is restored.

Assessing Progress

Monitor Output: The squirrel should begin urinating frequently. Urine should be pale yellow or clear.

Retest the Skin: Once rehydrated, the skin should “snap” back immediately when pinched.

Eye Check: Eyes should appear bright, moist, and no longer sunken.

Gradual Transition Back to Formula

Once the squirrel is fully hydrated and its “skin tent” has resolved, do not jump straight to full-strength formula.

Step 1: Start with a mix of electrolyte solution and formula for a few feedings.

Step 2: If the squirrel tolerates the initial mix without bloat, move to a higher concentration of formula.

Step 3: Return to full-strength formula once digestion is confirmed normal.

Advanced Care: Subcutaneous (SQ) Fluids

For squirrels that are too weak to swallow or in severe shock, oral rehydration may not be enough.

Lactated Ringers Solution (LRS): A veterinarian or experienced rehabber may administer warmed LRS under the skin (SQ) to bypass the digestive tract and rehydrate the squirrel directly. See Medication Chart for LRS compatibility.

heading: Ch. 33 — Diarrhea — Complete Clinical Guide (4-Way Split)
text:
## **33\. Diarrhea — Complete Clinical Guide (4-Way Split)**

Diarrhea can be caused by a wide variety of factors including overfeeding, too frequent of feeding, the wrong formula, parasites, and also from the use of antibiotics and mediation.

Diarrhea can kill quickly so the faster you identify what is wrong, the faster you can start treating it.

NOTE: It’s normal for poops to change color and consistency when you are transitioning a baby to formula. A wild baby will have small black, hard poops. Once they transition, they should become golden/yellow-orange in color and firm but not hard.

Type 1: Golden/Yellow “Smush” Stool (The Overfeeding Diarrhea)

This is the most common form of diarrhea in rehab. It is usually a mechanical issue—the gut is simply overwhelmed by the volume or richness of the formula and cannot process it fast enough.

Identification

Appearance: Soft, mustard-yellow or golden-colored stool with a “pudding” or “smushy” consistency. It is unformed but not necessarily watery.

Cause: Feeding too much volume per sitting, feeding too frequently, or using a formula concentration that is too rich for that specific individual.

TREATMENT PROTOCOL: DO THIS NOW

Reduce Volume: Immediately decrease the formula amount for the next 3–4 feedings.

Dilute the Richness: Mix the formula with an oral rehydration solution (like Pedialyte or warm water) for 2–4 feedings.

Probiotics: Add a mammal-specific probiotic (e.g., Bene-Bac) to every feeding to help the gut flora catch up.

Gradual Return: As the stool firms into pellets, slowly increase the concentration back to full strength.

Secondary Treatment Options

BRAT Diet Support: For older babies, offering small amounts of “BRAT” foods (Banana, Rice cereal, Applesauce) can help provide bulk to the stool.

This is the most common form of diarrhea in rehab. It is usually a mechanical issue—the gut is simply overwhelmed by the volume or richness of the formula and cannot process it fast enough.

Identification

Appearance: Soft, mustard-yellow or golden-colored stool with a “pudding” or “smushy” consistency. It is unformed but not necessarily watery.

Cause: Feeding too much volume per sitting, feeding too frequently, or using a formula concentration that is too rich for that specific individual.

TREATMENT PROTOCOL: DO THIS NOW

Reduce Volume: Immediately decrease the formula amount for the next 3–4 feedings.

Dilute the Richness: Mix the formula with an oral rehydration solution (like Pedialyte or warm water) for 2–4 feedings.

Probiotics: Add a mammal-specific probiotic (e.g., Bene-Bac) to every feeding to help the gut flora catch up.

Gradual Return: As the stool firms into pellets, slowly increase the concentration back to full strength.

Secondary Treatment Options

BRAT Diet Support: For older babies, offering small amounts of “BRAT” foods (Banana, Rice cereal, Applesauce) can help provide bulk to the stool.

(Neomycin Sulfate): While labeled for hamsters, anecdotal evidence in squirrel rehab suggests positive results for general gastric upset or overfeeding diarrhea. Consult a veterinarian for appropriate dosage if considering this option.

Prevention

Calculated Feedings: Always calculate feedings based on a percentage of the squirrel’s body weight in grams. Do not “eyeball” the amount.

Wait for Emptying: Ensure the squirrel’s tummy feels soft and empty before the next feeding. If the belly is still rounded from the previous meal, wait another hour.

WHITE DIARRHEA \- Coccidia

SEVERE \- Very common

What it is: Parasitic infection of intestinal tract. Very common in baby squirrels. Often presents with [Bordatella.](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/bordatella?authuser=0)

What you see: White, watery diarrhea (may have blood)

What you smell: Coccidia smells HORRIBLE.

Cause: Coccidian parasites (protozoal infection)

Other symptoms:

Dehydration

Weight loss despite eating

Lethargy

Loss of appetite

PREVENTATIVE TREATMENT (RECOMMENDED):

[Revolution\*(selemectin)](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/medical-dosing-information/revolution?authuser=0)at intake. NOTE: Do NOT use selemectin on neuro babies (lowers seizure threshold)

Larger babies: 1.5ml of formula mix

Repeat 7-10 days apart

Takes 2-3 days to work

TREATMENT:

NOTE: Ponazuril is the preferred treatment for Coccidia as it takes just two doses over a period of 48 hours. Albon is also a treatment, but due to the fact that it takes up to 21 days to treat, you run the risk of the baby dying of dehydration before the treatment is complete. If Albon is your only option, make sure to hydrate the baby between feedings.

Ponazuril: .2ml every 48 hours for a total of 2 doses.

\-OR-

Albon (sulfadimethoxine): 25mg/kg first dose, then 12.5mg/kg once daily for 10-21 days

Hydrate: Pedialyte between feedings if dehydrated

Fecal recheck after treatment to confirm clear

Sanitize environment: Coccidia is highly contagious, including to humans

CRITICAL: Can be fatal if untreated. Start Albon immediately.

Type 3: Green/Grey Diarrhea (Giardia)

Giardia is a protozoal parasite that infects the small intestine. It is notorious for causing malabsorption, meaning the squirrel cannot absorb nutrients from its formula, leading to rapid “wasting” even if the baby is eating well.

Identification

Appearance: Stool is typically green or grey, often described as having a “greasy” or oily sheen. The consistency is loose to watery.

The Smell: It has an extremely foul, distinctive odor that is different from the “sickly sweet” smell of Coccidia.

Cause: Ingestion of Giardia cysts, usually from contaminated water, soil, or contact with infected wildlife/feces.

Symptoms

Physical: Significant abdominal bloating and gas.

Systemic: Rapid weight loss or failure to thrive (“bony” appearance despite a full belly).

Dehydration: Due to the greasy nature of the stool, the body loses fluids and electrolytes very quickly.

Medication: Metronidazole (Flagyl) is the standard treatment.

Dosage: 20mg/kg administered twice daily for 5–7 days.

Probiotics: Use a mammal-specific probiotic (e.g., Bene-Bac) to support the gut during Flagyl treatment.

Zoonotic Risk: Giardia is highly contagious to humans and other pets. Always wear gloves when handling an infected squirrel or cleaning its bedding.

Sanitization: Use a bleach solution or high-heat steam to sanitize the enclosure. Cysts are hardy and can survive in the environment for a long time.

Isolation: Keep the infected squirrel strictly isolated from other rescues until the full course of treatment is finished and the stool has returned to normal.

Bloody Diarrhea

🔴 CRITICAL – Bloody diarrhea is a medical emergency. Your first priority should be to get your squirrel to a vet.

Bloody diarrhea in squirrels is a critical symptom usually indicating severe gastrointestinal distress, parasitic infection, internal bleeding due to injury or a fall, or infectious disease requiring immediate veterinary attention.

Primary Causes

• Intestinal Parasites (Coccidiosis): This is likely the most common cause. Coccidia is a parasitic infection of the intestinal tract caused by microscopic protozoa. While many adult squirrels carry it without symptoms, it can be fatal for babies or stressed adults. When coccidia diarrhea becomes bloody, the infection has progressed to a point where it is causing active intestinal damage and must be treated by a vet immediately.

• Salmonellosis: A bacterial infection often spread through contaminated bird feeders or feces. It causes severe gastrointestinal distress including bloody stools, cramps, and fever.

⚠ WARNING: ZOONOTIC: Salmonella can be transmitted to humans through handling infected squirrels. Wear gloves and wash hands thoroughly after contact.

• Rodenticide Poisoning: Ingesting anticoagulant rat poisons—often through “second-hand” poisoning by eating contaminated bait or poisoned insects—prevents blood from clotting. This leads to internal bleeding, which can manifest as bright red blood or dark, tarry stools. Warfarin-based products are the most common culprit.

• Tularemia (“Rabbit Fever”): Though less common than Coccidia, this bacterial infection is highly contagious and can cause diarrhea and intestinal pain if the squirrel ingests the bacteria. It often leads to sudden death in rodent populations.

⚠ WARNING: ZOONOTIC: Tularemia is transmissible to humans. If suspected, use strict PPE protocols and contact your State Wildlife Lab immediately.

• Dietary “Wrong Food” Syndrome: In orphans, feeding the wrong formula (cow’s milk, goat’s milk, or “homemade” recipes) can cause a bacterial bloom or severe inflammation in the gut, leading to bloody discharge. This is entirely preventable.

• Internal Trauma: A fall or a “clip” by a car can cause blunt force trauma to the abdominal organs, resulting in internal hemorrhaging that passes through the GI tract. The squirrel may show no external injuries.

• Hemorrhagic Gastroenteritis: A sudden, severe condition causing watery, bloody diarrhea. Can progress rapidly and requires immediate veterinary intervention.

• Toxic Ingestion: Ingestion of pesticides, poisonous plants, or contaminated food can cause gastrointestinal bleeding.

How to Assess: What Are You Actually Looking At?

Not all blood in stool is the same. The color, consistency, and volume tell you how serious this is.

Check External Sources First

Before assuming internal bleeding, check the squirrel’s body. Blood near the anus could be from an external wound, abrasion, or injury—not from the GI tract. A quick visual inspection can save you a panic.

Stool Color and Consistency Guide

• Light streaking or flecks of red: May indicate minor irritation, a small abrasion near the anal region, or early-stage parasitic damage. Monitor closely. Wait until the next bowel movement. If blood persists or worsens, consult your vet.

• Bright red blood mixed into stool: Suggests active bleeding in the lower GI tract (colon or rectum). More urgent than streaking. Contact your vet.

• Dark, tarry, or black stool: This is digested blood from higher in the GI tract (stomach or small intestine). The dark color means the blood has been partially broken down during digestion. This indicates significant internal bleeding and is a medical emergency.

• Coffee-ground texture: Similar to tarry stool but with a grainy consistency. Indicates gastric bleeding. Veterinary emergency.

• Volume that soaks bedding: Regardless of color, if the blood volume is soaking through bedding or is obviously causing further distress, this is a crisis. Do not wait for the next bowel movement.

Escalation Framework: When to Act

Level 1: Monitor

Small amount of blood, external source confirmed or single occurrence with bright streaking. Squirrel is alert, eating, and hydrated. Check next bowel movement. Clean the area and observe.

Level 2: Call Your Vet

Blood persists across multiple bowel movements. Blood is mixed into stool (not just surface streaking). Squirrel’s appetite or energy is declining. Stool is changing color toward darker shades.

Level 3: Emergency – Vet NOW

Any of the following require immediate veterinary care:

• Black, tarry, or coffee-ground stool

• Blood volume soaking bedding

• Pale or white gums

• Weakness, lethargy, or collapse

• Visible bruising on the abdomen

• Abdominal bloating or distension

• Known exposure to rat poison or toxic substances

• Sudden onset with no obvious dietary cause

Immediate Supportive Care (While Getting to the Vet)

1. Warmth: A squirrel losing blood is losing the ability to thermoregulate. Provide gentle, consistent heat.

2. Hydration: Bloody diarrhea causes rapid dehydration. Offer oral Pedialyte if the squirrel can swallow safely. If too weak for oral fluids, subcutaneous LRS may be necessary.

3. Stop Feeding: Do not offer formula or solid food until the cause is identified. Feeding can worsen GI bleeding or cause aspiration in a weakened animal.

4. Isolate: Until the cause is known, treat as potentially contagious. Bloody diarrhea from Coccidia, Salmonella, or Tularemia can spread to other animals in your care.

5. Collect a Sample: If possible, collect a stool sample for your vet. A fecal float can identify parasites. Note the color, consistency, volume, and any odor.

What NOT to Do

• Do not treat with over-the-counter anti-diarrheal medications (Immodium, Kaolin) without veterinary guidance. Stopping the diarrhea can trap toxins or bacteria in the gut.

• Do not assume it’s “just Coccidia” and self-treat with Albon or Ponazuril if the stool is bloody. Bloody coccidia has progressed beyond standard home treatment.

• Do not wait multiple days “to see if it improves.” Bloody diarrhea can lead to fatal dehydration, sepsis, or hemorrhagic shock within hours in a baby squirrel.

• Do not handle the squirrel without gloves until the cause is identified. Salmonella and Tularemia are zoonotic.

Cross-Reference: See Coccidia (White Diarrhea), Giardia (Green/Gray Diarrhea), Dehydration & Fluid Therapy, Rodenticide Poisoning (Ch. 60), Shock Protocol.

DEGLOVING

Degloving (Tail Injuries)

Tail injuries are common due to predator escapes.

The Assessment: If the skin is pulled off but the bone is intact, the exposed bone will eventually dry out and “self-amputate” (necrose and fall off).

The Care:

Do not try to “pull” the skin back over the bone.

Keep the area clean and apply a thin layer of Silvadene or triple-antibiotic ointment (without pain reliever).

Watch for “ascending infection.” if the tail base becomes hot or swollen, surgical amputation by a vet is required.

text:
### **⚕ Clinical Protocol — Golden/Yellow Diarrhea**

**DIARRHEA \- GOLDEN/YELLOW “SMUSH” (OVERFEEDING DIARRHEA)**

🟡 MANAGEABLE

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

Bright golden-yellow color \- Stool looks like mustard or baby food consistency

“Smush” texture \- Completely unformed, pudding-like, or liquid consistency

No blood, mucus, or unusual odor \- Stool is pure yellow without streaks or foul smell

Baby otherwise healthy \- Normal energy level, good appetite, no lethargy

Occurs after feeding \- Diarrhea appears shortly after meals, especially if baby ate large amount

Abdomen may feel slightly soft or “squishy” but not painful or distended

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Golden/yellow “smush” diarrhea is the most common and least dangerous type of diarrhea in baby squirrels. It’s caused by overfeeding \- giving too much formula at once or feeding too frequently, overwhelming the digestive system’s ability to process nutrients. The intestines respond by rushing food through without proper absorption, resulting in loose, unformed stool. While not immediately dangerous, prolonged overfeeding diarrhea leads to dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and malnutrition (nutrients aren’t being absorbed). It also increases risk of urine scald and skin irritation from frequent loose stools. The key distinction is that golden “smush” diarrhea is a husbandry issue, not an infection \- the baby is healthy but being fed incorrectly. This is easily corrected by adjusting feeding amounts and frequency.

#### *Immediate Action*

Reduce Formula Volume:

Cut feeding amount by 25-30% for next 2-3 feedings

Example: If feeding 5cc per meal, reduce to 3-3.5cc

Baby may act hungry but resist urge to overfeed \- smaller amounts more frequently is better than large amounts less often

Extend Time Between Feedings:

Add 30-60 minutes between feedings to give digestive system time to process

Example: If feeding every 2 hours, extend to every 2.5-3 hours

Watch baby’s cues \- should be actively seeking food, not just accepting it passively

Dilute Formula Temporarily:

For next 2-3 feedings, dilute formula slightly (add 10-15% more water than usual)

This reduces concentration and makes it easier to digest

Gradually return to full-strength formula over 24-48 hours as stool firms up

Add Probiotic:

Mix 1-2 drops plain yogurt (no sugar, no flavoring) into formula

OR use commercial probiotic powder (pinch mixed into formula)

Helps restore healthy gut bacteria and improve digestion

Monitor Hydration:

Check skin tent and gum moisture every 4-6 hours

If baby shows signs of dehydration, offer small amounts of Pedialyte between feedings

Golden diarrhea rarely causes severe dehydration but monitor closely

Keep Bottom Clean:

Gently clean genital area after each bowel movement with warm water

Pat dry thoroughly and apply thin layer of petroleum jelly or diaper cream to prevent urine scald

Change bedding frequently to keep baby dry

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

**PRIMARY MANAGEMENT (DIETARY ADJUSTMENT)**

Formula Reduction Protocol:

Day 1: Reduce feeding volume by 25-30%, extend feeding intervals by 30-60 minutes

Day 2: If stool is firming up, maintain reduced volume; if still loose, reduce another 10-15%

Day 3-4: Gradually increase volume back to normal as stool consistency improves

Goal: Find the feeding amount that baby can digest without producing loose stool

Dilution Protocol:

Feedings 1-3: Add 15% extra water to formula

Feedings 4-6: Add 10% extra water

Feedings 7-9: Add 5% extra water

Feedings 10+: Return to full-strength formula if stool is formed

Probiotic Supplementation:

Plain yogurt: 2-3 drops per feeding for 3-5 days

OR Probiotic powder (Bene-Bac, FortiFlora): Small pinch mixed into formula once or twice daily

Helps restore beneficial gut bacteria and improve nutrient absorption

**SUPPORTIVE CARE**

Hydration Monitoring: Check hydration status twice daily; offer Pedialyte between feedings if skin tent is slow or gums are tacky

Skin Protection: Apply barrier cream (petroleum jelly, A\\\&D ointment, or zinc oxide diaper cream) to genital area after each cleaning to prevent urine scald

Bedding Management: Change fleece or cloth bedding 2-3 times daily to keep baby dry; damp bedding increases risk of skin irritation

Weight Monitoring: Weigh baby daily; should continue gaining weight even with reduced feeding amounts (if weight loss occurs, increase volume slightly)

**WHEN TO ESCALATE TREATMENT**

If diarrhea persists beyond 48 hours despite dietary adjustments, consider other causes (infection, parasites)

If stool color changes from golden-yellow to green, grey, white, or bloody, treat as different type of diarrhea (see respective protocols)

### ⚕ Clinical Protocol — Golden/Yellow Diarrhea

DIARRHEA - GOLDEN/YELLOW “SMUSH” (OVERFEEDING DIARRHEA)

🟡 MANAGEABLE

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

Bright golden-yellow color - Stool looks like mustard or baby food consistency

“Smush” texture - Completely unformed, pudding-like, or liquid consistency

No blood, mucus, or unusual odor - Stool is pure yellow without streaks or foul smell

Baby otherwise healthy - Normal energy level, good appetite, no lethargy

Occurs after feeding - Diarrhea appears shortly after meals, especially if baby ate large amount

Abdomen may feel slightly soft or “squishy” but not painful or distended

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Golden/yellow “smush” diarrhea is the most common and least dangerous type of diarrhea in baby squirrels. It’s caused by overfeeding - giving too much formula at once or feeding too frequently, overwhelming the digestive system’s ability to process nutrients. The intestines respond by rushing food through without proper absorption, resulting in loose, unformed stool. While not immediately dangerous, prolonged overfeeding diarrhea leads to dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and malnutrition (nutrients aren’t being absorbed). It also increases risk of urine scald and skin irritation from frequent loose stools. The key distinction is that golden “smush” diarrhea is a husbandry issue, not an infection - the baby is healthy but being fed incorrectly. This is easily corrected by adjusting feeding amounts and frequency.

#### *Immediate Action*

Reduce Formula Volume:

Cut feeding amount by 25-30% for next 2-3 feedings

Example: If feeding 5cc per meal, reduce to 3-3.5cc

Baby may act hungry but resist urge to overfeed - smaller amounts more frequently is better than large amounts less often

Extend Time Between Feedings:

Add 30-60 minutes between feedings to give digestive system time to process

Example: If feeding every 2 hours, extend to every 2.5-3 hours

Watch baby’s cues - should be actively seeking food, not just accepting it passively

Dilute Formula Temporarily:

For next 2-3 feedings, dilute formula slightly (add 10-15% more water than usual)

This reduces concentration and makes it easier to digest

Gradually return to full-strength formula over 24-48 hours as stool firms up

Add Probiotic:

Mix 1-2 drops plain yogurt (no sugar, no flavoring) into formula

OR use commercial probiotic powder (pinch mixed into formula)

Helps restore healthy gut bacteria and improve digestion

Monitor Hydration:

Check skin tent and gum moisture every 4-6 hours

If baby shows signs of dehydration, offer small amounts of Pedialyte between feedings

Golden diarrhea rarely causes severe dehydration but monitor closely

Keep Bottom Clean:

Gently clean genital area after each bowel movement with warm water

Pat dry thoroughly and apply thin layer of petroleum jelly or diaper cream to prevent urine scald

Change bedding frequently to keep baby dry

Day 1: Reduce feeding volume by 25-30%, extend feeding intervals by 30-60 minutes

Day 2: If stool is firming up, maintain reduced volume; if still loose, reduce another 10-15%

Goal: Find the feeding amount that baby can digest without producing loose stool

Dilution Protocol:

Feedings 1-3: Add 15% extra water to formula

Feedings 4-6: Add 10% extra water

Feedings 7-9: Add 5% extra water

Feedings 10+: Return to full-strength formula if stool is formed

Plain yogurt: 2-3 drops per feeding for 3-5 days

### 33B. Bloody Diarrhea (Hemorrhagic)

heading: Ch. 33 — Diarrhea — Complete Clinical Guide (4-Way Split) › ⚕ Clinical Protocol — Bloody/Hemorrhagic Diarrhea
text:
### **⚕ Clinical Protocol — Bloody/Hemorrhagic Diarrhea**

**DIARRHEA \- BLOODY (HEMORRHAGIC DIARRHEA)**

🔴 LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

Visible blood in stool \- Ranges from pink streaks to bright red blood to dark tarry black (digested blood)

Mucus present \- Stool may be slimy or jelly-like with blood mixed in

Foul odor \- Strong, unpleasant smell (worse than normal stool)

Liquid to semi-liquid consistency \- Rarely formed; usually watery with blood

Frequent bowel movements \- Baby may pass bloody stool multiple times per hour

Abdominal pain \- Baby may cry, arch back, or show distress when defecating

Lethargy and weakness \- Baby becomes progressively less active as condition worsens

Dehydration signs \- Sunken eyes, tacky gums, poor skin tent, decreased urine output

**SEVERITY ASSESSMENT FRAMEWORK**

LEVEL 1 (MILD) \- Pink Streaks:

Faint pink streaks or tinge in otherwise normal-looking stool

Baby is alert, eating normally, no other symptoms

May indicate minor intestinal irritation or small amount of blood from straining

Action: Monitor closely, adjust diet, add probiotics; may resolve without medication

LEVEL 2 (MODERATE) \- Visible Red Blood:

Obvious bright red blood mixed throughout stool

Baby showing some lethargy or decreased appetite

Stool is loose but baby is still passing some formed portions

Action: Start antibiotics immediately, provide supportive care, monitor for progression

LEVEL 3 (SEVERE) \- Profuse Bleeding:

Large amounts of bright red blood, stool is mostly blood with little fecal matter

Baby is weak, lethargic, may be cold or unresponsive

Rapid dehydration occurring

Action: EMERGENCY \- aggressive antibiotic therapy, subcutaneous fluids, possible blood transfusion consideration, veterinary consultation

LEVEL 4 (CRITICAL) \- Black Tarry Stool (Melena):

Dark black, tar-like stool indicating digested blood from upper GI tract

Suggests severe internal bleeding, possible stomach or small intestine ulceration

Baby is in shock \- cold, unresponsive, barely breathing

Action: GRAVE PROGNOSIS \- emergency vet care, may require euthanasia if baby is suffering

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Bloody diarrhea is one of the most serious conditions in baby squirrels and indicates severe intestinal damage. Blood in stool means the intestinal lining is compromised \- either from bacterial infection (E. coli, Salmonella, Clostridium), viral infection, parasitic invasion, toxin exposure, or severe inflammation. The intestines are bleeding internally, and baby is losing blood, fluids, and electrolytes rapidly. Without immediate aggressive treatment, bloody diarrhea progresses to hemorrhagic shock, organ failure, and death within 12-24 hours. The most common cause is bacterial enteritis from contaminated formula, dirty feeding equipment, or exposure to fecal pathogens. Bloody diarrhea is also highly contagious between squirrels \- immediate isolation is critical. This is a true medical emergency requiring immediate antibiotic intervention and intensive supportive care.

#### *Immediate Action*

**ISOLATE IMMEDIATELY:**

Separate baby from all other squirrels

Use dedicated feeding supplies that never contact other animals

Wash hands thoroughly with antibacterial soap before and after handling

Disinfect all surfaces with bleach solution (1:10 dilution)

**ASSESS SEVERITY LEVEL:**

Use framework above to determine if Level 1, 2, 3, or 4

Level 1: Can monitor at home with dietary changes

Level 2-4: Requires immediate medical intervention

START ANTIBIOTICS IMMEDIATELY (Level 2-4):

Do NOT wait for vet appointment \- bloody diarrhea requires immediate treatment

Baytril (enrofloxacin) or Clavamox (amoxicillin-clavulanate) \- see dosing below

Every hour without antibiotics increases mortality risk

**STOP FORMULA TEMPORARILY:**

Do NOT feed regular formula for 6-12 hours

Intestines need rest to heal; formula will worsen diarrhea

Offer Pedialyte ONLY for first 6-12 hours

**AGGRESSIVE HYDRATION:**

Offer unflavored Pedialyte every 30-60 minutes in small amounts (0.5-1cc)

If baby is too weak to drink or showing severe dehydration, administer subcutaneous fluids immediately

Dehydration kills faster than the infection itself

**WARMTH:**

Keep baby on heating pad (LOW setting with thick towel barrier)

Target body temperature 98-100°F

Hypothermia is common with bloody diarrhea and worsens prognosis

**MONITOR VITAL SIGNS:**

Check consciousness level, body temperature, hydration status every 1-2 hours

Watch for deterioration \- increasing lethargy, cold extremities, labored breathing

If baby becomes unresponsive or goes into shock, seek emergency vet care

heading: Ch. 33 — Diarrhea — Complete Clinical Guide (4-Way Split) › ⚕ Veterinary Protocol
text:
### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

**PRIMARY ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY**

Baytril (enrofloxacin) \- FIRST CHOICE:

Dosage: 10-20 mg/kg orally twice daily for 10-14 days

Why Baytril: Broad-spectrum coverage against gram-negative bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella) commonly causing bloody diarrhea; excellent GI penetration

Administration: Give on empty stomach if possible; if baby vomits, give with small amount of Pedialyte

Duration: MUST complete full 10-14 day course even if symptoms improve; stopping early causes relapse

Clavamox (amoxicillin-clavulanate) \- ALTERNATIVE:

Dosage: 12.5-25 mg/kg orally twice daily for 10-14 days

Why Clavamox: Good broad-spectrum coverage, safer for very young babies, less likely to cause GI upset than Baytril

When to Use: If Baytril unavailable, or for babies under 3 weeks old

Limitation: Less effective against some gram-negative bacteria than Baytril

Metronidazole (Flagyl) \- ADD FOR SEVERE CASES:

Dosage: 10-20 mg/kg orally twice daily for 5-7 days

Why Metronidazole: Covers anaerobic bacteria and protozoal parasites; anti-inflammatory effect on intestines

When to Add: If bloody diarrhea is severe (Level 3-4) or not improving after 24-48 hours on Baytril alone

Combination Therapy: Can be used simultaneously with Baytril for dual coverage

**FLUID THERAPY**

Oral Rehydration (Level 1-2):

Unflavored Pedialyte: 0.5-1cc every 30-60 minutes for first 6-12 hours

Goal: Maintain hydration while intestines rest

Monitor urine output \- should see urination within 2-4 hours

Subcutaneous Fluids (Level 2-4):

Warmed LRS or saline: 5-10% of body weight twice daily

Technique: Inject under loose skin between shoulder blades; fluid should absorb within 4-6 hours

Frequency: Repeat every 8-12 hours until baby is drinking adequately on own

Monitoring: Check hydration status before each fluid administration; adjust volume based on skin tent and gum moisture

**INTESTINAL PROTECTANTS**

Pepto-Bismol (bismuth subsalicylate):

Dosage: 0.1-0.2cc per 100g body weight orally 2-3 times daily

Purpose: Coats intestinal lining, reduces inflammation, has mild antibacterial properties

Duration: Use for 3-5 days or until bloody diarrhea resolves

Note: Stool may turn black from Pepto-Bismol; this is normal and different from melena (digested blood)

Kaopectate (kaolin-pectin):

Dosage: 0.5-1cc orally 2-3 times daily

Purpose: Absorbs toxins, firms up stool, protects intestinal lining

Alternative to Pepto-Bismol: Use if Pepto unavailable or baby is very young

**PROBIOTIC THERAPY**

Timing: Do NOT give probiotics during first 24-48 hours of antibiotic treatment (antibiotics will kill beneficial bacteria)

When to Start: Begin probiotics on Day 3-4 of antibiotic treatment

Options:

Plain yogurt: 2-3 drops per feeding

Bene-Bac or FortiFlora: Small pinch mixed into formula once daily

Duration: Continue probiotics for 7-10 days after antibiotics are finished to restore gut flora

**DIETARY REINTRODUCTION PROTOCOL**

Hours 0-6: Pedialyte ONLY, no formula

Hours 6-12: If baby is alert and hydrated, offer 50% Pedialyte / 50% formula mixture

Hours 12-24: If tolerating mixture well, transition to 75% formula / 25% Pedialyte

Hours 24-48: Return to full-strength formula if stool is improving

Days 2-7: Continue full-strength formula; add probiotic; monitor stool closely

**MONITORING PROTOCOL**

First 24 Hours (CRITICAL): Check every 1-2 hours for consciousness, hydration, body temperature, stool quality

Days 2-3: Check every 4-6 hours; watch for improvement (less blood, firmer stool, increased energy)

Days 4-7: Check twice daily; stool should be transitioning from bloody to normal

Days 8-14: Monitor daily; complete full antibiotic course even if baby appears recovered

#### *Prognosis & Recovery*

Timeline: Mild bloody diarrhea (Level 1-2) improves within 24-48 hours with treatment; severe cases (Level 3-4) take 3-7 days if survival occurs

Success Rate by Severity:

Level 1 (Pink streaks): 90-95% recovery with dietary adjustment and monitoring

Level 2 (Visible red blood): 70-80% recovery with antibiotics and supportive care

Level 3 (Profuse bleeding): 30-50% survival rate; requires aggressive treatment

Level 4 (Melena/shock): 5-10% survival rate; grave prognosis

Critical 48-Hour Window: Most deaths occur within first 48 hours; babies who survive past this point have significantly better prognosis

Warning Signs of Poor Prognosis: Bloody diarrhea worsens despite antibiotics, baby becomes cold and unresponsive, breathing becomes labored, or no urine output for 12+ hours

Improvement Indicators: Blood in stool decreases, stool becomes more formed, baby becomes more alert and active, appetite returns, hydration improves

Long-term Effects: Survivors may have chronic GI sensitivity requiring careful diet management; some develop malabsorption issues requiring nutritional supplementation

#### *Prevention*

**STERILE FEEDING PRACTICES:**

Wash hands thoroughly before preparing formula and feeding

Sterilize all feeding equipment (syringes, nipples, mixing containers) after EVERY use

Use boiling water or dishwasher sanitize cycle

Never reuse formula \- mix fresh for each feeding

**PROPER FORMULA STORAGE:**

Refrigerate mixed formula; discard after 24 hours

Keep formula powder in sealed container in cool, dry place

Check expiration dates; discard expired formula

**CLEAN ENVIRONMENT:**

Change bedding daily minimum; more frequently if soiled

Disinfect cage/container weekly with bleach solution

Keep baby’s living area separate from areas where you prepare food or handle other animals

**QUARANTINE NEW ARRIVALS:**

Isolate new babies for 7-10 days before introducing to other squirrels

Watch for signs of illness during quarantine period

Use separate feeding supplies for quarantined babies

**AVOID CONTAMINATION:**

Never let baby come in contact with feces (own or other animals’)

Don’t house squirrels near areas where wild animals defecate

Keep dogs/cats away from baby squirrels and their supplies

**EARLY INTERVENTION:**

Monitor stool quality at every feeding

Address ANY abnormal stool immediately before it progresses

### **33C. White Diarrhea / Coccidia (Coccidiosis)**

*For the general causes of diarrhea (including Salmonella and rodenticide warnings), see the overview in 33A.*

### **⚕ Clinical Protocol — White Diarrhea / Coccidiosis**

**DIARRHEA \- WHITE/COCCIDIA (COCCIDIOSIS)**

🟠 URGENT

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

White, chalky, or pale yellow stool \- Distinctive color unlike any other type of diarrhea (hallmark sign)

Watery to pudding-like consistency \- Rarely formed; usually liquid or semi-liquid

Foul, sour odor \- Smells worse than normal stool; distinctive unpleasant smell

Mucus present \- Stool may be slimy or have jelly-like consistency

Frequent bowel movements \- Baby may pass white diarrhea multiple times per hour

Progressive weight loss \- Baby fails to gain weight or actively loses weight despite eating

Lethargy and weakness \- Baby becomes less active, sleeps more, shows decreased interest in surroundings

Dehydration \- Develops quickly due to fluid loss from diarrhea

Pot-bellied appearance \- Abdomen may look distended despite weight loss (fluid accumulation and intestinal inflammation)

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Coccidiosis is caused by Coccidia \- microscopic parasites that invade and destroy the intestinal lining. Baby squirrels become infected by ingesting Coccidia oocysts (eggs) from contaminated surfaces, bedding, or feces. Once inside the intestines, the parasites multiply rapidly, causing severe inflammation and damage to the intestinal walls. This prevents proper nutrient absorption, leading to malnutrition and wasting despite adequate food intake. The characteristic white color comes from undigested fats and proteins passing through the damaged intestines. Coccidia is highly contagious between squirrels and spreads rapidly through shared cages, feeding equipment, or caretaker hands. Without treatment, coccidiosis causes progressive dehydration, malnutrition, organ failure, and death within 5-10 days. Even with treatment, severe cases may have permanent intestinal damage requiring lifelong dietary management.

#### *Immediate Action*

CONFIRM DIAGNOSIS (if possible):

White, chalky diarrhea is highly suggestive of Coccidia

Definitive diagnosis requires fecal flotation test at vet (identifies oocysts under microscope)

However, treatment should begin immediately based on clinical signs \- don’t wait for lab confirmation

**ISOLATE IMMEDIATELY:**

Separate baby from all other squirrels

Use dedicated feeding supplies, bedding, and cleaning tools

Assume ALL squirrels in contact with affected baby are exposed

Quarantine entire group and monitor for symptoms

**START ANTIPARASITIC TREATMENT:**

Coccidia requires specific antiparasitic medication (see protocol below)

Do NOT use antibiotics alone \- they won’t kill parasites

Treatment must continue for full course even if symptoms improve

**AGGRESSIVE HYDRATION:**

Offer Pedialyte frequently (every 30-60 minutes) in small amounts

If baby is severely dehydrated or too weak to drink, administer subcutaneous fluids

Dehydration is the immediate threat to life

**CONTINUE FEEDING:**

Unlike bacterial diarrhea, do NOT withhold formula

Baby needs nutrition to fight parasitic infection

May need to increase feeding frequency to compensate for malabsorption

**ENVIRONMENTAL DECONTAMINATION:**

Coccidia oocysts are extremely hardy and survive in environment for months

Disinfect ALL surfaces with ammonia solution (10% ammonia in water) \- bleach does NOT kill Coccidia

Boil all feeding equipment, bedding, and toys for 10 minutes

Discard any porous items (cardboard, wood) that cannot be sterilized

Timeline: Mild bloody diarrhea (Level 1-2) improves within 24-48 hours with treatment; severe cases (Level 3-4) take 3-7 days if survival occurs

Success Rate by Severity:

Level 1 (Pink streaks): 90-95% recovery with dietary adjustment and monitoring

Level 2 (Visible red blood): 70-80% recovery with antibiotics and supportive care

Level 3 (Profuse bleeding): 30-50% survival rate; requires aggressive treatment

Level 4 (Melena/shock): 5-10% survival rate; grave prognosis

Critical 48-Hour Window: Most deaths occur within first 48 hours; babies who survive past this point have significantly better prognosis

Warning Signs of Poor Prognosis: Bloody diarrhea worsens despite antibiotics, baby becomes cold and unresponsive, breathing becomes labored, or no urine output for 12+ hours

Improvement Indicators: Blood in stool decreases, stool becomes more formed, baby becomes more alert and active, appetite returns, hydration improves

Long-term Effects: Survivors may have chronic GI sensitivity requiring careful diet management; some develop malabsorption issues requiring nutritional supplementation

#### *Prevention*

STERILE FEEDING PRACTICES:

Wash hands thoroughly before preparing formula and feeding

Sterilize all feeding equipment (syringes, nipples, mixing containers) after EVERY use

Use boiling water or dishwasher sanitize cycle

Never reuse formula - mix fresh for each feeding

PROPER FORMULA STORAGE:

Refrigerate mixed formula; discard after 24 hours

Keep formula powder in sealed container in cool, dry place

Check expiration dates; discard expired formula

CLEAN ENVIRONMENT:

Change bedding daily minimum; more frequently if soiled

Disinfect cage/container weekly with bleach solution

Keep baby’s living area separate from areas where you prepare food or handle other animals

QUARANTINE NEW ARRIVALS:

Isolate new babies for 7-10 days before introducing to other squirrels

Watch for signs of illness during quarantine period

Use separate feeding supplies for quarantined babies

AVOID CONTAMINATION:

Never let baby come in contact with feces (own or other animals’)

Don’t house squirrels near areas where wild animals defecate

Keep dogs/cats away from baby squirrels and their supplies

EARLY INTERVENTION:

Monitor stool quality at every feeding

Address ANY abnormal stool immediately before it progresses

### 33C. White Diarrhea / Coccidia (Coccidiosis)

*For the general causes of diarrhea (including Salmonella and rodenticide warnings), see the overview in 33A.*

### ⚕ Clinical Protocol — White Diarrhea / Coccidiosis

DIARRHEA - WHITE/COCCIDIA (COCCIDIOSIS)

🟠 URGENT

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

White, chalky, or pale yellow stool - Distinctive color unlike any other type of diarrhea (hallmark sign)

Watery to pudding-like consistency - Rarely formed; usually liquid or semi-liquid

Foul, sour odor - Smells worse than normal stool; distinctive unpleasant smell

Mucus present - Stool may be slimy or have jelly-like consistency

Frequent bowel movements - Baby may pass white diarrhea multiple times per hour

Progressive weight loss - Baby fails to gain weight or actively loses weight despite eating

Lethargy and weakness - Baby becomes less active, sleeps more, shows decreased interest in surroundings

Dehydration - Develops quickly due to fluid loss from diarrhea

Pot-bellied appearance - Abdomen may look distended despite weight loss (fluid accumulation and intestinal inflammation)

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Coccidiosis is caused by Coccidia - microscopic parasites that invade and destroy the intestinal lining. Baby squirrels become infected by ingesting Coccidia oocysts (eggs) from contaminated surfaces, bedding, or feces. Once inside the intestines, the parasites multiply rapidly, causing severe inflammation and damage to the intestinal walls. This prevents proper nutrient absorption, leading to malnutrition and wasting despite adequate food intake. The characteristic white color comes from undigested fats and proteins passing through the damaged intestines. Coccidia is highly contagious between squirrels and spreads rapidly through shared cages, feeding equipment, or caretaker hands. Without treatment, coccidiosis causes progressive dehydration, malnutrition, organ failure, and death within 5-10 days. Even with treatment, severe cases may have permanent intestinal damage requiring lifelong dietary management.

#### *Immediate Action*

CONFIRM DIAGNOSIS (if possible):

White, chalky diarrhea is highly suggestive of Coccidia

Definitive diagnosis requires fecal flotation test at vet (identifies oocysts under microscope)

However, treatment should begin immediately based on clinical signs - don’t wait for lab confirmation

ISOLATE IMMEDIATELY:

Separate baby from all other squirrels

Use dedicated feeding supplies, bedding, and cleaning tools

Assume ALL squirrels in contact with affected baby are exposed

Quarantine entire group and monitor for symptoms

START ANTIPARASITIC TREATMENT:

Coccidia requires specific antiparasitic medication (see protocol below)

Do NOT use antibiotics alone - they won’t kill parasites

Treatment must continue for full course even if symptoms improve

AGGRESSIVE HYDRATION:

Offer Pedialyte frequently (every 30-60 minutes) in small amounts

If baby is severely dehydrated or too weak to drink, administer subcutaneous fluids

Dehydration is the immediate threat to life

CONTINUE FEEDING:

Unlike bacterial diarrhea, do NOT withhold formula

Baby needs nutrition to fight parasitic infection

May need to increase feeding frequency to compensate for malabsorption

ENVIRONMENTAL DECONTAMINATION:

Coccidia oocysts are extremely hardy and survive in environment for months

Disinfect ALL surfaces with ammonia solution (10% ammonia in water) - bleach does NOT kill Coccidia

Boil all feeding equipment, bedding, and toys for 10 minutes

Discard any porous items (cardboard, wood) that cannot be sterilized

text:
### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

**PRIMARY ANTIPARASITIC THERAPY**

Sulfadimethoxine (Albon) \- FIRST CHOICE:

Loading Dose: 50 mg/kg orally on Day 1

Maintenance Dose: 25 mg/kg orally once daily for 10-14 days

Why Sulfadimethoxine: Most effective anticoccidial drug; prevents Coccidia reproduction and allows intestines to heal

Formulation: Available as liquid suspension (easier to dose for small babies) or tablets (can be crushed and mixed with formula)

Duration: MUST complete full 10-14 day course; stopping early allows parasites to rebound

Ponazuril (Marquis) \- ALTERNATIVE:

Dosage: 20-50 mg/kg orally once daily for 3-5 days

Why Ponazuril: Faster-acting than Sulfadimethoxine; good for severe cases

Limitation: More expensive and harder to source than Albon

When to Use: If Sulfadimethoxine unavailable or baby is critically ill requiring rapid treatment

Toltrazuril (Baycox) \- ALTERNATIVE:

Dosage: 10-25 mg/kg orally once, repeat in 5 days

Why Toltrazuril: Single-dose treatment (easier compliance); effective against multiple Coccidia species

Availability: Difficult to obtain in US; more commonly used in Europe

**SUPPORTIVE ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY**

Why Add Antibiotics: Damaged intestinal lining is vulnerable to secondary bacterial infection

Baytril (enrofloxacin): 10-20 mg/kg orally twice daily for 7-10 days

OR Clavamox (amoxicillin-clavulanate): 12.5 mg/kg orally twice daily for 7-10 days

Timing: Start antibiotics simultaneously with antiparasitic treatment

Duration: Continue for full course even if diarrhea resolves

**FLUID THERAPY**

Oral Rehydration: Pedialyte 0.5-1cc every 30-60 minutes between feedings

Subcutaneous Fluids (if moderate to severe dehydration): Warmed LRS or saline 5-10% of body weight twice daily

Monitoring: Check hydration status every 4-6 hours; adjust fluid volume based on skin tent and gum moisture

**NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT**

Increase Feeding Frequency: Feed every 1.5-2 hours instead of every 3-4 hours to compensate for malabsorption

High-Calorie Supplementation: Add Nutri-Cal or similar supplement (0.5-1cc) to formula to boost calorie intake

Probiotic Support: Add plain yogurt (2-3 drops per feeding) or probiotic powder to help restore gut flora (start after 48 hours of antiparasitic treatment)

Vitamin Supplementation: Consider adding liquid multivitamin (1 drop per feeding) since damaged intestines may not absorb vitamins properly

**INTESTINAL PROTECTANTS**

Pepto-Bismol: 0.1-0.2cc per 100g body weight orally 2-3 times daily to coat and soothe intestinal lining

Kaopectate: 0.5-1cc orally 2-3 times daily as alternative to Pepto-Bismol

**MONITORING PROTOCOL**

Days 1-3 (Critical Period): Check every 2-4 hours for hydration, energy level, stool quality, body temperature

Days 4-7: Check twice daily; stool should begin transitioning from white to yellow/brown as intestines heal

Days 8-14: Monitor daily; complete full antiparasitic course even if stool appears normal

Post-Treatment: Recheck fecal sample 7-10 days after finishing medication to confirm parasites are cleared

#### *Prognosis & Recovery*

Timeline: Stool color should begin improving within 3-5 days of starting treatment; full resolution takes 10-14 days; intestinal healing continues for 2-4 weeks after parasites are cleared

Success Rate: Good to excellent if caught early and treated appropriately; moderate if baby is severely debilitated at time of diagnosis

Warning Signs: White diarrhea persists or worsens after 5-7 days of treatment, baby becomes progressively weaker despite therapy, or severe dehydration develops that cannot be corrected with fluids

Improvement Indicators: Stool color transitions from white to yellow to normal brown, consistency becomes more formed, baby becomes more active and alert, weight gain resumes, appetite improves

Long-term Effects: Severe coccidiosis can cause permanent intestinal damage leading to chronic malabsorption, requiring lifelong dietary management; most babies recover fully with prompt treatment

Relapse Risk: Coccidia can recur if baby is re-exposed to contaminated environment or if treatment course was incomplete; thorough environmental decontamination is critical

#### *Prevention*

**ENVIRONMENTAL HYGIENE:**

Clean cages/containers daily with ammonia solution (10% ammonia in water) \- ONLY disinfectant that kills Coccidia oocysts

Boil all feeding equipment, bedding, and toys weekly

Discard porous items (cardboard, wood) that cannot be sterilized

Use fleece or cloth bedding that can be laundered in hot water with bleach

**PREVENT FECAL CONTAMINATION:**

Remove soiled bedding immediately; don’t let baby walk through or sleep in feces

Keep food and water containers elevated off floor

Stimulate baby to urinate/defecate away from sleeping area

**QUARANTINE PROTOCOL:**

Isolate new arrivals for 10-14 days before introducing to other squirrels

Monitor for white diarrhea during quarantine period

Consider prophylactic fecal testing for all new intakes

**HAND HYGIENE:**

Wash hands thoroughly with antibacterial soap before and after handling each baby

Use hand sanitizer between animals if washing not immediately possible

Never touch multiple squirrels without cleaning hands between

**STRESS REDUCTION:**

Minimize handling and environmental changes

Maintain consistent temperature and feeding schedule

Avoid overcrowding \- stress weakens immune system and increases susceptibility to Coccidia

**EARLY DETECTION:**

Monitor stool color and consistency at every feeding

Address ANY white or pale-colored stool immediately

Don’t wait to see if it resolves on its own \- early treatment dramatically improves outcomes

**FACILITY-WIDE OUTBREAK MANAGEMENT**

If multiple squirrels develop coccidiosis:

Treat ALL exposed animals prophylactically even if not showing symptoms

Complete facility shutdown \- no new intakes until outbreak is controlled

Intensive environmental decontamination \- ammonia solution on all surfaces, boil all equipment

Cohort management \- keep affected and unaffected groups completely separate with dedicated supplies

Extended monitoring \- watch all animals for 3-4 weeks after last case resolves

Consider consulting wildlife veterinarian for facility-wide treatment protocol

---

### **33D. Green/Grey Diarrhea (Giardia)**

**⚠ Zoonotic Risk:** Giardia is transmissible to humans via the fecal-oral route. Always wear gloves when handling animals with suspected Giardia. Wash hands thoroughly after cage cleaning. Treat all fecal material as potentially infectious.

### **⚕ Clinical Protocol — Giardia (Green/Grey Diarrhea)**

*F2 Clinical Note: Do not wait for lab confirmation — treat on clinical signs. Fecal ELISA antigen testing can confirm diagnosis but should not delay treatment when clinical presentation is consistent.*

**DIARRHEA \- GREEN/GREY (GIARDIA)**

🟠 URGENT

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

Green, grey, or clay-colored stool \- Distinctive color unlike normal brown or yellow stool (hallmark sign)

Greasy, fatty appearance \- Stool may look oily or shiny (steatorrhea from fat malabsorption)

Extremely foul odor \- Worse than any other type of diarrhea; distinctive rancid smell

Frothy or foamy consistency \- May have bubbles or foam mixed in

Watery to pudding-like texture \- Rarely formed; usually liquid or semi-liquid

Chronic, persistent diarrhea \- Lasts for days to weeks if untreated

Progressive weight loss \- Baby fails to gain weight or actively loses weight despite eating well

“Failure to thrive” appearance \- Baby looks thin, weak, and underdeveloped compared to age-matched peers

Pot-bellied appearance \- Abdomen may look distended despite overall thinness (gas and fluid accumulation)

Dehydration \- Develops gradually due to chronic fluid loss

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Giardiasis is caused by Giardia \- flagellated protozoan parasites that attach to the intestinal lining and interfere with nutrient absorption. Baby squirrels become infected by ingesting Giardia cysts from contaminated water, surfaces, or feces. Once in the intestines, Giardia parasites multiply and coat the intestinal walls, preventing proper absorption of fats, proteins, and vitamins. This causes severe malabsorption syndrome \- baby eats normally but cannot utilize nutrients, leading to progressive malnutrition and wasting. The characteristic green/grey color comes from undigested bile and fats passing through the damaged intestines. The greasy, foul-smelling stool (steatorrhea) is pathognomonic for fat malabsorption. Giardia is highly contagious and spreads easily through contaminated water sources or fecal-oral transmission. Without treatment, giardiasis causes chronic diarrhea, severe malnutrition, stunted growth, and eventual death from starvation despite adequate food intake. Even with treatment, severe cases may have permanent intestinal damage requiring lifelong dietary management.

#### *Immediate Action*

**SUSPECT GIARDIA IF:**

Stool is green, grey, or clay-colored (not normal brown or yellow)

Stool has greasy, oily appearance

Odor is extremely foul and distinctive

Baby is eating well but losing weight or failing to gain

CONFIRM DIAGNOSIS (if possible):

Definitive diagnosis requires fecal examination at vet (identifies Giardia cysts or trophozoites under microscope)

Giardia antigen test (ELISA) available at some vet clinics \- more sensitive than microscopy

However, treatment should begin immediately based on clinical signs \- don’t wait for lab confirmation

**ISOLATE IMMEDIATELY:**

Separate baby from all other squirrels

Use dedicated feeding supplies and cleaning tools

Assume ALL squirrels sharing water source or living space are exposed

Quarantine entire group and monitor for symptoms

**START ANTIPARASITIC TREATMENT:**

Giardia requires specific antiparasitic medication (see protocol below)

Do NOT use antibiotics alone \- they won’t kill parasites

Treatment must continue for full course even if symptoms improve

**HYDRATION SUPPORT:**

Offer Pedialyte between feedings to maintain hydration

If baby is dehydrated, provide subcutaneous fluids

Chronic diarrhea causes gradual dehydration that may not be immediately obvious

**CONTINUE FEEDING:**

Do NOT withhold formula \- baby needs nutrition to fight infection

May need to increase feeding frequency to compensate for malabsorption

Consider switching to easily digestible formula or adding digestive enzymes

**ENVIRONMENTAL DECONTAMINATION:**

Giardia cysts are hardy and survive in environment for weeks to months

Disinfect ALL surfaces with quaternary ammonium compounds or bleach solution (1:10 dilution)

Boil all feeding equipment and water containers for 10 minutes

Discard any porous items that cannot be sterilized

CRITICAL: Disinfect water sources \- Giardia spreads through contaminated water

text:
### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

**PRIMARY ANTIPARASITIC THERAPY**

Metronidazole (Flagyl) \- FIRST CHOICE:

Dosage: 15-25 mg/kg orally twice daily for 5-7 days

Why Metronidazole: Most effective anti-Giardia drug; kills trophozoites and reduces cyst shedding

Formulation: Available as liquid suspension or tablets (can be crushed and mixed with formula)

Taste: Extremely bitter \- mix with small amount of flavored Pedialyte or add to formula to mask taste

Duration: MUST complete full 5-7 day course; stopping early allows parasites to rebound

Side Effects: May cause decreased appetite or nausea; if baby refuses to eat, reduce dose slightly or give with food

Fenbendazole (Panacur) \- ALTERNATIVE:

Dosage: 50 mg/kg orally once daily for 3-5 days

Why Fenbendazole: Broad-spectrum antiparasitic; effective against Giardia and other intestinal parasites

When to Use: If Metronidazole unavailable or baby cannot tolerate it

Advantage: Better tolerated than Metronidazole; less likely to cause GI upset

Limitation: May be slightly less effective than Metronidazole for Giardia specifically

Combination Therapy (for severe or refractory cases):

Metronidazole 15 mg/kg twice daily PLUS Fenbendazole 50 mg/kg once daily for 5 days

When to Use: If single-drug therapy fails or baby has severe, chronic giardiasis

Rationale: Dual mechanism of action increases parasite kill rate

SUPPORTIVE ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY (if secondary bacterial infection suspected):

Baytril (enrofloxacin): 10-20 mg/kg orally twice daily for 7-10 days

When to Add: If baby has signs of bacterial overgrowth (foul odor worsens, fever develops, or bloody mucus appears in stool)

Note: Antibiotics alone will NOT treat Giardia \- antiparasitic medication is required

**FLUID THERAPY**

Oral Rehydration: Pedialyte 0.5-1cc every 1-2 hours between feedings

Subcutaneous Fluids (if dehydrated): Warmed LRS or saline 5-10% of body weight once or twice daily

Monitoring: Check hydration status daily; chronic diarrhea causes gradual dehydration that may not be immediately obvious

**NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT & MALABSORPTION MANAGEMENT**

Increase Feeding Frequency: Feed every 1.5-2 hours instead of every 3-4 hours to compensate for malabsorption

High-Calorie Supplementation: Add Nutri-Cal or similar supplement (0.5-1cc) to formula to boost calorie intake

Digestive Enzyme Supplementation: Add pancreatic enzyme powder (small pinch) to formula to aid digestion of fats and proteins

Low-Fat Formula (if steatorrhea is severe): Consider temporarily switching to lower-fat formula or diluting regular formula to reduce fat load on damaged intestines

Probiotic Support: Add plain yogurt (2-3 drops per feeding) or probiotic powder after 48 hours of antiparasitic treatment to restore gut flora

Vitamin Supplementation: Add liquid multivitamin (1 drop per feeding) since damaged intestines may not absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) properly

**INTESTINAL PROTECTANTS**

Pepto-Bismol: 0.1-0.2cc per 100g body weight orally 2-3 times daily to coat intestinal lining and reduce inflammation

Kaopectate: 0.5-1cc orally 2-3 times daily as alternative

**MONITORING PROTOCOL**

Days 1-3: Check twice daily for hydration, energy level, stool color/consistency, body temperature, weight

Days 4-7: Check daily; stool should begin transitioning from green/grey to yellow/brown as intestines heal

Days 8-14: Monitor every 2-3 days; weight should begin increasing as nutrient absorption improves

Post-Treatment: Recheck fecal sample 7-10 days after finishing medication to confirm parasites are cleared; Giardia can be difficult to eradicate and may require repeat treatment

#### *Prognosis & Recovery*

Timeline: Stool color should begin improving within 3-5 days of starting treatment; full resolution takes 7-14 days; intestinal healing and weight gain continue for 2-4 weeks after parasites are cleared

Success Rate: Good if caught early and treated appropriately; moderate if baby has severe malabsorption and malnutrition at time of diagnosis

Warning Signs: Green/grey diarrhea persists or worsens after 7 days of treatment, baby continues losing weight despite therapy, or severe dehydration develops

Improvement Indicators: Stool color transitions from green/grey to yellow to normal brown, greasy appearance resolves, odor improves, consistency becomes more formed, baby becomes more active, weight gain resumes

Treatment Failure: If no improvement after 7 days of Metronidazole, consider switching to Fenbendazole or using combination therapy; some Giardia strains are resistant to single-drug treatment

Long-term Effects: Severe giardiasis can cause permanent intestinal damage (villous atrophy) leading to chronic malabsorption requiring lifelong dietary management; most babies recover fully with prompt treatment

#### *Prevention*

Use only clean, filtered, or boiled water for formula preparation

Never use water from ponds, streams,

or other natural water sources that may be contaminated with Giardia cysts

Disinfect water bowls daily with bleach solution; rinse thoroughly before refilling

If using well water, have it tested for Giardia contamination

**PREVENT FECAL CONTAMINATION:**

Remove soiled bedding immediately; don’t let baby walk through or sleep in feces

Keep food and water containers elevated off floor

Stimulate baby to urinate/defecate away from sleeping/eating areas

Never house squirrels in areas where wild animals (especially beavers, which are common Giardia carriers) defecate

**QUARANTINE PROTOCOL:**

Isolate new arrivals for 10-14 days before introducing to other squirrels

Monitor for green/grey diarrhea during quarantine period

Consider prophylactic fecal testing for all new intakes, especially those from areas with known Giardia contamination

**HAND HYGIENE:**

Wash hands thoroughly with antibacterial soap before and after handling each baby

Use hand sanitizer between animals if washing not immediately possible

Never touch multiple squirrels without cleaning hands between

**STRESS REDUCTION:**

Minimize handling and environmental changes

Maintain consistent temperature and feeding schedule

Avoid overcrowding \- stress weakens immune system and increases susceptibility to parasites

**EARLY DETECTION:**

Monitor stool color and consistency at every feeding

Address ANY green, grey, or greasy-looking stool immediately

Don’t wait to see if it resolves on its own \- early treatment dramatically improves outcomes

---

### **33E. Salmonella**

**Salmonella moves fast in babies.** Symptoms appear **6–36 hours** after the bacteria are swallowed. Once acute symptoms start, a fragile baby can die within **24–48 hours** from rapid dehydration and septicemia (blood poisoning).

**Why so fast:** infants have immature immune systems and very little body mass, so severe diarrhea and systemic shock can overwhelm them in under two days. Death comes from acute fluid loss, profound electrolyte imbalance, and septicemia.

- Lethargy and refusal to feed
- Cold body temperature
- Severe, watery, or discolored diarrhea
- Bloating or abdominal pain

**Action:** this is a vet emergency. Warm first (Ch. 49); fluids and antibiotics are vet decisions. Salmonella spreads to people — gloves, handwashing, and separate bedding (Ch. 1).

heading: Ch. 34 — Dwarfism (Congenital Growth Stunting)
text:
## **34\. Dwarfism (Congenital Growth Stunting)**

Dwarfism in squirrels is a rare genetic or endocrine condition where the animal’s body does not grow at a normal rate or in normal proportions. While these squirrels are often “the favorites” due to their permanent baby-like appearance, they face significant physiological challenges.

1. It is difficult to diagnose dwarfism in pinkies. Most cases become apparent at the 6–10 week mark.

The “Puppy” Head: The head appears disproportionately large or “domed” compared to a short, compact body.

Shortened Extremities: The legs (especially the forelimbs) are significantly shorter and may have a “bowed” appearance.

Micropinna: The ears may remain small or fail to fully unfurl.

Delayed Teething: Incisors may erupt much later than the standard 4-week mark.

The “Forever Fuzzy”: They often retain their soft, juvenile fur texture long after they should have developed a coarse adult coat.

2. Diagnostic Distinction: Dwarfism vs. MBD/Malnutrition

Before labeling a squirrel as a dwarf, you must rule out “environmental” stunting:

Malnutrition/Refeeding: These squirrels will eventually “catch up” once on a proper diet. A true dwarf will stay small despite perfect nutrition.

MBD: If the legs are short because the bones are bowing or breaking, it is MBD (Ch. 54), not dwarfism.

Organ Failure: Congenital heart or liver issues can stunt growth, but these squirrels usually appear “sickly” (lethargic/pale), whereas dwarfs are often energetic and “bright.”

Environmental/Toxic Dwarfism (The “Cluster” Effect)

When multiple dwarves appear in a single litter or within the same geographic area in a single season, the cause is likely Teratogenic (toxin-induced) rather than purely genetic.

The “Clue” of the Cluster: Genetic dwarfism is exceedingly rare. If you have siblings showing these traits, it suggests the mother ingested toxins (such as lead-based paint, lawn chemicals, or contaminated water) that crossed the placental barrier.

Variable Stunting: Unlike “textbook” dwarfism, toxic stunting can be inconsistent. One sibling may have a shorter spine, while another has a “twisted” limb or missing toes.

The “Head-to-Body” Ratio: In toxic cases, the head often continues to grow at a near-normal rate while the long bones of the legs stop prematurely, creating a “bobblehead” appearance that is even more pronounced than in genetic cases.

Organ Fragility: These squirrels are at even higher risk for internal issues (heart murmurs or kidney insufficiency) because the toxins that stunted their bones likely impacted their developing organs as well.

3. Clinical Challenges

Dwarfism isn’t just about size; it’s about internal space.

Respiratory Crowding: Because the chest cavity is smaller, these squirrels are at a much higher risk for respiratory distress or pneumonia.

Dental Crowding: A smaller jaw means less room for elodont teeth. Dwarfs are highly prone to Malocclusion (Ch. 52) and must be monitored weekly for tooth overgrowth.

Arthritis: Their joints are not aligned for high-impact jumping. They often develop early-onset mobility issues.

4. Release Prospects

Dwarf squirrels are strictly non-releasable.

The “Prey” Factor: Their shorter limbs mean they cannot outrun predators or climb fast enough to reach safety.

Foraging Failures: They often lack the reach or strength to crack heavy mast (walnuts/hickory) or navigate long distances between trees.

Thermoregulation: Their small body mass makes them lose heat rapidly, making them unable to survive a standard winter.

5. Management in Sanctuary

If the squirrel has a high quality of life (breathing well, eating well, moving without pain), they can live a full life in a specialized sanctuary setting.

Low-Profile Housing: Use cages that are “long and wide” rather than tall to prevent fall injuries.

High-Nutrient Density: Because they eat less total volume, every bite must count. Stick to high-quality blocks (Henry’s) and limit “filler” veggies.

The “Toxic Cluster” Profile

When dwarfism is caused by prenatal environmental exposure, the squirrels often present with a specific “High-Burn” phenotype.

Metabolic Hyper-Drive: These squirrels are often faster and more “twitchy” than standard orphans. They may exhibit a lower threshold for “fight or flight” and require a much higher calorie intake relative to their size because they burn energy so rapidly.

Incomplete Pelage (Alopecia): Thin, patchy fur or large areas of permanent baldness are common. The skin may appear healthy (no crusting like mange), but the fur simply does not grow or remains in a “peach fuzz” state.

Neurological “Static”: Their “high-string” nature suggests the toxins may have impacted the development of the GABA receptors in the brain, leaving them in a state of constant neurological “noise.”

Care Note: Because of their speed and anxiety, these dwarves are at high risk for “bonking” (running into cage walls and causing head trauma). They need heavily padded enclosures and “soft” hiding spots (fleece cubes) rather than hard wooden houses.
