heading: Ch. 35 — Electrocution (High-Voltage Trauma)
text:
## **35\. Electrocution (High-Voltage Trauma)**

🔴 CRITICAL EMERGENCY – Watch for Delayed Systemic Collapse.

In area where power lines often cut through squirrel corridors, electrocution is a common and devastating trauma. For a seasoned rehabber, the challenge is that the external damage—the “entry and exit” wounds—is often just the tip of the iceberg. The real destruction is internal, affecting the heart, lungs, and nerves.

Electrocution occurs when a squirrel completes a circuit between a live wire and a grounded object (like a transformer or another wire). This causes immediate thermal burns, muscle contractions, and potential cardiac arrest.

Identifying the Damage

The “Entry/Exit” Wounds: Look for singed fur, blackened skin, or deep, “charred” holes, usually on the paws, mouth, or tail.

Flash Burns: General singeing of the fur without deep tissue damage.

Neurological: Stupor, blindness (temporary or permanent), or “stargazing” from the massive electrical jolt to the brain.

Respiratory: Labored breathing or “clicking” (Pulmonary Edema). The electrical current often causes fluid to leak into the lungs.

Emergency Stabilization Protocol

STEP 1: Cardiac & Respiratory Support

Oxygen: If the squirrel is gasping or has blue gums, provide flow-by oxygen immediately. Electrocution often causes pulmonary contusions.

Minimize Stress: The heart is electrically “unstable” after a shock. Any sudden noise or rough handling can trigger a fatal arrhythmia.

STEP 2: Managing the “Burn” (From Your List)

Wound Care: Do not apply thick ointments to fresh electrical burns, as they trap heat. Use a thin layer of SSD Cream (Silver Sulfadiazine) or [Betadine](https://henryspets.com/pages/baby-squirrel) once the tissue has cooled.

Hydration: Electrocution causes massive internal tissue death, which releases toxins that “clog” the kidneys. Start Sub-Q LRS immediately to flush the system.

STEP 3: Pharmaceutical Strategy (From Your List)

Meloxicam: Essential for the intense inflammation and pain of the burn sites.

Dexamethasone/Prednisone: If the squirrel is neurological or has “wet” lungs (edema), a vet may prioritize a Steroid burst over NSAIDs to reduce CNS swelling. Note: Choose one or the other; never mix.

Antibiotics: Burned tissue becomes necrotic (dies) and infects quickly. Start Baytril or Clavamox as a prophylactic.

The “72-Hour Rule”

Electrocution is famous for delayed necrosis.

The Slough: A limb that looks “fine” on Day 1 may turn black and literally fall off (slough) by Day 4 because the internal blood vessels were “cooked.”

Mouth Burns: If the squirrel bit a wire, the tongue and lips may swell or slough, making hand-feeding via a thin cannula or tube necessary.

Rehabber Insight: Cataracts

Squirrels that survive electrocution often develop electrical cataracts (cloudy eyes) weeks or months later. This is a common “late-stage” complication of the current passing through the head.

heading: Ch. 37 — Failure to Thrive (FTT) in Infants
text:
## **37\. Failure to Thrive (FTT) in Infants**

🔴 URGENT & FRUSTRATING – The “Fading” Baby Syndrome

Failure to Thrive (FTT) is one of the most heartbreaking challenges for a rehabber because there isn’t always a “smoking gun” like a cat bite or a fall. It’s a quiet, steady decline that requires detective work.

Failure to Thrive isn’t a disease itself; it’s a symptom of an underlying invisible wall. You have a baby who should be gaining weight but is either “stagnant” (plateaued) or losing ground despite proper feeding.

Identifying the FTT Baby

The “Old Man” Look: Wrinkled, loose skin despite hydration; a head that looks too large for the body.

The “Bony” Spine: You can feel every vertebrae and the pelvic “wings” (ilium) prominently.

Lethargy: They don’t “fight” the syringe; they are limp or fall asleep mid-feeding.

Developmental Lag: Eyes not opening on time, or ears remaining pinned long after they should have popped.

The “Rehabber’s Detective” Protocol

STEP 1: The Nutritional Audit

Caloric Density: Is your formula ratio correct? (Check for Proper Dilution).

Formula Intolerance: Is the baby bloated or having diarrhea? If they aren’t absorbing the nutrients, they can’t grow.

Feeding Volume: Are they being fed 5-7% of their body weight? (A 50g baby needs 2.5cc–3.5cc per feeding).

STEP 2: The “Silent Killer” Check (Internal Parasites)

Coccidia: This is the \#1 cause of FTT in “clumped” litters. It strips the intestinal lining.

Action: From your list, start Albon or Ponazuril immediately, even if the stool looks “okay.” Coccidia can be sub-clinical (invisible) while still stealing all the baby’s calories.

STEP 3: Metabolic & Congenital Issues

Inborn Errors: Some babies are born with heart murmurs or “shunts” that prevent growth.

Aspiration (Silent): They may have a low-grade, chronic Aspiration Pneumonia that is burning all their energy just to keep them breathing. Check for a faint “click.”

The “Rehabber’s Recovery” Plan

Boost the Calories: If the GI tract is stable, consider adding a tiny amount of Heavy Whipping Cream or a “fat booster” to the formula to increase caloric density without increasing volume.

B-Vitamin Boost: Ask your vet about a B-12 injection. It can act as an appetite stimulant and metabolic “jumpstart.”

Probiotics: Use [Bene-Bac](https://henryspets.com/pages/baby-squirrel) at every feeding to ensure maximum nutrient absorption.

Heat Management: FTT babies have zero body fat. They must be kept slightly warmer (around 90-95°F) than healthy siblings to prevent them from burning calories just to stay warm.

The Hard Truth

If a baby continues to fade despite [aggressive parasite treatment](https://www.nwrawildlife.org/page/Rehabilitator_Resources) and caloric boosting, they may have a genetic defect. Sometimes, “Mother Nature” selects against a baby, and despite our best efforts, they are simply “not meant for this world.”

Boost the Calories: If the GI tract is stable, consider adding a tiny amount of Heavy Whipping Cream or a “fat booster” to the formula to increase caloric density without increasing volume.

B-Vitamin Boost: Ask your vet about a B-12 injection. It can act as an appetite stimulant and metabolic “jumpstart.”

Probiotics: Use Bene-Bac at every feeding to ensure maximum nutrient absorption.

Heat Management: FTT babies have zero body fat. They must be kept slightly warmer (around 90-95°F) than healthy siblings to prevent them from burning calories just to stay warm.

The Hard Truth

If a baby continues to fade despite aggressive parasite treatment and caloric boosting, they may have a genetic defect. Sometimes, “Mother Nature” selects against a baby, and despite our best efforts, they are simply “not meant for this world.”

heading: Ch. 38 — Fever vs. Hyperthermia
text:
## **38\. Fever vs. Hyperthermia**

In squirrel rehab, a “hot” squirrel is usually facing one of two very different crises: Hyperthermia (external heatstroke) or a True Fever (internal infection). For a seasoned rehabber, the first 60 seconds are spent deciding which one it is, because treating a fever like heatstroke can send a sick baby into shock.

🔴 CRITICAL – Know the difference before you cool.

Hyperthermia / Heatstroke

🔴 EMERGENCY – Seconds count to prevent brain damage.

Hyperthermia happens when the squirrel’s body can no longer dump heat. It is unregulated and dangerous. This is an EMERGENCY and you need to go to [Hyperthermia](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/hyperthermia-too-hot?authuser=0) right now\!

2. True Fever (Pyrexia) Protocol

🟡 STEADY CARE – Manage the infection, not just the temp.

Fever is a regulated rise in temperature used by the immune system to kill bacteria.

Do NOT Flash-Cool: Forced cooling can cause the squirrel to shiver, which actually raises their internal temp and burns vital energy.

Supportive Warmth: Ironically, a feverish squirrel often feels cold and wants heat. Keep them in a room-temperature environment (75°F–80°F) with a soft blanket.

Hydration is Key: Fever causes rapid [dehydration](https://henryspets.com/pages/baby-squirrel). Give frequent, small amounts of warm LRS or Pedialyte.

Medication (From Your List):

Meloxicam: Your primary fever-reducer (antipyretic). It helps lower the “set point” in the brain and reduces pain.

Antibiotics: Since fever is almost always bacterial (URI, bite abscess), start Clavamox or Baytril as soon as the squirrel is hydrated.

The “Rabbit Fever” (Tularemia) Warning

While rare, if you encounter an epidemic where multiple squirrels are found dead or dying with lethargy, stupor, and high fever, consider [Tularemia](https://www.cdc.gov/tularemia/about/index.html).

Zoonotic: It is highly contagious to humans via ticks, fleas, or direct contact.

Action: Wear [disposable gloves](https://www.wildlifecenterflorida.org/wp-content/uploads/Rehabilitation-of-Eastern-Gray-Squirrels-2020Formatted-for-PDF-file-1.pdf) and eye protection. If you suspect Tularemia, contact your State Wildlife Lab immediately.

heading: Ch. 39 — Fly Strike (Myiasis)
text:
## **39\. Fly Strike (Myiasis)**

Fly strike occurs when flies lay eggs on a compromised squirrel (usually neonates or those with wounds/diarrhea). Once hatched, maggots eat living tissue and release toxins that cause rapid shock.

Step 1: Immediate Knockdown [(Capstar)](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/medical-dosing-information/capstar?authuser=0)

Oral: Administer one age-appropriate dose of [Capstar (Nitenpyram)](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/medical-dosing-information/capstar?authuser=0)immediately. It begins killing maggots from the “inside out” within 30 minutes as they ingest the squirrel’s blood/fluids.

Topical: Dissolve a [Capstar](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/medical-dosing-information/capstar?authuser=0)tablet in a small amount of warm sterile saline. Apply this solution directly into the wound or infested area (ears, anus, nose). This causes maggots to scramble out of hiding for easier removal.

Step 2: Physical Removal & Flushing

Manual Extraction: Dust the fur thoroughly with cornstarch and rub the powder into the fur, making sure to avoid the eyes and nose. Use blunt-tipped forceps to remove visible maggots. Do not leave any behind; even one can cause massive tissue damage overnight.

Warm Flush: DO NOT USE WATER \- WATER TRIGGERS FLY EGGS TO HATCH AND WILL DRIVE MAGGOTS DEEPER INTO FUR/WOUNDS/ORIFICES. Use a syringe (no needle) to flush the wound gently with warm Diluted Betadine, Chlorhexidine, or [Capstar.](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/medical-dosing-information/capstar?authuser=0) This drowns remaining larvae and cleans the tract.

The “Orifice” Check: Carefully check the ears, nose, mouth, and genitals. If maggots are in the ear canal, consult a vet immediately to prevent brain entry. Flush [IMMEDIATELY WITH CAPSTAR](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/medical-dosing-information/capstar?authuser=0) per directions.

Step 3: Stabilization & Hydration

Shock Treatment: Fly strike victims are almost always in shock. Keep the squirrel on low, consistent heat.

Sub-Q Fluids: If permitted and trained, administer warm sub-Q LRS or Saline. Maggots cause extreme dehydration and toxic buildup in the bloodstream.

Step 4: Systemic Defense

Antibiotics: Start a broad-spectrum antibiotic (like Baytril or Clavamox) immediately. Maggots carry bacteria that cause rapid sepsis.

Pain Management: Once hydrated, administer Meloxicam to reduce the intense inflammation and pain caused by tissue burrowing.

Step 5: The 24-Hour Watch

Re-Check: Maggot eggs are tiny and look like “yellow rice.” If you see eggs, they must be brushed off with a toothbrush or fine-tooth comb before they hatch.

Secondary Wave: Re-examine the squirrel every 4 hours for 24 hours. A single missed egg can lead to a new infestation overnight.

Rehabber’s Pro-Tip:

Remind: “If you see ‘yellow rice’ (eggs), the clock is ticking.” It is much easier to comb off eggs than it is to surgically remove maggots. Using a flea comb, a soft-bristle toothbrush, or a mascara wand is the best way to clear eggs from the fur.

heading: Ch. 40 — Genital Nursing (Suckling Trauma)
text:
## **40\. Genital Nursing (Suckling Trauma)**

🔴 URGENT & PERSISTENT – Can lead to permanent mutilation.

This is arguably the most common “nursery nightmare” for a rehabber. When a litter is hungry or separated from mom too early, their natural suckling instinct misfires, and they begin to “nurse” on the most prominent thing they can find: their sibling’s genitals.

What starts as a misplaced nursing instinct can quickly escalate into severe tissue damage, infections, and “urethral plugs” that prevent the squirrel from urinating.

The Targets

Genitals: Most commonly the penis of male littermates.

Extremities: Ears, tails, and toes.

The Damage: Constant suction causes “hickies,” severe bruising, swelling (edema), and can eventually lead to a Penile Prolapse or the inability to urinate due to tissue damage.

If left unchecked, suckle-sucking causes scarring that can block the urethra. If a male squirrel cannot pass urine, his bladder will rupture. A “wet” belly on a male squirrel is often not urine he passed—it’s saliva from a sibling.

Signs of Trauma

The “Suckling” Position: Finding two babies head-to-tail in the nest.

Physical: Swollen, bright red, or scabbed penis or clitoris.

The Crust: Dried formula or saliva creating a “plug” over the urinary opening.

Distended Bladder: The baby has a hard, “bloated” lower belly because they physically cannot pee through the swollen tissue.

Why Does It Happen?

Under-feeding: If the squirrels are hungry, they seek a nipple wherever they can find a protrusion.

Premature Weaning: Being taken from the mother too early triggers a desperate “suckling reflex.”

Boredom/Stress: In older juveniles, it becomes a self-soothing mechanism similar to thumb-sucking in humans.

The Protocol: Detection & Intervention

The Daily Check: Every time you feed, inspect the genitals of every male in the litter. If the area looks red, wet, or “puffy,” someone is being sucked on.

Immediate Separation: This is the only 100% effective cure.

Separate the “sucker” from the “suckee.”

If you have a large litter, you may need to divide them into pairs, but ensure the “victim” is housed alone or with a non-aggressive sibling.

The “Bitter” Method (Optional/Caution): Some rehabbers apply a very tiny amount of bitter apple spray or a safe oil to the target area, but this is often ineffective against a determined squirrel and can irritate the sensitive mucosal tissue. Physical separation is always preferred.

The “Stop the Cycle” Protocol

STEP 1: Immediate Separation

The Divider: If you see any redness, the offending “sucker” and the “suckee” must be separated immediately. Once this behavior starts, it is nearly impossible to stop while they remain in the same cage.

Individual Housing: Use a temporary divider or separate bins. They can still see and smell each other through a mesh barrier to reduce stress, but physical contact must be zero.

STEP 2: Medical Treatment (From Your List)

Cleaning: Gently soak the area in a warm Chlorhexidine or Betadine solution to remove crusts and bacteria.

Topical Protection: Apply a thin layer of SSD Cream (Silver Sulfadiazine) or Neosporin to the area. SSD is superior for reducing inflammation and preventing infection in sensitive tissue.

NSAIDs: Use Meloxicam to bring down the swelling. If the tissue is too swollen, the squirrel cannot urinate, which leads to a bladder crisis.

STEP 3: Ensuring Elimination

Manual Expression: You must ensure the squirrel can actually pee. If the opening is “scabbed over,” you may need to gently soak the scab off to allow urine to flow.

Frequency: Check and clean the area before and after every feeding.

Prevention for the “Naughty” Litter

Increase Feedings: Suckling usually happens because babies are hungry or their caloric needs aren’t being met. Ensure you are feeding a full 5–7% of body weight.

The “Nipple” Fix: Some rehabbers find that adding a “pacifier” (a spare Miracle Nipple attached to nothing) in the nest can redirect the urge.

Bitter Deterrents: As a last resort, some apply a tiny amount of diluted Bitter Apple around (not on) the genital area of the victim.

The Long-Term Risk

If the damage is severe, the urethra can scar shut as it heals (stricture). If a male squirrel loses the tip of the penis or the urethra is permanently blocked, they are not releasable and may require specialized veterinary surgery.

heading: Ch. 41 — GI Stasis — Bloat, Constipation & Sludge › 1. Bloat (The Emergency)
text:
## **41\. GI Stasis — Bloat, Constipation & Sludge**

Digestive issues are the leading cause of death in orphaned squirrels. Whether it’s simple constipation or life-threatening “sludge” from a finder feeding the wrong formula, you must act systematically.

### **1\. Bloat (The Emergency)**

Action: STOP ALL FEEDING until the tummy goes down.

Medication: Mylicon (Simethicone) drops every 4 hours.

The Reset: After the bloat subsides, give 1/2 Pedialyte and 1/2 Water for three feedings (5% of body weight only).

The Formula: Use Esbilac Puppy (Dry Powder). Start at 3 parts water to 1 part formula with a tiny pinch of Fox Valley Probiotics.

### **2\. Constipation (The “Move-It” Recipes)**

**The Constipation Ladder.** Work up one step at a time. Before any step, make sure the baby is **warm and hydrated** and the belly is **soft**. A hard, drum-tight, red, or purple belly is bloat or sludge (sections 1 and 3) — not simple constipation.

1. **Toothbrush technique** (section 4), alternated with warm-water rectal stimulation
2. **Applesauce-molasses mix** (Method B)
3. **Lactulose** (see Veterinary Protocol)
4. **Sennosides** — field report, [PROVISIONAL] (see Veterinary Protocol), only if lactulose fails and no vet is available
5. **Vet:** enema or manual disimpaction

**When every baby goes down at once, suspect the formula.** If several babies become constipated — or sick — at the same time, suspect a bad formula lot first. Throw out the Esbilac and Fox Valley you're using and start over with **different lot numbers**. Write the lot number on your daily log (Ch. 95) so you can trace it.

If the baby hasn’t pooped in 12–24 hours, try these in order:

Method A: The “Fruit Flush”

Give warm Apple Juice via syringe between feedings.

If no results in 12 hours, move to Prune Juice.

Mommy’s Bliss Laxative: 0.01 to 0.02 ml.

Method B: The Applesauce-Molasses Mix

Recipe: 1 tsp unsweetened applesauce \+ 1/2 tsp unsulfured molasses.

Prep: Microwave for 3 seconds to remove “hot spots.” It must be formula-warm.

Feeding: Use a Miracle Nipple as a “spoon.” Scoop a bit (half-pea size) and tickle their lips. Most will gobble it. If they refuse, gently pry the lips and push in a tiny bit.

Goal: Get roughly the volume of 2–3 sweet peas into them.

Follow-up: Warm bath and stimulation after 1–2 hours. Repeat up to 3 times if needed.

heading: Ch. 41 — GI Stasis — Bloat, Constipation & Sludge › 3. The “Sludge” Protocol (The KMR/Cow’s Milk Rescue)
text:
### **3\. The “Sludge” Protocol (The KMR/Cow’s Milk Rescue)**

If a finder fed the squirrel KMR, Cow’s Milk, or Condensed Milk, the proteins often “curdle” into a hard, clay-like sludge in the gut.

The Sign: The belly feels hard and “angry red” (septic) or purple. Once it turns red, the prognosis is grave. Check bellies after every feeding; they should always be squishy.

The Water Flush: You must get plain water in as quickly as possible to break up the crud. Give 0.2ml–0.3ml of plain water every hour.

Crucial Step: Stimulate after every water dose. You must empty the bladder to make room and keep the system moving.

The Transition: Once the poop becomes watery (usually after 8–10 hours), slowly reintroduce Approved Formula (Esbilac Puppy Dry):

Phase 1: 25% Formula / 75% Water (Half day)

Phase 2: 50% Formula / 50% Water (Half day)

Phase 3: 75% Formula / 25% Water (One day)

Phase 4: Full strength.

| Item | Purpose |
| :---: | :---: |
| Infant Simethicone (Mylicon) | Gas/Bloat. |
| White Granulated Sugar | Prolapse (Sugar Cure). |
| Plain Canned Pumpkin / Applesauce | Constipation. |
| Unsulfured Molasses | Energy boost / Constipation mix. |
| Activated Charcoal | Suspected Poisoning. |
| Tums (Fruit Flavored) | Emergency Calcium for MBD. |
| Coconut Oil / K-Y Jelly | Lubrication for prolapse or thermometers. |
| Pedialyte (Unflavored) | Dehydration and re-feeding. |
| Styptic Powder | To stop bleeding from a shattered tooth or nail. |
| Miracle Nipples (Multiple sizes) | For feeding and “spooning” meds. |

1. The Symptoms

The “Banana” Back: The squirrel hunches excessively while trying to go.

Firm Abdomen: The belly feels tight or “lumpy” to the touch.

Strained Output: Small, dry, black stones, or no output for 24+ hours.

2. The “Move-It” Recipe This is the standard safe intervention before moving to harsher laxatives:

Base: 1 teaspoon of pureed canned Pumpkin (NOT pumpkin pie filling—plain pumpkin only).

The Slip: Add 2–3 drops of extra virgin Olive Oil or Coconut Oil.

The Sweetener: A tiny drop of blackstrap molasses (optional, but the iron and sugar help stimulate the gut).

3. The Protocol

Offer the mix via syringe or on a small spoon. Most squirrels love the taste.

Hydration is Key: You cannot move stool through a dry gut. Give Sub-Q fluids or extra Pedialyte alongside the pumpkin mix.

The “Warm Soak”: While waiting for the mix to work, soak the squirrel’s lower half in warm water and gently massage the abdomen in a clockwise motion.

4. The Toothbrush Technique \- AKA Vibrating Gastric Stimulation

When a neonate’s gut shuts down (Stasis), gas bubbles become trapped in the stomach and intestines. Because neonates cannot burp effectively, this gas creates pressure on the diaphragm, leading to respiratory distress and shock. While medications like Simethicone help break down bubbles, mechanical vibration is often required to move the “sludge” through the system.

I. Equipment Needed

An electric toothbrush (standard oscillating or sonic).

A thin fleece or soft cloth.

Infant Simethicone (Gas-X).

2. The Protocol (The 3-Step Move)

Chemical Prep: Administer 0.1 mL of Infant Simethicone orally. Wait 5–10 minutes for the medication to begin breaking the surface tension of the gas bubbles.

The “Buffer” Layer: Wrap the squirrel snugly in a thin fleece (The “Burrito”). This prevents the vibration from being too harsh on the skin and keeps the baby calm (preventing Capture Myopathy).

The Application: Turn the toothbrush on. Gently press the back of the vibrating head (not the bristles) against the lower left side of the abdomen, just below the rib cage.

Movement: Use tiny, circular motions, moving slowly from the left side toward the center and down toward the vent. \#\#\#\# III. The Physics of Why It Works  
The high-frequency vibration mimics the natural peristalsis (muscle contractions) of a healthy gut. It physically “shakes” the trapped gas and fermented formula, breaking it loose from the stomach lining so it can pass into the lower intestines to be expelled.

4. Critical Safety Rules

Pressure: Use the weight of the toothbrush only. Do not “push” into the organs.

Duration: 2–3 minutes of vibration, followed by 5 minutes of rest. Repeat until you hear a “rumble” or the baby passes gas/sludge.

The “Burp” Check: Occasionally hold the baby upright (vertical) during the rest period to allow any upper-gastric gas to escape.

#### **The Alternation Method (Toothbrush + Warm Water)**

When a baby is bloated, hard-bellied, or simply hasn’t passed stool after stimulation, the electric toothbrush technique can help get things moving. The gentle vibration stimulates gut motility in a way that warm-water stimulation alone sometimes can’t.

**What you need:** \- A soft electric toothbrush (the vibration is what matters — use the flat back of the head, not the bristles) \- A basin of warm water \- Cotton ball or soft cloth for rectal stimulation

**The technique:**

1. **Electric toothbrush belly massage:** Turn on the toothbrush and hold the back of the head gently against the baby’s belly. Use a soft, downward stroke from mid-sternum to just above where the genitals begin — following the direction of the gut, from stomach toward the exit. About **five slow downward swipes** per pass.

⚠️ **Gentle pressure only.** The vibration is doing the work — you are not scrubbing or pressing hard. You are guiding a vibration across a tiny belly. This is a baby, not a stuck drawer. Think of it as coaxing, not forcing.

2. **Warm water stimulation:** Return to a warm water bath and gentle rectal stimulation with a damp cotton ball — the same stimulation you’d do after every feeding, but extended and deliberate. Warm water relaxes the muscles; stimulation tells the body it’s time to go.

3. **Alternate and repeat:** Go back and forth — toothbrush belly massage, then warm water and rectal stimulation, then toothbrush again — until stool passes. Don’t rush. Don’t push harder. Let the alternation do its work.

That’s an emergency; get help

**Age range:** This technique is most useful in Pinky through Toddler stage babies (≤200g) who are still fully dependent on stimulation for elimination. Older babies and juveniles should be toileting on their own — if they’re not, that’s a different problem.

**Why it works:** In the wild, the mother’s grooming provides constant tactile stimulation to the baby’s belly and genital area, keeping the gut moving between feedings. In rehab, we stimulate after feedings but not continuously. A constipated baby is often one whose gut has slowed between stimulations — the toothbrush vibration mimics the kind of sustained gentle pressure that nudges things along.

heading: Ch. 41 — GI Stasis — Bloat, Constipation & Sludge › ⚕ Veterinary Protocol — Constipation & Sludge
text:
### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol — Constipation & Sludge**

MILD CONSTIPATION (No stool for 12-24 hours, baby otherwise normal):

Increased Hydration: Offer Pedialyte or diluted formula between regular feedings for 24-48 hours

Pumpkin Supplement: 0.5-1cc pure pumpkin puree mixed with formula before each feeding for 2-3 days

Warm Soaks: 2-3 times daily for 5-10 minutes with gentle abdominal massage

Proper Stimulation: Ensure stimulation is performed after EVERY feeding until baby is 5-6 weeks old

Formula Dilution: Reduce formula concentration by 10-20% for next 3-4 feedings

MODERATE CONSTIPATION (No stool for 24-48 hours, sludge consistency, mild discomfort):

Mineral Oil: 0.1-0.2cc orally once or twice daily for 1-2 days maximum (lubricates intestines)

Lactulose (if available): 0.5-1cc orally twice daily \- gentle osmotic laxative that draws water into intestines

Increased Warm Soaks: 3-4 times daily with vigorous but gentle abdominal massage

“Move-It” Recipe: Pumpkin mixture before every feeding until stool normalizes

Subcutaneous Fluids (if dehydrated): Warmed saline or LRS 5% of body weight once daily to improve hydration status

SEVERE CONSTIPATION/IMPACTION (No stool for 48+ hours, hard distended abdomen, baby in distress):

Veterinary Evaluation Required \- May need enema or manual disimpaction

Warm Water Enema (vet-administered): 1-2cc warm saline gently inserted into rectum with small syringe (do NOT attempt at home without training)

Lactulose: 1cc orally every 6-8 hours until impaction clears

Pain Management: Meloxicam 0.1-0.2 mg/kg orally once daily if baby is showing significant discomfort

Aggressive Hydration: Subcutaneous fluids 10% of body weight twice daily

NPO (Nothing by Mouth) Temporarily: May need to withhold formula for 6-12 hours while focusing on hydration and stool passage; offer Pedialyte only

Monitoring: Once impaction clears, baby may have diarrhea for 12-24 hours as backed-up stool passes; this is normal

ONGOING MANAGEMENT

Probiotic Supplementation: Add small amount of plain yogurt (1-2 drops) or probiotic powder to formula once daily to support healthy gut bacteria

Consistent Stimulation: Never skip stimulation after feedings; set timer if needed to ensure it’s done every time

Formula Consistency Check: Weigh formula powder and water to ensure accurate mixing ratios

Gradual Formula Changes: If changing formula brands, transition slowly over 5-7 days to prevent GI upset

Monitor Stool Daily: Keep log of stool frequency, consistency, and color to catch problems early

#### **Sennosides (Senna) — Evidence: [B] RODENT ANALOG + [C] REHAB PRECEDENT + [PROVISIONAL]**

*A fellow rehabber's field report. Not veterinarian-validated.*

- **What it is:** a stimulant laxative that triggers the bowel's pushing contractions.
- **When:** last resort for confirmed constipation after lactulose has failed and no vet is available.
- **Never when:** the belly is hard or bloated, an impaction or blockage is possible, or the baby is dehydrated. Forcing a blocked gut to push causes cramping and can damage the bowel.
- **Product:** plain sennosides only — never a senna + docusate combination. Check the label for xylitol.
- **Preparation:** crush one 25 mg sennoside tablet (to break the coating) and dissolve it in 25 mL of warm apple juice. It dissolves slowly but completely. Concentration: **1 mg/mL**. Mix thoroughly before each use.
- **Starting dose:** **5 mg/kg every 12 hours** = **0.5 mL per 100 g** body weight. Stop once stool passes.
- **Evidence note:** the safety reference is a rat toxicology study (Mengs U., "Toxic effects of sennosides in laboratory animals and in vitro," *Pharmacology* 1988;36 Suppl 1:180–187). There, 20 mg/kg was the top dose of the short-term rat studies and caused no specific toxicity; rats tolerated up to 100 mg/kg for 6 months. Its harms came from diarrhea itself — fluid and electrolyte loss — which is the real danger for a tiny, dehydration-prone baby. That's why the dose stays low and hydration comes first. Rats are not squirrels, and adults are not babies. In the original report senna was given alongside a Pedialyte/apple juice/molasses mix and the underlying cause was a bad formula lot, so senna's own effect is uncertain. A higher first round (10 mg/kg every 6 hours = 40 mg/kg/day) is **not** recommended.

heading: Ch. 42 — Glue Traps — How to Remove
text:
## **42\. Glue Traps — How to Remove**

Glue Trap Rescue & Oil Management

A squirrel caught in a glue trap is a Category 1 Emergency. The animal is likely in “Compensated Shock” from struggling and may have inhaled toxic fumes from the adhesive or chemical attractants in the trap.

1. The First Step: Stabilize, Don’t Scrub

The “Mistake”: Most volunteers want to start pulling the squirrel off immediately. Stop. \* The Fix: Cover all exposed “sticky” areas of the trap with paper towels, tissues, or cornstarch so the squirrel doesn’t get more stuck while you work.

The Calm: Drape a light fleece over the squirrel’s head. If they can’t see you, their heart rate will drop, reducing the risk of a stress-induced cardiac arrest.

2. The Removal Protocol (The Oil & Flour Method)

We use Vegetable, Canola, or Mineral Oil to break the bond. Avoid using “Goo Gone” or industrial solvents, which are toxic to squirrel skin.

Warm the Oil: Run the oil bottle under warm water. Cold oil on a stressed squirrel can trigger a shock crash.

Massage: Using a cotton swab or gloved finger, gently massage the oil into the interface between the fur and the trap. Go slow. If you see skin tearing or fur pulling out by the roots, you are moving too fast.

The Flour/Cornstarch Trick: As the squirrel’s limbs become free, immediately dust the freed area with flour or cornstarch.

Why? This “neutralizes” the remaining glue and oil so the limb doesn’t just stick right back down or slide into the squirrel’s mouth.

The “Slide”: Once the squirrel is free, slide a piece of paper over the trap and move the squirrel to a clean, warm box.

3. The “Oiled Squirrel” Crisis

A squirrel covered in oil cannot regulate its body temperature. They will freeze to death even in a warm room if not dried.

The Bath: Only once the squirrel is stable and warm (wait at least 2–4 hours post-removal) should you give a Dawn Dish Soap bath.

The Temperature: Use very warm water (100°F). Work the soap into the fur to strip the oil, rinse thoroughly, and blow-dry on the lowest/warmest setting until bone-dry.

The Risk: A wet, oily squirrel is a dead squirrel. Dryness is life.

4. Post-Removal Medical Check

Skin Tears: Check for “degloving” where the trap may have ripped the top layer of skin off. Treat with the Sugar Cure (Ch. 61).

Self-Mutilation: Squirrels will often chew their own limbs to escape a trap. Check for bone fractures or missing toes.

Hydration: These squirrels have usually been struggling for hours. Sub-Q fluids are almost always required.

heading: Ch. 43 — Head Trauma & CNS Crisis
text:
## **43\. Head Trauma & CNS Crisis**

🔴 CRITICAL – The First 24 Hours Determine the Outcome.

The “Eyes as a Window” Pupil Response Guide

In a neurological emergency, the eyes are your most direct link to the squirrel’s brain function. By using a simple phone flashlight, you can perform a Pupil Response Test to gauge the severity of a concussion or brain bleed.

1. The Prep

Dim the lights in the room for a moment to allow the squirrel’s pupils to naturally dilate (get larger).

Use your phone’s flashlight, but never shine it directly into the center of the eye. Approach from the side.

2. What to Look For (The “Big Three”)

Normal Response (PERRL): When you shine the light, the pupil should quickly “zip” shut (constrict). When you pull the light away, it should slowly grow large again. Both eyes should do this at the same time.

Anisocoria (Unequal Pupils): One pupil is large (blown) while the other is small.

What it means: This is a classic sign of a brain bleed or localized head trauma on one side.

Fixed and Dilated (The “Blown” Pupil): The pupil stays large and does not react to light at all.

What it means: High intracranial pressure. This is a Stage 3 Emergency.

Pinpoint Pupils: Both pupils are tiny, even in low light.

What it means: Often indicates severe brainstem injury or toxicity.

3. The “Nystagmus” Check (The Flickering Eye)

Watch the eyes without the light. Are they “flickering” back and forth or up and down rapidly (like they are watching a fast ping-pong match)?

The Insight: This is Nystagmus. It indicates the squirrel’s “inner ear” or “vestibular system” is haywire. It’s why they feel like the room is spinning, leading to the “rolling” behavior.

4. Action Steps Based on Findings

If Pupils are Responsive but Slow: Continue with Stage 1 Sensory Deprivation (Dark, quiet, Meloxicam).

If Pupils are Fixed/Unequal: This squirrel needs a vet for Dexamethasone or Mannitol to reduce brain pressure immediately.

Pro-Tip: If you see a “blown” pupil, do not tilt the squirrel’s head down when handling. Keep the head slightly elevated to help decrease intracranial pressure.

Neurological Red Flags

Mentation: Dullness, “staring through” you, or stupor.

Physical: Listing to one side, circling, or “knuckling” (walking on the tops of paws).

Ocular: Uneven pupils (anisocoria) or rapid, involuntary eye movement (nystagmus).

Posture: [Opisthotonus](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7322266/) (head arched back) or rigid, extended limbs.

Emergency Stabilization (The “Quiet Brain” Protocol)

Elevate the Head: Prop the squirrel’s head at a 30-degree angle. This uses gravity to encourage [venous drainage](https://www.vin.com/apputil/content/defaultadv1.aspx?pId=11268&catId=32731&id=3866654) and lower ICP.

Oxygen is Fuel: If available, provide flow-by oxygen. Hypoxia (low oxygen) causes brain vessels to dilate, which drastically increases pressure.

Strict Isolation: Even minor noises trigger a stress response that spikes blood pressure. Use a dark, padded “silent chamber.” Even the smell of a predator (dog/cat) can spike blood pressure and increase brain bleeding.

.Managing Inflammation: The Choices

In a head trauma crisis, you must choose one path. Mixing these causes fatal GI bleeding.

Path A: Prednisone (Steroid). Useful if the squirrel is in shock or has severe cord/brain swelling. It stabilizes cell membranes but can delay healing if used long-term.

Path B: Meloxicam/Ibuprofen (NSAID). Best for mild-to-moderate trauma where pain management is the priority. Meloxicam is generally preferred for its safety profile in small mammals.

2. Managing CNS Excitation & Pain

Gabapentin: Excellent for “quieting” the central nervous system. It helps manage neuropathic pain and can provide a mild sedative effect to prevent the squirrel from thrashing.

Trazodone: If the squirrel is panicked or hyper-reactive to light/sound, Trazodone provides the chemical restraint needed to keep them still enough for the brain to heal.

3. Fluid Support

LRS (Lactated Ringers): Be conservative. Over-hydrating a head trauma patient can worsen Cerebral Edema. Give just enough to maintain blood pressure, but do not “slug” them with fluids.

The “Wait and See” Window

48-Hour Rule: Brain tissue heals slowly. A squirrel that appears “comatose” but has a blink reflex and deep pain sensation often makes a dramatic recovery if kept supported and quiet.

Secondary Watch: Monitor for “clicking” (Aspiration Pneumonia) as head trauma patients often lose the ability to swallow properly.

Rehabber Insight: If you must use steroids, never combine them with [NSAIDs (like Metacam)](https://www.protocols.io/view/chapter-5-severe-nutritional-deficiencies-emaciati-bmjek4je.html), as this combination causes fatal GI ulceration.

Secondary Monitoring

Poisoning Mimic: Always cross-reference head trauma signs with [Rodenticide Toxicity](https://www.squirrelmender.com/adult_squirrels.html). If the squirrel is bleeding from the nose/mouth, it may be an anticoagulant issue rather than a fall.

The “Miracle” Recovery: Brain-injured squirrels often look “dead to the world” for 48 hours and then suddenly “wake up.” Don’t euthanize too early unless there is an open skull fracture or total lack of deep pain reflex.

FOLLOW UP NOTE: IN THE EVENT OF split mandibular symphysis (the chin is split in two from a fall) THE SQUIRREL should be flagged for a follow-up dental check 6 months later. Those are the prime candidates for future Odontomas.

### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

PRIMARY ANTI-INFLAMMATORY PROTOCOL

Dexamethasone (PREFERRED for head trauma): 0.5-2 mg/kg subcutaneously or intramuscularly as initial emergency dose, then 0.1-0.5 mg/kg orally once daily for 3-5 days

Why Dexamethasone: More potent anti-inflammatory effect on brain tissue than other steroids; crosses blood-brain barrier effectively; reduces cerebral edema rapidly

Dosing Note: Use higher end of range (1-2 mg/kg) for severe trauma with altered consciousness; lower end (0.5 mg/kg) for mild trauma with normal consciousness

Administration: Injectable form works fastest for emergency; switch to oral after first dose if baby can swallow

ALTERNATIVE ANTI-INFLAMMATORY

Meloxicam (if dexamethasone unavailable): 0.2 mg/kg orally once daily for 5-7 days

Why Meloxicam: Safer for long-term use, less immunosuppressive than dexamethasone

Limitation: Less effective for acute brain swelling; better for mild trauma or as follow-up after initial dexamethasone treatment

When to Use: Mild head trauma with no loss of consciousness, or as maintenance therapy after emergency phase

CHOOSING BETWEEN DEXAMETHASONE AND MELOXICAM

Use Dexamethasone if: Pink nose present, altered consciousness, abnormal pupils, seizures, or severe trauma \- these indicate significant brain swelling requiring aggressive treatment

Use Meloxicam if: Minor head bump, baby fully conscious and alert, no pink nose, normal pupils \- mild trauma with low risk of significant swelling

Sequential Protocol: Start with dexamethasone for first 24-48 hours in severe cases, then switch to meloxicam for remaining recovery period

SUPPORTIVE CARE

Oxygen Support (if available): Provide supplemental oxygen if baby shows respiratory distress or altered consciousness \- brain needs maximum oxygen during recovery

Fluid Therapy: Subcutaneous fluids (LRS or saline) 5-10% of body weight once or twice daily if baby is not drinking \- maintain hydration without overloading (excess fluids worsen brain swelling)

Nutritional Support: Do NOT force-feed if baby is unconscious or has poor swallow reflex (aspiration risk); wait until consciousness improves, then offer small amounts of formula frequently

Temperature Regulation: Maintain body temperature at 98-100°F; hypothermia worsens brain injury, but hyperthermia increases metabolic demand

Seizure Management (if needed): Diazepam 0.5-1 mg/kg rectally or intramuscularly for active seizures; midazolam 0.2-0.3 mg/kg intranasally if available

First 6 Hours (Critical Period): Check every 30-60 minutes for consciousness level, pupil response, breathing pattern, and body temperature

6-24 Hours: Check every 2-3 hours; watch for “delayed crash” \- sudden deterioration as brain swelling peaks

24-48 Hours: Check every 4-6 hours; most babies either stabilize or decline by this point

Improvement Signs: Increased alertness, normal pupil response returns, pink nose clears, baby begins eating/drinking independently

Deterioration Signs: Decreasing consciousness, pupils become fixed and dilated, breathing becomes irregular, seizures develop, body temperature drops

## 43. Head Trauma & CNS Crisis

🔴 CRITICAL – The First 24 Hours Determine the Outcome.

The “Eyes as a Window” Pupil Response Guide

In a neurological emergency, the eyes are your most direct link to the squirrel’s brain function. By using a simple phone flashlight, you can perform a Pupil Response Test to gauge the severity of a concussion or brain bleed.

1. The Prep

Dim the lights in the room for a moment to allow the squirrel’s pupils to naturally dilate (get larger).

Use your phone’s flashlight, but never shine it directly into the center of the eye. Approach from the side.

2. What to Look For (The “Big Three”)

Normal Response (PERRL): When you shine the light, the pupil should quickly “zip” shut (constrict). When you pull the light away, it should slowly grow large again. Both eyes should do this at the same time.

Anisocoria (Unequal Pupils): One pupil is large (blown) while the other is small.

What it means: This is a classic sign of a brain bleed or localized head trauma on one side.

Fixed and Dilated (The “Blown” Pupil): The pupil stays large and does not react to light at all.

What it means: High intracranial pressure. This is a Stage 3 Emergency.

Pinpoint Pupils: Both pupils are tiny, even in low light.

What it means: Often indicates severe brainstem injury or toxicity.

3. The “Nystagmus” Check (The Flickering Eye)

Watch the eyes without the light. Are they “flickering” back and forth or up and down rapidly (like they are watching a fast ping-pong match)?

The Insight: This is Nystagmus. It indicates the squirrel’s “inner ear” or “vestibular system” is haywire. It’s why they feel like the room is spinning, leading to the “rolling” behavior.

4. Action Steps Based on Findings

If Pupils are Responsive but Slow: Continue with Stage 1 Sensory Deprivation (Dark, quiet, Meloxicam).

If Pupils are Fixed/Unequal: This squirrel needs a vet for Dexamethasone or Mannitol to reduce brain pressure immediately.

Pro-Tip: If you see a “blown” pupil, do not tilt the squirrel’s head down when handling. Keep the head slightly elevated to help decrease intracranial pressure.

Neurological Red Flags

Mentation: Dullness, “staring through” you, or stupor.

Physical: Listing to one side, circling, or “knuckling” (walking on the tops of paws).

Ocular: Uneven pupils (anisocoria) or rapid, involuntary eye movement (nystagmus).

Posture: Opisthotonus (head arched back) or rigid, extended limbs.

Emergency Stabilization (The “Quiet Brain” Protocol)

Elevate the Head: Prop the squirrel’s head at a 30-degree angle. This uses gravity to encourage venous drainage and lower ICP.

Oxygen is Fuel: If available, provide flow-by oxygen. Hypoxia (low oxygen) causes brain vessels to dilate, which drastically increases pressure.

Strict Isolation: Even minor noises trigger a stress response that spikes blood pressure. Use a dark, padded “silent chamber.” Even the smell of a predator (dog/cat) can spike blood pressure and increase brain bleeding.

.Managing Inflammation: The Choices

In a head trauma crisis, you must choose one path. Mixing these causes fatal GI bleeding.

Path A: Prednisone (Steroid). Useful if the squirrel is in shock or has severe cord/brain swelling. It stabilizes cell membranes but can delay healing if used long-term.

Path B: Meloxicam/Ibuprofen (NSAID). Best for mild-to-moderate trauma where pain management is the priority. Meloxicam is generally preferred for its safety profile in small mammals.

2. Managing CNS Excitation & Pain

Gabapentin: Excellent for “quieting” the central nervous system. It helps manage neuropathic pain and can provide a mild sedative effect to prevent the squirrel from thrashing.

Trazodone: If the squirrel is panicked or hyper-reactive to light/sound, Trazodone provides the chemical restraint needed to keep them still enough for the brain to heal.

3. Fluid Support

LRS (Lactated Ringers): Be conservative. Over-hydrating a head trauma patient can worsen Cerebral Edema. Give just enough to maintain blood pressure, but do not “slug” them with fluids.

The “Wait and See” Window

48-Hour Rule: Brain tissue heals slowly. A squirrel that appears “comatose” but has a blink reflex and deep pain sensation often makes a dramatic recovery if kept supported and quiet.

Secondary Watch: Monitor for “clicking” (Aspiration Pneumonia) as head trauma patients often lose the ability to swallow properly.

Rehabber Insight: If you must use steroids, never combine them with NSAIDs (like Metacam), as this combination causes fatal GI ulceration.

Secondary Monitoring

Poisoning Mimic: Always cross-reference head trauma signs with Rodenticide Toxicity. If the squirrel is bleeding from the nose/mouth, it may be an anticoagulant issue rather than a fall.

The “Miracle” Recovery: Brain-injured squirrels often look “dead to the world” for 48 hours and then suddenly “wake up.” Don’t euthanize too early unless there is an open skull fracture or total lack of deep pain reflex.

FOLLOW UP NOTE: IN THE EVENT OF split mandibular symphysis (the chin is split in two from a fall) THE SQUIRREL should be flagged for a follow-up dental check 6 months later. Those are the prime candidates for future Odontomas.

PRIMARY ANTI-INFLAMMATORY PROTOCOL

Dexamethasone (PREFERRED for head trauma): 0.5-2 mg/kg subcutaneously or intramuscularly as initial emergency dose, then 0.1-0.5 mg/kg orally once daily for 3-5 days

Why Dexamethasone: More potent anti-inflammatory effect on brain tissue than other steroids; crosses blood-brain barrier effectively; reduces cerebral edema rapidly

Dosing Note: Use higher end of range (1-2 mg/kg) for severe trauma with altered consciousness; lower end (0.5 mg/kg) for mild trauma with normal consciousness

Administration: Injectable form works fastest for emergency; switch to oral after first dose if baby can swallow

ALTERNATIVE ANTI-INFLAMMATORY

Meloxicam (if dexamethasone unavailable): 0.2 mg/kg orally once daily for 5-7 days

Why Meloxicam: Safer for long-term use, less immunosuppressive than dexamethasone

Limitation: Less effective for acute brain swelling; better for mild trauma or as follow-up after initial dexamethasone treatment

When to Use: Mild head trauma with no loss of consciousness, or as maintenance therapy after emergency phase

CHOOSING BETWEEN DEXAMETHASONE AND MELOXICAM

Use Dexamethasone if: Pink nose present, altered consciousness, abnormal pupils, seizures, or severe trauma - these indicate significant brain swelling requiring aggressive treatment

Use Meloxicam if: Minor head bump, baby fully conscious and alert, no pink nose, normal pupils - mild trauma with low risk of significant swelling

## **44\. Hemorrhage & Internal Bleeding**

🔴 CRITICAL – The “Invisible” Killer.

A squirrel that looks “fine” immediately after a fall is often in a state of compensated shock. Internal hemorrhaging into the thoracic or abdominal cavities is common and requires a very specific “low-pressure” approach to stabilization. When a baby squirrel falls from a high canopy (often 30–60 feet), the impact causes deceleration trauma. Even if no bones are broken, the kinetic energy is absorbed by the vascular system and internal organs, leading to “hidden” crises that manifest hours later.

Signs of Internal Trauma

The “Pink Nose” (Epistaxis): Blood or pink-tinged fluid from the nostrils suggests lung trauma or a skull base fracture.

Abdominal Distension: A belly that feels tight, “doughy,” or looks bruised/purple.

Orthopnea: The squirrel sits with its elbows flared out and neck extended to catch its breath (indicates blood in the chest cavity).

The “Crash”: Sudden lethargy, gasping, or death 4–12 hours after a fall, often due to a slow internal leak finally causing organ failure.

Emergency Stabilization Protocol

STEP 1: The “Fragile Handling” Rule

No Palpation: Do not “squeeze” the belly or chest to check for breaks. This can dislodge a blood clot that is currently preventing a fatal bleed.

Minimal Movement: Keep the squirrel in a small, padded carrier where it cannot move much. Every movement increases blood pressure and the risk of re-bleeding.

STEP 2: Fluid Management (Crucial Distinction)

Hypovolemic Shock: If the squirrel is bleeding internally, its blood pressure is dropping.

Conservative Hydration: Do not “slug” the squirrel with a full dose of Lactated Ringers (LRS). If you raise the blood pressure too fast or too high, you will “pop the clot” and cause the squirrel to bleed out internally. Give small, frequent amounts (boluses) rather than one large injection.

STEP 3: Pharmaceutical Support

Pain & Inflammation: Use Meloxicam only after the squirrel is hydrated and stable.

Warning: Avoid Ibuprofen in suspected internal bleeds, as it can interfere with platelet function (clotting) more significantly than Meloxicam.

Secondary Infection: High-velocity falls often cause “bruised lungs” (pulmonary contusions). These are magnets for bacteria. Prophylactic Amoxicillin/Clavamox is often started to prevent secondary pneumonia.

The “Bruise” Timeline

Day 1: Shock management and heat.

Day 2–3: The peak of bruising. The squirrel may look worse (more purple/blue skin) as the blood from the internal injury migrates to the surface.

Day 4+: If they survive to day four without respiratory distress, the internal clots are likely stable and the “crush” injury is healing.

### **⚕ Clinical Protocol — Hemorrhage & Internal Trauma**

**HEMORRHAGE & INTERNAL TRAUMA**

🔴 LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

External Hemorrhage:

Active bleeding from wounds

Blood pooling around baby

Blood-soaked fur or bedding

Pale or white gums (indicates blood loss)

Internal Hemorrhage:

Pink nose (epistaxis) \- Blood in nasal passages; hallmark sign of internal bleeding or head trauma

Pale or white gums despite no visible external bleeding

Distended, firm abdomen (blood accumulating in abdominal cavity)

Labored breathing (blood in chest cavity compressing lungs)

Progressive weakness and lethargy

Cold extremities

Rapid, weak pulse

Shock Symptoms:

Cold body temperature

Lethargic or unresponsive

Pale or blue-tinged gums

Rapid, shallow breathing

Weak, rapid heartbeat

“Delayed Crash” Warning:

Baby seems okay initially after trauma

Deteriorates suddenly 2-12 hours later as internal bleeding progresses

This is why ALL trauma cases require 24-hour monitoring even if they appear stable

**HEMORRHAGE SEVERITY ASSESSMENT**

CLASS I (MILD) \- \\\<15% Blood Volume Loss:

Baby is alert and responsive

Gums are pink or slightly pale

Heart rate normal or slightly elevated

No signs of shock

Action: Monitor closely; may not require intervention

CLASS II (MODERATE) \- 15-30% Blood Volume Loss:

Baby is lethargic but responsive

Gums are pale pink

Heart rate elevated

Mild shock symptoms

Action: Stop bleeding, provide fluids, monitor closely

CLASS III (SEVERE) \- 30-40% Blood Volume Loss:

Baby is very lethargic, minimally responsive

Gums are white or grey

Heart rate very rapid

•Moderate to severe shock (cold body, weak pulse, rapid shallow breathing)

**Action:** Aggressive hemostasis, immediate fluid resuscitation with small conservative boluses, emergency vet transport

**CLASS IV (SHOCK/CRITICAL) \- \\\>40% Blood Volume Loss:**

Baby is unresponsive or semi-comatose

Gums are white, blue, or mottled

Heart rate extremely rapid and thready, or bradycardic (slowing \- ominous sign)

Severe shock (icy cold, gasping respirations, absent or barely palpable pulse)

**Action:** This is often non-survivable without immediate veterinary intervention including blood transfusion; focus on warmth, oxygen if available, and emergency transport

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Hemorrhage—whether external or internal—rapidly depletes the body’s blood volume, starving organs of oxygen and triggering hypovolemic shock. External bleeding is obvious, but internal hemorrhage is insidious: blood pools silently in body cavities while the squirrel appears deceptively stable, then crashes suddenly hours later as compensatory mechanisms fail. The “pink nose” (epistaxis) is a critical red flag indicating blood in the nasal passages from head trauma or internal bleeding. Without intervention, progressive blood loss leads to organ failure, brain damage from hypoxia, and death. Even squirrels that survive the initial trauma can die 6-24 hours later from undetected internal bleeding—this is why the 24-hour monitoring window is non-negotiable for all trauma cases.

#### *Immediate Action*

1\. **Stop External Bleeding Immediately** \- Apply direct pressure with clean gauze or cloth for 5-10 minutes without lifting to check (lifting restarts bleeding). For severe arterial bleeding (bright red, spurting), maintain continuous pressure and seek emergency vet care.

2\. **Assess for Shock** \- Check gum color (should be pink, not white/grey/blue), feel body temperature (should be warm, not cold), and observe breathing (should be steady, not rapid/shallow). If shock signs present, move to step 3 immediately.

3\. **Warm the Baby** \- Hypothermia kills faster than blood loss in small animals. Place baby on heating pad set to LOW with towel barrier, or against your skin under your shirt. Do NOT use high heat—this causes peripheral vasodilation and worsens shock.

4\. **Provide Conservative Fluid Support** \- If baby is in shock (Class II or higher), give **small boluses** of warmed oral rehydration solution or subcutaneous Lactated Ringer’s Solution (LRS). Give 1-2 mL per 100g body weight every 30-60 minutes. **DO NOT “slug” with a full large dose**—overloading a compromised cardiovascular system can cause pulmonary edema and death.

5\. **Monitor for Internal Bleeding** \- Check for pink nose (blood in nostrils), distended/firm abdomen, labored breathing, or progressive lethargy. Gently palpate abdomen—if it feels tight or fluid-filled, suspect internal hemorrhage and transport to vet immediately.

6\. **Establish 24-Hour Monitoring Protocol** \- Even if baby appears stable, check every 2 hours for: gum color, body temperature, respiratory rate, responsiveness, and abdominal distension. The “delayed crash” window is 2-12 hours post-trauma. If baby deteriorates suddenly, this is internal bleeding and requires emergency vet care.

heading: Ch. 44 — Hemorrhage & Internal Bleeding › ⚕ Veterinary Protocol
text:
### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

**Primary Hemostasis (Stopping Bleeding):**

**External Wounds:** Direct pressure for 5-10 minutes; if bleeding continues, apply styptic powder or silver nitrate stick to small vessels; larger vessels may require cauterization or ligation by vet

**Internal Hemorrhage:** Supportive care only—cannot be stopped without surgical intervention; focus on stabilization and allowing body’s clotting mechanisms to work

**Clotting Support:** Vitamin K (phytonadione) may be administered if rodenticide poisoning suspected (causes failure to clot); otherwise, body’s natural clotting factors should engage within 5-10 minutes if animal is warm and adequately perfused

**Hypovolemic Shock Management:**

**Conservative Fluid Resuscitation:** Administer warmed subcutaneous or intravenous Lactated Ringer’s Solution in **small, frequent boluses** (1-2 mL per 100g body weight every 30-60 minutes). Do NOT give large single doses—this can overwhelm the cardiovascular system and cause fluid to leak into lungs (pulmonary edema) or worsen internal bleeding by increasing blood pressure before clotting has occurred.

**Warmth is Critical:** Maintain body temperature at 98-100°F (36.5-37.8°C)—cold animals cannot clot blood or maintain blood pressure

**Oxygen Support:** If available, provide supplemental oxygen via flow-by or oxygen chamber (especially for Class III/IV hemorrhage)

**Pharmaceutical Support:**

**Pain Management:** Meloxicam (Metacam) 0.2 mg/kg orally or subcutaneously once daily ONLY after baby is stable and adequately hydrated (NSAIDs can worsen kidney function in hypovolemic patients). **Do NOT use Ibuprofen**—it is toxic to many wildlife species and can cause gastric ulceration and kidney failure.

**Prophylactic Antibiotics:** If wounds are contaminated (dirt, saliva from predator attack, road debris), administer Clavamox or Baytril to prevent sepsis. Internal hemorrhage alone does not require antibiotics unless gut perforation suspected.

**Avoid Aspirin/Blood Thinners:** Never administer aspirin, heparin, or other anticoagulants—these will worsen bleeding

**Monitoring:**

Check gum color every 30-60 minutes (should gradually return to pink over 4-12 hours)

Monitor respiratory rate and effort (should stabilize as shock resolves)

Palpate abdomen every 2-4 hours (should remain soft; increasing firmness indicates ongoing internal bleeding)

Track urine output (should resume within 6-12 hours if kidney perfusion adequate)

Watch for “rebound crash” 6-24 hours post-trauma

**Duration:**

Acute stabilization phase: 4-12 hours

Critical monitoring window: 24-48 hours

Full recovery from shock: 3-7 days depending on severity

**Bruise Timeline (Recovery Progression):**

**Day 1:** Fresh bruising appears dark red/purple; swelling peaks; baby may be painful and reluctant to move

**Day 2-3:** Bruising begins to darken to deep purple/black; swelling starts to decrease; baby becomes more alert and mobile

**Day 4+:** Bruising transitions through green/yellow/brown as blood breaks down and reabsorbs; swelling resolves; function returns to affected areas. Complete bruise resolution can take 7-14 days.

#### *Prognosis & Recovery*

**Timeline:**

**Class I (Mild):** Recovery within 24-48 hours with monitoring only

**Class II (Moderate):** Stabilization within 4-12 hours; full recovery in 3-5 days with supportive care

**Class III (Severe):** Touch-and-go for first 24 hours; if baby survives initial crisis, recovery takes 7-14 days

**Class IV (Critical):** Survival rate extremely low without blood transfusion and intensive veterinary care; if baby survives, recovery is prolonged (2-4 weeks) with high risk of organ damage

**Success Rate:**

**External hemorrhage (controlled quickly):** 80-90% survival if shock prevented

**Internal hemorrhage (mild to moderate):** 60-70% survival with aggressive supportive care and 24-hour monitoring

**Internal hemorrhage (severe with shock):** 20-30% survival; often fatal despite intervention

**Delayed crash (undetected internal bleeding):** 10-20% survival once crash occurs—this is why early detection and monitoring are critical

**Warning Signs (Recovery is Failing):**

Gums remain white or become progressively paler despite treatment

Body temperature drops or cannot be maintained despite warming efforts

Respiratory rate increases or breathing becomes labored/gasping

Baby becomes less responsive or unresponsive after initial stabilization

Abdomen becomes progressively more distended or firm

Pink nose (epistaxis) persists or worsens

No urine output after 12-24 hours (indicates kidney failure from prolonged shock)

“Rebound crash” 6-24 hours after apparent stabilization (delayed internal bleeding)

**Release Considerations:**

**Minor external wounds with full recovery:** Releasable once healed and baby demonstrates normal strength, coordination, and wild behavior

**Significant internal trauma with full recovery:** Requires extended rehabilitation (4-6 weeks minimum) to ensure no delayed complications; assess climbing ability, foraging behavior, and predator avoidance before release

**Neurological deficits from hypoxic brain injury:** May be non-releasable if coordination, balance, or cognitive function permanently impaired

**Chronic pain or mobility issues:** Non-releasable; requires permanent sanctuary placement

**Successful recovery from Class III/IV hemorrhage:** Extended observation period (6-8 weeks) to ensure no organ damage; full functional assessment required before release clearance

#### *Prevention*

**Minimize Handling Stress:** Excessive handling, rough restraint, or chasing terrified squirrels can cause capture myopathy, which leads to muscle breakdown and internal bleeding. Handle gently, minimize stress, and use proper restraint techniques.

**Predator-Proof Housing:** Ensure outdoor enclosures have secure wire mesh (no gaps larger than ½ inch), buried barriers to prevent digging predators, and overhead protection from raptors. Cat and dog attacks are the leading cause of traumatic hemorrhage in rehabilitation settings.

**Safe Transport Protocols:** Always transport squirrels in secure, padded carriers. Loose animals in vehicles can be thrown during sudden stops, causing head trauma and internal injuries. Never transport in open boxes or on laps.

in Rehabilitation:\*\* Baby squirrels are notorious climbers with poor judgment. Use enclosures with appropriate height limits for developmental stage, provide soft bedding to cushion falls, and avoid slick surfaces (glass, smooth plastic) that cause slipping injuries.

**Early Intervention for Minor Trauma:** Any squirrel involved in a fall, predator encounter, or vehicle strike should be assessed immediately and monitored for 24 hours—even if appearing normal. The “delayed crash” from undetected internal bleeding is preventable with proper observation protocols.

### **When Sugar Isn't Working: Hypovolemic Shock from Internal Bleeding**

**The baby who keeps crashing.** If a baby is warm and well-hydrated but has clear abdominal trauma, and keeps crashing over and over, assume hypovolemic shock from internal bleeding — not simple low blood sugar.

Primary Hemostasis (Stopping Bleeding):

External Wounds: Direct pressure for 5-10 minutes; if bleeding continues, apply styptic powder or silver nitrate stick to small vessels; larger vessels may require cauterization or ligation by vet

Internal Hemorrhage: Supportive care only—cannot be stopped without surgical intervention; focus on stabilization and allowing body’s clotting mechanisms to work

Clotting Support: Vitamin K (phytonadione) may be administered if rodenticide poisoning suspected (causes failure to clot); otherwise, body’s natural clotting factors should engage within 5-10 minutes if animal is warm and adequately perfused

Hypovolemic Shock Management:

Conservative Fluid Resuscitation: Administer warmed subcutaneous or intravenous Lactated Ringer’s Solution in small, frequent boluses (1-2 mL per 100g body weight every 30-60 minutes). Do NOT give large single doses—this can overwhelm the cardiovascular system and cause fluid to leak into lungs (pulmonary edema) or worsen internal bleeding by increasing blood pressure before clotting has occurred.

Warmth is Critical: Maintain body temperature at 98-100°F (36.5-37.8°C)—cold animals cannot clot blood or maintain blood pressure

Oxygen Support: If available, provide supplemental oxygen via flow-by or oxygen chamber (especially for Class III/IV hemorrhage)

Pharmaceutical Support:

Pain Management: Meloxicam (Metacam) 0.2 mg/kg orally or subcutaneously once daily ONLY after baby is stable and adequately hydrated (NSAIDs can worsen kidney function in hypovolemic patients). Avoid Aspirin/Blood Thinners: Never administer aspirin, heparin, or other anticoagulants—these will worsen bleeding

Check gum color every 30-60 minutes (should gradually return to pink over 4-12 hours)

heading: Ch. 45 — Hiccups vs. Seizures
text:
## **45\. Hiccups vs. Seizures**

It is a rite of passage for every new rehabber: the “Midnight Hiccup Panic.” Because squirrels have such high metabolic rates, their hiccups are often much more forceful and “full-body” than human hiccups, leading to frequent misidentification as seizures.

1. The “Hiccup” Profile

The Rhythm: Perfect, metered timing. A hiccup will occur every 2 to 4 seconds with robotic precision.

The Look: A sudden “jerk” of the entire torso, often causing the head to bob forward.

The Context: Usually happens immediately after a feeding or when a baby wakes up and begins to move.

Duration: Can last anywhere from 30 seconds to several minutes.

The “Tell”: The squirrel remains conscious and alert. If you touch them, they react normally; if you offer a nipple, they may even try to suckle between “hic-s.”

2. The “Seizure” Profile (The Real Emergency)

The Rhythm: Erratic, “clonic” (shaking) movements. There is no steady beat.

The Look: “Paddling” of the limbs, jaw clamping/chomping, or “star-gazing” (neck arching back).

The Context: Often triggered by MBD (Calcium crash), head trauma, or high fever.

The “Tell”: The squirrel is unconscious or “checked out.” Their eyes may roll back, they will not respond to your voice, and they often lose control of their bladder/bowels.

3. Why Do Squirrels Get Hiccups?

Gulping Air: The \#1 cause. If the nipple flow is too fast or the squirrel is “greedy,” they swallow air into the stomach, irritating the diaphragm.

Temperature Shift: Moving a baby from a warm incubator into a cooler room for feeding can trigger diaphragmatic spasms.

Immature Nervous System: In pinkies, the connection between the brain and the diaphragm is still “wiring up.” Sometimes the system just misfires.

4. What to Do (The “Don’t Panic” Protocol)

Stop Feeding: If they start hiccuping mid-meal, pull the syringe. Do not risk aspiration by forcing formula during a spasm.

Burp Them: Gently rub the squirrel’s back or side while they are upright to help move any air bubbles.

Check Your Technique: If hiccups happen every time you feed, your syringe transition might be too fast (e.g., moving to a 3cc too early) or your formula might be too cold.

Wait It Out: Hiccups are harmless. They do not hurt the squirrel, and they do not require medical intervention.

heading: Ch. 46 — Hydrocephalus (Water on the Brain)
text:
## **46\. Hydrocephalus (Water on the Brain)**

🔴 CHRONIC & PROGRESSIVE – Managing Intracranial Pressure (ICP)

Hydrocephalus occurs when CSF builds up within the ventricles of the brain, causing the skull to enlarge (if the sutures haven’t fused) or the brain tissue to be compressed against the bone.

Identifying the “Hydro” Squirrel

The “Dome” Head: A noticeably rounded, prominent forehead or an abnormally large, “bulbous” skull.

The “Setting Sun” Eyes: Eyes that appear to be looking downward, with the white (sclera) showing at the top.

Neurological Deficits: Persistent circling, head-pressing, high-pitched vocalizing, or “staring” spells (absence seizures).

Coordination: A “clumsy” or high-stepping gait (hypermetria).

STEP 1: Reducing the Pressure

Prednisone: This is the primary steroid used to reduce the production of CSF and decrease brain inflammation. Note: Long-term use requires a slow “taper” to avoid adrenal crisis.

Omeprazole: Interestingly, Omeprazole (Prilosec) has shown some evidence in veterinary medicine for reducing CSF production by inhibiting certain enzymes in the brain’s choroid plexus.

Gabapentin: Essential for managing the neuropathic pain and “electric” headaches caused by the internal pressure.

STEP 2: Seizure Watch

Hydrocephalus lowers the seizure threshold.

Environment: Keep the squirrel in a low-stimulus environment. Sudden loud noises or bright flashing lights can trigger a pressure spike.

Safety: Ensure their area is heavily padded. A seizure in a hydro squirrel can be more violent due to the existing brain compression.

STEP 3: Positioning

The “Inclined” Bed: Just like with head trauma, keepingtheir head slightly elevated (about 30 degrees) when he sleeps can help with venous drainage and slightly lower the resting pressure in his skull.

The Quality of Life (QoL) Baseline

With hydrocephalus, the “end” often comes when the pressure can no longer be managed by meds.

Monitor for: “Head Pressing.” If the squirrel starts pushing their head firmly against the wall or corner of their cage, they are most likely experiencing an agonizing pressure headache.

Appetite Loss/Weight Loss: As the brainstem becomes compressed, the “hunger” signal is often the first to go.

Note: Hydrocephalus (“Water on the Brain”) is rare in squirrels, usually appearing as a congenital defect or the result of severe neonatal head trauma that blocks the flow of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

For a squirrel with hydrocephalus, the prognosis for release and life in the wild is poor, which is why many end up as sanctuary squirrels. With a sanctuary squirrel, the goal isn’t a “cure,” but managing the pressure and keeping them comfortable for as long as their[quality of life](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/quality-of-life-scale?authuser=0)remains high.

heading: Ch. 47 — Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar)
text:
## **47\. Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar)**

🔴 CRITICAL EMERGENCY – Immediate Glucose Required.

For a seasoned rehabber, Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is the “Great Crasher.” It is a common secondary complication in neonates, starved rescues, and squirrels with MBD or Refeeding Syndrome. Because squirrels have such a high metabolic rate, they can burn through their glucose reserves in a matter of hours, leading to a rapid, life-threatening spiral.

Hypoglycemia occurs when the body’s fuel supply drops below the level needed to support brain and heart function. In squirrels, this is often a “silent” crisis that looks like death until the sugar hits the system.

Signs of a “Sugar Crash”

The “Limp” Baby: Sudden, extreme lethargy or “floppiness.”

Temperature Drop: Body feels chilly despite being in a warm incubator.

Neurological: Glassy eyes, unresponsiveness, or Hypoglycemic Seizures (often characterized by slow, rhythmic twitching or “paddling”).

Pale Gums: Gums appear white or very light pink.

Emergency Resuscitation Protocol

STEP 1: The “Gum Rub” (Immediate Action)

Do NOT Force Liquid: If the squirrel is unconscious or seizing, forcing liquid into the mouth will cause fatal aspiration.

Mucosal Absorption: Take a drop of Honey, Karo Syrup, or Sugar Water on your finger and rub it directly onto the gums and inside the cheeks. The glucose will absorb directly through the mucous membranes into the bloodstream.

Wait: You should see a response (movement, blinking, or improved color) within 2–5 minutes. Repeat every 10 minutes until the squirrel is alert enough to swallow.

STEP 2: Stabilization & Internal Support

Warmth: Hypoglycemic squirrels cannot maintain body heat. Place on a Heating Pad immediately.

Hydration: Once alert, offer oral LRS or Pedialyte with a pinch of extra sugar added.

Transition to Protein: Glucose is “fast fuel,” but it burns off quickly. As soon as the squirrel is stable, offer a small feeding of diluted formula or a High-Protein Block to provide long-lasting energy and prevent a “rebound” crash.

Common Triggers for Rehabbers

Missed Feedings: Especially in neonates (under 4 weeks) who lack fat stores.

Diarrhea/Enteritis: Nutrients are passing through too fast to be absorbed.

Septicemia: Serious infections (like a cat bite) can consume the body’s glucose at an alarming rate.

Refeeding: As discussed in Refeeding Syndrome, a sudden insulin spike can drive blood sugar too low.

Rehabber Insight: If you have an “Old Man” like Ein or a neurological sanctuary resident, they may experience occasional crashes if they have a particularly active day. Keeping a small bottle of Karo Syrup or Honey in your first aid kit is a literal lifesaver.

heading: Ch. 48 — Hyperthermia & Heatstroke
text:
## **48\. Hyperthermia & Heatstroke**

In summers, temperatures over 100°F turn attics and nests into ovens. For a squirrel, hyperthermia isn’t just “being hot”—it is a physiological crisis where the heart and brain begin to fail.

🔴 EMERGENCY – Immediate cooling required. Seconds count.

Hyperthermia occurs when a squirrel’s internal temperature rises above its ability to dissipate heat. Because squirrels cannot sweat, they rely on “splooting” (lying flat on cool surfaces) and panting, which fail quickly in extreme Idaho heat.

Identifying the Stages of Heat Stress

Mild: Damp fur (saliva spreading), rapid heartbeat, and “splooting” behavior.

Moderate: Open-mouth panting, drooling or “foaming” at the mouth, and labored breathing.

Severe (Heatstroke): Loss of balance (staggering), [seizures](https://thesquirrelboard.com/forums/showthread.php?17786-Hyperthermia-%28Heat-Stroke%29), bloody diarrhea, or total collapse.

Emergency Cool-Down Protocol

STEP 1: Immediate Thermal Reduction

The “Dip”: Submerge the squirrel up to its neck in cool (not ice-cold) water. Using ice-cold water can trigger shock or [rebound hypothermia](https://www.facebook.com/groups/108046649534931/posts/2587710948235143/).

Evaporative Cooling: Lay the squirrel on a damp cloth in front of a fan. Focus on wetting the head and tail areas, as these are primary heat-exchange points.

Elevation: Keep the head slightly elevated to prevent aspiration if they are drooling or vomiting.

STEP 2: Monitor the “Stop Point”

Temperature Check: Use a digital ear or rectal thermometer if possible.

The 103°F Rule: You must stop all cooling procedures once the squirrel’s temperature drops to 103°F. Continuing past this point often causes a dangerous crash into hypothermia.

STEP 3: Post-Stabilization Hydration

Oral Fluids: Once the squirrel is alert and their temperature is stable, offer cool (room temp) unflavored Pedialyte or LRS drop-by-drop.

Sub-Q Fluids: Most severe cases will not survive without [subcutaneous fluids](https://www.facebook.com/groups/108046649534931/posts/1221288518210733/) to address internal organ dehydration.

The “Delayed Crash” Warning

Organ Damage: Even if a squirrel seems to recover, permanent organ damage (kidney or liver failure) may not manifest for 24–48 hours.

Observation: Keep any heatstroke intake under strict 48-hour observation. If they become lethargic or stop urinating, they require immediate veterinary intervention.

heading: Ch. 49 — Hypothermia & Critical Cooling
text:
## **49\. Hypothermia & Critical Cooling**

Hypothermia is a common and deadly condition for orphaned squirrels, especially those found on the ground in spring or fall. A cold squirrel cannot digest food, and its heart rate and metabolism will continue to drop until it becomes unresponsive.

Warning Signs

Physical: The baby feels cold or “room temperature” to the touch. The skin may have a blue or greyish tint (cyanosis), indicating poor oxygenation.

Behavioral: Extreme lethargy, unresponsive to touch, or completely limp.

Respiratory: Breathing is very slow, shallow, or labored.

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

CRITICAL RULE: You must warm the squirrel SLOWLY. Raising the body temperature too rapidly can cause “rewarm shock,” which is often fatal.

Step 1: Use Your Own Body Heat First:

Place the baby directly against your skin (inside your shirt against your chest is best).

Cup the squirrel in your hands to provide steady, safe warmth. This is the safest way to begin the thawing process.

Step 2: External Warming:

Once the baby begins to show signs of life, move them to an incubator or a box with a heating pad set to LOW, placed under several layers of fleece or towels.

Alternatively, use a warm (not hot) rice sock or water bottle wrapped in a thick cloth.

Step 3: Frequent Temperature Checks:

Check the squirrel every 5 minutes. The goal is a steady, gradual climb to a normal body temperature (approx. 98–100°F).

Step 4: The “No Food” Rule:

NEVER feed a cold squirrel. Their digestive tract is shut down; formula will simply sit in the gut and ferment, causing fatal bloat.

Only once the squirrel is fully warm and moving should you begin oral rehydration with warm Pedialyte or a 5% dextrose/LRS solution.

Safety Cautions

NO Direct Heat: Never place a squirrel directly on a heating pad or under a heat lamp without a buffer.

NO Hot Water: Do not submerge a hypothermic squirrel in hot water; this can cause immediate cardiovascular collapse.

NO Microwaves: Never use a microwave to warm the animal itself.

Recovery Indicators

Positive Signs: The squirrel begins to squirm, cry, or its skin transitions from blue/grey to a healthy pink.

Maintenance: Once warmed, the squirrel must stay on a heat source (with “cool” spots to crawl to) until it is fully stabilized and eating regularly.

Behavioral: Extreme lethargy, unresponsive to touch, or completely limp.

Respiratory: Breathing is very slow, shallow, or labored.

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

CRITICAL RULE: You must warm the squirrel SLOWLY. Raising the body temperature too rapidly can cause “rewarm shock,” which is often fatal.

Step 1: Use Your Own Body Heat First:

Place the baby directly against your skin (inside your shirt against your chest is best).

Cup the squirrel in your hands to provide steady, safe warmth. This is the safest way to begin the thawing process.

Step 2: External Warming:

Once the baby begins to show signs of life, move them to an incubator or a box with a heating pad set to LOW, placed under several layers of fleece or towels.

Alternatively, use a warm (not hot) rice sock or water bottle wrapped in a thick cloth.

Step 3: Frequent Temperature Checks:

Check the squirrel every 5 minutes. The goal is a steady, gradual climb to a normal body temperature (approx. 98–100°F).

Step 4: The “No Food” Rule:

NEVER feed a cold squirrel. Their digestive tract is shut down; formula will simply sit in the gut and ferment, causing fatal bloat.

Only once the squirrel is fully warm and moving should you begin oral rehydration with warm Pedialyte or a 5% dextrose/LRS solution.

Safety Cautions

NO Direct Heat: Never place a squirrel directly on a heating pad or under a heat lamp without a buffer.

NO Hot Water: Do not submerge a hypothermic squirrel in hot water; this can cause immediate cardiovascular collapse.

NO Microwaves: Never use a microwave to warm the animal itself.

Recovery Indicators

Positive Signs: The squirrel begins to squirm, cry, or its skin transitions from blue/grey to a healthy pink.

Maintenance: Once warmed, the squirrel must stay on a heat source (with “cool” spots to crawl to) until it is fully stabilized and eating regularly.
