heading: Ch. 51 — Leptospirosis (The “Silent” Zoonosis)
text:
## **51\. Leptospirosis (The “Silent” Zoonosis)**

🔴 HIGH ZOONOTIC RISK – Protect the Rehabber First.

For a seasoned rehabber, Leptospirosis is less about the squirrel’s health and more about yours. In squirrels, it is a quiet, “carrier-state” infection. They often show zero symptoms while shedding the live bacteria in their urine for months—effectively turning their cage and bedding into a zoonotic hazard.

Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection caused by Leptospira. While it can cause fatal organ failure in dogs and humans, most squirrels are maintenance hosts, meaning they carry and spread the disease without ever appearing sick.

Signs in Squirrels (Rarely Seen)

Asymptomatic: Most squirrels look perfectly healthy while actively shedding bacteria in their urine.

Renal/Hepatic Distress: In rare, acute cases, you may see:

Jaundice: Yellowing of the gums or whites of the eyes.

Hydration Changes: Increased drinking and urination followed by a sudden “crash” into kidney failure.

Vague Illness: Fever, lethargy, and muscle stiffness.

The “Rehabber Safety” Protocol

STEP 1: PPE & Transmission Barrier

The bacteria enter humans through broken skin, eyes, nose, or mouth after contact with infected urine or contaminated water/bedding.

Gloves: Never handle bedding or clean cages without [disposable gloves](https://www.cdc.gov/leptospirosis/about/index.html).

Eye Protection: Wear a [face shield](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/infectious-diseases/leptospirosis/leptospirosis-in-animals-overview) when cleaning with spray bottles or hosing down enclosures to prevent aerosolized urine from hitting your eyes.

No High-Pressure Hoses: High-pressure water creates a fine mist of bacteria that you can inhale.

STEP 2: Decontamination (From Your List)

Leptospires are fragile once they leave a moist environment but can live for months in wet bedding or puddles.

Bleach: Use a 1:10 [Bleach Solution](https://acphd.org/health-advisory/leptospirosis/) on all hard surfaces; let it sit for 10 minutes before rinsing.

Laundry: Wash all bedding in hot water with bleach and dry on high heat.

Chlorhexidine: While on your list, [Iodine-based disinfectants](https://hilo.hawaii.edu/panr/get_attachment.php?file=NWLeptospirosis.pdf) or 1% bleach are generally more effective against Leptospira.

STEP 3: Treatment (From Your List)

If you are treating a squirrel for a suspected URI or “mystery fever,” you may already be treating Lepto.

Doxycycline: The gold standard for clearing the “carrier state” in the kidneys.

Amoxicillin/Clavamox: Effective for the initial blood-borne phase but less effective at clearing the bacteria from the kidneys than Doxycycline.

Important Public Health Note

If you develop sudden flu-like symptoms, high fever, or severe leg/back pain after handling a litter of squirrels, seek medical attention immediately and [tell your doctor](https://uhs.berkeley.edu/health-promotion/health-topics/leptospirosis) you are a wildlife rehabilitator.

heading: Ch. 52 — Malocclusion (Misaligned Teeth)
text:
## **52\. Malocclusion (Misaligned Teeth)**

🟡 CHRONIC MANAGEMENT – The “Trim or Starve” Reality

For a seasoned rehabber, Malocclusion is a high-maintenance but often manageable condition. However, the distinction between “genetic/trauma misalignment” and “Odontoma” is the most critical call you will make. While an Odontoma is a death sentence in the wild, a simple malocclusion can sometimes be corrected—or managed in a sanctuary setting.

For more information on Odotnoma, for more on why these “calcified clusters” at the root are non-correctable and lead to respiratory distress.

Squirrels are elodonts, meaning their incisors grow continuously (up to 6 inches a year\!). If the top and bottom teeth do not meet perfectly to grind against each other, they will overgrow, curl back into the roof of the mouth, or pierce the skull.

Identifying Malocclusion

The “Tusk” Look: Teeth that are visibly too long, curving sideways, or growing in a “spiral.”

The “Chunky” Face: Drooling, matted fur on the chin, or a squirrel that “fumbles” its food.

Weight Loss: A squirrel with a “starvation” feel to its spine despite plenty of food being available.

Orange vs. White: Healthy adult teeth are dark orange. Pale or white teeth often indicate a nutritional deficiency or trauma to the tooth bud.

The “Age” Factor: Note that pinky and fuzzy squirrels have white/pale teeth naturally; the orange “enamel iron” doesn’t usually set in until they have been on solid food for a few weeks. This prevents a new volunteer from panicking when they see a 5-week-old’s white teeth.

The “Art of the Tooth Trim” (Rehabber Protocol)

Note: This is a two-person job. One person must securely wrap the squirrel in a “burrito” while the other performs the trim.

Tools of the Trade: Use sterilized High-Quality Side-Cutters or a specialized dental dremel. Never use dull clippers, as they can shatter the tooth down into the sensitive pulp/root.

The “Score” Technique: If using side-cutters on very thick teeth, “score” (dent) the tooth all the way around before making the final snip. This encourages the tooth to snap cleanly at the score line rather than splintering vertically toward the root.

The “Speculum”: Use a tongue depressor or a sturdy piece of plastic behind the teeth to protect the tongue and soft palate from accidental nicks. The Trick: Some rehabbers drill a small hole in a tongue depressor and slide the tooth through the hole before clipping. This provides a 360-degree “shield” for the mouth and tongue so that even if the squirrel jerks, you can’t accidentally clip the lip.

The Cut: Aim for the “natural” length (where the teeth would normally meet). Trim in small increments. If you see a tiny pink dot in the center of the cut, you have hit the pulp (nerve/blood supply). Stop immediately.

Capping: If the tooth shatters or the pulp is exposed, apply a tiny dab of Styptic Powder and monitor for infection.

Management & Release Prospects

Temporary Malocclusion: If caused by a one-time injury (falling and knocking a tooth loose), regular trims for 4–8 weeks may allow the tooth to “re-set” into the proper groove. If the teeth eventually meet and self-grind, the squirrel can be [released](https://www.nwrawildlife.org/page/Rehabilitator_Resources).

Permanent Malocclusion: If the jaw is broken/offset or the alignment is genetic, the squirrel cannot be released. They will eventually starve or the teeth will pierce their brain.

The “Sanctuary” Life: Permanent malocclusion squirrels require life-long tooth trims every 2–4 weeks and a specialized diet of softened blocks and shaved veggies.

Note: The “Sore Mouth” Period: Add a note that for 24 hours after a major trim (especially if you got close to the pulp), the squirrel may be reluctant to eat hard blocks. Suggest offering a “warm mash” of blocks or baby food for that first day.

The “MBD” Connection

Sometimes, “soft” teeth that move or drift out of alignment are actually a symptom of Metabolic Bone Disease (MBD). Before assuming the jaw is broken, check for other MBD signs like “rubber jaw” or hind-leg weakness.

heading: Ch. 53 — Major Wound Care: Tears, Muscle Trauma & Degloving
text:
## **53\. Major Wound Care: Tears, Muscle Trauma & Degloving**

🔴 URGENT – Stabilize for Shock Before Cleaning

VET LEVEL INJURIES REQUIRE IMMEDIATE CARE \- DO NOT ATTEMPT TO SELF TREAT

When dealing with significant injuries like “degloving” or deep muscle tears in squirrels, it is crucial to prioritize the animal’s well-being and seek professional help. Attempting to treat such severe wounds without proper veterinary training can cause further harm and distress to the animal.

When a squirrel comes in with a “degloving” injury (common in cat attacks or fence snags) or a deep muscular tear, a seasoned rehabber knows that the goal isn’t just closing the gap—it’s managing the dead space underneath. Squirrel skin is incredibly mobile, which can hide massive pockets of infection.

🔴 URGENT – Seek Professional Veterinary Care

If you encounter a squirrel with a large tear or deep muscle trauma, the most responsible action is to contact your veterinarian who is experienced with wildlife. They have the knowledge, sterile equipment, and access to necessary medications to properly assess and treat these complex injuries.

When a squirrel suffers a massive tear or degloving injury, your role is to stop the clock. Your goal isn’t to fix the wound, but to prevent the squirrel from dying of shock or infection before the vet can debride and close it.

Stabilizing Major Trauma & Degloving

🔴 CRITICAL – The “Clean, Cover, and Calm” Protocol

Large skin tears (common from hawk strikes or fence snags) and muscle trauma create a massive “open door” for bacteria and rapid heat loss.

STEP 1: Immediate Hemostasis (Stop the Bleed)

Direct Pressure: Use sterile gauze or a clean, lint-free cloth. Apply firm, steady pressure for a full 5 minutes without “peeking.”

Avoid Tourniquets: Never tie off a limb; squirrels have fragile vasculature and this often leads to unnecessary amputation.

Silver Sulfadiazine (SSD) Cream: If you have it on your list, a thin layer on the wound edges can help prevent the exposed tissue from drying out (necrosis) while in transit.

STEP 2: The “Wet-to-Dry” Protection

Keep it Moist: If muscle or bone is exposed, it must stay moist to remain viable for surgical repair. Dampen sterile gauze with Lactated Ringers (LRS) or Saline Solution and lay it gently over the wound.

Loose Wrap: Use Vet Wrap or a soft cloth to hold the gauze in place. Do not wrap tightly; swelling will occur, and a tight wrap can cut off circulation.

STEP 3: Pain & Infection Loading

NSAID Support: Administer Meloxicam from your list immediately to address the massive inflammatory response.

Antibiotic Loading: Large tears are contaminated the second they happen. Start a “broad-spectrum” load of Amoxicillin/Clavamox or Baytril as soon as the squirrel is hydrated and warm.

STEP 4: The “Safe Transport” Box

Plastic over Bars: Use a solid-walled pet carrier rather than a wire cage. A panicked squirrel with a large tear can easily snag the wound on wire, turning a repairable tear into a fatal one.

No Loose Substrate: Avoid wood shavings or shredded paper, which will stick to the wound. Use flat fleece only.

When a squirrel has been injured and requires transport to a veterinarian or wildlife rehabilitator, ensuring the animal is as stable and comfortable as possible during the journey is important.

Safe Transport Checklist

Before transport, consider these steps to help the squirrel:

Prepare a suitable carrier: Use a clean, secure container that is appropriately sized for the squirrel. A carrier with solid sides is preferable to prevent the squirrel from injuring itself further. Line the carrier with soft, clean material, like a towel or fleece, that won’t snag on any injuries.

Handle with care: If you need to move the squirrel, do so gently and minimize stress. Use thick gloves or a towel to protect yourself and to handle the squirrel calmly.

Provide warmth: Injured animals can easily become hypothermic. Place a heat source under one half of the carrier, like a hot water bottle wrapped in a towel, to allow the squirrel to move away if it gets too warm. Do not place the heat source inside the carrier without protection, and avoid direct contact with the animal.

Keep it calm and dark: Cover the carrier with a towel or blanket to create a dark, quiet environment. This helps reduce stress during transport. Avoid loud noises and sudden movements.

Minimize stops: Plan the route to the vet or rehabilitator to be as direct as possible, reducing the time and potential stress of the journey.

Do not offer food or water: It’s generally best not to give food or water to an injured or stressed animal unless specifically instructed by a professional. This is because they may aspirate it or it could interfere with potential veterinary treatments.

Contact ahead: Call the veterinarian or wildlife rehabilitator while en route or before leaving if possible. Provide details about the squirrel’s condition so they can be prepared for your arrival.

Following these steps can help stabilize the squirrel for transport and give it the best chance of receiving successful treatment.

Treating severe wounds in wild animals involves:

Thorough Assessment: Evaluating the extent of the injury, checking for dead space and potential infection.

Wound Cleaning and Debridement: Carefully cleaning the wound and removing any damaged tissue or debris.

Infection Control: Administering appropriate antibiotics and topical treatments to prevent or manage infection.

Wound Closure: Determining if sutures are necessary or if the wound should heal through secondary intention.

Pain Management: Providing appropriate pain relief to the animal.

Ongoing Care: Monitoring the wound’s healing progress and providing necessary follow-up care.

For these reasons, treating large wounds is not a do-it-yourself option. Seek professional help and give the squirrel and yourself the best chance at success.

WARNING: Attempting these steps at home without expertise can lead to improper cleaning, increased risk of infection, incorrect wound closure, and inadequate pain management, all of which can severely compromise the squirrel’s recovery and even lead to its death.

text:
### **⚕ Clinical Protocol — Trauma & Degloving (Large Skin Tears)**

**TRAUMA & DEGLOVING (LARGE SKIN TEARS)**

🔴 LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

Large area of missing skin \- Skin completely torn away, exposing underlying muscle, fat, or bone

“Degloving” appearance \- Skin peeled back like removing a glove; may still be partially attached

Severe bleeding \- Active hemorrhage from torn blood vessels

Exposed tissue \- Muscle appears red/pink; fat appears yellow; bone appears white

Shock symptoms \- Baby is cold, lethargic, pale gums, rapid breathing

Contamination \- Wound contains dirt, debris, or predator saliva

Pain and distress \- Baby may vocalize, thrash, or be unresponsive from pain/shock

**COMMON CAUSES**

Hawk/Raptor Strikes: Talons tear large strips of skin from back, sides, or limbs

Cat Attacks: Claws rake across body, peeling skin away

Vehicle Strikes: Dragging on pavement causes road rash and degloving

Entanglement: Caught in wire, fencing, or machinery that tears skin

Falls: High-impact falls onto rough surfaces

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Degloving injuries and large skin tears are catastrophic wounds that threaten life through multiple mechanisms. First, massive blood loss from torn vessels can cause hypovolemic shock and death within minutes if not controlled. Second, exposed tissue loses moisture rapidly through evaporation, leading to tissue death and severe dehydration. Third, contaminated wounds (especially from predator attacks) carry high infection risk \- bacteria from talons, claws, or environment enter deep tissue. Fourth, extensive skin loss eliminates the body’s protective barrier and temperature regulation, causing hypothermia. Fifth, the pain from these injuries is extreme and can trigger neurogenic shock. Without immediate intervention, babies with degloving injuries die from hemorrhage, shock, infection, or hypothermia within hours. Even with treatment, these wounds take weeks to months to heal and often result in permanent scarring, contractures, or non-releasability. The “golden hour” principle applies \- outcomes are dramatically better if treatment begins within 60 minutes of injury.

#### *Immediate Action*

**CLEAN \- COVER \- CALM PROTOCOL**

1\. CLEAN (Hemorrhage Control & Decontamination):

Stop Bleeding FIRST:

Apply direct pressure with clean gauze or cloth for 5-10 minutes

Do NOT remove pressure to “check” if bleeding stopped \- this disrupts clot formation

If bleeding soaks through, add more gauze on top \- don’t remove original layer

For severe arterial bleeding (pulsing bright red blood), apply pressure and transport immediately

Tourniquet use: ONLY as absolute last resort for limb hemorrhage that cannot be controlled with pressure

Wound Cleaning (ONLY after bleeding controlled):

Flush wound with copious sterile saline or clean water

Remove visible dirt, debris, and contamination

Do NOT scrub \- gentle irrigation only

If predator attack, assume bacterial contamination \- start antibiotics immediately

If wound is heavily contaminated and bleeding is controlled, continue flushing for 5-10 minutes

2\. COVER (Protect Exposed Tissue):

Immediate Covering:

Cover wound with sterile, non-stick gauze pad moistened with sterile saline

### ⚕ Clinical Protocol — Trauma & Degloving (Large Skin Tears)

TRAUMA & DEGLOVING (LARGE SKIN TEARS)

🔴 LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY

#### *Quick Identifier — What You’ll See*

Large area of missing skin - Skin completely torn away, exposing underlying muscle, fat, or bone

“Degloving” appearance - Skin peeled back like removing a glove; may still be partially attached

Severe bleeding - Active hemorrhage from torn blood vessels

Exposed tissue - Muscle appears red/pink; fat appears yellow; bone appears white

Shock symptoms - Baby is cold, lethargic, pale gums, rapid breathing

Contamination - Wound contains dirt, debris, or predator saliva

Pain and distress - Baby may vocalize, thrash, or be unresponsive from pain/shock

COMMON CAUSES

Hawk/Raptor Strikes: Talons tear large strips of skin from back, sides, or limbs

Cat Attacks: Claws rake across body, peeling skin away

Vehicle Strikes: Dragging on pavement causes road rash and degloving

Entanglement: Caught in wire, fencing, or machinery that tears skin

Falls: High-impact falls onto rough surfaces

#### *Why It Matters — Consequences if Untreated*

Degloving injuries and large skin tears are catastrophic wounds that threaten life through multiple mechanisms. First, massive blood loss from torn vessels can cause hypovolemic shock and death within minutes if not controlled. Second, exposed tissue loses moisture rapidly through evaporation, leading to tissue death and severe dehydration. Third, contaminated wounds (especially from predator attacks) carry high infection risk - bacteria from talons, claws, or environment enter deep tissue. Fourth, extensive skin loss eliminates the body’s protective barrier and temperature regulation, causing hypothermia. Fifth, the pain from these injuries is extreme and can trigger neurogenic shock. Without immediate intervention, babies with degloving injuries die from hemorrhage, shock, infection, or hypothermia within hours. Even with treatment, these wounds take weeks to months to heal and often result in permanent scarring, contractures, or non-releasability. The “golden hour” principle applies - outcomes are dramatically better if treatment begins within 60 minutes of injury.

#### *Immediate Action*

CLEAN - COVER - CALM PROTOCOL

1. CLEAN (Hemorrhage Control & Decontamination):

Stop Bleeding FIRST:

Apply direct pressure with clean gauze or cloth for 5-10 minutes

Do NOT remove pressure to “check” if bleeding stopped - this disrupts clot formation

If bleeding soaks through, add more gauze on top - don’t remove original layer

For severe arterial bleeding (pulsing bright red blood), apply pressure and transport immediately

Tourniquet use: ONLY as absolute last resort for limb hemorrhage that cannot be controlled with pressure

Wound Cleaning (ONLY after bleeding controlled):

Flush wound with copious sterile saline or clean water

Remove visible dirt, debris, and contamination

Do NOT scrub - gentle irrigation only

If predator attack, assume bacterial contamination - start antibiotics immediately

If wound is heavily contaminated and bleeding is controlled, continue flushing for 5-10 minutes

2. COVER (Protect Exposed Tissue):

Immediate Covering:

Cover wound with sterile, non-stick gauze pad moistened with sterile saline

If sterile supplies unavailable, use clean cloth moistened with clean water

CRITICAL: Keep exposed tissue moist - drying causes tissue death

Do NOT use cotton balls or fluffy gauze directly on wound - fibers stick to exposed tissue

Bandaging:

Cover moistened gauze with dry gauze or bandage material

Wrap loosely - tight bandaging cuts off circulation

If degloving involves limb, immobilize limb gently to prevent further tissue damage

Change bandage every 12-24 hours or if it becomes soaked with blood/fluid

Skin Flap Management:

If skin is torn but still partially attached, do NOT remove it

Position skin flap back over wound as much as possible

Cover with moist gauze

Veterinarian will assess if skin can be salvaged or must be debrided

heading: Ch. 53 — Major Wound Care: Tears, Muscle Trauma & Degloving › ⚕ Veterinary Protocol
text:
### **⚕ Veterinary Protocol**

**EMERGENCY STABILIZATION**

Shock Treatment:

IV fluids (if available) or aggressive subcutaneous fluids

Oxygen supplementation if respiratory distress present

Warming to correct hypothermia

Pain management with opioids (Buprenorphine or Morphine)

Hemorrhage Control:

Identify and ligate (tie off) bleeding vessels

Cauterize small bleeders

Blood transfusion if severe anemia (rarely available for squirrels)

**SURGICAL WOUND MANAGEMENT**

Debridement (Removal of Dead/Contaminated Tissue):

Remove all devitalized (dead) tissue \- will not heal and becomes infected

Remove heavily contaminated tissue

Trim wound edges to create clean margins

Assess skin flaps \- remove if not viable, preserve if blood supply intact

Wound Closure Options:

Primary Closure (immediate suturing): ONLY for clean wounds with minimal tissue loss; rarely appropriate for degloving injuries

Delayed Primary Closure: Clean wound, treat with antibiotics for 3-5 days, then suture once infection risk reduced

Secondary Intention Healing: Leave wound open to heal from inside out; used for contaminated wounds or extensive tissue loss

Skin Grafting: May be necessary for very large wounds; rarely performed in squirrels due to cost and complexity

Drain Placement:

Surgical drains may be placed to allow fluid drainage and prevent seroma (fluid pocket) formation

Remove drains after 3-5 days once drainage decreases

**ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY**

For ALL Degloving Injuries:

Clavamox 25 mg/kg orally twice daily for 14-21 days minimum

OR Baytril 20 mg/kg orally twice daily for 14-21 days

Start immediately \- these wounds WILL become infected without antibiotics

If predator attack, use high-end dosing and consider combination therapy (see Cat/Dog Attack protocol)

**PAIN MANAGEMENT**

Acute Phase (First 5-7 days):

Buprenorphine 0.01-0.05 mg/kg subcutaneously or orally every 8-12 hours

OR Tramadol 5-10 mg/kg orally twice daily

PLUS Meloxicam 0.2 mg/kg orally once daily

Maintenance Phase (After first week):

Meloxicam 0.2 mg/kg orally once daily for duration of healing

Add Tramadol as needed for breakthrough pain

**WOUND CARE**

Daily Bandage Changes:

Clean wound gently with sterile saline or diluted chlorhexidine

Remove any loose dead tissue

Apply topical antibiotic (Silver Sulfadiazine cream or triple antibiotic ointment)

Cover with non-stick gauze moistened with saline

Wrap with gauze bandage \- change every 12-24 hours

Monitoring for Complications:

Infection: Increased swelling, heat, purulent discharge, foul odor

Tissue necrosis: Black, dead tissue developing at wound edges

Seroma formation: Fluid pocket under skin

Wound dehiscence: Sutured wound opens up

**NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT**

High-Calorie, High-Protein Diet:

Wound healing requires 2-3× normal caloric intake

Add protein supplement to formula

Offer high-calorie supplements (Nutri-Cal) 2-3 times daily

Vitamin Supplementation:

Vitamin C: 10-20 mg/kg daily (supports collagen formation)

Vitamin E: Supports tissue healing

Zinc: Supports wound healing if deficiency suspected

**MONITORING PROTOCOL**

First 48 Hours:

Check every 2-4 hours for shock, hemorrhage, infection, pain level

Monitor body temperature, hydration, appetite

Watch for wound complications

Days 3-14:

Daily wound care and assessment

Monitor for infection and tissue necrosis

Ensure adequate nutrition and pain control

Watch for granulation tissue formation (pink, bumpy new tissue \- good sign)

Weeks 2-8:

Continue wound care until fully healed

Monitor for contracture formation if wound is over joint

Assess range of motion

Physical therapy may be needed

#### *Prognosis & Recovery*

Timeline:

Small wounds (\\\<2 cm): Heal in 2-4 weeks

Medium wounds (2-5 cm): Heal in 4-8 weeks

Large wounds (\\\>5 cm): Take months to heal; may never fully close without grafting

Success Rate:

Clean wounds, prompt treatment: 70-80% survival and recovery

Contaminated wounds, delayed treatment: 40-50% survival

Extensive degloving (\\\>20% body surface): 20-30% survival; high risk of complications

Warning Signs of Poor Prognosis:

Uncontrollable hemorrhage

Severe shock that doesn’t respond to fluids

Extensive tissue necrosis

Overwhelming infection despite antibiotics

Wound involves critical structures (major blood vessels, joints, spine)

Complications:

Infection: Most common; requires aggressive antibiotic therapy

Tissue necrosis: Dead tissue must be surgically removed

Contractures: Scar tissue tightens, restricting movement

Chronic pain: Nerve damage from injury

Seroma formation: Fluid pockets that may require drainage

Long-term Effects:

Permanent scarring and hair loss

Reduced range of motion if contractures develop

Chronic pain or sensitivity

May require ongoing wound care for months

Release Considerations:

Must have complete wound healing before release

Must demonstrate full mobility and climbing ability

Contractures or reduced range of motion make squirrel non-releasable

Extensive scarring may affect thermoregulation

Test in large outdoor enclosure for 2-3 weeks before release

#### *Prevention*

& Pain Management):

Treat for Shock:

Warm baby immediately \- place on heating pad (LOW setting with thick towel barrier)

Target body temperature 98-100°F

Administer subcutaneous fluids (warmed LRS or saline, 5-10% of body weight)

Minimize handling and stress

Pain Management:

Administer Meloxicam 0.2 mg/kg orally if available

For severe pain, Buprenorphine 0.01-0.05 mg/kg subcutaneously

Pain control is critical \- severe pain worsens shock

Calm Environment:

Place baby in dark, quiet container

Cover container with towel to reduce visual stimulation

Speak softly; avoid sudden movements

**4\. TRANSPORT:**

**MINIMIZE STOPS:**

Get to veterinarian as quickly as safely possible

Every minute of delay increases tissue death and infection risk

Do NOT stop to “stabilize” further \- basic first aid done, now baby needs surgery

Call ahead so vet can prepare for emergency surgery

Transport Protocol:

Keep baby warm during transport

Keep wound covered with moist dressings

Drive smoothly to avoid jostling injured baby

If transport will take more than 30 minutes, re-moisten wound dressings during trip

Predator Protection: Secure outdoor enclosures against hawks, cats, and other predators

Safe Transport: Use secure carriers to prevent escape and injury during transport

Habitat Safety: Remove hazards (wire, fencing, machinery) from rehabilitation areas

Public Education: Teach people to watch for injured wildlife and seek help immediately

Early Intervention: The sooner treatment begins, the better the outcome \- educate public about “golden hour”

heading: Ch. 54 — Metabolic Bone Disease (MBD)
text:
## **54\. Metabolic Bone Disease (MBD)**

🔴 CRITICAL EMERGENCY – The Metabolic Collapse

MBD is the “Great Imitator”—it looks like head trauma, spinal injury, or a seizure disorder, but it is actually a systemic nutritional failure. Because squirrels have an incredibly high metabolic rate, they can go from “seeming fine” to “seizing and paralyzed” in less than 24 hours.

1. The MBD Triage (What You Will See)

Early Signs: Reluctance to jump, sleeping more than usual, and the “Tell” (nails getting caught in fabric because they are too weak to retract them).

Neurological: “Electric” tremors, full-body seizures, or “star-gazing.”

Physical: The “Flat-Track” walk (dragging the belly), “The Bunny Hop” (hind-end weakness), or “Rubber Jaw” (the lower jaw feels flexible or soft).

Pain: The squirrel may scream, growl, or become aggressive when touched because their entire skeleton hurts.

The “Hunch”: A sudden curvature of the spine (kyphosis) as the vertebrae soften.

2. Emergency “Right Now” Treatment

DO NOT WAIT. If you see these symptoms, begin treatment immediately. If they respond to the calcium, it was MBD.

The “Calcium Load”: Goal is to raise blood calcium immediately to stop seizures and heart failure.

The Method: Crush one Calcium pill (Tums, Rolaids, or plain Calcium Carbonate). Add a tiny bit of water or fruit juice to make a “toothpaste” consistency.

The Dose: Smear the paste on the gums or force-feed via syringe.

Initial “Blast”: 100 mg (50 mg for flyers or squirrels under 12 weeks).

The 15-Minute Rule: You should observe a reduction in tremors within 15–30 minutes. If symptoms persist, repeat dosing.

Stability Phase (First 24 Hours): Give 100 mg every 4 hours. This is about saturation—getting levels up is more important than the brand of calcium.

3. The “Refeed” Warning

If you intake an emaciated squirrel, do not start high-protein formula immediately. \> Danger: Sudden high-calorie intake causes a phosphorus spike that drives blood calcium to zero, triggering a fatal MBD seizure. Start with Pedialyte and slow-transition to food (See Ch. 63, Refeeding Syndrome).

4. Long-Term Recovery & Maintenance

It takes months to rebuild bone density. Do not stop therapy the moment symptoms vanish.

| Phase | Action & Dosage |
| :---: | :---: |
| Day 2–14 | 500 mg elemental calcium daily (250 mg for flyers), divided into 5 doses. |
| Dietary Reset | Remove ALL seeds, nuts, corn, and fruit. These are “metabolic poison” (high phosphorus) during recovery. |
| The “Block” Rule | Squirrel MUST eat 2 Henry’s Healthy Blocks per day. Once eating blocks, cut extra calcium dosage in half. |
| The Food Trap | Mix calcium with peanut butter or yogurt to avoid the stress of force-feeding. |

5. Monitoring the “Sweet Spot”

Increase Dose If: The squirrel has “ups and downs” or tremors return.

Decrease Dose If: You see white feces or a white film on dried urine. This means the body is excreting excess calcium and you are stressing the kidneys.

6. Critical Safety & Environmental Support

Fracture Watch: MBD bones are like glass. Use a “low-profile” bin with no bars or climbing branches. A 1-foot fall can snap a femur during recovery.

Sunlight (The D3 Factor): Calcium cannot be absorbed without Vitamin D.

Natural: Provide 20 minutes of unfiltered sunlight (not through a window) daily.

Artificial: Use a Full-Spectrum UVB light (5.0 or 10.0) for 12 hours a day, placed at the appropriate distance above the enclosure.

Soothing Heat: Use a heating pad on LOW (half-on, half-off the cage) to soothe aching joints.

Warning: Never give Vitamin D drops without vet supervision; it can quickly become toxic.

heading: Ch. 55 — Mites and Mange
text:
## **55\. Mites and Mange**

*Free-roaming adult with mange? See the Mange Ball variation of Recipe 4 (Ch. 5, 11D) — adults only.*

Finding patches of missing fur or irritated skin on a squirrel can be unsettling, but it is one of the most common issues rehabbers encounter. While a sleek, full coat is a hallmark of a healthy squirrel, hair loss (alopecia) and “crusty” textures are usually the body’s visible response to microscopic invaders. Whether the culprit is a fungal infection like ringworm or one of the three main types of parasitic mange, identifying the specific look and behavior of the skin is your first step toward the right cure. Use the following guides to help you distinguish between the “stubbled” circles of fungus and the “thickened” skin of mites so you can treat the patient—and protect yourself—effectively.

Critical Diagnostic Tip: The “Wrinkle Test”

If you see the bare skin is smooth (even if it’s red or scaly), it is likely [Ringworm or a Fungal Infection](https://www.wildagainrescue.com/post/help-for-your-backyard-wildlife). If the skin looks like “elephant skin”—thickened, dark, and deeply creased—it is almost certainly [Mange](https://cwhl.vet.cornell.edu/resource/mange).

heading: Ch. 55 — Mites and Mange › Ringworm (Dermatophytosis)
text:
## **Ringworm (Dermatophytosis)**

🟡 MODERATE – Contagious but non-emergency.

Signs of Ringworm

Hair Loss: Circular patches of baldness, often starting on the face, ears, or paws.

Stubble: Unlike mange (which often leaves skin raw), ringworm causes hair to break off at the skin line, leaving a fine “stubble”.

Skin Condition: The skin may appear dry, scaly, or crusty, sometimes with a classic raised red “ring” (though this is less common on squirrels than on humans).

Fluorescence: Under a [Wood’s Lamp](https://www.tvmf.org/articles/ringworm/) (UV light), some species of ringworm will glow a bright “apple green”.

Treatment Protocol

STEP 1: Strict Quarantine

Isolate: Move the infected squirrel to a separate room immediately.

PPE: Always wear gloves and wash your arms thoroughly after handling.

Laundry: Wash all bedding in hot water with bleach.

STEP 2: Topical Therapy

Lime Sulfur Dip: This is the gold standard for killing spores on the coat. Mix 8oz per gallon of warm water and sponge it onto the squirrel twice a week. Warning: It smells like rotten eggs and will stain jewelry and surfaces.

Antifungal Creams: For small, localized spots, you can apply a thin layer of [Clotrimazole (Lotrimin)](https://www.animalhumanesociety.org/health/treating-ringworm-shelter) or Miconazole once daily. Ensure the squirrel does not lick it off immediately.

STEP 3: Nutritional Support

Boost Immunity: Healthy squirrels often clear fungal infections naturally. Ensure they are receiving high-quality Squirrel Blocks and consider a drop of coconut oil in their food, as it contains antifungal lauric acid.

Environmental Decontamination

Fungal spores are incredibly hardy and can live in carpets or wood for over a year.

Bleach Solution: Use a 1:10 bleach-to-water ratio on all non-porous surfaces.

Vacuuming: Vacuum daily and immediately discard the bag or empty the canister outside to prevent spores from blowing back into the room.

Skin Condition: The skin may appear dry, scaly, or crusty, sometimes with a classic raised red “ring” (though this is less common on squirrels than on humans).

Fluorescence: Under a Wood’s Lamp (UV light), some species of ringworm will glow a bright “apple green”.

Treatment Protocol

STEP 1: Strict Quarantine

Isolate: Move the infected squirrel to a separate room immediately.

PPE: Always wear gloves and wash your arms thoroughly after handling.

Laundry: Wash all bedding in hot water with bleach.

STEP 2: Topical Therapy

Lime Sulfur Dip: This is the gold standard for killing spores on the coat. Mix 8oz per gallon of warm water and sponge it onto the squirrel twice a week. Warning: It smells like rotten eggs and will stain jewelry and surfaces.

Antifungal Creams: For small, localized spots, you can apply a thin layer of Clotrimazole (Lotrimin) or Miconazole once daily. Ensure the squirrel does not lick it off immediately.

STEP 3: Nutritional Support

Boost Immunity: Healthy squirrels often clear fungal infections naturally. Ensure they are receiving high-quality Squirrel Blocks and consider a drop of coconut oil in their food, as it contains antifungal lauric acid.

Environmental Decontamination

Fungal spores are incredibly hardy and can live in carpets or wood for over a year.

Bleach Solution: Use a 1:10 bleach-to-water ratio on all non-porous surfaces.

Vacuuming: Vacuum daily and immediately discard the bag or empty the canister outside to prevent spores from blowing back into the room.

heading: Ch. 55 — Mites and Mange › Sarcoptic Mange (The “Itch” Mite)
text:
## **Sarcoptic Mange (The “Itch” Mite)**

🔴 HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS – Protect yourself and your other animals\!

Sarcoptic mange is caused by microscopic Sarcoptes scabiei mites that tunnel under the skin to lay eggs. This causes an allergic reaction so intense that squirrels often injure themselves trying to stop the itch.

Signs of Sarcoptic Mange

The “Elephant Skin”: Skin becomes grey, incredibly thick, and develops deep, crusty wrinkles.

Intense Pruritus (Itching): The squirrel will scratch, bite, and chew at its skin until it bleeds.

Crusty Eyes/Ears: Thick, yellow-grey crusts often form around the eyes, sometimes sealing them shut.

Smell: A distinct, “musty” or “yeasty” odor often develops due to secondary skin infections.

Emergency Treatment Protocol

STEP 1: Immediate Lockdown

Total Isolation: This mite can travel on your clothes. Keep the squirrel in a separate room and use “dedicated” tools (bowls, fleece) that never leave that room.

PPE: Wear Disposable Gloves and a long-sleeved shirt that you can bleach or discard.

STEP 2: Medical Intervention

Diet alone will not cure Sarcoptic mange. The mites must be killed chemically.

Revolution (Selamectin): This is the gold standard. A single topical drop between the shoulder blades (where they can’t lick it) is often effective.

Ivermectin: Some rehabbers use [Diluted Ivermectin](https://www.wildagainrescue.com/post/help-for-your-backyard-wildlife), but dosing is extremely sensitive—consult a Wildlife Veterinarian to avoid neurotoxicity (overdose).

Antibiotics: Because they scratch so much, most “mange squirrels” have staph infections and need a course of Clavamox or Baytril.

STEP 3: Environmental Sanitization

High Heat: Mites can fall off and live in bedding. Wash all fleece in hot water with bleach.

Deep Clean: Scrub cages with a 10% Bleach Solution and let it sit for 10 minutes before rinsing.

Crucial Note: The “Zoonotic” Risk

Sarcoptic mange can jump to humans and domestic dogs. In humans, it is known as “Scabies.” If you develop small, red, intensely itchy bumps on your wrists or between your fingers, contact your doctor immediately.

heading: Ch. 55 — Mites and Mange › Demodectic Mange (The “Internal” Mite)
text:
## **Demodectic Mange (The “Internal” Mite)**

🟢 LOW CONTAGION – A sign of a weakened immune system.

Unlike other mites, Demodex lives naturally in small numbers in the hair follicles of almost all squirrels. It only becomes a “disease” when the squirrel’s immune system crashes, allowing the mites to overpopulate.

Signs of Demodectic Mange

Thinning Fur: Generally starts around the eyes, muzzle, and forehead.

The “Moth-Eaten” Look: Fur looks thin and sparse rather than falling out in thick chunks.

Skin Quality: The skin is usually pink and dry, not the thick, “elephant-skin” texture of Sarcoptic mange.

Non-Itchy: Most squirrels with Demodex do not scratch excessively.

Treatment Protocol

STEP 1: Boost the Immune System

Because this is a “vulnerability” issue, medicine alone won’t fix it if the diet is poor.

Nutrition: Transition immediately to high-quality Squirrel Blocks and limit nuts/fruit.

Stress Reduction: Move the squirrel to a low-traffic area. High cortisol (stress hormone) prevents the immune system from fighting off the mites.

STEP 2: Medication

Consult a Professional: While Ivermectin or Selamectin are often used, they may not be necessary if the squirrel’s health improves through diet.

Watch for Secondary Infection: If the skin becomes red or “oozy,” the squirrel may need [Antibiotics](https://www.wildagainrescue.com/post/help-for-your-backyard-wildlife) for a staph infection.

Important Note: Demodectic mange is not considered contagious to humans or healthy pets. It is a “red flag” that the squirrel is likely struggling with an underlying issue like poor nutrition, Metabolic Bone Disease, or recent severe trauma.

heading: Ch. 55 — Mites and Mange › Notoedric Mange (The “Squirrel-Specific” Mite)
text:
## **Notoedric Mange (The “Squirrel-Specific” Mite)**

🟡 MODERATE – Highly contagious to other squirrels, but rarely affects humans.

NOT TO BE CONFUSED WITH SQUIRREL MITES WHICH ARE COMMONLY FOUND ON RECENTLY ACQUIRED SQUIRRELS AND WHICH ARE DISCUSSED HERE

In many regions, this is actually the most common form of mange found in wild gray and fox squirrels. It is often a “winter killer,” as squirrels that lose their fur to these mites often die from exposure to the cold.

Signs of Notoedric Mange

Progressive Fur Loss: Typically starts on the chest and shoulders before spreading across the entire body.

Skin Changes: The skin becomes very dark (pigmented), dry, and thickened.

Lack of Crust: Unlike Sarcoptic mange, Notoedric mange in squirrels [does not usually form thick, foul-smelling crusts](https://www.purdue.edu/fnr/extension/sp_faq/squirrel-with-missing-fur-is-it-sick/).

Intense Itching: The squirrel will spend a significant portion of its day scratching and biting at the affected areas.

Treatment Protocol

STEP 1: Quarantine

Separate: Even though it doesn’t easily jump to humans, it spreads rapidly between squirrels through shared nests and direct contact.

Clean: Disinfect all cages and [wash bedding in hot water](https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN953) to kill mites that have fallen off the host.

STEP 2: Medication

Ivermectin or Selamectin: Like Sarcoptic mange, this requires a miticide. [Topical Selamectin (Revolution)](https://cwhl.vet.cornell.edu/resource/mange) is often the safest and most effective choice for rehabilitators.

In addition, simple mite spray readily available at most grocery stores as well as all pet stores is a fast and easy way to treat both the squirrel and yourself (not contagious to humans, but the little bastards love to chew on you for a few hours before realizing you’re not their target and moving on.)

Wait for Regrowth: Fur regrowth can take 3–6 weeks. Do not release a squirrel treated in winter until they have a full “winter coat” to protect them from the elements.

STEP 3: Nutritional Support

High-Calorie Diet: These squirrels are often emaciated because they spend more energy scratching than eating. Provide extra squirrel blocks and healthy fats like [coconut oil](https://www.wildagainrescue.com/post/help-for-your-backyard-wildlife) to support skin repair.

Key Difference: The “Good News”

The best part about Notoedric mange for the rehabber is its host specificity. While Sarcoptic mange is a major risk to you and your pets, [Notoedric mites generally stay on squirrels](https://albionpleiad.com/2017/10/squirrels-are-going-bald-in-albion-but-dont-worry-its-just-mange/) and do not colonize non-hosts like humans or dogs.

heading: Ch. 55 — Mites and Mange › Not Every Bald Squirrel Has Mange: Hair Follicle Dysplasia (American Red Squirrels)
text:
## **Not Every Bald Squirrel Has Mange: Hair Follicle Dysplasia (American Red Squirrels)**

**Before you treat for mange — or decide a bald baby can't be saved — rule this out.** A 2023 Cornell case series described 8 juvenile American red squirrels (pine squirrels) with dramatic hair loss that was **not mange, not ringworm, and not pox**. Every squirrel that was kept long enough **grew a normal coat back**.

**What it looks like**

- Widespread hair loss on **both sides equally**, covering the trunk and neck and often running down the legs, with a **sharp edge** (one squirrel had a clean line at the hock)
- **Normal hair on the muzzle and the tops of the paws**; the head and tail may or may not be bald
- Skin that looks **normal** — normal color, texture, and thickness, with no redness or swelling. A few tiny crusts may be present.
- No intense itching, and **skin scrapes are negative**

**Who gets it:** juveniles, about 6–8 weeks old, mostly found in **September through November** (one in April). Five of the eight were found with or near other bald red squirrels, so the authors suspect a **genetic** cause. It resembles seasonal flank alopecia in dogs.

**What happens:** every squirrel that was followed **regrew its coat**. Two littermates had full coats by March (about 6 months), and a third had nearly full hair within 2 months. All three were released. In the same series, several others were **euthanized out of fear of contagious disease**, or because they were too bald to release.

**What to do**

1. **Rule out the treatable causes first:** skin scrape for mites (see above), a vet check for ringworm, and a look for pox nodules (Ch. 71). Under a microscope, a vet biopsy shows malformed, bent or coiled hair shafts with clumped pigment.
2. **If it fits this pattern, it isn't a reason to euthanize.** Nothing in the study showed it to be contagious.
3. **Overwinter them in care.** A bald juvenile can't survive a cold winter outside. Hold them until the coat grows back, then release (Ch. 86, Overwintering).
4. **Keep them warm** like a younger baby, and watch for chilling.

**The honest caveats:** this was a small study (8 squirrels) in one species, the American red squirrel, so we don't know whether gray or fox squirrels get the same thing. Two of the squirrels that regrew had been treated with ivermectin, lime sulfur, antibiotics, and meloxicam, and one regrew with no treatment, so the treatment probably isn't what fixed it. The authors also point out that if the condition is inherited, overwintering and releasing affected squirrels may pass the trait on. That's a judgment call for each rehabber.

*Source: Gordon DL, Peters-Kennedy J, Childs-Sanford SE. Widespread, symmetric, noninflammatory alopecia associated with follicular dysplasia in the American red squirrel (Tamiasciurus hudsonicus). Veterinary Pathology. 2023;60(6):905–909. doi:10.1177/03009858231176556*

heading: Ch. 56 — Nystagmus (The “Ping-Pong” Eye)
text:
## **56\. Nystagmus (The “Ping-Pong” Eye)**

Nystagmus is the involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyeballs. To the observer, it looks like the squirrel is watching an incredibly fast tennis match. It is a symptom of Vestibular Dysfunction—the squirrel’s internal “gyroscope” is broken.

1. Types of Movement

The direction of the flick tells us a lot about the location of the injury:

Horizontal Nystagmus: The eyes move side-to-side. This is the most common form and often indicates a peripheral issue (like an inner ear infection) or mild head trauma.

Vertical Nystagmus: The eyes flick up and down. This is a Red Flag. It almost always indicates a central nervous system (brainstem) injury.

Rotary Nystagmus: The eyes appear to roll in a circular motion. This is common in severe trauma or advanced raccoon roundworm.

2. Why Does it Happen?

The “Fall” (Head Trauma): The most common cause in juveniles. Swelling in the brain puts pressure on the vestibular nerve.

Inner Ear Infections: A “silent” infection can cause a sudden head tilt and nystagmus.

Toxicity: Exposure to certain pesticides or chemicals can cause neurological “misfiring.”

Severe Dehydration: When the brain shrinks due to fluid loss, it can pull on the delicate cranial nerves.

3. The “Nausea” Connection

Imagine being on a Tilt-A-Whirl that never stops. That is what a squirrel with nystagmus is experiencing.

The Result: They are often profoundly nauseous. They may refuse food, or if they do eat, they may vomit or aspirate because the world won’t stop spinning.

The “Rolling” Link: Nystagmus is the primary driver behind “rolling.” The squirrel is trying to align its body with what its eyes are seeing.

4. Stabilization Protocol

Stop the Spin (Darkness): The absolute best medicine for nystagmus is complete darkness. Close the squirrel’s eyes for them by placing them in a dark, padded box. If they can’t see the world spinning, the brain can begin to recalibrate.

Anti-Inflammatories: Use Meloxicam (Metacam) as directed by your vet to reduce the swelling around the vestibular nerve.

Hydration (Sub-Q): Do not attempt to bottle-feed a squirrel with active nystagmus. The risk of aspiration is nearly 100%. Use Sub-Q fluids until the eye flickering slows down.

Meclizine (Optional/Vet Consult): In some chronic cases, vets may suggest a micro-dose of Meclizine (motion sickness medication) to help the squirrel stop “rolling” so they can eat.

heading: Ch. 57 — Ocular Emergencies & Care
text:
## **57\. Ocular Emergencies & Care**

A squirrel’s eyes are their primary defense. When infection strikes before the eyes even open, or when trauma leads to permanent blindness, the care protocol must be precise to save the globe or prepare the animal for a non-releasable life.

1. “Pop-Eye” (Neonatal Ophthalmia)

This is a bacterial infection that develops behind the sealed eyelid of a pinky or fuzzy. The eye looks massively swollen, often appearing as a dark or purple “bulge” under the skin.

The Cause: Bacteria trapped in the ocular cavity during development or introduced via a small scratch.

The Protocol:

DO NOT USE HEAT: Heat increases blood flow and bacterial activity, which can cause the eye to rupture. Use COOL compresses only to reduce inflammation.

Topical Treatment: Apply a thin line of Terramycin (ophthalmic ointment) along the “slit” where the eye is meant to open. The medication will slowly seep behind the lid.

Internal Support: This is a systemic risk. The squirrel must be seen by a vet for internal antibiotics (Baytril or Clavamox) to prevent the infection from reaching the brain.

2. Assessment of Blindness

Blindness in squirrels can be congenital (born with it), caused by untreated “Pop-eye,” or the result of head trauma.

The Menace Reflex Test: Move your hand quickly toward the squirrel’s eye (without touching the whiskers). A sighted squirrel will blink or flinch. A blind squirrel will remain still.

The “Tracking” Test: Move a colorful object or a nut in a quiet arc in front of them. If the eyes don’t follow the movement, vision is likely compromised.

Cataracts: Look for a cloudy, milky, or “shattered glass” appearance inside the lens.

3. Living with Blindness: The “Ambassador” Decision

A completely blind squirrel cannot be released. They are unable to navigate the 3D environment of the canopy or spot predators.

Rehabilitation Goal: If the blindness is permanent, the squirrel must either be euthanized or transferred to a permitted facility as a non-releasable educational animal.

Habitat Management: Blind squirrels (like “Grizzle Bear” types) rely entirely on scent and whisker-mapping. If they are in a permanent sanctuary, never move their furniture. They “map” their cage and can navigate perfectly until you move their food bowl or sleeping box.

4. Corneal Ulcers (The “Blue Haze”)

If an eye looks cloudy or has a “crater” on the surface after a cat attack or a poke from a branch:

Diagnosis: A vet will use Fluorescein stain to see the ulcer.

Treatment: Requires frequent antibiotic drops (often every 4-6 hours). Never use a steroid drop (like Maxitrol) on an eye unless an ulcer has been ruled out, as it will “melt” the cornea.

“Star Cornea” (Dehydration Triage)

When a squirrel is severely dehydrated, the fluid inside the eye (aqueous humor) decreases, causing the cornea to lose its tension and “crinkle” or “fold.”

The Appearance: When you shine a light on the eye, instead of a smooth, glassy reflection, you will see a “starburst” pattern or jagged, splintered lines across the surface of the eye.

What it Means: This is a Stage 2 or 3 Emergency. It indicates at least 10-12% dehydration.

The Protocol: \* Immediate Sub-Q Fluids: Oral hydration is often not enough at this stage; the gut may not be absorbing properly.

Do Not Flush the Eye: The “starring” is internal, not external. Focus on systemic rehydration.

The Recovery Sign: As the squirrel becomes hydrated, the “star” will vanish, and the cornea will become plump and glassy again. If the star remains after 24 hours of fluids, the squirrel may have permanent ocular damage or underlying kidney failure.

Topical Treatment: Apply a thin line of Terramycin (ophthalmic ointment) along the “slit” where the eye is meant to open. The medication will slowly seep behind the lid.

Internal Support: This is a systemic risk. The squirrel must be seen by a vet for internal antibiotics (Baytril or Clavamox) to prevent the infection from reaching the brain.

2. Assessment of Blindness

Blindness in squirrels can be congenital (born with it), caused by untreated “Pop-eye,” or the result of head trauma.

The Menace Reflex Test: Move your hand quickly toward the squirrel’s eye (without touching the whiskers). A sighted squirrel will blink or flinch. A blind squirrel will remain still.

The “Tracking” Test: Move a colorful object or a nut in a quiet arc in front of them. If the eyes don’t follow the movement, vision is likely compromised.

Cataracts: Look for a cloudy, milky, or “shattered glass” appearance inside the lens.

3. Living with Blindness: The “Ambassador” Decision

A completely blind squirrel cannot be released. They are unable to navigate the 3D environment of the canopy or spot predators.

Rehabilitation Goal: If the blindness is permanent, the squirrel must either be euthanized or transferred to a permitted facility as a non-releasable educational animal.

Habitat Management: Blind squirrels (like “Grizzle Bear” types) rely entirely on scent and whisker-mapping. If they are in a permanent sanctuary, never move their furniture. They “map” their cage and can navigate perfectly until you move their food bowl or sleeping box.

4. Corneal Ulcers (The “Blue Haze”)

If an eye looks cloudy or has a “crater” on the surface after a cat attack or a poke from a branch:

Diagnosis: A vet will use Fluorescein stain to see the ulcer.

Treatment: Requires frequent antibiotic drops (often every 4-6 hours). Never use a steroid drop (like Maxitrol) on an eye unless an ulcer has been ruled out, as it will “melt” the cornea.

When a squirrel is severely dehydrated, the fluid inside the eye (aqueous humor) decreases, causing the cornea to lose its tension and “crinkle” or “fold.”

The Appearance: When you shine a light on the eye, instead of a smooth, glassy reflection, you will see a “starburst” pattern or jagged, splintered lines across the surface of the eye.

What it Means: This is a Stage 2 or 3 Emergency. It indicates at least 10-12% dehydration.

The Protocol: * Immediate Sub-Q Fluids: Oral hydration is often not enough at this stage; the gut may not be absorbing properly.

Do Not Flush the Eye: The “starring” is internal, not external. Focus on systemic rehydration.

The Recovery Sign: As the squirrel becomes hydrated, the “star” will vanish, and the cornea will become plump and glassy again. If the star remains after 24 hours of fluids, the squirrel may have permanent ocular damage or underlying kidney failure.

heading: Ch. 58 — Odontoma (Elodontoma)
text:
## **58\. Odontoma (Elodontoma)**

🔴 CRITICAL & PROGRESSIVE – A “Quiet” Killer.

For a seasoned rehabber, an Odontoma is one of the most heartbreaking diagnoses. Unlike a simple malocclusion that can be managed with regular trims, an odontoma is a progressive, life-threatening structural failure of the tooth root itself.

An odontoma is a benign but invasive tumor-like mass of dental tissue at the root of the upper incisors. Because squirrels are “elodonts” (ever-growing teeth), if the root becomes traumatized or infected, it can begin to grow backward and upward into the nasal cavity and toward the skull.

Identifying the Signs

Respiratory Distress: This is often the first sign. As the mass grows, it blocks the nasal passages. You will hear labored breathing, “snuffling,” or persistent sneezing that doesn’t respond to antibiotics.

The “Bulge”: A hard, bony swelling on the bridge of the nose or the roof of the mouth.

Upper Incisor Stunting: The visible top teeth may become thin, brittle, discolored (chalky white instead of orange), or stop growing entirely as the energy shifts to the root mass.

Eye Involvement: In advanced cases, the mass presses against the back of the eye socket, causing one or both eyes to bulge (Exophthalmos).

Whistling: Another symptom or sign of an odontoma can be the presence of a high-pitched whistle or “clicking” during rest. Because squirrels are obligate nasal breathers, even a tiny obstruction at the root creates a distinct “whistle” that is different from the “clicking” of pneumonia.

Gap Teeth: Sometimes an odontoma causes the two upper incisors to splay apart (forming a ‘V’ shape) because the mass at the root is pushing the bases away from each other. This is a great “at-a-glance” red flag to look for during an oral exam.

WARNING NOTE: The “Pseudo-Odontoma” (Clinical Nuance)

Rehabber Tip: Don’t confuse a persistent sinus infection or a simple abscess with an Odontoma. If the “snuffling” clears up 100% with a 14-day course of antibiotics and the X-ray is clear, you dodged the bullet. If the “cold” keeps coming back the moment the meds stop, it’s likely an Odontoma. If in doubt, a vet visit is always a worthwhile trip.

The Diagnostic Roadmap

Oral Exam: Check the roof of the mouth for a “doming” effect or inflammation behind the upper incisors.

X-Ray/Radiology: This is the only definitive way to diagnose an odontoma. A Skull Radiograph will show a “club-like” or “calcified mass” at the base of the tooth roots.

Management & Treatment

Surgical Extraction: This is a high-level specialized surgery. A vet must remove the entire tooth and the associated mass. If even a small piece of the germinal tissue remains, the odontoma will return.

The “Non-Releasable” Reality: A squirrel that has undergone a full incisor extraction cannot be released. They cannot crack nuts, groom properly, or defend themselves.

Medication Support: While waiting for a surgical consult, use Meloxicam to manage the intense pressure/pain and Doxycycline or Baytril if a secondary sinus infection is present.

Post-Surgical Care (For Sanctuaries)

If you have a squirrel that survives the extraction:

The “Tongue” Issue: Without upper incisors, the tongue often hangs out slightly. Not only is this a cosmetic issue, it can also lead to dehydration as the squirrel may have trouble “scooping” water when drinking. They need deep water bowls or specialized “lapping” stations.

The Hard Truth

Odontomas are often caused by early life trauma (falling from a nest and hitting the face on pavement) which “shocks” the tooth bud. If the mass has already invaded the sinus cavity or is pressing on the brain, the most compassionate path is [Humane Euthanasia](https://www.nwrawildlife.org/page/Rehabilitator_Resources). A squirrel that cannot breathe through its nose lives in a constant state of “suffocation panic.”

heading: Ch. 59 — Oral Formula Burns
text:
## **59\. Oral Formula Burns**

🔴 URGENT – Occurs when formula is heated over 105°F.

A common mistake for new rehabbers is not “shaking and testing” every single syringe. A hot “pocket” in the formula can scald the mouth and throat instantly.

THIS REQUIRES IMMEDIATE VET INTERVENTION AS THE SWELLING OF BOTH THE MOUTH AND THROAT CAN CUT OFF AIR, AS WELL AS MAKE EATING PAINFUL, RESULTING IN STARVATION.

Symptoms: Swelling of the lips/tongue, refusal to eat, drooling, or white/grey patches inside the mouth (dead tissue).

Immediate Action: Flush the mouth with cool (not cold) water or LRS.

Treatment:

Pain: Use Buprenorphine (OTM) or Meloxicam immediately. Oral burns are excruciating and prevent the squirrel from nursing.

Topical: If the lips are burned, apply a thin layer of SSD Cream.

Feeding: Use a [thinner cannula or specialized nipple](https://www.wildlifecenterflorida.org/wp-content/uploads/Rehabilitation-of-Eastern-Gray-Squirrels-2020Formatted-for-PDF-file-1.pdf) and feed room-temperature formula. You may need to tube-feed if the tongue is too swollen to swallow.

Secondary Bacterial Pneumonia (Non-Aspiration)

🔴 HIGH URGENCY – The infection has moved into the “Chest.”

When an Upper Respiratory Infection (URI) is left untreated, the bacteria (Bordetella bronchiseptica, Pasteurella, or Staph) can migrate from the nasal passages into the lower respiratory tract. Unlike “aspiration” pneumonia, which is a sudden mechanical event, this “plain old” bacterial pneumonia is a progressive inflammatory takeover of the lung tissue.

Signs of Progression (URI to Pneumonia)

The “Chest Click”: Rhythmic clicking or popping sounds that remain even after the nose is cleared. This indicates fluid or exudate deep in the lungs.

Abdominal Breathing: The squirrel’s belly is visibly working hard to pull in air (heaving), rather than just the chest moving.

“Puffed” Appearance: The squirrel sits hunched with fur “spiked” or puffed out to trap heat, as the body struggles to maintain its internal temperature while fighting infection.

Deep Lethargy: The squirrel is difficult to rouse and may have a “staring” or unfocused look.

Treatment Protocol (Bacterial Clearance)

STEP 1: Antibiotic Strategy

Since this is a systemic infection of the lung tissue, you need antibiotics that penetrate deeply and handle common respiratory pathogens.

Baytril (Enrofloxacin): Often the first-line choice for bacterial pneumonia in squirrels.

Doxycycline: Highly effective for secondary lung infections, especially if Bordetella or Mycoplasma are suspected.

Amoxicillin/Clavamox: While effective for some, some rehabbers prefer [Baytril or SMZ-TMP](https://www.squirrelrehabilitation.com/aspiration%20pneumonia.htm) to avoid the gastrointestinal “shutdown” often seen with penicillin-based drugs in squirrels. Always use a probiotic like [Bene-Bac](https://henryspets.com/pages/baby-squirrel) 2 hours after any antibiotic dose.

STEP 2: Airway Management

Nebulization: The most effective way to deliver moisture and meds to the lungs. Use a [nebulizer](https://www.facebook.com/groups/108046649534931/posts/2703138016692435/) with 0.9% sterile saline for 10–15 minutes, 2–3 times a day.

Steam Treatment: If no nebulizer is available, use a steamy bathroom to help “thin” the mucus in the lungs so it can be moved out.

STEP 3: Supportive Nursing

Hydration: Pneumonia causes rapid fluid loss through respiration. Use LRS or Pedialyte to keep the mucus “sol” (watery) so the squirrel can clear it.

Heat: Provide constant, low-level warmth on half of the bin to support the immune system.

Propping: Place a small roll of fleece under the chest to [keep the head elevated](https://www.justanswer.com/pet/rt9tp-believe-baby-squirrel-aspiration-pneumonia.html) and reduce the effort needed to breathe.

The “Red Flag” Warning

If you ever see bright red or pink frothy foam coming from a squirrel’s nose or mouth during respiratory distress, this is a sign of acute pulmonary hemorrhage otherwise known as Hemorrhagic-Necrotizing Pneumonia. At that point, the lungs are actively failing, and the prognosis is grave without immediate, high-level veterinary intervention.

Rehabber Warning: The “Hemorrhagic” Risk

Certain rare viral or aggressive bacterial strains can cause “Hemorrhagic-Necrotizing Pneumonia,” where the lungs begin to bleed. If you see pink or bloody discharge from the nose or mouth, the prognosis is grave and immediate Veterinary Intervention is mandatory.

SANITY CHECK: Fortunately, Hemorrhagic-Necrotizing Pneumonia is extremely rare in a standard rehabilitation setting. While it is a terrifying “worst-case scenario,” the actal chances of it being HNP is incredibly rare because it typically requires a perfect storm of a highly virulent bacterial strain and a severely compromised immune system.

What is it?

This is a “flesh-eating” version of pneumonia where the infection is so aggressive that it literally kills the lung tissue (necrosis) and causes it to bleed (hemorrhage). The bacteria—often specialized strains of Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae—release toxins that destroy blood vessels in the lungs, leading to rapid tissue death.

Why it’s Rare

Aspiration vs. Bacterial: Most pneumonia you see is Aspiration Pneumonia, which is a “mechanical” injury from inhaled fluid. While dangerous, it doesn’t typically involve the necrotizing toxins found in these rare bacterial strains.

Pathogen Exposure: These specific necrotizing strains are more common in overcrowded, high-stress environments like laboratory colonies or high-intake “mega-shelters” rather than individual home-rehab settings.

Immune Strength: Even a sick baby squirrel usually has enough “fight” to prevent an infection from becoming necrotizing unless they are also battling something like Metabolic Bone Disease (MBD) or severe starvation.

Honestly, you have a better chance of winning the million-dollar lottery than encountering HNP.

heading: Ch. 60 — Poisoning & Toxin Ingestion
text:
## **60\. Poisoning & Toxin Ingestion**

Poisoning is a rapid-onset emergency. Whether it’s a squirrel that ate a toxic plant (Cycad/Sago Palm) or a victim of secondary rodenticide poisoning, your goal is to stop absorption and reverse the chemical effects.

CRITICAL WARNING: These steps are a “last resort” for when veterinary care is unavailable. If you suspect poisoning, take the squirrel to an experienced vet IMMEDIATELY.

1. Activated Charcoal (The “Sponge”)

Purpose: Prevents poison from being absorbed into the bloodstream.

Dose: 5 grams per kilogram (5g/kg).

Example: For a 500g squirrel, you need 2.5g of charcoal. (If using a 520mg capsule, dissolve 5 capsules in 1-2 mL of water).

When to Use: Effective for most organic poisons, pesticides, and toxic plants.

DO NOT USE FOR: Corrosive agents (lye, acids, cleaning fluids), petroleum products (gasoline/oil), or alcohols. Charcoal will not bind to these and can mask damage.

2. Vitamin K1 (Rodenticide Antidote)

If a squirrel has white/grey gums, is bruising easily, or has blood in the stool/urine after being found in a residential area, assume Anticoagulant Rodenticide (Rat Poison).

Preferred Route: Subcutaneous (Sub-Q). Never give K1 Intravenously (IV) due to high risk of anaphylaxis.

Dosage (Warfarin/First-Gen):

Initial: 2.2 mg/kg Sub-Q.

Follow-up: 1.1 mg/kg Sub-Q every 12 hours until bleeding stops.

Maintenance: Transition to oral K1 for 7 days.

Dosage (Long-acting/Second-Gen):

Follow the initial dose above, but maintain treatment for at least 2 weeks, tapering the dose slowly.

Note: Vitamin K3 is NOT effective for rodenticide poisoning. Always use K1.

3. N-Acetyl Cysteine (NAC) – The “Liver Saver”

NAC is a powerful antioxidant that protects the liver from catastrophic failure, specifically from Acetaminophen (Tylenol) or Cycad (Sago Palm) poisoning.

Success Rate: Highly effective for “down” squirrels who have consumed toxic berries or seeds.

Protocol:

1st Dose: 200 mg powder mixed with liquid (force-feed).

Follow-up: 100 mg orally every 2 hours until the squirrel stabilizes.

The “Zombie” Effect: If a squirrel is unresponsive or acting “mentally gone” due to toxic exposure, NAC can help flush the liver and clear the brain.

4. Poison Triage Flowchart

| If they ate… | Use this… |
| :---: | :---: |
| Toxic Plants / Berries | NAC (N-Acetyl Cysteine) \+ Activated Charcoal. |
| Rat Poison (Anticoagulant) | Vitamin K1 (Sub-Q) \+ Strict cage rest. |
| Pesticides / Chemicals | Activated Charcoal immediately. |
| Cleaning Fluids / Lye | NO CHARCOAL. Flush mouth with water/milk and get to a Vet. |

### **Rodenticide (Rat Poison) Poisoning**

Anticoagulant rat poisons don't kill instantly. They stop the liver from recycling vitamin K, so the body can't make new clotting factors. The squirrel keeps running on the clotting factors already in its blood until they're used up.

**Phase 1 — The silent window (roughly the first 1–3 days).** No symptoms yet. If you know a squirrel ate poison, this is your best chance: start prescription **Vitamin K1** right away, before bleeding begins. Treated in this window, the prognosis is excellent.

**Phase 2 — Bleeding (usually day 3–7).** Once the clotting factors run out, spontaneous internal bleeding starts. **If you see symptoms, the squirrel is already bleeding internally — you have hours, not days.**

Signs it is almost too late:

- Extreme lethargy or weakness; acting "tame" or unresponsive
- Cold or pale paws, ears, and mouth
- Heavy, labored, or rapid breathing (blood in the chest or lungs)
- Blood from the nose or mouth, or in the stool

**Modern rat poison is worse.** Older poisons were warfarin-based and clear the body in about a week. Most products sold today are second-generation anticoagulants (SGARs) such as **brodifacoum** and **bromadiolone** — "superwarfarins" that stay in the liver and remain toxic for months. One dose of vitamin K1 will not save a squirrel that ate an SGAR: it needs **daily oral vitamin K1 for at least 4 weeks**, as your vet directs, or it will relapse and bleed again when treatment stops.

**Never give Vitamin K3 (menadione).** It's sold over the counter as a supplement, it doesn't work against rodenticides, and it is toxic to organs. Only prescription **Vitamin K1 (phytonadione)** works.

One dose of vitamin K1 will not save a squirrel that ate an SGAR: it needs daily oral vitamin K1 for at least 4 weeks, as your vet directs, or it will relapse and bleed again when treatment stops.

Never give Vitamin K3 (menadione). It's sold over the counter as a supplement, it doesn't work against rodenticides, and it is toxic to organs. Only prescription Vitamin K1 (phytonadione) works.

heading: Ch. 61 — Prolapse (Tissue Displacement)
text:
## **61\. Prolapse (Tissue Displacement)**

A prolapse is internal tissue — rectal, vaginal, or penile — pushed out of the body and trapped outside. This tissue is meant to stay moist and internal; outside, it swells, dries, and dies quickly. **Treat it as urgent.**

### **Types**

- **Rectal (most common):** a red "doughnut" at the anus. Causes: severe diarrhea (parasites, bad formula), constipation and straining, or extreme dehydration.
- **Vaginal/uterine:** uncommon in infants; seen in adult females after difficult labor or trauma.
- **Penile (paraphimosis):** see 61A below.

### **Triage — Treat at Home or Go to the Vet?**

| What you see | What it means | Action |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Small, pea-sized, moist, bright pink bubble; no bleeding | Minor | Home care: the Sugar Shrink below. If it stays in after 1–2 treatments, monitor 24 hours. |
| More than about **1/4 inch** out, a "tube," dark red or purple, or bleeding | Significant | **Vet immediately** — often needs a purse-string suture or surgical reduction. |
| Dripping blood, or black, grey, or cold tissue | Dying (necrotic) | **Do not push it back in** — pushing dead tissue inside can cause fatal internal rot. Needs surgical debridement or amputation. |

**Transport:** keep the tissue soaked in warm saline or coated in K-Y Jelly the whole drive. Never let it dry out.

### **The Sugar Shrink (Home Care for Small, Pink Prolapses)**

Sugar is a powerful osmotic agent: it draws the excess fluid out of swollen tissue so it shrinks and can slide back where it belongs.

1. **Cleanse:** flush gently with warm saline or plain water to remove debris and hair.
2. **Keep it moist:** if you can't start right away, coat with unscented water-soluble lubricant (K-Y Jelly) or plain Vitamin E oil.
3. **Sugar:** coat the tissue with **granulated white table sugar** — dry, or as a thick paste with a few drops of water. Sugar substitutes do not work.
4. **Wait 15–30 minutes.** You'll see the tissue shrink and shift from dark red/purple toward pink as the sugar draws out the fluid.
5. **Rinse and lubricate:** rinse with lukewarm saline, then apply K-Y Jelly, plain coconut oil, or warm saline.
6. **The nudge:** with a gloved finger or a lubricated cotton swab, guide the tissue back gently. **Never force it.** If it won't go easily, re-sugar and wait longer.
7. **If sugar isn't enough:** a cool (not freezing) saline compress helps the tissue retreat.

**Sugar vs. honey:** sugar is preferred — because it's dry, it draws moisture out faster. Honey works if it's all you have.

### **After It's Back In**

- **Preparation H without lidocaine** (and without the "cooling" menthol) can help keep swelling down. Never use products containing lidocaine, pramoxine, or benzocaine — see the Never-Use list (Ch. 80).
- **Purse-string suture:** if it keeps popping out, a vet will need to place one while the inflammation heals. Many squirrels need one even after a successful reduction.
- **Diet:** low-residue or liquid diet (mashed blocks, formula) for 24–48 hours to prevent straining.
- **Hydration:** prolapse is often a sign of a stressed gut. Increase Sub-Q fluids (Ch. 32).

### **Fix the Cause — or It Comes Back Within the Hour**

- **Diarrhea:** BRAT diet (Ch. 5, 11D); check for coccidia and Giardia (Ch. 33).
- **Constipation:** the Constipation Ladder in Ch. 41.
- **Parasites:** fecal check and deworming (Formulary: Panacur, Ponazuril).
- **Nursing siblings:** separate them immediately. "Suckle-shaming" doesn't work — physical separation is the only way to save the genitals of the victim (see Ch. 40).

### **61A. Paraphimosis (Penile Prolapse)**

*Contributed by Danielle Bourgeois, Licensed Wildlife Rehabber.*

Paraphimosis is when the penis is trapped outside the sheath (prepuce) and can't retract. It does occur in squirrels — especially males in care — and it can quickly become serious. Exposed tissue dries, swells, gets injured, and can become infected; severe cases progress to necrosis and may need surgery.

**Causes**

- Sibling nursing or self-suckling — common in lonely orphans (Ch. 40)
- Hair, bedding fibers, or debris constricting the area (hair rings)
- Dehydration, which reduces tissue elasticity
- Trauma
- Infection or inflammation
- Neurological problems affecting retraction
- Hormonal influences in juveniles or during breeding season

**Early signs**

- The penis is visible and does not retract
- Swelling or redness
- Dry, darkened, or cracked tissue
- Excessive grooming or biting at the area
- Lethargy or reduced appetite (advanced cases)

**Immediate first aid** — time is critical.

1. **Keep it moist:** sterile water-based lubricant (plain K-Y Jelly). Nothing medicated unless your vet directs it.
2. **Reduce swelling:** granulated sugar (preferred) or honey. Apply gently and give it time.
3. **Clean gently:** sterile saline to remove debris. Check for — and gently remove — any hair ring.
4. **Retract if mild and early:** with clean hands or gloves, guide the penis back into the sheath very gently. Do not force it.

**Stop and get to a vet if**

- Swelling is significant or getting worse
- Tissue is dark, cold, or damaged
- You can't easily retract it
- It has been out for more than a short time
- **He can't urinate**
- He is in pain or declining

**Prevention:** no loose threads or fibrous nesting material; keep babies well hydrated and fed; minimize unnecessary handling; check males visually during routine care; separate siblings who nurse on each other.

**Prognosis:** with early care, many cases resolve with no lasting effects. Delay sharply raises the risk of complications.

heading: Ch. 62 — Rabies & Small Rodents — National Guidance
text:
## **62\. Rabies & Small Rodents — National Guidance**

**The CDC Position:** According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, small rodents (including squirrels, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chipmunks, rats, and mice) and lagomorphs (including rabbits and hares) are almost never found to be infected with rabies and have not been known to transmit rabies to humans. A squirrel is extremely unlikely to transmit rabies, and post-exposure prophylaxis is almost never indicated following contact with rodents.

**Transmission reality:** While technically possible, rabies transmission from small rodents to humans is documented only in extremely rare circumstances. The primary rabies vectors in North America are bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes — not squirrels.

**Local protocols:** State regulations governing rabies reporting, animal testing, and post-exposure protocols vary significantly. Contact your **state fish and wildlife agency** and local health department for jurisdiction-specific guidance.

⚪️ EXTREMELY RARE – A “Dead-End” Host.

In the world of rehab, the “R-word” is the ultimate boogeyman. For a seasoned rehabber, the conversation about Rabies isn’t about fear—it’s about Risk Assessment and Public Health protocol.

The short version? It is statistically microscopic in squirrels, but because it is 100% fatal to humans, we never, ever play “cowboy” with the rules.

According to the CDC (Centers for Disease Control), small rodents like squirrels, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chipmunks, rats, and mice, as well as rabbits and hares, are almost never found to be infected with rabies and have not been known to transmit rabies to humans.

Why Squirrels Don’t “Carry” Rabies

The “Size” Problem: Rabies is transmitted via a bite from a predator (raccoon, skunk, fox, bat). If a predator big enough to carry rabies bites a squirrel, the squirrel usually dies from the physical trauma of the attack before the virus can ever incubate.

Viral Load: Even if they survive the bite, their small body mass doesn’t typically support the viral shedding necessary to pass it on through their own saliva.

The “Mimic” Signs (What People Confuse for Rabies)

Most “rabies scares” reported by the public are actually one of these common rehab issues:

Head Trauma: Circling, “stargazing,” or lack of fear of humans.

Raccoon Roundworm (Baylisascaris procyonis): This parasite migrates to the brain, causing severe neurological “zombie-like” behavior that looks exactly like the “dumb” form of rabies.

Severe MBD: Twitching, spasming, and “foaming” at the mouth during a calcium-crash seizure.

Heat Stroke: Staggering, drooling, and disorientation.

Emergency Triage: The “If” Protocol

In the one-in-a-million chance you encounter a squirrel that is aggressively lunging, biting inanimate objects, or showing extreme hydrophobia (fear of water):

Zero Contact: Use a hard-sided carrier and thick welding gloves. Do not let the animal’s saliva touch your skin or mucous membranes.

No Rehabilitation: If an animal is a legitimate rabies suspect, State Wildlife Protocols usually mandate immediate euthanasia and testing. You cannot “treat” rabies.

The Bite Rule: If you are bitten by any wild animal showing neurological signs, you must contact your local Health Department immediately. They will decide if Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) is required.

Rehabber Reality Check

In many states, squirrels aren’t even on the “High-Risk Vector” list. However, as a permitted rehabber, your State Permit likely requires you to report any “neurological animal of unknown origin.”

The Bottom Line: You are 1,000 times more likely to get Cat Scratch Fever or Tularemia from a squirrel than you are to ever see a case of Rabies.
