heading: Ch. 63 — Refeeding Syndrome (The Hunger Trap)
text:
## **63\. Refeeding Syndrome (The Hunger Trap)**

🔴 CRITICAL DANGER – Do NOT feed a starved squirrel immediately.

In the world of animal rescue, “starving” is a physiological trap. When a squirrel has been without food for days, its intracellular electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus) are depleted. If you suddenly flood the system with glucose or high-protein formula, a massive insulin spike occurs, driving those already-low electrolytes into the cells and causing the heart to stop.

Refeeding syndrome is a metabolic crash that happens when a “hollow” body is given calories too quickly. You will see a squirrel that looks like it’s recovering suddenly “crash” and die 12–72 hours after its first big meal.

Signs of Severe Emaciation

The “Hollow” Look: Sunken eyes (dehydration), prominent spine/pelvis, and “tucked” abdomen.

The “Chill”: Body temperature is below 97°F (36°C) because they have no fat to burn for heat.

Mentation: Lethargic, slow to respond, or “flat.”

Emergency Stabilization Protocol (The 24-Hour Rule)

STEP 1: Restore Heat First

Internal Engine: A cold squirrel cannot digest. If you feed a squirrel whose body temp is below 98°F, the food will sit in the gut and rot (bloat).

Action: Incubate or place on a heating pad for at least 2 hours until the torso and extremities feel warm to the touch.

STEP 2: The Hydration Bridge (Hours 0–12)

Electrolyte Push: Do not start with formula. Start with Lactated Ringers (LRS) or Unflavored Pedialyte.

The Goal: Dilute the concentrated toxins in the blood and “wake up” the kidneys before they have to process protein.

STEP 3: The Slow Introduction (Hours 12–48)

The “Dilution” Method: Start with a 1:4 ratio (1 part formula to 4 parts water/LRS).

Frequency: Small, frequent feedings (every 2 hours) are safer than one large “fill-up.”

The Transition: Only increase the concentration (1:3, then 1:2) if the squirrel has normal stool and no Bloat.

Monitoring for “The Crash”

Watch for these signs of Refeeding Syndrome during the first 3 days:

Sudden Edema: Swelling of the limbs or “puffy” face (heart/kidney failure).

Muscle Weakness: Sudden inability to lift the head or “paddling” limbs.

Respiratory Distress: Fluid in the lungs caused by the sudden shift in electrolytes.

Rehabber Insight: The Phosphorus Spike

The biggest killer in refeeding is Phosphorus. Many high-quality formulas are phosphorus-dense. If the squirrel’s phosphorus levels spike too fast, it will drive their blood calcium to zero, triggering an MBD Seizure. Have your Calcium/Tums “Glop” ready during the first 48 hours of refeeding just in case.

heading: Ch. 64 — Screwworm (New World Screwworms)
text:
## **64\. Screwworm (New World Screwworms)**

🔴 CRITICAL – A Reportable, Flesh-Eating Emergency.

Unlike common maggots that eat dead tissue, [Screwworms](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/cattle/ticks/screwworm) eat live, healthy flesh.

Symptoms: Wounds that “shimmer” with movement; a foul, distinct odor; and deep, “bored” holes that look like a screw being driven into wood.

Treatment:

Removal: Do not just flush; they must be physically removed with forceps.

Chemical: Use Ivermectin from your list; it is highly effective at killing larvae internally.

Legal: Screwworm is a USDA-reportable disease in many states. If you find them, you must notify your State Veterinarian.

Severe Bleeding & Hemorrhage Control

Hemorrhage in small mammals can lead to rapid onset of shock and death. Immediate, calm intervention is required.

Warning Signs of Critical Blood Loss

Active, pulsing, or pooling blood that does not slow with initial pressure.

Systemic Signs: Gums becoming pale or white, weakness, cool extremities, or gasping (signs of hypovolemic shock).

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

Apply Direct Pressure: Use a clean cloth, sterile gauze, or a finger. Apply firm, constant pressure directly onto the wound.

The “5-Minute Rule”: Hold pressure for 5 to 10 full minutes without lifting the cloth to “check.” Lifting the gauze too early tears away the initial clot and restarts the bleeding.

Manage Shock: Keep the squirrel warm and quiet. Wrap the body (excluding the wound area) in a fleece or “snuggle” to maintain core body temperature during blood loss.

If Bleeding Persists

Hemostatic Agents: Apply Styptic Powder (Kwik Stop) or a silver nitrate stick to the wound site if pressure alone is failing.

Secondary Pressure: Apply a second layer of gauze over the first (do not remove the soaked original layer) and hold for another 10 minutes.

VETERINARY EMERGENCY: If bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes of continuous pressure, the animal requires professional ligation or surgical glue. Keep pressure applied during transport.

Post-Bleeding Care

Do Not Disturb the Clot: Once bleeding stops, do not clean the wound or “scrub” the area, as this will re-trigger the hemorrhage.

Infection Control: Once stable, start a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics (Baytril or Clavamox) as most traumatic bleeds (bites, cat attacks, or fence injuries) carry high bacterial loads.

Monitor for Re-bleeding: Check the site every hour for the first 4 hours.

Special Case: Broken Toenails

While they look dramatic, nail bleeds are rarely life-threatening but very painful.

Pack the Nail: Use Styptic Powder. If unavailable, pack the nail with flour or cornstarch.

Pressure: Maintain firm pressure on the toe for 5 minutes.

Prevention: Keep claws trimmed in older rehablings to prevent snagging on fleece bedding.

Prevention: Keep claws trimmed in older rehablings to prevent snagging on fleece bedding.

heading: Ch. 65 — Seizures
text:
## **65\. Seizures**

🔴 CRITICAL EMERGENCY – Stay Calm and Protect the Patient

A seizure is a sudden surge of electrical activity in the brain. While frightening to watch, your primary goal is to prevent the squirrel from injuring itself during the episode.

Signs of a Seizure

Physical: Uncontrolled shaking, rigid limbs, or “paddling” (legs moving as if swimming).

Loss of Control: Loss of consciousness, drooling, or accidental bladder/bowel release.

The “Freeze”: Some seizures involve a vacant stare or total lack of responsiveness rather than active shaking.

Emergency Response Protocol

STEP 1: Immediate Safety (The “Hands-Off” Rule)

DO NOT Restrain: Forcing the squirrel to stay still can cause broken bones or hyperthermia.

Clear the Area: Remove hard objects, water bowls, or climbing toys the squirrel could hit.

Padding: Gently slide a soft fleece or towel under the squirrel if possible, but DO NOT put anything in their mouth.

Time It: Note the exact start and end time. A seizure lasting more than 2-3 minutes is a Status Epilepticus emergency.

STEP 2: The Recovery Phase (Post-Ictal)

Isolation: Once the shaking stops, place the squirrel in a dark, warm, quiet box.

Reorientation: Expect them to be blind, disoriented, or aggressive for 15–30 minutes as they wake up. This is normal.

Minimal Handling: Keep touch to an absolute minimum to prevent triggering a second seizure.

STEP 3: Triage & Cause Assessment

If the squirrel is alert enough to swallow, place one drop of Sugar Water or Honey on their gums. This can be life-saving if the cause is Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar).

Common Causes to Report to Your Vet:

Head Trauma: Did the squirrel fall recently?

Metabolic Bone Disease (MBD): Calcium deficiency is a leading cause of seizures in captives.

Toxin Exposure: Could they have nibbled a toxic plant or been exposed to chemicals?

Overheating: Check if the enclosure is too close to a heat source.

Medical Warnings

Medication Interaction: DO NOT apply Revolution (Selamectin) or other parasite treatments to a squirrel prone to seizures, as these can lower the seizure threshold.

Veterinary Care: Seek a Wildlife Veterinarian immediately if seizures recur or last longer than 2 minutes. Anti-seizure medication (like Phenobarbital) may be required.

Seizures & Muscle Tremors

Seizures and tremors in squirrels are neurological emergencies. While they can be caused by head trauma or low blood sugar, the most frequent cause in a rehab setting is a “Calcium Crash” associated with Metabolic Bone Disease (MBD).

Warning Signs

Physical: Full-body tremors, “paddling” of the limbs (as if swimming), or rhythmic twitching of the face and paws.

Behavioral: Inability to stand, loss of consciousness, or star-gazing (head tilted back sharply).

Post-Ictal State: After a seizure, the squirrel may be blind, disoriented, or extremely exhausted for several minutes.

EMERGENCY RESPONSE: DO THIS NOW

Ensure Safety: Move the squirrel to a small, heavily padded carrier with soft fleece. Remove all hard objects, branches, or water bowls to prevent self-injury during a fit.

DO NOT Restrain: Do not attempt to hold the squirrel down. This can cause broken bones or over-heating.

Immediate Calcium (The “Rescue” Dose):

If the squirrel is conscious enough to swallow, rub Liquid Calcium Gluconate or a dissolved Tums/water slurry directly onto the gums.

Absorption through the oral mucous membranes is the fastest way to stop an MBD-related seizure.

Sugar Boost: If you suspect low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), rub a drop of Karo Syrup or honey on the gums as well.

Secondary Treatment & Stabilization

Follow-Up Calcium: If the tremors stop after the first dose, continue administering oral calcium every 4 to 6 hours until the squirrel is fully stable and eating. Refer to the MBD Protocol for long-term dosing.

Quiet & Dark: Keep the squirrel in a completely dark, silent room. Sensory input (light/noise) can trigger another seizure.

Hydration: Once the seizure has passed and the squirrel is alert, offer warm oral rehydration fluids (Pedialyte).

Identifying the Cause

Metabolic Bone Disease (MBD): Most common. Usually seen in squirrels on poor diets (nuts only) or those transitioning off formula too early.

Head Trauma: Likely if the squirrel was a fall victim or “hit by car.” Note: Do not use Doxycycline in these cases as it may lower the seizure threshold.

Toxin Ingestion: If the tremors are accompanied by vomiting or extreme salivation.

heading: Ch. 66 — Self-Mutilation (Automutilation)
text:
## **66\. Self-Mutilation (Automutilation)**

🔴 URGENT BEHAVIORAL CRISIS – Stop the Cycle Immediately

Self-mutilation is rarely about behavioral “craziness”; it is a physiological response to nerve pain or numbness. If a squirrel begins to chew its own paws, tail, or surgical sites, it can cause more damage in ten minutes than the original injury did in the first place.

Identifying the Triggers

Neuropathic Pain: “Phantom” sensations or stinging as spinal/nerve injuries heal.

The “Numb” Factor: If a limb has no feeling, the squirrel may treat it as a foreign object attached to its body and try to remove it.

Stress & Confinement: Intense “cage rage” in high-energy older juveniles or adults.

The Intervention Protocol

STEP 1: Immediate Chemical Restraint

You cannot “reason” with a squirrel in this state. You must address the internal “noise” in their nervous system.

Gabapentin: This is your primary tool for Neuropathic Pain. It “quiets” the misfiring nerves that cause the chewing urge.

Trazodone: Provides necessary sedation to lower the squirrel’s overall drive to obsess over the injury site.

Meloxicam: Essential if the chewing is driven by active inflammation or “throbbing” pain.

STEP 2: Physical Barriers (The “Hardware” Store)

The E-Collar: For squirrels, a standard “cone” is often useless. Use a “Neck Pillow” or “Donut” collar made of soft fleece or vet wrap. It must be wide enough to prevent them from reaching their hindquarters but light enough to allow them to eat.

The “Squirrel Burrito” (Temporary): If the squirrel is actively self-destructing, wrap them in a snug Fleece Wrap to provide “swaddled” security while other interventions take effect.

Bitters: Applying a bitter spray (like Grannick’s Bitter Apple) around the wound (never in it) can sometimes act as a deterrent, though many squirrels will power through the taste.

STEP 3: Environment & Distraction

Texture Management: If they are chewing a foot, ensure the bedding is not “loopy” (like terry cloth) which can snag and cause further frustration. Use flat Anti-Pill Fleece.

Heavy Enrichment: Provide safe items to chew instead of their bodies—fresh apple branches, antler chews, or hard nut shells.

When to Call It

Self-mutilation has a high rate of secondary infection (Sepsis). If a squirrel has chewed down to the bone or removed significant portions of a limb, the prognosis for release drops to near zero.

The “Deep Pain” Check: If they are chewing a limb because they cannot feel it, and there is no return of sensation after 14–21 days, the limb may require Veterinary Amputation or euthanasia.

When a squirrel suffers major trauma—especially severe burns or deep cat bites—the primary threat shifts from the initial injury to Sepsis (blood poisoning). For a seasoned rehabber, catching the “Septic Shift” early is the only way to prevent a total organ collapse.

heading: Ch. 67 — Sepsis & Septic Shock
text:
## **67\. Sepsis & Septic Shock**

🔴 CRITICAL – Systemic failure due to overwhelming infection.

When a squirrel suffers major trauma—especially severe burns or deep cat bites—the primary threat shifts from the initial injury to Sepsis (blood poisoning). For a seasoned rehabber, catching the “Septic Shift” early is the only way to prevent a total organ collapse.

Sepsis is the body’s extreme, life-threatening response to an infection. In burn victims, the loss of the skin barrier allows bacteria to flood the bloodstream, triggering a “cytokine storm” that causes the heart, kidneys, and lungs to shut down.

Stage 1: Early Sepsis (The Red Alert)

In the early “hyperdynamic” stage, the squirrel’s body is fighting hard.

The “Septic Blush”: Gums and the skin on the belly may look bright, “brick red” (injected) due to massive vessel dilation.

Rapid Vitals: Tachycardia (racing heart) and tachypnea (rapid, shallow breathing).

The Temperature Swing: A sudden spike in fever (\>104°F) or, conversely, a sudden drop into hypothermia (\<97°F).

Bounding Pulse: The pulse feels very strong and “thumping” against your fingers.

Stage 2: Septic Shock (The Crash)

This is the stage of cardiovascular collapse where blood pressure bottom outs.

Mentation: The squirrel becomes disoriented, confused, or “glassy-eyed”.

Poor Perfusion: Gums turn “muddy,” grey, or pale.

Cold Extremities: Paws and tail feel icy as the body pulls blood to the core.

Urine Output: The squirrel stops peeing because the kidneys are failing.

Emergency Intervention (From Your Formulary)

1. Aggressive Hydration (LRS)

Push Fluids: Septic shock is “distributive shock.” The fluid is in the body, but it’s “leaking” out of the blood vessels. You must provide warm Sub-Q or IV Lactated Ringers (LRS) to maintain blood pressure.

2. The “Big Guns” Antibiotic Load

Baytril \+ Clavamox: In a septic crisis, you often need a combination to cover both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria.

Loading Dose: Do not wait for the “next scheduled dose.” If you suspect sepsis, administer the first dose immediately.

3. Anti-Inflammatory Support

Meloxicam: Use to address the massive systemic inflammation. However, if the squirrel is severely dehydrated, ensure they have received fluids first to protect the kidneys.

4. Glucose Support

The Honey/Karo Rub: Sepsis consumes glucose at an astronomical rate. Rub honey or sugar water on the gums every 30 minutes to prevent a fatal hypoglycemic crash.

The “Burn Sepsis” Timeline

Day 1-2: Usually “Burn Shock” (fluid loss).

Day 3-5: This is the peak window for Septicemia. If a burn victim makes it to Day 3 and suddenly stops eating or develops “brick red” gums, they are likely septic.

heading: Ch. 68 — Shootings
text:
## **68\. Shootings**

BBS VERSUS PELLETS VERSUS BULLETS

Ballistic Injuries (BBs vs. Pellets)

Squirrels are frequent victims of “nuisance” shooting. When a squirrel arrives with a small, circular puncture wound, you must determine what is inside. The composition of the projectile dictates the entire course of treatment.

1. The BB (Steel/Copper-Coated)

Appearance on X-ray: A perfect, bright white circle.

Material: Usually steel or zinc-coated steel.

The “Leave It” Rule: Steel is relatively inert. If a BB is lodged in muscle tissue or under the skin and is not near a joint, a major vessel, or the spinal cord, it is often safer to leave it in place.

The Outcome: The body will form a fibrous capsule (scar tissue) around the BB. Digging for a BB often causes more trauma than the projectile itself.

2. The Pellet (Lead Airgun Ammunition)

Appearance on X-ray: Often looks like a “mushroom” or a flattened, irregular white shape (because lead is soft and deforms on impact).

Material: Soft Lead.

The “Must Remove” Rule: Lead is toxic. Over time, the body’s acidic fluids break down the lead, allowing it to enter the bloodstream. This leads to Lead Poisoning, causing seizures, blindness, and organ failure.

The Outcome: If a lead pellet is present, it must be surgically removed by a vet once the squirrel is stable.

3. Triage & Stabilization

| Action | Protocol |
| :---: | :---: |
| Wound Cleaning | Flush the entry hole with dilute Betadine. Never flush a wound if you suspect the projectile entered the chest or abdominal cavity (this can cause drowning/sepsis). |
| Antibiotics | Non-negotiable. Projectiles carry fur and bacteria deep into the wound. Start Baytril or Clavamox immediately. |
| Pain Management | These injuries are excruciating. Use Meloxicam for inflammation and, if available through a vet, an opioid for the first 48 hours. |
| Fracture Check | Projectiles often shatter bone. If the squirrel is dragging a limb near a puncture, assume a “comminuted fracture” (shattered bone) and stabilize with a wrap. |

4. Lead Poisoning “Chelation”

If you suspect a lead pellet has been in the squirrel for a while (chronic injury), watch for neurological signs.

Signs: Grinding teeth, star-gazing, or “lead palsy” (wrist drop/weakness).

Treatment: Vets may use Calcium EDTA or Succimer to “bind” the lead and flush it out of the system.

5. Critical “Do Not Touch” Zones

Regardless of whether it is a BB or a Pellet, if the projectile is in the Chest (Thorax) or Brain, the prognosis is guarded.If a chest wound is present, see §29 Collapsed Lung (Pneumothorax).

heading: Ch. 69 — Spinal Trauma & Hind-Limb Paralysis
text:
## **69\. Spinal Trauma & Hind-Limb Paralysis**

🟠 MODERATE TO HIGH URGENCY – The “Wait and See” Game

Spinal injuries usually result from falls (“flat-back” landings) or crushing trauma. In squirrels, the difference between a temporary “spinal shock” and permanent paralysis often comes down to inflammation management and time.

Triage: Assessing the Damage

A thorough assessment is crucial to understand the extent of the injury:

Deep Pain Reflex: Gently stimulate a back toe to see if the squirrel shows a brain response, such as pulling back or vocalizing. A simple leg twitch is a local reflex and does not indicate deep pain sensation.

Proprioception: Position the paw so the knuckles are on the ground. Observe if the squirrel can immediately correct the paw’s position.

The “Step-Off”: Carefully feel along the spine for any abnormal gaps or changes in alignment.

Emergency Management

Initial care focuses on reducing inflammation and preventing further injury:

Anti-Inflammatory Support: Managing swelling is critical for spinal cord injuries. A veterinarian can recommend appropriate anti-inflammatory medications.

Pain Management: Addressing potential nerve pain is important. Medications can help alleviate discomfort and prevent the squirrel from self-mutilating.

Strict Rest: Confine the squirrel to a small, secure enclosure to prevent movement that could worsen the injury. Avoid any opportunity for climbing or jumping.

Rehabber “Best Practices”

The “Hamster Wheel” Warning: Do not allow a spinal patient to climb. Use a “flat-only” enclosure with high-loft fleece to prevent pressure sores (decubital ulcers).

The 3-Week Window: Nerve tissue heals at a snail’s pace. Many squirrels regain function after 21 days of strict cage rest. If there is no improvement after 3 weeks, quality-of-life discussions are necessary.

Critical Nursing Care

Ongoing care involves addressing potential complications:

Bladder Management: Paralyzed squirrels may need assistance with bladder emptying. A trained professional can demonstrate how to express the bladder manually to prevent complications.

Skin Care: Maintaining clean and dry skin is essential, especially in the groin area, to prevent irritation and infection.

Comfortable Bedding: Use soft, supportive bedding to prevent pressure sores on immobile areas.

Note for Experienced Individuals: If a squirrel shows no deep pain sensation after a week, the prognosis for full recovery and release is significantly reduced. However, some squirrels initially presenting as paralyzed can regain function within a few weeks as swelling subsides.

heading: Ch. 70 — Squirrel King (Tail Entanglement)
text:
## **70\. Squirrel King (Tail Entanglement)**

This is a rare but critical emergency. It occurs when pine sap, nesting material, and feces fuse the tails of a litter together. As the squirrels grow and move in different directions, the knot tightens, cutting off circulation and leading to panic, mutual biting, and necrosis.

1. The Golden Rule: Sedation or “The Hood”

Do not attempt to untangle a Squirrel King while the animals are fully alert and frantic.

The Risk: They will bite each other and you. The more they pull, the more they damage the delicate tail vertebrae.

The Action: If you have access to a vet, Isoflurane (gas sedation) is the only way to do this safely. If you are in the field, cover the entire “cluster” with a heavy, dark fleece to induce a “freeze” response.

2. The Solvent Protocol (Sap Removal)

Do not use scissors initially. You cannot see where one tail ends and the other begins in a sap-clot.

Vegetable/Mineral Oil: Saturate the entire knot in warm oil. This begins to break down the sticky resins in the pine sap.

Alcohol (Isopropyl): Use a cotton swab soaked in alcohol to “dissolve” the sap bond.

Warning: Alcohol is chilling. Only use small amounts and keep the squirrels on a heating pad.

The “Slow Pick”: Use a blunt-nosed pair of tweezers or a seam ripper to slowly tease the hairs apart. Do not pull. If the hair is bonded to the skin, you must dissolve the bond, not rip the hair.

3. Medical Triage: Post-Separation

Once the squirrels are free, you must assess the damage to each individual tail.

Circulation Check: If a tail is cold, hard, or “wooden” to the touch, the blood supply has been cut off for too long.

Degloving: If the skin has been pulled off during the struggle, refer to Ch. 53 (Degloving).

Self-Mutilation: Check for “chew sites.” Squirrels in a King cluster often bite at the tails of their siblings to try and free themselves. These punctures need immediate antibiotics (Baytril/Clavamox) to prevent infection.

4. The “Stink” of Necrosis

If the cluster has a foul, rotting smell, at least one tail is already necrotic.

The Fix: The dead portion of the tail will eventually dry up and fall off (self-amputation), or a vet will need to perform a surgical amputation. A squirrel can survive and be released with a partial tail, but they must have enough “stump” for balance.

heading: Ch. 71 — Squirrel Pox (Fibromatosis)
text:
## **71\. Squirrel Pox (Fibromatosis)**

🔴 HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS – The “Quarantine” Nightmare.

A viral infection that causes multiple tumors (fibromas) across the body.

Symptoms: Multiple raised, [skin-colored or dark nodules](https://www.in.gov/dnr/fish-and-wildlife/wildlife-resources/wildlife-diseases-in-indiana/squirrel-pox/) around the eyes, nose, and joints.

Treatment:

Isolation: Strict 21-day to 4-month quarantine%20Squirrel%20Poxvirus.pdf).

Supportive: While there is no “cure,” Acyclovir (Zovirax) may be used to slow viral replication. Use Meloxicam for the pain of ulcerated nodules.

Secondary: If nodules are “leaky,” start Baytril to prevent sepsis.

The Squirrel Pox Virus Disease is usually fatal to red squirrels. Grey squirrels are carriers of the infection and can spread the disease to red squirrels. Greys have developed immunity to the disease having been exposed to the virus for many years.

In sharp contrast, the mortality rate for untreated infected red squirrels in the wild appears to be 100%, most dying within 15 days of being infected.

[Squirrel pox](https://www.google.com/search?q=Squirrel+pox&rlz=1C1ONGR_enUS1030US1030&oq=is+squirrel+pox+fatal+to+fox+squirrels&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIHCAEQIRigAdIBCDUwOTVqMGo0qAIAsAIB&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8&mstk=AUtExfAAKlstx7-EO8N1lQPvF_A3j7kKDB3LAo-P1b2CQ_u8M4iC6HUsnC9kCvcUTDAJy6uGslmRx7A2sJ2NnNx8uy-jV8sgnOrcjQcSsBKgFL8v2BVw0IGOOrg8ZRwu1xIj8K16NASque_rQVBoiuZ9oXDYNXYlgWMgt8H6Kk3oPevlmB3mCGgBxwbZUpQ3A75XR15kTICuRPmqIL0GSHNY11I-nzkz0NEHGrs-gb-GD1RCgM77rtW7WWAtxKHCNul1rpdCCaCzW7t2EJmjFv3BQyWF&csui=3&ved=2ahUKEwjp6fGQvdKSAxXaITQIHeC2OSYQgK4QegQIARAB) (squirrel fibroma virus) can be fatal to fox squirrels, particularly in severe cases, although it is not always 100% fatal. The virus causes tumors on the skin, which can lead to death from starvation if they obstruct vision, feeding, or cause secondary infections. While often affecting juveniles more, the disease can be severe, with no known cure.

heading: Ch. 72 — Starvation
text:
## **72\. Starvation**

Starvation & Metabolic Collapse

A starved squirrel is not just “thin.” Their body has entered Catabolism, a state where it is literally digesting its own muscle and organ tissue to stay alive. Their electrolyte balance is precarious, and their insulin response is “sleeping.”

1. Clinical Signs of Starvation

The “Razor Back”: The spine and shoulder blades are prominent, with deep hollows where the thigh muscles should be.

Sunken Eyes: A sign of both dehydration and the loss of the fat pads behind the eyeballs.

Hypothermia: Starved squirrels cannot generate body heat. They will feel like “ice cubes.”

Lethargy: They may be too weak to lift their heads or even swallow.

2. The Starvation Triage Protocol

DO NOT GIVE FORMULA YET. If you put complex proteins or fats into a starved gut, the squirrel will bloat and die.

Heat First: Warm the squirrel slowly over 1–2 hours. A cold gut cannot move food (peristalsis).

Hydrate & Energize: Start with warm Pedialyte or 5% Dextrose. This “wakes up” the kidneys and provides immediate glucose to the brain without requiring complex digestion.

The 24-Hour Rule: For a severely emaciated squirrel, stay on clear fluids/dextrose for the first 12–24 hours to ensure they are urinating and “priming” the system.

3. Introducing Food (The “Dilution” Method)

When you finally move to formula, you must go slow:

Step 1: 25% Formula / 75% Water (or Pedialyte) for 2–3 feedings.

Step 2: 50/50 mix for the next 24 hours.

Step 3: Only move to full-strength formula once the squirrel is passing normal (though perhaps small) stools and shows no signs of bloating.

4. Refeeding Syndrome (The Internal Crash)

See Ch. 63, Refeeding Syndrome. Key Concept: When a starved body suddenly receives a “payload” of calories (especially carbohydrates), it triggers a massive insulin spike. This causes Potassium, Magnesium, and Phosphorus to be pulled out of the blood and into the cells. This sudden drop in blood electrolytes causes heart failure, seizures, and death.

5. The “Golden Spoon” Rule

In starved adults or older juveniles, offer “easy” calories first:

Beef Baby Food: High protein, easy to lick, and requires minimal chewing effort.

Avocado (No skin/pit): High in “good fats” to help rebuild weight quickly once the gut is stable.

heading: Ch. 73 — Tapeworms (Cestodes)
text:
## **73\. Tapeworms (Cestodes)**

Tapeworms are internal parasites that live in the squirrel’s small intestine, stealing nutrients from the food the squirrel eats. Unlike roundworms, tapeworms require an intermediate host (usually a flea or a beetle) to complete their life cycle.

1. Identification: The “Moving Rice” Sign

The Segments (Proglottids): You will see small, white, flat segments that look like grains of rice. These may be seen in the feces or stuck to the fur around the squirrel’s tail/anus.

Movement: When fresh, these segments often “inch” or wiggle. As they dry out, they look like hard, yellowed sesame seeds.

Secondary Signs: Pot-bellied appearance (despite being thin), voracious appetite with no weight gain, and “scooting” or biting at the tail area due to itching.

2. The Transmission Cycle (How they got it)

The Flea Connection: The most common tapeworm (Dipylidium caninum) is transmitted when a squirrel swallows an infected flea while grooming.

The “Prey” Connection: If you have an older rehab squirrel that has been catching insects, they may have ingested a beetle or other intermediate host.

3. Treatment: Praziquantel

Tapeworms do not respond to standard “over-the-counter” roundworm medications like Pyrantel. You must use Praziquantel (found in brands like Droncit or Drontal).

The Protocol: \* Dose: 5–10 mg/kg orally or by injection.

Frequency: Usually a single dose is sufficient to kill the adult worms. However, many rehabbers repeat the dose in 10–14 days to ensure any newly matured worms (from recently ingested fleas) are cleared.

The “Dissolve” Factor: You won’t usually see “dead worms” in the stool after treatment. Praziquantel works by disintegrating the worm’s skin, allowing the squirrel’s body to actually digest the parasite.

4. Triage & Volunteer Safety (Zoonotic Risk)

Can Humans Get It? Technically, yes, but only if you swallow the intermediate host (the flea). You cannot get tapeworms from touching the squirrel or the segments in the stool.

Prevention: \* Wash Hands: Standard protocol after every handling.

Flea Control: You cannot cure tapeworms if you don’t kill the fleas. Treat the squirrel and the bedding immediately (Formulary: Capstar, Revolution), or the squirrel will just re-infect itself within days.

heading: Ch. 75 — Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
text:
## **75\. Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)**

🟡 MODERATE TO HIGH URGENCY – Prevent Kidney Failure.

n a rehab setting, a Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) is rarely a standalone issue. It is almost always a secondary complication of Spinal Trauma, Genital Nursing, or Dehydration. For a seasoned rehabber, catching a UTI early prevents the bacteria from traveling up to the kidneys (Pyelonephritis), which is often fatal.

A UTI occurs when bacteria (often E. coli from fecal contamination) travel up the urethra and colonize the bladder. This is a constant risk for squirrels that require manual expression or have urine scald.

Identifying the Signs

The “Smell”: A strong, pungent ammonia or “fishy” odor that persists even after the squirrel is cleaned.

The “Cloud”: Urine that looks milky, opaque, or contains visible “grit” (sediment).

Hematuria: Pink, orange, or bright red blood in the urine.

Straining: The squirrel may hunch, grunt, or “pump” their tail while trying to pee.

Lethargy: A sudden “dullness” or loss of appetite in a previously stable spinal patient.

The “Clear the Track” Protocol

STEP 1: Immediate Hydration Flush

Dilution is the Solution: Increase oral fluids immediately using Lactated Ringers (LRS) or Pedialyte. Pushing fluids thins the urine and helps “wash” bacteria out of the bladder.

Frequency: Offer extra hydration between every regular feeding.

STEP 2: Antibiotic Therapy (From Your List)

You need antibiotics that concentrate in the urine to kill the bacteria at the source.

Baytril (Enrofloxacin): Often the first-line choice. It is highly effective against most gram-negative bacteria that cause UTIs in rodents.

Amoxicillin/Clavamox: An excellent second-choice, especially if the infection is persistent.

Probiotics: Mandatory. Always give Bene-Bac or a squirrel-safe probiotic 2 hours after each antibiotic dose to prevent GI shutdown.

STEP 3: Pain & Inflammation (From Your List)

Meloxicam: Essential for reducing the swelling of the bladder wall and urethra. If the urethra is too swollen, the squirrel cannot empty its bladder, leading to Urinary Stasis.

Rehabber Home Testing

If you suspect a UTI but aren’t sure, you can use Urinary Reagent Strips (Dipsticks).

Leukocytes & Nitrites: High levels indicate active bacterial infection.

Protein/Blood: Indicates inflammation or trauma to the bladder lining.

Prevention for “Special Needs” Residents

The “Double Clean”: Always clean the genital area before and after manual expression using your diluted Chlorhexidine.

Cranberry Support: Some sanctuary owners use a tiny drop of sugar-free cranberry extract to help prevent bacteria from sticking to the bladder wall, but this is a supplement, not a cure for an active infection.

heading: Ch. 76 — Urine Scald (Ammonia Burn)
text:
## **76\. Urine Scald (Ammonia Burn)**

🟡 PAINFUL & CONTAMINATED – Requires aggressive hygiene management.

For a seasoned rehabber, Urine Scald is more than just a rash; it is a chemical burn. When a squirrel is unable to groom itself due to [Spinal Trauma](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/spinal-traumahind-end-paralysis?authuser=0), Neurological Deficits, or [Genital Nursing](https://sites.google.com/view/thesquirrelbible/treatment-protocols/nursing-on-genitals?authuser=0), the ammonia in trapped urine literally eats away the skin, leading to painful ulcerations and secondary infections.

Urine scald occurs when skin is in prolonged contact with damp, urine-soaked bedding or fur. It is most common in “special needs” sanctuary residents (like your Old Man) or spinal patients who “leak” throughout the day.

Identifying the Stages of Scald

Stage 1 (Mild): Pink, damp skin with slight fur thinning in the groin, belly, or inner thighs.

Stage 2 (Moderate): Bright red, raw skin. The squirrel may flinch or vocalize when touched. A strong ammonia smell is present.

Stage 3 (Severe): “Sloughing” or peeling skin, open sores, and yellowish crusts. This is an invitation for Septicemia and fly strike.

The “Dry & Protect” Protocol

STEP 1: The “Waterless” Clean

Avoid Constant Baths: Over-washing with water strips the skin’s natural oils and can worsen the burn.

The Wipe: Use a soft cloth dampened with a diluted Chlorhexidine or Betadine solution to neutralize the ammonia.

The Dry: Use a hairdryer on the cool/low setting or blot gently with a microfiber towel until the skin is 100% dry.

STEP 2: The Moisture Barrier (From Your List)

SSD Cream (Silver Sulfadiazine): This is the gold standard for urine scald. It is soothing, antibacterial, and creates a protective barrier that prevents urine from touching the raw skin.

A\&D Ointment / Vaseline: If SSD is unavailable, use a thick layer of White Petroleum Jelly to “waterproof” the skin.

Avoid Cornstarch/Powders: These can clump, trap bacteria, and be inhaled by the squirrel.

STEP 3: Environmental Engineering

The “Wick” Bedding: Switch to high-quality anti-pill fleece over a layer of absorbent puppy pads. Fleece wicks moisture downward, keeping the squirrel’s skin dry.

Frequent Rotations: Change bedding immediately as soon as it feels damp.

Medical Management

Pain Relief: Scald is incredibly painful. Use Meloxicam from your list to reduce skin inflammation.

Antibiotics: If the skin is broken or “oozing,” start Amoxicillin/Clavamox to prevent a localized skin infection from turning into a systemic crisis.

Rehabber Insight: The “Belly Shave”

In severe cases, you may need to carefully clip the fur in the groin area. Fur traps urine against the skin like a wet sponge; removing the hair allows the skin to breathe and stay dry.

In severe cases, you may need to carefully clip the fur in the groin area. Fur traps urine against the skin like a wet sponge; removing the hair allows the skin to breathe and stay dry.

heading: Ch. 78 — West Nile Virus (WNV)
text:
## **78\. West Nile Virus (WNV)**

While birds (especially corvids) are the primary reservoirs, tree squirrels (Fox, Gray, and Western Gray) are highly susceptible to the neuroinvasive form of West Nile Virus. In a rehabilitation setting, WNV is often mistaken for head trauma or Raccoon Roundworm.

1. Clinical Signs: The “Summer Neuro” Profile

WNV typically peaks in late summer and early fall (mosquito season). If a squirrel arrives with the following signs between July and October, suspect WNV:

Neurological Triad: Tremors (head or body), uncoordinated movement (ataxia), and circling.

Lethargy & Lack of Fear: The squirrel may sit out in the open, unresponsive to predators or humans.

Vision Loss: Apparent blindness or lack of “menace reflex” despite clear eyes.

Seizures/Paralysis: In advanced cases, the virus causes severe encephalitis (brain swelling), leading to hind-limb paralysis or full-body seizures.

2. WNV vs. Roundworm vs. Trauma

| Feature | West Nile Virus | Raccoon Roundworm | Head Trauma |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Onset | Rapid (days). | Progressive (weeks). | Instant (minutes). |
| Season | Mosquito Season (Summer). | Any. | Any. |
| Fever | Often present. | Absent. | Absent. |
| Pupils | Usually normal/responsive. | Normal. | Often unequal/blown. |

3. The “Viremia” Warning (Safety & Shedding)

Unlike humans and horses (who are “dead-end hosts”), some squirrels develop high enough viral loads in their blood to potentially infect a mosquito that bites them.

Shedding: WNV has been detected in the oral secretions, urine, and feces of infected squirrels for up to 20 days.

Zoonotic Risk: While you cannot “catch” WNV from a squirrel bite or scratch (it requires a mosquito vector), you should still use strict PPE (gloves and masks) when cleaning cages of suspected WNV patients to avoid accidental contact with infected fluids.

4. Stabilization & Treatment

There is no “cure” for WNV; the body must fight the virus. Treatment is 100% supportive.

Reduce Brain Swelling: Use Meloxicam or, in severe cases, a vet-prescribed steroid (Dexamethasone) to manage encephalitis.

Hydration: Sub-Q fluids are critical, as the virus often causes secondary kidney involvement.

Secondary Infection: Squirrels with WNV are immunocompromised. Watch for pneumonia and start Baytril if breathing becomes labored.

Vector Control: Keep suspected WNV squirrels in a mosquito-proof room or use fine mesh screening. You do not want a local mosquito biting the squirrel and then biting you or your other patients.

5. Prognosis & Release

The “Wait” Period: Neurological recovery can be slow. If a squirrel survives the acute phase (the first 7 days), they may still have a head tilt or “wobble” for weeks.

Release Criteria: A WNV survivor must be 100% symptom-free for at least 30 days before release. If permanent neurological deficits remain (blindness, circling), the squirrel is non-releasable.

heading: Ch. 79 — White Tears (Chromodacryorrhea)
text:
## **79\. White Tears (Chromodacryorrhea)**

⚪️ MONITORING – The Squirrel’s “Check Engine” Light.

White tears are not milk, pus, or a localized eye infection. They are a porphyrin-rich secretion from the Harderian gland (located behind the eyeball). While many rodents produce “red” porphyrin (looking like blood), squirrels produce a “milky white” version.

What the “White” is Telling You

Systemic Stress: The squirrel’s body is under significant physiological duress.

Acute Pain: This is the most common cause. If you see white tears, look for a hidden injury, MBD, or a fracture.

Severe Dehydration: The electrolytes are so imbalanced that the glands begin to over-secrete.

Respiratory Distress: Often seen in the early stages of Pneumonia or severe URI.

Triage & Response Protocol

STEP 1: The “Wipe and Watch” Test

Action: Take a soft, damp cloth and gently wipe the “milk” away.

The Result: If the eye underneath is clear, bright, and the squirrel isn’t squinting, the eye is fine. The problem is internal.

The Follow-up: If the white discharge returns within minutes, the squirrel is in active crisis.

STEP 2: The “Pain Audit” (From Your List)

Check the Mouth: Look for Oral Burns or Malocclusion.

Check the Limbs: Do a “toe-pinch” test. Are they responding to pain equally?

Check the Belly: Is it hard? (See Bloat Protocol).

Consider Pain Management: If you cannot find the source but the squirrel appears to be in distress and is “tearing,” consider administering pain relief medication such as Meloxicam or Buprenorphine under the guidance of a veterinarian. If the tearing subsides after medication is given, it can indicate that pain was the underlying cause.

STEP 3: Environmental Stabilization

Heat: Ensure the incubator isn’t too hot (see Hyperthermia).

Quiet: High-decibel noise (barking dogs, loud TVs) can trigger chromodacryorrhea in high-strung juveniles.

Rehabber “Pro Tip” for the Guide

“Don’t Treat the Eye, Treat the Squirrel.”

Applying topical eye treatments like Terramycin or saline drops to a squirrel with white tears will not address the underlying systemic issue and may cause additional stress to the animal, potentially exacerbating the tearing. Focus on identifying and treating the root cause of the stress or pain.

The “Star” of Dehydration (Corneal Opacity)

⚪️ MONITORING – Reversible vs. Permanent Damage.

When a squirrel’s hydration levels drop into the “danger zone,” the cornea (the clear front “window” of the eye) can actually change shape and develop white, opaque spots or star-like patterns.

The Appearance: It looks like a permanent scar or a “white film” in a jagged, starburst, or “lace” pattern across the eye.

The Science: Without enough fluid, the collagen fibers in the cornea lose their uniform spacing (which is what makes them clear). This causes light to scatter, making the eye look white and cloudy.

The “Plump” Effect: As you noted, this is often reversible. Once you restore systemic hydration through Sub-Q Fluids (LRS) or oral rehydration, the stromal tissue re-hydrates, the collagen fibers realign, and the “star” disappears as the eye becomes transparent again.

Emergency Hydration Protocol for “Star Eyes”

If you intake a squirrel with these “white stars,” they are likely at 10% dehydration or higher—a life-threatening level.

Immediate Sub-Q Fluids: This is a case where oral hydration may not be fast enough. Use warm Lactated Ringers (LRS) immediately to bypass the digestive tract.

Topical Protection: While the body hydrates from the inside, protect the eyes from the outside. Use Terramycin or a sterile lubricant (like Hylo-Gel) to prevent the dry surface from developing a real [Corneal Ulcer](https://www.willseye.org/corneal-dystrophies-and-scars/).

The “Check” Interval: Monitor the eyes every 4 hours. You should see the white patterns begin to “melt away” as the squirrel’s hydration improves.

Differentiating the “Star” from a True Scar

Dehydration Star: Usually appears in both eyes; has a jagged, translucent look; and improves within hours of fluid therapy.

Permanent Scar: Usually in one eye (from a scratch or poke); has a distinct, solid white “dense” center; and does not change with hydration.

Medical Dosing & Medication Reference

heading: Ch. 80 — Medical Dosing & Medication Reference › How to Use the Medication Compatibility Chart
text:
## **How to Use the Medication Compatibility Chart**

In wildlife rehabilitation, managing multiple medications is common, but “stacking” certain drugs can lead to treatment failure or fatal organ damage. Use this chart before every administration to ensure your patient’s safety.

The Color Code System

🟩 OK (SAFE): These medications are generally safe to administer concurrently or within the same treatment window.

🟥 NO (DANGEROUS): NEVER combine these medications. This combination is highly toxic and can lead to rapid GI perforation, kidney failure, or neurological distress. If a squirrel needs to switch from one to the other (e.g., Prednisone to Meloxicam), a “wash-out period” of 5–7 days is typically required.

🟨 US (USE SPARINGLY): These drugs can be used together but carry a higher risk of side effects. Watch closely for extreme lethargy (“Floppy Squirrel Syndrome”), loss of appetite, or severe diarrhea. Consult your lead rehabber or veterinarian if these signs appear.

🟧 WT (WAIT TIME): These medications “clash” in the digestive tract. If given at the same time, one will neutralize the other, making it ineffective.

The 2-Hour Rule: For any “WT” interaction (especially Antibiotics \+ Calcium/Formula), you must separate the doses by at least 2 hours.

NFP (NOT FOR PINKIES): These drugs cause permanent developmental delays and may result in disabilities.

The full-color compatibility chart is available in the printed edition and as a downloadable quick-reference card.

Critical Protocol Reminders

1. Hydration First: Regardless of the chart color, Albon, Ponazuril, and all NSAIDs (Meloxicam/Ibuprofen) should ONLY be given to a 100% hydrated squirrel to prevent permanent kidney crystallization.

2. The “Pinky” Exception: Even if marked “OK,” powerful antibiotics like Baytril should be used with extreme caution in unweaned neonates due to potential joint development issues. Nuflor should NOT be used with pinkies at all.

3. When in Doubt, Pause: If you are unsure about a combination not listed on this chart, DO NOT administer the medication. Contact your supervisor or attending veterinarian immediately.

Prednisone/Prednisolone: Special Interaction Warnings

Due to prednisone’s widespread effects on multiple body systems, it interacts with more medications than almost any other drug in your kit. The following medications should be used with extreme caution or avoided entirely when a squirrel is on prednisone therapy:

amphotericin B

anticholinesterases

aspirin

barbiturates

bupropion

cholestyramine

cyclophosphamide

cyclosporine

digoxin

potassium-depleting diuretics

ephedrine

estrogens

fluroquinolones

insulin

ketoconazole

macrolide antibiotics

mitotane

mycophenolate

non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

phenobarbital

rifampin

vaccines

warfarin

This product may also interact with laboratory tests, such as allergy tests, as well as cholesterol, urine glucose, potassium, and thyroid levels. Be sure to tell your veterinarian about any medications (including vitamins, supplements, or herbal therapies) that your pet is taking.

The “Never Mix” Rule (Absolute Contraindications)

NSAIDs \+ Corticosteroids: Never combine Meloxicam or Ibuprofen with Prednisone. This combination causes severe gastrointestinal ulceration and potentially fatal internal bleeding.

NSAID Stacking: Never use Meloxicam and Ibuprofen together. Using two different NSAIDs significantly increases the risk of acute kidney failure and liver stress.

NSAIDs \+ Aminoglycosides: Do not use Gentamicin with any NSAID. Both are toxic to the kidneys, and combined use can lead to rapid renal failure.

The “Wash-Out” Protocol

When switching between incompatible classes (e.g., moving from a steroid to an NSAID), a “wash-out period” is required to allow the first drug to clear the body.

Duration: A standard safety window is 5 to 7 days between these drug classes.

Wait Time & Feeding Rules

Formula & Cations: Do not give Baytril (Enrofloxacin) or Doxycycline at the same time as squirrel formula or Calcium/Tums.

Timing: Wait at least 2 hours between dosing these antibiotics and feeding formula to ensure full absorption.

CNS & Sedation Safety

Sedation Stacking: Be extremely cautious when using Trazodone, Gabapentin, and Benadryl concurrently. These drugs have additive sedative effects that can lead to profound CNS depression or respiratory arrest in compromised animals.

Pinkies/Neonates: Nuflor (Florfenicol) is generally avoided in neonates due to potential bone marrow suppression risks.

General Administration Best Practices

Hydration First: Never administer NSAIDs or Gentamicin to a dehydrated squirrel, as this drastically increases the risk of permanent kidney damage.

Route Matters: SSD Cream, Neosporin, and Clotrimazole are for topical use only; ensure squirrels do not ingest these through grooming.

Extra-Label Use: Most medications in wildlife rehab are used “extra-label,” meaning they are not specifically FDA-approved for squirrels. Always operate under the guidance of a licensed veterinarian.

heading: Ch. 80 — Medical Dosing & Medication Reference › How to Use the Medication Compatibility Chart › 80A. How to Use the Medication Compatibility Chart
text:
### **80A. How to Use the Medication Compatibility Chart**

These are medications available without a prescription that rehabbers can access and use safely with proper guidance. This is your “what you can do right now” toolkit.

Aloe Vera Gel

CATEGORY: TOPICAL BURN & SKIN TREATMENT

Primary Uses: Burns, sunburn (pinkies frequently arrive sunburned from exposure), and minor skin irritation. Provides cooling relief and supports skin healing.

Forms: Pure aloe vera gel. Avoid products with added fragrances, alcohol, or dyes.

How it Works: Creates a moist healing environment, reduces inflammation, and provides mild analgesic properties.

Safety: Generally very safe topically. Ensure the squirrel does not ingest large amounts.

Treatment Course: Apply gently to affected area as needed.

Bactine Spray — DO NOT USE

CATEGORY: DO NOT USE — CONTAINS LIDOCAINE

Not safe for squirrels: Bactine contains lidocaine (see the Never-Use list). For wound cleaning, use diluted chlorhexidine or Betadine (the color of weak tea).

Banocin Powder

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTIBIOTIC POWDER

Primary Uses: Oozing cuts and wounds that will not hold gel or cream-based antibiotics. When Neosporin slides off, this stays put.

Forms: Antibiotic powder.

How it Works: Provides a dry antimicrobial barrier over wounds, allowing healing while preventing infection in areas where ointments fail.

Safety: For external use only. Particularly useful for weeping wounds where moisture prevents cream adhesion.

Treatment Course: Apply to clean wound as needed. Reapply after cleaning.

Base Numb Topical Anorectal Cream

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANESTHETIC / PROLAPSE SUPPORT

Primary Uses: Minor rectal prolapse. Helps reduce discomfort and swelling to allow tissue to retract.

Forms: Topical anorectal cream.

How it Works: Contains a topical anesthetic that reduces pain and inflammation in the prolapsed tissue.

Safety: For external use only. Monitor closely—if prolapse does not resolve, veterinary intervention is required.

Rehabber’s Note: Yes, you will have to order this on Amazon. No, you will never live it down. But it works, and that’s what matters.

Benadryl (Diphenhydramine)

CATEGORY: ANTIHISTAMINE / ALLERGY & INFLAMMATORY REDUCTION

Primary Uses: Insect stings (bees/wasps), ant bites, and severe localized allergic swelling. Can also be used as a mild sedative for highly stressed animals.

Form 1: Children’s liquid (cherry is common) or compounded liquid. DO NOT USE ADULT STRENGTH.

Form 2: Topical cream for localized reactions.

How it Works: Blocks H1 receptors, preventing histamine from binding and causing swelling, itching, and redness.

Safety: Causes drowsiness/sedation. Overdosing can lead to extreme lethargy or respiratory depression.

⚠ WARNING: If the squirrel is on Trazodone, Gabapentin, or Benadryl, monitor for “Floppy Squirrel Syndrome.” Excessive sedation can lead to aspiration pneumonia because the squirrel loses the ability to swallow effectively.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Topical Treatment: Apply cream directly to the affected area following product instructions.

Betadine (Povidone-Iodine)

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTISEPTIC

Primary Uses: Cleaning superficial wounds, cuts, and site preparation for lancing abscesses. Preferred for “dirty” wounds with soil or debris. DO NOT USE ON WOUNDS WITH BLOOD OR PUS—use Chlorhexidine instead.

Dilution Protocol: Never use full-strength on open tissue. Mix with sterile saline or clean water until it reaches the “color of weak tea” (approx. 1:10 dilution).

Safety: Iodine is inactivated by organic matter (blood or pus). Avoid use in individuals with known iodine sensitivities.

Rehabber’s Note: If it’s too dark (dark brown), it is cytotoxic and can actually DELAY wound healing by killing the very cells trying to repair the skin.

Bitter Balm

CATEGORY: BEHAVIORAL DETERRENT

Primary Uses: Genital sucking deterrent and self-mutilation prevention. Applied to areas the squirrel is obsessively chewing or licking.

Forms: Topical balm or spray with extremely bitter taste.

How it Works: The intensely unpleasant taste discourages the squirrel from licking or chewing the treated area.

Safety: Non-toxic. The taste is the active mechanism. May need frequent reapplication.

Treatment Course: Apply to affected area as needed. Monitor for effectiveness and reapply as the squirrel grooms it away.

Calcium / Tums (Calcium Carbonate)

CATEGORY: MINERAL SUPPLEMENT / ANTACID

Primary Uses: Emergency treatment for MBD (calcium crashes/seizures), bone health support during growth, and occasionally as a mild antacid.

Forms: Oral suspension (compounded), crushed Tums (fruit-flavored is often accepted), or calcium carbonate powder.

How it Works: Restores blood calcium levels critical for proper bone density, muscle contraction, and neurological function.

Safety & Interactions:

Antibiotic Binding (Critical): Calcium binds to Doxycycline and Baytril, preventing absorption. You must separate calcium/formula dosing from these antibiotics by at least 2 hours.

Over-supplementation can lead to soft tissue mineralization or kidney stones. Use as targeted treatment, not a permanent dietary additive for healthy squirrels on a balanced block diet.

Emergency Administration: For crashes (seizures/paralysis), a concentrated calcium syrup or crushed Tums in water can be given orally for rapid absorption through the mucous membranes.

Treatment Course: High-frequency dosing during an active crash (every 2–4 hours), tapering as symptoms stabilize. Transition to a balanced diet for long-term maintenance.

Castor Oil U.S.P.

CATEGORY: EMERGENCY LAXATIVE

⚠ WARNING: EMERGENCY USE ONLY. This is an absolute last resort medication for life-threatening constipation/impaction when all other interventions have failed and the baby is actively dying.

Primary Uses: Severe, life-threatening constipation or gut impaction where no other treatment has worked.

Forms: U.S.P. grade oil.

How it Works: Stimulates intestinal contractions and draws water into the intestines to soften and move impacted stool.

Safety: Can cause severe cramping and rapid dehydration. This is not a routine laxative—it is a Hail Mary when the alternative is losing the animal.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Chlorhexidine (Nolvasan / Hibiclens)

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTISEPTIC

Primary Uses: Best for visible infections, abscesses, and surgical site prep. Remains active even in the presence of blood or pus, unlike Betadine.

Dilution Protocol: For a 2% solution, dilute 1 ounce per gallon of water for general cleaning. For flushing open wounds, use a 0.05% solution (approx. 1 part 2% chlorhexidine to 40 parts saline).

⚠ WARNING: Never use in or near the EYES or EARS. It is ototoxic (causes permanent deafness) if it reaches the middle ear through a ruptured eardrum and can cause corneal ulcers if splashed in eyes.

Rehabber’s Note: Use the “Solution,” not the “Scrub.” The scrub contains detergents (soap) that are TOXIC to open tissue and should only be used on intact skin.

Clear Moisture Barrier Ointment

CATEGORY: SKIN PROTECTANT

Primary Uses: Urine scald protection and treatment. Creates a barrier between the skin and urine to prevent further damage.

Forms: Clear ointment.

How it Works: Forms a protective moisture barrier on the skin surface, allowing damaged skin to heal underneath.

Safety: Does contain petrolatum, but is safer than zinc-based alternatives for squirrels. Zinc oxide products should be avoided due to ingestion risk during grooming.

Treatment Course: Apply to clean, dry skin on affected area as needed. Reapply after cleaning.

colostrum

Clotrimazole (Lotrimin)

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTIFUNGAL

Primary Uses: Ringworm (fungal skin infection), which often appears as circular patches of hair loss with crusty or red edges.

Forms: 1% cream or solution.

How it Works: Inhibits the growth of fungus by altering the permeability of the fungal cell wall.

⚠ WARNING: ZOONOTIC WARNING: Ringworm is highly contagious to humans and other animals. Always wear gloves when applying. Ensure the squirrel does not ingest large amounts while grooming.

Treatment Course: Applied twice daily. Treatment must continue for 7 to 14 days AFTER the skin appears totally healed to prevent recurrence.

Decongestants (Oxymetazoline)

CATEGORY: NASAL SWELLING REDUCTION

Primary Uses: Upper respiratory infections that make breathing difficult. Used via nebulizer, not direct application.

Forms: Nose drops, diluted in saline for nebulizer use.

How it Works: Constricts blood vessels in the nasal passages (vasoconstriction), reducing swelling and mucus production.

Safety: Overuse can cause “rebound congestion.” Do not use for more than 3 days in a row.

Treatment Course: Dilute drops in saline and nebulize in an enclosed space. Adjust drop count by age—fewer drops for younger squirrels.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Hylands Homeopathic Cough & Mucous Syrup (Daytime)

CATEGORY: SUPPORTIVE SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT

Primary Uses: Supportive symptom management for congestion, cough, and throat irritation—particularly as a comfort companion during Bordetella treatment. This manages symptoms to improve comfort and rest. It is NOT a treatment for infection.

Forms: Children’s liquid syrup.

How it Works: Provides mild relief from cough and mucous symptoms, helping the animal rest better during antibiotic treatment.

Safety: Specifically chosen because it is alcohol-free, sugar-free, and xylitol-free with no known interactions with Bordetella medications (Doxycycline, Nuflor, Baytril).

Rehabber’s Note: This is supportive symptom management, not treatment. It works alongside your antibiotic protocol to make the animal more comfortable. Use the homeopathic version specifically because it avoids dangerous inactive ingredients found in standard OTC cough medicines.

Ibuprofen (Infant Concentrated Drops)

CATEGORY: PAIN RELIEF / FEVER REDUCER / INFLAMMATION REDUCER

⚠ WARNING: THIS IS A LAST RESORT MEDICATION. Use ONLY if no other pain relievers are available. Dosing should be kept as small as possible, no more than every 4 hours, for a maximum of 4 days. DO NOT USE ON SQUIRRELS 12 WEEKS AND YOUNGER.

Primary Uses: Minor pain and fever reduction. Many rehabbers have replaced it with Meloxicam due to a safer profile.

Forms: Infant Concentrated Drops (NOT Children’s—Children’s is half the strength and will be less effective).

How it Works: Inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes to block prostaglandins that trigger pain and inflammation.

Safety: Very narrow safety margin in squirrels. Overdose or use in dehydrated animals can lead to rapid gastric ulcers and kidney failure. NEVER mix with steroids. NEVER use in squirrels 12 weeks and younger.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Immodium AD (Loperamide)

CATEGORY: ANTI-DIARRHEAL

⚠ WARNING: Use Children’s formula ONLY (labeled for ages 6 and up). Never use adult strength. Squirrel age minimum: consult your veterinarian for species-appropriate age cutoff.

Primary Uses: Mild diarrhea management in older juveniles and adults.

Forms: Children’s liquid formula.

How it Works: Slows intestinal motility, allowing more water absorption from stool.

Safety: Can be dangerous in young animals. Do not use in neonates or young babies. Can mask symptoms of serious underlying conditions—if diarrhea persists, investigate the cause rather than continuing to treat the symptom.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Ivermectin Paste

CATEGORY: ANTI-PARASITIC

Primary Uses: External parasites like ear mites and sarcoptic mange (common in older juveniles), as well as some internal nematodes (worms).

Forms: Apple-flavored paste available at most farm and ranch supply stores.

How it Works: Causes paralysis and death of the parasite by interfering with nerve and muscle cell function.

Safety: Neurotoxicity is a risk if overdosed; signs include tremors, stargazing, and lethargy. Do not use alongside Revolution.

Treatment Course: Usually one dose (approximately a grain-of-rice sized amount on a piece of walnut), repeated once 7 to 14 days later to catch the parasite life cycle.

Kaolin

CATEGORY: ANTI-DIARRHEAL / GI PROTECTANT

Primary Uses: Mild diarrhea management. Gentler alternative to Immodium for less severe cases.

Forms: Oral liquid suspension.

How it Works: Adsorbs toxins and bacteria in the GI tract and forms a protective coating on the intestinal lining.

Safety: Generally very safe. May reduce absorption of other oral medications if given simultaneously—separate by 1–2 hours.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Lactated Ringer’s Solution (LRS)

CATEGORY: REHYDRATION / ELECTROLYTE SUPPORT

Primary Uses: Correcting dehydration, treating shock, and flushing the system during toxin/poison ingestion or fly strike.

Forms: Sterile fluid bag for Sub-Q (subcutaneous) injection.

How it Works: Unlike plain saline, LRS contains sodium lactate, potassium, and calcium, which helps buffer the blood and replace essential electrolytes lost during illness or trauma.

⚠ WARNING: MUST be warmed to body temperature before administration. Cold fluids can put a compromised baby squirrel into fatal cardiac arrest.

Treatment Course: Dosing is weight-based (usually 5–10% of body weight) and split into multiple sessions over 24 hours until skin tenting resolves.

Lidocaine 4% Pain Relieving Cream — DO NOT USE

CATEGORY: DO NOT USE

Not safe for squirrels — see the Never-Use list. For pain, ask your vet about meloxicam (inflammation) or gabapentin (nerve pain).

Little Remedies Saline Spray

CATEGORY: NASAL CARE

Primary Uses: Bloody noses and nasal dryness. Helps gently clear nasal passages without medication.

Forms: Pediatric saline nasal spray.

How it Works: Sterile saline moisturizes nasal passages and helps loosen dried blood or mucus.

Safety: Extremely safe. No medication—just saline.

Treatment Course: Use as needed for nasal dryness or to gently clean bloody noses.

Mylicon / Simethicone (Baby Gas Drops)

CATEGORY: ANTI-GAS

Primary Uses: Bloat and gas in formula-fed baby squirrels, which can be life-threatening if the abdomen becomes hard and distended.

Forms: Pediatric oral drops (often unflavored or berry).

How it Works: Breaks down the surface tension of gas bubbles in the GI tract, allowing the squirrel to pass gas more easily. It is not absorbed into the bloodstream.

Safety: Extremely safe with virtually no side effects—it acts mechanically rather than chemically. It does not treat the cause of bloat (like overfeeding), only the symptom.

Rehabber’s Note: You cannot overdose a baby on simethicone. One of my squirrels (Scootch) ate an entire blister pack of GasX and the worst thing that happened was minty burps for 24 hours. VERY SAFE.

Treatment Course: Given as needed (PRN) before or after feedings until the abdomen is soft again.

Neosporin (Triple Antibiotic Ointment)

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: Minor cuts, scrapes, and superficial wounds to prevent bacterial infection.

Forms: Topical ointment or cream.

How it Works: Creates a physical barrier while three antibiotics (bacitracin, neomycin, polymyxin B) kill bacteria on the skin’s surface.

Safety: Use sparingly. Squirrels are groomers—if they lick off large amounts, the neomycin can cause GI upset. Ensure it is rubbed in well or used in areas they cannot easily reach. Do not use in deep puncture wounds (like cat bites), which require systemic antibiotics.

Treatment Course: Applied 1 to 3 times daily until the skin has healed.

Omeprazole (Prilosec)

CATEGORY: GI PROTECTION / CSF REDUCTION FOR HYDROCEPHALUS

Primary Uses:

GI Protection: Used as a preventative to protect the stomach lining when a squirrel is on Prednisone or other steroids, which significantly increase the risk of gastric ulcers.

Hydrocephalus Support: Sometimes used to help reduce production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), lowering intracranial pressure.

Forms: Liquid from compounding pharmacies (prescription) or by opening capsules and retrieving the beads inside. Because Omeprazole is a time-release drug, the beads must remain UNCRUSHED. Mix with a carrier like peanut butter.

How it Works: Irreversibly binds to proton pumps in the stomach’s parietal cells, shutting down acid secretion more effectively than H2 blockers.

Safety: Generally very safe. Long-term use can interfere with absorption of certain nutrients (B12, Calcium). Should be given 30–60 minutes BEFORE a meal or other medications for maximum efficacy.

Treatment Course: Usually once daily. For GI protection, continue for the duration of the steroid course plus 48 hours. For capsule administration: 3 beads 30–60 minutes prior to Prednisone mixed into a carrier paste.

When using Omeprazole for Hydrocephalus, it is often paired with Prednisone. While Omeprazole helps reduce fluid, the Prednisone handles brain tissue inflammation. Omeprazole is dosed 30–60 minutes prior to Prednisone for maximum GI protection.

Orasol Benzocaine 20% Oral Anesthetic Gel

CATEGORY: ORAL PAIN RELIEF — VET-DIRECTED ONLY

Primary Uses: Oral burns (from overheated formula), mouth injuries, and teething pain.

Forms: 20% benzocaine oral gel.

How it Works: Topical anesthetic that numbs oral tissue on contact, providing immediate pain relief for mouth injuries.

Safety: Use only if your vet directs it. Benzocaine can cause methemoglobinemia (blood that can't carry oxygen), and a tiny body gets a large dose fast. Never use on neonates without vet direction.

Treatment Course: Apply tiny amount directly to affected area in the mouth as needed for pain.

Preparation H

CATEGORY: RECTAL PROTECTANT / PROLAPSE SUPPORT

Primary Uses: Minor rectal prolapse. Helps reduce swelling and protect exposed tissue.

Forms: Cream or ointment.

How it Works: Contains phenylephrine (vasoconstrictor) to reduce swelling, plus protectants to soothe and protect irritated tissue.

Safety: For external use only. If prolapse is severe or does not resolve with supportive care, veterinary intervention is required immediately.

Treatment Course: Apply gently to prolapsed tissue as needed while working to resolve the underlying cause.

Sugar: The “Sugar Cure” (Hypertonic Therapy)

This is an old-school clinical technique that is highly effective for “wet,” infected, or sloughing wounds.

The Science: Sugar is “hygroscopic.” It draws moisture out of the wound, dehydrating bacteria and reducing edema (swelling) without the need for harsh chemicals.

The Method:

Clean the wound with dilute Betadine or Saline.

Pack the wound with plain, granulated white sugar.

Cover with a sterile dressing if the location allows.

Change the packing every 12–24 hours as the sugar dissolves into a “syrup.”

CLINICAL NOTE: Rectal Prolapse In cases of mild rectal prolapse (often caused by diarrhea or straining), the tissue becomes engorged with fluid, making it impossible to retract.

The Fix: Apply a generous coating of granulated sugar directly to the prolapsed tissue. Wait 15–20 minutes. The sugar will pull the fluid out, causing the tissue to shrink significantly, often allowing it to slip back into place naturally or with very gentle assistance.

Super H Antiseptic Powder (with Menthol)

CATEGORY: ANTISEPTIC / SELF-MUTILATION DETERRENT

Primary Uses: Self-mutilation prevention and wound healing. The menthol creates a cooling sensation that discourages continued chewing/scratching while the antiseptic powder promotes healing.

Forms: Antiseptic powder with menthol.

How it Works: Dual action: the antiseptic component prevents infection while the menthol provides a sensory distraction that interrupts the self-mutilation cycle and gives wounds a chance to heal.

Safety: For external use only. The menthol sensation may initially startle the animal.

Treatment Course: Apply to affected area. Reapply as needed, especially after the squirrel grooms it away.

Vicks VapoRub

CATEGORY: RESPIRATORY / CONGESTION SUPPORT

⚠ WARNING: DO NOT apply directly to the squirrel. Indirect use ONLY via the incubator plate method. A SMALL swipe being key.

Primary Uses: Congestion relief. Used indirectly to help clear nasal passages in congested babies.

Forms: Topical rub (used on a plate, NOT on the animal).

How it Works: The menthol and eucalyptus vapors help open nasal passages when the squirrel breathes the ambient fumes in an enclosed incubator space.

The Incubator Plate Method: Place a small swipe of Vicks on a paper plate and set it inside the incubator (not touching the animal or bedding). The gentle fumes help with congestion. Small swipe is critical—too much will overwhelm the animal.

Safety: NEVER apply directly to any animal. The camphor, menthol, and eucalyptus are toxic if ingested or applied to skin. Indirect vapor use only.

Vitamin E Skin Oil

CATEGORY: TOPICAL SKIN & BURN TREATMENT

Primary Uses: Burns, healing skin, and scar tissue management. Promotes skin cell regeneration.

Forms: Pure vitamin E oil (can be squeezed from gel capsules).

How it Works: Antioxidant properties promote skin healing and reduce scarring. Moisturizes damaged tissue.

Safety: Generally very safe topically. Minimal concern for ingestion in small amounts.

Treatment Course: Apply to healing burns or skin damage as needed.

──────────────────────────────

### 80A. How to Use the Medication Compatibility Chart

These are medications available without a prescription that rehabbers can access and use safely with proper guidance. This is your “what you can do right now” toolkit.

CATEGORY: TOPICAL BURN & SKIN TREATMENT

Primary Uses: Burns, sunburn (pinkies frequently arrive sunburned from exposure), and minor skin irritation. Provides cooling relief and supports skin healing.

Forms: Pure aloe vera gel. Avoid products with added fragrances, alcohol, or dyes.

How it Works: Creates a moist healing environment, reduces inflammation, and provides mild analgesic properties.

Safety: Generally very safe topically. Ensure the squirrel does not ingest large amounts.

Treatment Course: Apply gently to affected area as needed.

Bactine Spray — DO NOT USE

CATEGORY: DO NOT USE — CONTAINS LIDOCAINE

Not safe for squirrels: Bactine contains lidocaine (see the Never-Use list). For wound cleaning, use diluted chlorhexidine or Betadine (the color of weak tea).

Banocin Powder

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTIBIOTIC POWDER

Primary Uses: Oozing cuts and wounds that will not hold gel or cream-based antibiotics. When Neosporin slides off, this stays put.

Forms: Antibiotic powder.

How it Works: Provides a dry antimicrobial barrier over wounds, allowing healing while preventing infection in areas where ointments fail.

Safety: For external use only. Particularly useful for weeping wounds where moisture prevents cream adhesion.

Treatment Course: Apply to clean wound as needed. Reapply after cleaning.

Base Numb Topical Anorectal Cream

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANESTHETIC / PROLAPSE SUPPORT

Primary Uses: Minor rectal prolapse. Helps reduce discomfort and swelling to allow tissue to retract.

Forms: Topical anorectal cream.

How it Works: Contains a topical anesthetic that reduces pain and inflammation in the prolapsed tissue.

Safety: For external use only. Monitor closely—if prolapse does not resolve, veterinary intervention is required.

Rehabber’s Note: Yes, you will have to order this on Amazon. No, you will never live it down. But it works, and that’s what matters.

Benadryl (Diphenhydramine)

CATEGORY: ANTIHISTAMINE / ALLERGY & INFLAMMATORY REDUCTION

How it Works: Blocks H1 receptors, preventing histamine from binding and causing swelling, itching, and redness.

Safety: Causes drowsiness/sedation. Overdosing can lead to extreme lethargy or respiratory depression.

⚠ WARNING: If the squirrel is on Trazodone, Gabapentin, or Benadryl, monitor for “Floppy Squirrel Syndrome.” Excessive sedation can lead to aspiration pneumonia because the squirrel loses the ability to swallow effectively.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Topical Treatment: Apply cream directly to the affected area following product instructions.

Betadine (Povidone-Iodine)

Safety: Iodine is inactivated by organic matter (blood or pus). Avoid use in individuals with known iodine sensitivities.

Rehabber’s Note: If it’s too dark (dark brown), it is cytotoxic and can actually DELAY wound healing by killing the very cells trying to repair the skin.

Bitter Balm

CATEGORY: BEHAVIORAL DETERRENT

Primary Uses: Genital sucking deterrent and self-mutilation prevention. Applied to areas the squirrel is obsessively chewing or licking.

Forms: Topical balm or spray with extremely bitter taste.

How it Works: The intensely unpleasant taste discourages the squirrel from licking or chewing the treated area.

Safety: Non-toxic. The taste is the active mechanism. May need frequent reapplication.

Treatment Course: Apply to affected area as needed. Monitor for effectiveness and reapply as the squirrel grooms it away.
