Treatment Course: Use as needed for nasal dryness or to gently clean bloody noses.

Mylicon / Simethicone (Baby Gas Drops)

CATEGORY: ANTI-GAS

Primary Uses: Bloat and gas in formula-fed baby squirrels, which can be life-threatening if the abdomen becomes hard and distended.

Forms: Pediatric oral drops (often unflavored or berry).

How it Works: Breaks down the surface tension of gas bubbles in the GI tract, allowing the squirrel to pass gas more easily. It is not absorbed into the bloodstream.

Safety: Extremely safe with virtually no side effects—it acts mechanically rather than chemically. It does not treat the cause of bloat (like overfeeding), only the symptom.

Rehabber’s Note: You cannot overdose a baby on simethicone. One of my squirrels (Scootch) ate an entire blister pack of GasX and the worst thing that happened was minty burps for 24 hours. VERY SAFE.

Treatment Course: Given as needed (PRN) before or after feedings until the abdomen is soft again.

Neosporin (Triple Antibiotic Ointment)

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: Minor cuts, scrapes, and superficial wounds to prevent bacterial infection.

Forms: Topical ointment or cream.

How it Works: Creates a physical barrier while three antibiotics (bacitracin, neomycin, polymyxin B) kill bacteria on the skin’s surface.

Safety: Use sparingly. Squirrels are groomers—if they lick off large amounts, the neomycin can cause GI upset. Ensure it is rubbed in well or used in areas they cannot easily reach. Do not use in deep puncture wounds (like cat bites), which require systemic antibiotics.

Treatment Course: Applied 1 to 3 times daily until the skin has healed.

Omeprazole (Prilosec)

CATEGORY: GI PROTECTION / CSF REDUCTION FOR HYDROCEPHALUS

Primary Uses:

GI Protection: Used as a preventative to protect the stomach lining when a squirrel is on Prednisone or other steroids, which significantly increase the risk of gastric ulcers.

Hydrocephalus Support: Sometimes used to help reduce production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), lowering intracranial pressure.

Forms: Liquid from compounding pharmacies (prescription) or by opening capsules and retrieving the beads inside. Because Omeprazole is a time-release drug, the beads must remain UNCRUSHED. Mix with a carrier like peanut butter.

How it Works: Irreversibly binds to proton pumps in the stomach’s parietal cells, shutting down acid secretion more effectively than H2 blockers.

Safety: Generally very safe. Long-term use can interfere with absorption of certain nutrients (B12, Calcium). Should be given 30–60 minutes BEFORE a meal or other medications for maximum efficacy.

Treatment Course: Usually once daily. For GI protection, continue for the duration of the steroid course plus 48 hours. For capsule administration: 3 beads 30–60 minutes prior to Prednisone mixed into a carrier paste.

When using Omeprazole for Hydrocephalus, it is often paired with Prednisone. While Omeprazole helps reduce fluid, the Prednisone handles brain tissue inflammation. Omeprazole is dosed 30–60 minutes prior to Prednisone for maximum GI protection.

Orasol Benzocaine 20% Oral Anesthetic Gel

CATEGORY: ORAL PAIN RELIEF — VET-DIRECTED ONLY

Primary Uses: Oral burns (from overheated formula), mouth injuries, and teething pain.

Forms: 20% benzocaine oral gel.

How it Works: Topical anesthetic that numbs oral tissue on contact, providing immediate pain relief for mouth injuries.

Safety: Use only if your vet directs it. Benzocaine can cause methemoglobinemia (blood that can't carry oxygen), and a tiny body gets a large dose fast. Never use on neonates without vet direction.

Treatment Course: Apply tiny amount directly to affected area in the mouth as needed for pain.

Preparation H

CATEGORY: RECTAL PROTECTANT / PROLAPSE SUPPORT

Primary Uses: Minor rectal prolapse. Helps reduce swelling and protect exposed tissue.

Forms: Cream or ointment.

How it Works: Contains phenylephrine (vasoconstrictor) to reduce swelling, plus protectants to soothe and protect irritated tissue.

Safety: For external use only. If prolapse is severe or does not resolve with supportive care, veterinary intervention is required immediately.

Treatment Course: Apply gently to prolapsed tissue as needed while working to resolve the underlying cause.

Sugar: The “Sugar Cure” (Hypertonic Therapy)

This is an old-school clinical technique that is highly effective for “wet,” infected, or sloughing wounds.

The Science: Sugar is “hygroscopic.” It draws moisture out of the wound, dehydrating bacteria and reducing edema (swelling) without the need for harsh chemicals.

The Method:

Clean the wound with dilute Betadine or Saline.

Pack the wound with plain, granulated white sugar.

Cover with a sterile dressing if the location allows.

Change the packing every 12–24 hours as the sugar dissolves into a “syrup.”

CLINICAL NOTE: Rectal Prolapse In cases of mild rectal prolapse (often caused by diarrhea or straining), the tissue becomes engorged with fluid, making it impossible to retract.

The Fix: Apply a generous coating of granulated sugar directly to the prolapsed tissue. Wait 15–20 minutes. The sugar will pull the fluid out, causing the tissue to shrink significantly, often allowing it to slip back into place naturally or with very gentle assistance.

Super H Antiseptic Powder (with Menthol)

CATEGORY: ANTISEPTIC / SELF-MUTILATION DETERRENT

Primary Uses: Self-mutilation prevention and wound healing. The menthol creates a cooling sensation that discourages continued chewing/scratching while the antiseptic powder promotes healing.

Forms: Antiseptic powder with menthol.

How it Works: Dual action: the antiseptic component prevents infection while the menthol provides a sensory distraction that interrupts the self-mutilation cycle and gives wounds a chance to heal.

Safety: For external use only. The menthol sensation may initially startle the animal.

Treatment Course: Apply to affected area. Reapply as needed, especially after the squirrel grooms it away.

Vicks VapoRub

CATEGORY: RESPIRATORY / CONGESTION SUPPORT

⚠ WARNING: DO NOT apply directly to the squirrel. Indirect use ONLY via the incubator plate method. A SMALL swipe being key.

Primary Uses: Congestion relief. Used indirectly to help clear nasal passages in congested babies.

Forms: Topical rub (used on a plate, NOT on the animal).

How it Works: The menthol and eucalyptus vapors help open nasal passages when the squirrel breathes the ambient fumes in an enclosed incubator space.

The Incubator Plate Method: Place a small swipe of Vicks on a paper plate and set it inside the incubator (not touching the animal or bedding). The gentle fumes help with congestion. Small swipe is critical—too much will overwhelm the animal.

Safety: NEVER apply directly to any animal. The camphor, menthol, and eucalyptus are toxic if ingested or applied to skin. Indirect vapor use only.

Vitamin E Skin Oil

CATEGORY: TOPICAL SKIN & BURN TREATMENT

Primary Uses: Burns, healing skin, and scar tissue management. Promotes skin cell regeneration.

Forms: Pure vitamin E oil (can be squeezed from gel capsules).

How it Works: Antioxidant properties promote skin healing and reduce scarring. Moisturizes damaged tissue.

Safety: Generally very safe topically. Minimal concern for ingestion in small amounts.

Treatment Course: Apply to healing burns or skin damage as needed.

──────────────────────────────

### **80C. Prescription Medications**

These medications require veterinary prescription and direction. This section teaches what each drug does, when it’s used, what it interacts with, and what to watch for—so you can communicate effectively with your vet and administer safely under their guidance.

Albon (Sulfadimethoxine)

CATEGORY: ANTI-PARASITIC

Primary Uses: Most frequently prescribed to treat coccidiosis (a parasitic intestinal infection). Also treats bacterial infections affecting the respiratory, urinary, and digestive tracts.

Forms: Oral suspension. Requires a prescription.

How it Works: Bacteriostatic agent that prevents bacteria and protozoa from producing folic acid, which they need to multiply.

Safety: Common side effects include vomiting, diarrhea, and loss of appetite. Must only be given to fully hydrated animals to prevent kidney crystallization.

Treatment Course: 1 dose daily for 10 to 21 days.

USE ONLY IF PONAZURIL IS UNAVAILABLE. Ponazuril kills coccidia in 2 doses over 48 hours versus Albon’s 21-day course.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Amoxicillin / Clavamox (Amoxicillin/Clavulanate)

CATEGORY: ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: Soft tissue injuries—abscesses, cat-bite wounds (kills Pasteurella), and secondary skin infections.

Forms: Powder for oral suspension (must be refrigerated after mixing).

Mixing from Powder: Mix only what you need: 5ml water to 3/8 teaspoon Clavamox powder. Keep both powder and mixed solution refrigerated. Discard mixed solution after 10 days. Powder keeps safely refrigerated for up to 3 months.

How it Works: Bactericidal agent that disrupts bacteria’s cell wall synthesis, causing bacteria to rupture.

Safety: Can cause GI upset or diarrhea. High risk of disrupting gut flora in rodents; often paired with a probiotic (given 2 hours apart).

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Baytril (Enrofloxacin)

CATEGORY: ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: The “gold standard” for aspiration pneumonia and severe respiratory infections in squirrels. Also used for deep tissue infections.

Forms: Injectable solution (often given orally by rehabbers) or flavored tablets/compounded liquid.

How it Works: Inhibits the enzyme DNA gyrase, preventing bacteria from transcribing or replicating its DNA.

Safety:

Can cause cartilage abnormalities in rapidly growing neonates. Use only when benefit outweighs risk in pinkies.

Do not give with calcium/formula. Separate by at least 2 hours.

May lower the seizure threshold—should not be used in squirrels with known head trauma or history of seizures.

Treatment Course: Usually 1 dose daily for 5 to 10 days.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Buprenorphine (Opioid Analgesic)

CATEGORY: CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE – HIGH-LEVEL PAIN MANAGEMENT

⚠ WARNING: CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE. Must be kept in a double-locked, secure location. Handle with extreme care.

Primary Uses: Severe pain that Meloxicam cannot touch—electrocution, crushing injuries, open fractures, surgical recovery (first 24–48 hours after amputation or debridement), severe burns, and end-of-life comfort care.

Forms: Injectable solution, often administered OTM (Oral Transmucosal).

The OTM Method: Buprenorphine is highly absorbed through the cheek/gum tissue. A drop inside the lip works without making them swallow—this is the preferred method for squirrels as it’s less stressful than injection.

How it Works: Partial mu-opioid agonist that provides superior analgesia for breakthrough pain, especially bone trauma, major surgery, and severe burns.

Recognizing Buprenorphine Effects

The squirrel will become very relaxed, eyes may “droop,” breathing will slow.

Do not mistake opioid sedation for “dying.” A squirrel on Buprenorphine should still be rousable but significantly less reactive to pain.

Critical Interactions

🔴 RED ALERT – Gabapentin: Both are CNS depressants. Combined use can cause severe respiratory depression and extreme sedation. If you must use together, reduce doses of both and monitor breathing closely for the first 2 hours.

🟡 YELLOW ALERT – Benadryl: Additive sedation can make the squirrel so drowsy they stop eating or become unresponsive. If already “nodding off” from Buprenorphine, skip the Benadryl or wait at least 4 hours.

🟢 SAFE STACKING – Meloxicam: No known negative interactions. This is your GOLD STANDARD for pain: Meloxicam handles inflammation while Buprenorphine handles the brain’s pain signal. Allows lower opioid dosing.

⚠ CAUTION – Steroids: No direct clash, but both steroids and opioids slow the digestive tract. Monitor for Bloat or GI Stasis.

✅ Antibiotics: Most common squirrel antibiotics do not interfere with Buprenorphine. Primary concern is GI Stasis—be aggressive with Probiotics (Bene-Bac) to prevent fatal Bloat.

Over-Potentiation Warning Signs

Pale/Blue Gums: Indicates insufficient breathing depth (Hypoxia).

Pinpoint Pupils: Classic sign of opioid overdose.

Inability to Rouse: If the squirrel doesn’t wake when you gently touch its whiskers, the combined sedation is too high.

Storage: Keep in original amber glass or dark box. Opioids lose potency if exposed to light or extreme temperatures.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Doxycycline

CATEGORY: ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: Respiratory infections (especially Bordetella) and tick-borne diseases.

Forms: Oral suspension.

How it Works: Bacteriostatic; binds to the 30S ribosomal subunit, preventing bacteria from synthesizing proteins.

Safety:

Can cause permanent yellowing of teeth in neonates.

Extremely caustic if it sits in the esophagus—always follow with a tiny drop of water or formula.

May lower the seizure threshold—should not be used in squirrels with known head trauma or history of seizures.

⚠ WARNING: CRITICAL CALCIUM INTERACTION: Calcium binds to Doxycycline and prevents absorption. Do NOT mix Doxy into formula. Do NOT give with calcium supplements, Tums, or mineral-containing products. Separate dosing from formula by at least 2 hours. In neonates who feed constantly, perfect timing may be impossible—work with your vet. Inconsistent absorption is still better than no coverage.

Treatment Course: Usually 2 doses daily for 5 to 10 days.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Gabapentin

CATEGORY: PAIN RELIEF / ANTI-CONVULSANT / NEUROLOGICAL DISTRESS

Primary Uses: Nerve pain from spinal injuries, head trauma, or severe limb fractures. Also manages “phantom” pain after amputation.

Forms: Oral solution (MUST be checked for Xylitol, which is toxic) or compounded liquid.

How it Works: Gabapentin is a structural analogue of GABA whose principal recognized target is the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels; it does not simply act as a GABA-receptor agonist.

Safety: Can cause significant sedation and ataxia (wobbliness). Introduce at a low dose and taper off rather than stopping abruptly.

⚠ WARNING: If the squirrel is on Trazodone, Gabapentin, or Benadryl, monitor for “Floppy Squirrel Syndrome.” Excessive sedation can lead to aspiration pneumonia because the squirrel loses the ability to swallow effectively.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Nebulized Gentamicin (Gentocin)

CATEGORY: ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: Reserved for high-risk aspiration pneumonia or chronic respiratory infections that have not responded to first-line oral antibiotics like Baytril and Doxycycline.

Forms: Injectable gentamicin solution diluted with sterile saline for use in a jet or ultrasonic nebulizer.

How it Works: The nebulizer turns liquid medication into a fine mist that the squirrel breathes in, allowing the antibiotic to bypass the bloodstream and directly target bacteria in the lungs.

Safety:

Bronchoconstriction: Some animals may react with coughing or constricted airways. Many protocols include a bronchodilator (like Albuterol) in the nebulizer mixture.

Equipment must be thoroughly cleaned after every use.

Treatment Course: Often administered for 15 to 30 minutes, 2 to 3 times daily, for 7 to 14 days, frequently as complementary therapy alongside systemic (oral) antibiotics.

Nebulization is a SUPPLEMENT to, not always a replacement for, systemic treatment. If infection has spread beyond the lungs, oral or injectable antibiotics are still necessary.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Meloxicam (Metacam)

CATEGORY: PAIN RELIEF / FEVER / INFLAMMATION REDUCTION

Primary Uses: Reducing pain, fever, and inflammation from trauma (falls, breaks) or post-surgery.

Forms: Highly palatable honey-flavored oral suspension (0.5mg/mL or 1.5mg/mL).

How it Works: Inhibits COX-2 enzymes, reducing prostaglandins that cause pain and swelling.

⚠ WARNING: NEVER use with steroids (Prednisone). Must only be used in well-hydrated animals to prevent kidney failure. FATAL TO CATS.

Treatment Course: Usually 1 dose daily for 5 to 10 days.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Nuflor (Florfenicol) – Oral Compounded

CATEGORY: ADVANCED BROAD SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: Severe aspiration pneumonia and refractory respiratory infections, specifically Bordetella bronchiseptica.

Forms: Most commonly sourced as a 300 mg/mL injectable solution.

Compounding Protocol: To achieve a safer concentration of 30 mg/mL, the solution MUST BE DILUTED. Mix at a 1:9 ratio (1 part Nuflor to 9 parts sterile water or flavoring agent).

How it Works: Bacteriostatic agent that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. Highly lipid-soluble, allowing excellent lung tissue penetration.

Safety:

GI Stasis: Extremely harsh on rodent gut flora. Monitor for bloat or severe diarrhea; pair with a high-potency probiotic (given 2 hours apart).

Palatability: Raw injectable solution is caustic and bitter. Dilution is mandatory to prevent oral burns or food aversion.

Developmental Risk: Use in pinkies is STRONGLY discouraged unless no other alternatives exist.

Storage:

Stock Vial: Room temp. Do NOT refrigerate (becomes too thick). Discard 30 days after first puncture.

Compounded Oral Solution: Discard after 7 days at room temp or 14 days refrigerated. Check for crystallization.

Treatment Course: 1 initial dose with second dose 72 hours later. NOT TO EXCEED 2 DOSES. If the second dose is ineffective, consult the Bordetella protocol to follow up with Doxycycline.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Panacur (Fenbendazole)

CATEGORY: ANTI-PARASITIC

Primary Uses: Roundworms, hookworms, whipworms, and effective against certain protozoa like Giardia.

Forms: Oral suspension.

How it Works: Interferes with the parasite’s energy metabolism by binding to tubulin.

Safety: Generally high safety margin. Rare side effects include mild vomiting or loose stools, particularly with high parasite loads.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Ponazuril (Marquis)

CATEGORY: ANTI-PARASITIC

Primary Uses: Coccidiosis. Often preferred over Albon because it kills the parasite rather than just inhibiting growth, and works in 2 doses over 48 hours versus 21 days.

Forms: Compounded liquid or thick equine paste that must be diluted. Comes in multiple strengths—KNOW YOUR MG/ML BEFORE DOSING.

How it Works: Targets the apicoplast organelle within coccidia, killing the parasite at multiple life stages.

Safety: Generally safe, but recommended for fully hydrated animals only. Acts faster than Albon.

Treatment Course: 1 dose every 48 hours for a total of 2 doses. Dosing varies significantly by concentration—verify strength with your vet.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Prednisone (Prednisolone)

CATEGORY: IMMUNE SUPPRESSANT / INFLAMMATION REDUCTION

⚠ WARNING: CONSULT WITH A VET BEFORE ADMINISTERING. Should not be given alongside NSAIDs (Meloxicam/Ibuprofen). Has numerous drug interactions \- see “Prednisone Drug Interactions” in the Drug Uses & Interactions section before administering with any other medication. Requires tapering—never discontinue abruptly.

Primary Uses: Emergency cases of head trauma, spinal cord injuries, or severe allergic shock.

Forms: Oral syrup (Prednisolone is the form more easily absorbed by the liver).

How it Works: Inhibits inflammatory pathways and suppresses the immune response to reduce tissue swelling.

Safety: Long-term use suppresses the immune system. Requires tapering off slowly; abrupt discontinuation should be avoided.

Treatment Course: Often involves an initial higher dose followed by a decreasing taper over several days.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Revolution (Selamectin)

CATEGORY: ANTI-PARASITIC

Primary Uses: Fleas, ear mites, and sarcoptic mange. May be considered safer for neonates than some other flea treatments.

Forms: Topical liquid applied to the skin.

How it Works: Enters the bloodstream through the skin and redistributes into skin and sebaceous glands, affecting the nervous system of parasites.

Safety: Generally safe. Apply where the animal cannot lick. Should NOT be used simultaneously with Ivermectin.

Treatment Course: Single topical application, remains active for a period of time.

Silvadene (Silver Sulfadiazine) SSD

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTIMICROBIAL / BURN TREATMENT

Primary Uses: The “gold standard” for thermal burns (from heating pads) and electrical burns (from chewing wires). Also effective for road rash or degloving injuries.

Forms: 1% white cream.

How it Works: Releases silver ions lethal to bacteria and fungi, while the sulfonamide provides additional antibiotic protection.

Safety: Do not use on squirrels with a known sulfa allergy. Apply in a thick layer (“buttering” the wound) but clean and reapply every 12–24 hours to prevent hardening into a crust.

Treatment Course: Applied daily until a healthy bed of granulation tissue (new pink skin) forms.

Terramycin (Oxytetracycline)

CATEGORY: ANTIBIOTIC – OPHTHALMIC

Primary Uses: Eye infections (conjunctivitis), inflamed eyelids, or “sticky eye” in weanling squirrels. Also effective against Mycoplasma and Chlamydia.

Forms: Sterile ophthalmic ointment.

How it Works: Interferes with bacteria’s ability to produce essential proteins, stopping infection at the site of the eye.

Safety: Very safe for topical use. Never let the tip of the tube touch the squirrel’s eye to prevent contaminating the remaining medication.

Treatment Course: Applied to affected eye(s) 2 to 4 times daily until the infection is resolved.

Trazodone

CATEGORY: ANTI-ANXIETY / SEDATIVE

Primary Uses: Enforced cage rest. Calms high-stress juveniles or adults with spinal injuries, fractures, or post-surgical hardware. Also reduces self-mutilation behaviors from capture stress or neurological trauma.

Forms: Tablets (human generic) or compounded flavored oral liquids.

How it Works: Increases serotonin while blocking specific serotonin receptors (5-HT2A), producing a calming effect without heavy knockout or dissociative state.

⚠ WARNING: Must be prescribed and dosed by a licensed veterinarian. Overdosage can lead to severe lethargy, “Floppy Squirrel Syndrome,” or serotonin syndrome. Excessive sedation can lead to aspiration pneumonia.

Treatment Course: Usually 1 to 2 times daily depending on injury severity.

Rehabber’s Note: Trazodone varies significantly in effect based on the individual squirrel’s metabolism. It is recommended to do a “test dose” while a veterinarian is present to monitor for excessive sedation or respiratory depression.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

──────────────────────────────

CATEGORY: PAIN RELIEF / ANTI-CONVULSANT / NEUROLOGICAL DISTRESS

Primary Uses: Nerve pain from spinal injuries, head trauma, or severe limb fractures. Also manages “phantom” pain after amputation.

Forms: Oral solution (MUST be checked for Xylitol, which is toxic) or compounded liquid.

How it Works: Gabapentin is a structural analogue of GABA whose principal recognized target is the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels; it does not simply act as a GABA-receptor agonist.

Safety: Can cause significant sedation and ataxia (wobbliness). Introduce at a low dose and taper off rather than stopping abruptly.

⚠ WARNING: If the squirrel is on Trazodone, Gabapentin, or Benadryl, monitor for “Floppy Squirrel Syndrome.” Excessive sedation can lead to aspiration pneumonia because the squirrel loses the ability to swallow effectively.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Nebulized Gentamicin (Gentocin)

CATEGORY: ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: Reserved for high-risk aspiration pneumonia or chronic respiratory infections that have not responded to first-line oral antibiotics like Baytril and Doxycycline.

Forms: Injectable gentamicin solution diluted with sterile saline for use in a jet or ultrasonic nebulizer.

How it Works: The nebulizer turns liquid medication into a fine mist that the squirrel breathes in, allowing the antibiotic to bypass the bloodstream and directly target bacteria in the lungs.

Safety:

Bronchoconstriction: Some animals may react with coughing or constricted airways. Many protocols include a bronchodilator (like Albuterol) in the nebulizer mixture.

Equipment must be thoroughly cleaned after every use.

Treatment Course: Often administered for 15 to 30 minutes, 2 to 3 times daily, for 7 to 14 days, frequently as complementary therapy alongside systemic (oral) antibiotics.

Nebulization is a SUPPLEMENT to, not always a replacement for, systemic treatment. If infection has spread beyond the lungs, oral or injectable antibiotics are still necessary.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Meloxicam (Metacam)

CATEGORY: PAIN RELIEF / FEVER / INFLAMMATION REDUCTION

Primary Uses: Reducing pain, fever, and inflammation from trauma (falls, breaks) or post-surgery.

Forms: Highly palatable honey-flavored oral suspension (0.5mg/mL or 1.5mg/mL).

How it Works: Inhibits COX-2 enzymes, reducing prostaglandins that cause pain and swelling.

⚠ WARNING: NEVER use with steroids (Prednisone). Must only be used in well-hydrated animals to prevent kidney failure. FATAL TO CATS.

Treatment Course: Usually 1 dose daily for 5 to 10 days.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Nuflor (Florfenicol) – Oral Compounded

CATEGORY: ADVANCED BROAD SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTIC

Primary Uses: Severe aspiration pneumonia and refractory respiratory infections, specifically Bordetella bronchiseptica.

Forms: Most commonly sourced as a 300 mg/mL injectable solution.

Compounding Protocol: To achieve a safer concentration of 30 mg/mL, the solution MUST BE DILUTED. Mix at a 1:9 ratio (1 part Nuflor to 9 parts sterile water or flavoring agent).

How it Works: Bacteriostatic agent that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. Highly lipid-soluble, allowing excellent lung tissue penetration.

Safety:

GI Stasis: Extremely harsh on rodent gut flora. Monitor for bloat or severe diarrhea; pair with a high-potency probiotic (given 2 hours apart).

Palatability: Raw injectable solution is caustic and bitter. Dilution is mandatory to prevent oral burns or food aversion.

Developmental Risk: Use in pinkies is STRONGLY discouraged unless no other alternatives exist.

Storage:

Stock Vial: Room temp. Do NOT refrigerate (becomes too thick). Discard 30 days after first puncture.

Compounded Oral Solution: Discard after 7 days at room temp or 14 days refrigerated. Check for crystallization.

Treatment Course: 1 initial dose with second dose 72 hours later. NOT TO EXCEED 2 DOSES. If the second dose is ineffective, consult the Bordetella protocol to follow up with Doxycycline.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Panacur (Fenbendazole)

CATEGORY: ANTI-PARASITIC

Primary Uses: Roundworms, hookworms, whipworms, and effective against certain protozoa like Giardia.

Forms: Oral suspension.

How it Works: Interferes with the parasite’s energy metabolism by binding to tubulin.

Safety: Generally high safety margin. Rare side effects include mild vomiting or loose stools, particularly with high parasite loads.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Ponazuril (Marquis)

CATEGORY: ANTI-PARASITIC

Primary Uses: Coccidiosis. Often preferred over Albon because it kills the parasite rather than just inhibiting growth, and works in 2 doses over 48 hours versus 21 days.

Forms: Compounded liquid or thick equine paste that must be diluted. Comes in multiple strengths—KNOW YOUR MG/ML BEFORE DOSING.

How it Works: Targets the apicoplast organelle within coccidia, killing the parasite at multiple life stages.

Safety: Generally safe, but recommended for fully hydrated animals only. Acts faster than Albon.

Treatment Course: 1 dose every 48 hours for a total of 2 doses. Dosing varies significantly by concentration—verify strength with your vet.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Prednisone (Prednisolone)

CATEGORY: IMMUNE SUPPRESSANT / INFLAMMATION REDUCTION

⚠ WARNING: CONSULT WITH A VET BEFORE ADMINISTERING. Should not be given alongside NSAIDs (Meloxicam/Ibuprofen). Has numerous drug interactions - see “Prednisone Drug Interactions” in the Drug Uses & Interactions section before administering with any other medication. Requires tapering—never discontinue abruptly.

Primary Uses: Emergency cases of head trauma, spinal cord injuries, or severe allergic shock.

Forms: Oral syrup (Prednisolone is the form more easily absorbed by the liver).

How it Works: Inhibits inflammatory pathways and suppresses the immune response to reduce tissue swelling.

Safety: Long-term use suppresses the immune system. Requires tapering off slowly; abrupt discontinuation should be avoided.

Treatment Course: Often involves an initial higher dose followed by a decreasing taper over several days.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

Revolution (Selamectin)

CATEGORY: ANTI-PARASITIC

Primary Uses: Fleas, ear mites, and sarcoptic mange. May be considered safer for neonates than some other flea treatments.

Forms: Topical liquid applied to the skin.

How it Works: Enters the bloodstream through the skin and redistributes into skin and sebaceous glands, affecting the nervous system of parasites.

Safety: Generally safe. Apply where the animal cannot lick. Should NOT be used simultaneously with Ivermectin.

Treatment Course: Single topical application, remains active for a period of time.

Silvadene (Silver Sulfadiazine) SSD

CATEGORY: TOPICAL ANTIMICROBIAL / BURN TREATMENT

Primary Uses: The “gold standard” for thermal burns (from heating pads) and electrical burns (from chewing wires). Also effective for road rash or degloving injuries.

Forms: 1% white cream.

How it Works: Releases silver ions lethal to bacteria and fungi, while the sulfonamide provides additional antibiotic protection.

Safety: Do not use on squirrels with a known sulfa allergy. Apply in a thick layer (“buttering” the wound) but clean and reapply every 12–24 hours to prevent hardening into a crust.

Treatment Course: Applied daily until a healthy bed of granulation tissue (new pink skin) forms.

Terramycin (Oxytetracycline)

CATEGORY: ANTIBIOTIC – OPHTHALMIC

Primary Uses: Eye infections (conjunctivitis), inflamed eyelids, or “sticky eye” in weanling squirrels. Also effective against Mycoplasma and Chlamydia.

Forms: Sterile ophthalmic ointment.

How it Works: Interferes with bacteria’s ability to produce essential proteins, stopping infection at the site of the eye.

Safety: Very safe for topical use. Never let the tip of the tube touch the squirrel’s eye to prevent contaminating the remaining medication.

Treatment Course: Applied to affected eye(s) 2 to 4 times daily until the infection is resolved.

Trazodone

CATEGORY: ANTI-ANXIETY / SEDATIVE

Primary Uses: Enforced cage rest. Calms high-stress juveniles or adults with spinal injuries, fractures, or post-surgical hardware. Also reduces self-mutilation behaviors from capture stress or neurological trauma.

Forms: Tablets (human generic) or compounded flavored oral liquids.

How it Works: Increases serotonin while blocking specific serotonin receptors (5-HT2A), producing a calming effect without heavy knockout or dissociative state.

⚠ WARNING: Must be prescribed and dosed by a licensed veterinarian. Overdosage can lead to severe lethargy, “Floppy Squirrel Syndrome,” or serotonin syndrome. Excessive sedation can lead to aspiration pneumonia.

Treatment Course: Usually 1 to 2 times daily depending on injury severity.

Rehabber’s Note: Trazodone varies significantly in effect based on the individual squirrel’s metabolism. It is recommended to do a “test dose” while a veterinarian is present to monitor for excessive sedation or respiratory depression.

📋 DOSING: Specific dosing must be determined by your veterinarian based on the individual animal’s weight, age, and condition.

──────────────────────────────

heading: Ch. 80 — Medical Dosing & Medication Reference › Dangerous Drug Interactions
text:
## **Dangerous Drug Interactions**

Doxycycline \+ Calcium – THE MINERAL TRAP

⚠ WARNING: Doxycycline binds to minerals and those minerals block absorption. DO NOT mix Doxy into formula. EVER. That single rule will prevent treatment failures you didn’t even know were happening.

Doxy is blocked by: calcium, magnesium, aluminum, iron, and zinc.

Common rehab items that sabotage Doxycycline:

Milk replacers (including Esbilac)

Calcium supplements

Mineral-added electrolytes

Antacids (calcium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide)

Fortified vitamins

Many probiotics (depending on formulation)

This does NOT mean Doxy “never works” in nursing babies. It means absorption may be unpredictable. Partial absorption is still better than no coverage. Neonates eat too frequently to allow perfect timing separation, and most wildlife vets prescribe Doxy anyway because inconsistent absorption beats letting Bordetella win.

NSAIDs \+ Corticosteroids – THE GI KILLER

⚠ WARNING: NEVER combine Meloxicam or Ibuprofen with Prednisone. This combination causes severe gastrointestinal ulceration and potentially fatal internal bleeding.

If switching between these classes, a 5–7 day wash-out period is required.

NSAID Stacking – DOUBLE KIDNEY DAMAGE

⚠ WARNING: NEVER use Meloxicam and Ibuprofen together. Two NSAIDs dramatically increase the risk of acute kidney failure and liver stress.

NSAIDs \+ Aminoglycosides – RENAL FAILURE

⚠ WARNING: Do not use Gentamicin with any NSAID. Both are toxic to the kidneys; combined use can cause rapid renal failure.

Sedation Stacking – RESPIRATORY ARREST RISK

Trazodone \+ Gabapentin \+ Benadryl all have additive sedative effects. Using multiple CNS depressants together can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, and aspiration risk. If combination use is necessary, reduce doses and monitor breathing constantly.

Nuflor \+ Lactated Ringer’s Solution – PRECIPITATE RISK

Do not mix Nuflor with LRS in the same syringe—it can precipitate (turn cloudy/solid). Administer separately.

heading: Ch. 80 — Medical Dosing & Medication Reference › Substances That Should NEVER Be Used on Squirrels
text:
## **Substances That Should NEVER Be Used on Squirrels**

The following should NEVER be administered to a squirrel under any circumstances:

Dog or cat flea medications (even “safe” ones) – can be fatal Exception: Capstar for Kittens

Permethrin – do not use. Contraindicated under 16 weeks (most squirrels in care), fatal to cats, and toxic to fish. For fleas use Capstar or Revolution; for mites, Revolution or the ivermectin protocols.

Pyrethroids – neurotoxic

Human adult-strength pain medications (Tylenol, adult Advil, aspirin)

Human combination cold/flu medications – extremely dangerous

Adult-strength Imodium

Essential oils (applied or diffused near animals) – toxic

“Natural wormers” – ineffective and delay real treatment

Ivermectin in neonates – neurotoxicity risk

Any medication containing Xylitol – toxic to small mammals

Topical anesthetics — lidocaine and pramoxine ("+ Pain Relief" antibiotic ointments, Bactine, lidocaine creams) — especially on babies, kits under 8 weeks, or raw, broken, or necrotic skin. A tiny body absorbs them through damaged skin, and grooming means they get swallowed: risks include a dangerously slow heart or abnormal rhythm, tremors, seizures, or "the spins." Use instead: vet-approved systemic pain relief (meloxicam, gabapentin); for wounds, silver sulfadiazine (SSD), plain original triple antibiotic ointment, or medical-grade Manuka honey.

Benzocaine (Orasol) — vet-directed only (methemoglobinemia risk)

Fox Valley 32/40 — we do not use this formula. If you have some, save it for homemade treats for older kids only (Ch. 5, 11D).

When in doubt: DO NOT administer. Contact your veterinarian. The 15 minutes you spend making a phone call could save an animal’s life.

──────────────────────────────

heading: Ch. 81 — Euthanasia Protocols and Decision-Making
text:
## **81\. Euthanasia Protocols and Decision-Making**

Rehabilitation is the art of returning animals to the wild. When that goal becomes impossible and the animal’s quality of life is compromised, euthanasia is the most compassionate clinical tool we have. It is a mercy that ends “suffocation panic,” unmanageable pain, and fear.

⚠️ CRITICAL WARNING: Professional Administration

Euthanasia must be performed by a licensed veterinarian or a certified euthanasia technician. Attempts to perform “at-home” euthanasia (such as blunt force, cervical dislocation, or drowning) are not only inhumane but carry the following severe risks:

The “Botched” Attempt: Squirrels have incredibly dense bone structures and a high “will to live.” Inexperienced attempts often result in severe injury without death, leaving the animal in a state of agonizing terror and increased pain.

The Risk of Injury: A squirrel in a state of panic or partial consciousness can inflict deep, infectious “fear-bites” (Ch. 2) or scratches on the handler.

Chemical Hazards: Using non-approved substances is agonizing for the animal. Professional euthanasia involves a “two-step” process: first, a heavy sedative to induce deep sleep, followed by the final medication that stops the heart. This is the only way to ensure a painless transition.

Legal Consequences: In many jurisdictions, attempting to kill wildlife yourself—even for mercy—can be classified as animal cruelty or a violation of your state rehab permit.

Always have a “Mercy Vet” on speed-dial. Most clinics will provide low-cost or free euthanasia for confirmed wildlife cases. It is better to drive an hour to a vet than to have the squirrel’s final moments be ones of avoidable trauma.

1. When Euthanasia Is the Right Call

The decision should be based on the “Wild Path” or the “Sanctuary Path.” If neither exists, euthanasia is indicated.

Irreparable Physical Damage: Severed spines with no deep pain sensation, multiple crushed limbs, or “shattered” jaws that cannot be surgically repaired.

Progressive “Quiet Killers”: Advanced Odontomas that have invaded the sinus cavity or eyes, or neurological decay from West Nile Virus that prevents the animal from self-feeding.

Incurable Suffering: Severe, third-degree thermal burns or advanced septicemia where the squirrel is in a state of active organ failure.

The “Panic” Factor: If a squirrel’s condition (like severe bloat or respiratory obstruction) causes constant gasping and “air hunger,” immediate mercy is required to end the panic.

2. How to Make the Decision

Use the “Three Pillar” test. If the answer to any of these is “No,” the squirrel is a candidate for euthanasia:

Can the squirrel live without pain? (Can their pain be managed without keeping them in a permanent state of sedation?)

Can the squirrel perform natural behaviors? (Can they eat, groom, and move without distress?)

Is there a viable future? (Is there a release site or a permanent sanctuary spot available that meets their specific needs?)

3. Talking to Finders About Euthanasia

Finders often feel a sense of “heroism” and may be resistant to the idea of the animal dying.

The “Quality of Life” Script: “Our goal is always a wild life. Unfortunately, this little one’s injuries are so severe that he would spend the rest of his life in pain and fear. The most heroic thing we can do now is ensure he doesn’t suffer anymore.”

Be Direct but Gentle: Avoid euphemisms like “putting to sleep” if they cause confusion. Use terms like “humane transition” or “medical mercy.”

The “Closed Door” Policy: You are never required to have the finder present. In fact, it is usually better for the squirrel’s stress levels if the room is quiet and only contains the rehabber/vet.

4. Aftercare and What to Do with Remains

Handling the remains with dignity is part of the rehabber’s closure.

Burial: If local laws allow, bury at least 2 feet deep to prevent scavengers from digging up the remains (especially if euthanasia drugs were used, as these can be toxic to predators).

Incineration/Cremation: Most vets offer communal or individual cremation.

The “Natural Cycle”: If the squirrel died naturally (not through chemical euthanasia) and was not diseased/poisoned, some rehabbers choose to return the body to a remote wooded area to allow the “circle of life” to continue.

Acknowledge the Toll: Taking a life, even mercifully, causes Compassion Fatigue. Take a moment to acknowledge the work you did for that squirrel. You gave them a warm, safe place to spend their final hours instead of a cold sidewalk.

heading: Ch. 82 — Release Site Selection — Choosing the Forever Home
text:
## **82\. Release Site Selection — Choosing the Forever Home**

You have spent months saving this life; do not lose it in the final hour by choosing a dangerous location. A release site is not just a place with trees—it is a complex ecosystem that must meet four primary criteria.

1. The “Canopy Highway” (Connectivity)

Squirrels are safest when they don’t have to touch the ground.

The Test: Look up. Can a squirrel travel at least two blocks (or several hundred yards) by jumping from limb to limb without descending?

Why: Ground travel is where they meet cars, dogs, and cats. A “fragmented” forest is a death trap for a newly released juvenile.

2. Mast-Producing Trees (The Natural Larder)

A squirrel cannot survive on your supplemental feeding alone. They need “Hard Mast” to survive the winter.

Identify the Trees: Ensure the site has a high density of Oak (acorns), Walnut, Hickory, or Beech.

The Variety Rule: A site with only one type of tree is risky. If that specific crop fails one year, the squirrel may starve. A diverse forest is a stable forest.

3. The Water Requirement

Especially in drier climates like Idaho, water is the limiting factor for wildlife.

Proximity: There should be a reliable, year-round water source within 100 yards of the release cage.

Safety: Deep, steep-sided cattle tanks or pools without “critter escapes” are drowning hazards. Look for sloped creek banks or birdbaths maintained by “squirrel-friendly” neighbors.

4. The “Human Factor” (Safety & Policy)

The “No-Poison” Zone: Talk to the neighbors. If anyone in a 3-block radius uses rodenticide (rat poison), do not release there. A squirrel eating a poisoned bait or a poisoned carcass is a slow, painful death.

Predator Density: Avoid areas with high populations of outdoor/feral cats.

Legality: Ensure the landowner is 100% on board. You don’t want a “No Trespassing” sign to go up while you still need to provide supplemental food to your “Soft Release” cage.

Group Releases (The Buddy System)

Whenever possible, release squirrels in small groups (2–4), ideally siblings or “matched pairs” that have lived together in your pre-release cage.

Strength in Numbers: They will often share a drey for the first winter, sharing body heat to survive the cold.

Shared Vigilance: More eyes in the canopy means a better chance of spotting a hawk before it strikes.

The “Bully” Check: If one squirrel is aggressively dominant in the cage, they may need to be released 24 hours apart to give the submissive squirrel time to find a hiding spot.

Safety: Deep, steep-sided cattle tanks or pools without “critter escapes” are drowning hazards. Look for sloped creek banks or birdbaths maintained by “squirrel-friendly” neighbors.

4. The “Human Factor” (Safety & Policy)

The “No-Poison” Zone: Talk to the neighbors. If anyone in a 3-block radius uses rodenticide (rat poison), do not release there. A squirrel eating a poisoned bait or a poisoned carcass is a slow, painful death.

Predator Density: Avoid areas with high populations of outdoor/feral cats.

Legality: Ensure the landowner is 100% on board. You don’t want a “No Trespassing” sign to go up while you still need to provide supplemental food to your “Soft Release” cage.

Group Releases (The Buddy System)

Whenever possible, release squirrels in small groups (2–4), ideally siblings or “matched pairs” that have lived together in your pre-release cage.

Strength in Numbers: They will often share a drey for the first winter, sharing body heat to survive the cold.

Shared Vigilance: More eyes in the canopy means a better chance of spotting a hawk before it strikes.

The “Bully” Check: If one squirrel is aggressively dominant in the cage, they may need to be released 24 hours apart to give the submissive squirrel time to find a hiding spot.

heading: Ch. 83 — The Soft Release Protocol
text:
## **83\. The Soft Release Protocol**

A “Hard Release”—simply opening a cage and walking away—is a death sentence for a hand-reared squirrel. They have no “map” of the area, no cached food, and no awareness of local predators. We use the Soft Release method: a gradual transition that allows them to “wild up” while keeping a safety net.

1. The 30-Day Countdown (Outdoor Acclimation)

Once a squirrel is 10–12 weeks old, fully weaned, and physically agile, they move to an outdoor release cage.

The Goal: To reset their internal clock to the sun, thicken their fur for the local climate, and introduce them to the sights and sounds of the neighborhood.

The Rule: The cage should be in a quiet area of the yard, away from dogs and heavy human traffic.

Duration: Minimum of 2 to 3 weeks in the outdoor cage before the door is ever opened.

2. “Wilding Up” Behavior

During this month, you will notice a personality shift. This is a good thing.

They should stop seeking your hand and start “barking” at you or hiding when you approach.

Your Job: Become the “Ghost Provider.” Stop talking to them. Stop petting them. Wear a mask or a hoodie if you have to. You are now just the source of food, not a friend.

3. Release Site Criteria

Not every backyard is a release site. A perfect site needs:

The Canopy: Interlocking trees (so they can travel without touching the ground).

Water: A year-round water source (creek, pond, or a birdbath you commit to filling).

Food: Mast-producing trees (Oak, Walnut, Hickory) or neighbors who have “wild-friendly” yards.

The Predator Check: Low outdoor-cat population and no neighbors who use poison/snap traps.

4. Opening the Door (The Big Day)

The Timing: Choose a string of at least 3–5 days of clear, fair weather. Never release on the eve of a storm.

The Method: Open the door in the morning and walk away. Do not chase them out. Let them discover the exit on their own.

The Safety Net: Leave the cage open and continue to provide fresh water and food inside/on top of the cage for at least 2–4 weeks after release. This is their “Home Base” until they build a drey.

5. The Winter Release Dilemma

In Idaho and similar climates, the “Release Window” usually closes by late September or early October.

The Rule: If a squirrel is not ready for release by the time the nights are consistently freezing, you must Overwinter them.

Why? They haven’t had time to cache enough food to survive the winter. Releasing a “fall baby” in November is a death sentence. They stay with you until the first buds appear in Spring.

heading: Ch. 84 — The Danger of the “Hard Release”
text:
## **84\. The Danger of the “Hard Release”**

A Hard Release occurs when a captive-raised squirrel is taken to a random location, the carrier door is opened, and the animal is left to fend for itself. In the world of professional rehabilitation, a Hard Release is considered a failure of care.

1. Why It Is a “No-No” (The Biological Reality)

Zero Geographic Map: A squirrel’s survival depends on knowing exactly where the “escape routes” are. They need to know which branch leads to a hollow and which leads to a dead end. A hard-released squirrel has no map; when a hawk strikes, they hesitate—and hesitation is fatal.

The “Larder” Problem: Squirrels spend their entire lives caching food. A squirrel released in the fall without a “Soft Release” period has zero food stores. They cannot catch up to the local squirrels who have been burying nuts for months.

Territorial Warfare: Squirrels are social but highly territorial. Dropping a “stranger” into an established colony is like dropping a person into a neighborhood where they don’t speak the language and are trying to sleep on someone’s porch. The resident squirrels will often relentlessly bully, chase, or even kill the newcomer.

The Shelter Crisis: Building a drey (nest) takes time and skill. A hand-reared juvenile may not have perfected the “weaving” technique yet. Without a “Soft Release” cage or a provided nesting box to retreat to, they are exposed to the elements and predators on night one.

2. The Psychological Impact

A squirrel raised by humans has a “safety bias.” In a hard release, they are suddenly stripped of their food source, their “nest,” and their protector all at once. This leads to Capture Myopathy or extreme stress-responses, where the squirrel may simply sit on the ground in a “trance,” making them an easy meal for a roaming cat.

3. When is a Hard Release acceptable?

Almost never. The only exception is for a Short-Term Adult Intake.

Example: If you trapped a healthy adult squirrel to treat a minor wound for 3 days, you can “Hard Release” them—but only at the exact location where they were trapped. They already have their map, their caches, and their nest waiting for them.

heading: Ch. 85 — The “Nesting Box” Head Start
text:
## **85\. The “Nesting Box” Head Start**

To bridge the gap between the cage and the wild, we highly recommend the Starter Nesting Box.

The Strategy: Mount a sturdy, wooden squirrel box (with a predator-guarded entrance) in the release tree.

The Advantage: It gives them an immediate, “bomb-proof” shelter while they learn to build their own dreys. It also provides a familiar scent-marker that tells them, “This is home base.”

heading: Ch. 86 — Overwintering (The “Winter Guests”)
text:
## **86\. Overwintering (The “Winter Guests”)**

Overwintering is the process of holding a squirrel through the cold months to release them in the spring. In the Pacific Northwest/Idaho, the general rule is: If they aren’t out by October 1st, they stay until April.

1. The “Cutoff” Logic

Why can’t we release in November?

The Food Cache: Squirrels need weeks to bury nuts and establish a “pantry” for the winter. A squirrel released late has zero food stores.

The Nest (Drey): Building a winter-proof drey takes time and experience.

The “Toughness” Factor: A 12-week-old baby doesn’t have the body fat or the coarse “winter guard hairs” to survive a sub-zero night.

2. Housing During Overwintering

You have two choices: Inside vs. Outside.

Inside (The Controlled Hold):

Best for: Injured, underweight, or “special needs” squirrels (like your dwarves).

Pros: Prevents frostbite and keeps metabolic needs lower.

Cons: They may “de-wild” or lose their acclimation to the cold.

Outside (The Cold Hold):

Best for: Healthy, late-season juveniles.

Setup: A large, predator-proof outdoor enclosure with heavily insulated nesting boxes. Use straw or “virgin” sheep’s wool (never fleece, as it holds moisture/ice) inside the boxes.

Pros: They stay “wild” and maintain their winter coats.

3. The “Soft” Winter Diet

Overwintered squirrels are prone to “cage laziness” and obesity.

Limit the “Easy” Sugars: Cut back on fruit. Stick to high-quality blocks and sturdy winter veggies (squash, kale).

Work for Food: Give them nuts in the shell to keep their teeth trim and their minds busy.

Hydration: If outside, ensure their water hasn’t frozen. Use heated pet bowls or change the water twice daily.

4. Preventing “Zoo-osis” (Boredom)

Spending 5–6 months in a cage is mentally taxing for a wild animal.

Rotate Enrichment: Move branches around, add “dig boxes,” and hide food.

The Buddy System: Never overwinter a squirrel alone if you can help it. They need the social interaction and the “cuddle heat” to stay sane and warm.

5. The Spring Release Protocol

Do not open the door on the first warm day in March.

The “Green Leaf” Rule: Wait until the trees have leaves and the first green shoots appear. This ensures there is natural food available and that the squirrels will have natural cover to hide under.

The Hardening Off: If they were kept inside, move them to an outdoor cage for 2 weeks before release to get their bodies used to the temperature fluctuations. See Soft Release for full details.

heading: Ch. 87 — Release Failure and Boomerang Babies
text:
## **87\. Release Failure and Boomerang Babies**

Release is not a single event; it is a process. Some squirrels “take” to the wild instantly, while others need a second (or third) try. Monitoring your “graduates” is just as important as feeding your pinkies.

1. What’s Normal: The “Checking In” Phase

For the first 7–14 days, it is perfectly normal for a squirrel to:

The Snack Run: Return to the release cage or your back porch for a “easy meal.” They are learning to forage, but their bellies aren’t full yet.

The Sleepover: Sleep in the release cage or a provided nesting box for several nights before building their own drey.

The Recognition: Sit on a branch and “bark” at you or watch you through the window. As long as they are active and alert, this is fine.

2. What’s NOT Normal: Red Flags

If you see these signs, the release is failing, and the squirrel’s life is at risk:

The “Huddle”: The squirrel is sitting on the ground or a low branch, puffed up, with eyes squinted or closed.

Weight Loss: You can see the “razor back” spine or hip bones (Refeeding Syndrome risk—Ch. 63).

Approachability: If the squirrel tries to climb your leg or begs to be picked up, they have “de-wilded” due to hunger or fear.

Injury/Myopathy: Limping, dragging limbs, or signs of “Capture Myopathy” (extreme lethargy and lack of flight response).

3. When to Re-Trap

Do not hesitate. If a squirrel is failing, 24 hours can be the difference between a recovery and a carcass.

The Trap: Use the original release cage. Place high-value treats (nut butters, avocado) inside and use a manual pull-string or a Havahart trap.

The Protocol: Bring them back inside. Provide Heat, Hydration, and Darkness immediately.

4. Re-Integration into Pre-Release

Once stabilized, a returner shouldn’t necessarily go back to a small indoor cage.

The Assessment: If it was just an injury, treat and hold. If they “failed” because they weren’t wild enough, they need more time in the outdoor acclimation cage with zero human interaction.

The “Ghost” Treatment: This is the time to be the “Ghost Provider” (Ch. 83). They must learn that humans provide food, but they are not “friends.”

5. When a Release Becomes a “Non-Release”

Sometimes, despite our best efforts, a squirrel is mentally or physically unable to survive.

Physical: Chronic malocclusion, neurological deficits (West Nile/Trauma), or permanent stunted growth (Dwarfism).

Psychological: “Deep Imprinting.” If a squirrel shows zero fear of predators (cats/dogs) after 30 days of “wilding up,” they cannot be released. They will not survive 48 hours in a real forest.

AT-A-GLANCE: Release Readiness Checklist

Before the door opens, check these boxes. If any are “No,” wait another week.

\[ \] Weight: Is the squirrel at the target weight for their species?

\[ \] Agility: Can they leap between branches and “spiral” a trunk at high speed?

\[ \] Fear Response: Do they hide or “scold” when they see a dog or hear a loud noise?

\[ \] Foraging: Can they successfully open a hard-shell nut (Walnut/Hickory) on their own?

\[ \] Weather: Is there a 3-5 day window of clear, mild weather ahead?

\[ \] Water: Have you identified the specific water source they will use?

heading: Ch. 88 — The Sanctuary Environment
text:
## **88\. The Sanctuary Environment**

When a squirrel is deemed non-releasable due to physical disability (dwarfism, malocclusion) or deep imprinting, your goal shifts to Quality of Life (QoL). A cage that was “fine” for a 6-week recovery is not sufficient for a 10-year life span.

1. The “Horizontal over Vertical” Rule

While wild squirrels love height, many non-releasables (especially dwarves or those with neurological issues) are prone to falls.

The Design: Prioritize floor space and width over extreme height. If using a tall cage, install “Safety Baffles”—fleece hammocks or platforms staggered every 2 feet to catch a squirrel if they lose their grip.

The Flooring: Never use wire mesh bottoms; they cause bumblefoot and snag long nails. Use solid flooring covered in fleece, newspaper, or kiln-dried aspen shavings.

2. Strategic Accessibility

For squirrels with limited mobility:

Ramps over Ladders: Use wide, shallow-angle wooden ramps instead of vertical ladders.

The “Lapping” Station: If a squirrel has a malocclusion or jaw injury, they may struggle with traditional water bottle tubes. Provide a heavy, ceramic “no-tip” water crock that is shallow and easy to lap from.

Lowered Resources: Keep food, water, and the primary nesting box in the bottom 1/3 of the cage to conserve their energy.

3. Environmental Enrichment (Preventing “Stereotypy”)

Captive squirrels often develop “stereotypical behaviors” like obsessive pacing or wire-chewing due to boredom.

The Rotation: Change out toys, branches, and “puzzle feeders” weekly.

Safe Chews: Provide fresh, pesticide-free branches (Apple, Pear, Magnolia) to satisfy their gnawing instinct and keep teeth trim.

The “Dig Box”: A small bin filled with sterile coconut coir or shredded paper allows them to perform their natural caching (burying) behaviors.

4. Social Needs

The Companion Factor: If you have multiple non-releasables of the same species and sex, or a neutered/spayed pair, housing them together is the \#1 way to improve QoL. They groom, sleep, and play together, which no human can replicate.

Safe Human Interaction: Unlike release candidates, sanctuary squirrels need your interaction. Establish a routine for “out of cage” time in a squirrel-proofed room to maintain their muscle tone and mental health.

5. The “Sanctuary Diet” Caution

Non-releasable squirrels are prone to Obesity, which puts immense strain on their already compromised joints.

The 80/20 Rule: 80% high-quality rodent blocks (Henry’s/Mazuri) and 20% fresh veggies.

Nuts as Medicine: Nuts should be used only as a reward for tooth trims, medication taking, or extreme enrichment—never as a daily meal component.

heading: Ch. 89 — Feeding Your Non-Releasable Squirrels
text:
## **89\. Feeding Your Non-Releasable Squirrels**

This is where the “Science of Sanctuary” really comes into play. For a non-releasable squirrel, food is no longer just fuel for growth; it is their primary source of entertainment, their main health risk (obesity/MBD), and their strongest bond with you.

In a long-term captive setting, we have to be much stricter than we are with release candidates because “dietary indiscretions” (too many nuts) add up over years, not just weeks.

Feeding the Permanent Resident

The goal for a sanctuary squirrel is to maintain a lean body weight while providing maximum mental stimulation. An overweight squirrel is a squirrel with heart disease, pododermatitis (foot sores), and joint pain.

1. The “Power of the Block” (The 80% Rule)

Rodent blocks are the only way to ensure 100% nutritional coverage.

The Foundation: High-quality blocks (like Henry’s Healthy Blocks) must make up the vast majority of their caloric intake.

The Routine: Feed blocks first thing in the morning when the squirrel is hungriest. Do not offer veggies or treats until the blocks have been consumed.

For Dwarves/Seniors: If the squirrel has dental issues, soak the blocks in a tiny bit of warm water or unsweetened almond milk to create a “mash.”

2. The “Greens and Garden” (The 20% Rule)

Fresh produce provides hydration and fiber.

The Best Choices (High Ca:P Ratio): Kale, collard greens, turnip greens, squash, sugar snap peas, and bell peppers.

The “Limit” List: Fruits (berries, apple slices) should be viewed as sugar-bombs. Offer them in thumbnail-sized portions only 2–3 times a week.

The “Never” List: Avoid starchy “fillers” like corn, white potatoes, or dried fruit blends sold in pet stores.

3. The “Nut Myth” (Treats vs. Food)

In the wild, squirrels work hard for every nut. In a cage, a nut is “free” fat.

Nuts are Medicine/Rewards: Only use nuts for:

Positive reinforcement during tooth trims.

Taming/Bonding sessions.

Delivering oral medications (crushing a pill into a piece of walnut).

The Limit: One almond or half a walnut per day is the absolute maximum for a healthy adult. For a dwarf, reduce this by half.

4. Foraging Enrichment (Making them Work)

A sanctuary squirrel’s biggest enemy is boredom.

Hide the Food: Don’t just use a bowl. Hide blocks in fleece braids, inside cardboard toilet paper rolls, or tucked into crevices of clean branches.

The “Shell” Rule: If the squirrel’s teeth are healthy, always provide nuts (the rare ones they get) in the shell. The act of gnawing through the shell provides 15 minutes of “work” and natural tooth wear.

Antler Chews: Provide a piece of naturally shed deer antler. It’s a great source of calcium and a durable chew toy that won’t rot.

5. Weight Monitoring

The “Spine Test”: You should be able to feel the spine and ribs with light pressure, but they shouldn’t be “sharp.” If you see a “roll” of fat behind the front legs (the “armpits”), the squirrel is obese.

The Scale: Weigh your non-releasables once a month. Sudden weight gain can indicate a lack of exercise, while sudden loss can be the first sign of dental failure or internal illness.

heading: Ch. 90 — Aggression, Hormones, and the Neuter Question
text:
## **90\. Aggression, Hormones, and the Neuter Question**

As squirrels reach sexual maturity (usually between 8–12 months), their behavior changes. For a non-releasable squirrel, this “wild surge” can manifest as sudden aggression toward their favorite human. Understanding these warnings is key to maintaining a safe sanctuary.

1. Decoding the Warning Signs

A squirrel rarely bites without “telling” you first. Learn to read the body language:

The “Tail Flag”: A sharp, rhythmic waving of the tail. This is not “wagging” like a dog; it is a signal of high agitation or a warning to back off.

The “Stomp”: Rapidly tapping the front paws on a flat surface.

The “Chatter”: Audible grinding or clicking of the teeth. This is a clear signal that the squirrel is ready to use them.

The “Lunging Poke”: The squirrel may lunge and “boop” you with its nose without biting. This is a “final warning” shot.

2. “Winter Aggression” (The Seasonal Shift)

Even the tamest sanctuary squirrel can become a “demon” during the winter months.

The Trigger: Shorter days and colder temps trigger a biological drive to protect their food cache (you and their cage) and find a mate.

The Strategy: During “mean season,” limit physical handling. Use a “back-scratcher” or a long toy for interaction, and provide extra foraging puzzles to burn off that nervous energy.

3. To Neuter or Not to Neuter?

This is a frequent debate in the sanctuary community. Unlike dogs and cats, neutering a squirrel is a high-risk procedure with mixed behavioral results.

The Pros:

Reduced Aggression: In some males, it can significantly dampen “seasonal” aggression and territorial spraying (urine marking).

Co-Housing: It allows you to house a male and female together without the risk of “backyard” breeding.

The Cons:

Surgical Risk: Small mammals struggle with anesthesia. Many squirrels do not wake up from the procedure.

The “Hidden” Testicles: Squirrels have retractable testicles. A vet who is not a wildlife specialist may struggle to locate them or accidentally cause a hernia.

Inconsistent Results: If the aggression is “learned” (imprinted/fear-based) rather than purely hormonal, neutering will not fix it.

Squirrel Doc Verdict: Only consider neutering if you have a highly experienced exotics vet and a specific medical or social reason (like pairing with a female). Do not neuter as a “first resort” for behavioral issues; try environmental enrichment and “hands-off” periods first.

4. Managing the “Bitey” Squirrel

If a sanctuary resident becomes aggressive:

Check for Pain: Is there a tooth issue? An old injury flaring up? Aggression is often the only way a squirrel can say “I hurt.”

Respect the “No”: If they flag their tail when you open the cage, don’t force the interaction. Give them space.

Protective Gear: Keep a pair of heavy welding gloves or a thick fleece “sacrifice towel” nearby for when you must handle them (e.g., for cage cleaning or medical checks).

heading: Ch. 91 — Public Interaction & Social Media
text:
## **91\. Public Interaction & Social Media**

This is the chapter that makes experienced rehabbers cry with relief. We often spend as much time managing humans as we do managing squirrels. Protecting your boundaries is the only way to prevent burnout.

1. What NOT to Post (Legal & Safety)

The “Illegal” Cuddle: In many states (including Idaho), wildlife must be kept in a “non-display” fashion. Posting videos of squirrels playing with your domestic pets or sitting on your shoulder while you drink coffee can be used as evidence by Fish & Game to revoke your permit.

The “Location” Leak: Never post the exact location of your release sites. “Poaching” isn’t just for big game; people will go to release sites to try and find “tame” squirrels to take as pets.

The “Home” Danger: Avoid showing the exterior of your house or identifiable landmarks. You do not want “drop-offs” appearing on your porch at 3 AM because someone found your address online.

2. How to Prevent “Finder Entitlement”

Finders often feel they “own” the squirrel because they saved it.

The Script: “Once the squirrel enters my care, it is a Ward of the State. For the safety of the animal, I do not provide daily updates, photos, or ‘visitation.’ My goal is to make them forget humans exist so they can survive in the wild.”

The Boundary: You are a medical facility, not a petting zoo. If a finder becomes demanding, refer them to the state wildlife agency’s general policy on rehabilitation.

3. Handling “Armchair Rehabbers” & Harassment

Social media is full of people who “had a squirrel once” and will criticize your protocol.

The “Don’t Engage” Rule: You do not owe an explanation to someone on the internet. If someone is harassing you about your weaning schedule or cage size, Block and Move On. \* The Fact-Check: If someone is spreading dangerous advice (e.g., “Feed them cow’s milk\!”), post a single link to the official protocol and turn off comments. Do not get into a “comment war.”

4. Protecting Release Sites from the Public

The “Silent” Release: Never invite the public or “the media” to a release. The crowd’s noise and energy will terrify the squirrel, leading to a “Hard Release” panic (Ch. 84).

The Non-Disclosure: If a neighbor asks what you are doing, you are “monitoring local wildlife diversity.” You don’t need to specify that you just released six juveniles.

5. The Psychological Toll of Being Watched

Rehab is hard enough without the “Performance” aspect.

Compassion Fatigue: This is exacerbated when you feel you have to “justify” a euthanasia or a loss to an online audience.

The “Private” Win: Learn to celebrate the wins (a successful release) and mourn the losses privately or with a small circle of fellow rehabbers. You do not need to “content-create” your grief.

The “I Found a Baby” Call Script

To save your sanity, use a template for the hundreds of calls you will receive.

Safety First: “Is the animal in a box? Is it on heat? Do not give it any food or water yet.”

Reunion Check: “Is it truly orphaned, or did the mom just drop it? (See Ch. 3: Reunion Protocol).”

The Hand-off: “I am at capacity/can take it. Here is the neutral drop-off location.”

The “No-Update” Policy: “To focus on the animals, I cannot provide individual status reports. Thank you for understanding.”

This is the “Heart of the Manual.” You can have all the medical supplies in the world, but if the rehabber breaks, the mission stops. This section is a quiet acknowledgement that what we do is emotionally expensive.

heading: Ch. 92 — Rehabber Mental Health & Sustainability
text:
## **92\. Rehabber Mental Health & Sustainability**

Rehabilitation is a marathon run at a sprinter’s pace. Because we are driven by deep empathy, we are uniquely vulnerable to the emotional weight of this work. To save the squirrels, you must first save yourself.

1. Compassion Fatigue vs. Burnout

Compassion Fatigue: The “cost of caring.” It is the physical and emotional exhaustion that comes from witnessing the suffering of others. You might feel “numb,” lose your ability to feel empathy, or find yourself crying over a broken syringe.

Burnout: This is about the workload. It’s the feeling of being overwhelmed by too many feedings, too little sleep, and an endless pile of laundry.

2. The Emotional Toll of Losses & Euthanasia

The “Weight of the World”: It is normal to feel a sense of failure when a squirrel dies, especially one you fought for. Remember: You are not the cause of their trauma; you are the mercy that met it.

The Euthanasia Hangover: Making the call to end a life is a heavy burden. It often leads to “moral injury”—doubting if you did the right thing. Trust your protocols (Ch. 81) and trust your “past self” who made the decision with the facts at hand.

3. Peak Season Survival (The May/August Crunch)

In Idaho, the baby booms in spring and late summer can be relentless.

The “No” is a Tool: Learning to say “I am at capacity” is a life-saving skill. Taking one more squirrel when you are exhausted puts all the other squirrels in your care at risk of a mistake.

Micro-Breaks: Even 10 minutes away from the “peeping” of the incubator can reset your nervous system. Step outside, breathe the air, and remember what a tree looks like without a squirrel in it.

4. How to Know When to Step Back

It is time for a “Sabbatical” or a break if you notice:

Resentment: You start to feel angry at the finders or the animals themselves.

Neglect: You find yourself “cutting corners” on protocols or skipping cleanings.

Physical Toll: Chronic insomnia, headaches, or a weakened immune system.

Isolation: You stop talking to friends/family because “they don’t understand the work.”

5. Sustainability: How to Do This for Years

Build a Support Network: Join a private rehabber group (like the one we are building this Bible for). You need people who won’t say “It’s just a squirrel” when you lose a favorite resident.

Celebrate the Wins: We tend to remember the 5 we lost and forget the 50 we released. Keep a “Success Jar” or a folder of release photos to look at during the dark months.

Set Boundaries with the Public: (See Ch. 91: Public Relations). Do not give out your personal cell phone number to every finder. Use a dedicated line or app.

6. The “Oxygen Mask” Rule

You cannot pour from an empty cup. If you are not eating, sleeping, and hydrating, you cannot provide high-level medical care. Taking care of yourself is not “selfish”—it is a requirement for being a high-quality rehabilitator.

heading: Ch. 93 — Founder Syndrome & the Savior Complex
text:
## **93\. Founder Syndrome & the Savior Complex**

The “Savior Complex” is the belief that you are the only thing standing between an animal and death. While technically true for that specific orphan, this mindset can lead to a “God Complex” that destroys your health and the quality of care for your existing patients.

1. Recognizing the Savior Complex in Yourself

Ask yourself these hard questions:

Do I feel like I am the only capable rehabber in the state?

Do I feel a secret sense of pride in being “the most exhausted” person in my circle?

Am I taking in animals even though my quarantine area is full, or I’m skipping my own meals?

The Symptom: If your first thought when a call comes in is “Oh god, not another one” followed by an immediate “But I have to,” you are moving from Compassion to Compulsion.

2. The Math: Why “One More” Hurts Everyone

Let’s look at the “Squirrel Math” of being over-capacity:

The 10% Rule: Every new squirrel takes 10% of your time away from the others. If you have 10 squirrels and take an 11th, you are now providing 90% care to everyone.

The Mistake Threshold: Fatigue is the leading cause of Aspiration Pneumonia (Ch. 16). When you are tired, your hand slips on the syringe.

The Hygiene Decline: More squirrels \= more laundry, more dishes, and more cross-contamination risk. One case of Coccidia in a crowded room can wipe out a whole season’s work.

3. How to Say “No” (Without Feeling Like a Murderer)

When you are at capacity, saying “No” is an act of advocacy for the animals already in your cages.

The Script: “I am currently at my legal and medical capacity. If I take one more, I cannot provide the life-saving care that the squirrels currently in my nursery require. My priority is ensuring the survivors actually survive.”

The Referral: Keep a list of other rehabbers, even if they are far away. If everyone is full, the responsibility lies with the State Wildlife Agency, not your living room.

The Hard Truth: You are a human being with limits, not a limitless biological machine. If a squirrel dies because you couldn’t take it, you didn’t kill it. Nature, or the trauma that found it, did.

4. Managing Public Expectations

Finders will try to guilt-trip you. They will say, “If you don’t take it, it will die/I’ll throw it in the trash.”

Don’t Negotiate: Once you’ve said you are at capacity, stop the conversation. “I understand this is a difficult situation, but my capacity is firm for the health of my current patients.”

The “Drop-Off” Danger: If someone leaves a squirrel on your porch after you said no, do not feel obligated to keep it long-term. Stabilize it (Heat/Hydration) and immediately call your supervisor or the state to find a placement.

5. Setting Boundaries That Protect You

The Blackout Window: No calls or intakes after 9:00 PM (unless it’s an extreme emergency you’ve cleared). You need sleep to be a safe “Squirrel Doc” the next day.

The “Incubator Only” Rule: If you only have one incubator, you only have one litter. Never “MacGyver” a heating setup out of desperation; that’s how fires or burns happen.

Physical Distance: If possible, keep the nursery in a room you can walk away from. You need a “Human Space” where you don’t hear the peeping and the scratching.

heading: Ch. 94 — Record Keeping and Documentation
text:
## **94\. Record Keeping and Documentation**

If it isn’t written down, it didn’t happen. Documentation is your best friend when a vet asks for a history, when your state agency comes for an inspection, or when you are trying to remember what worked for a similar case three years ago.

1. How to Photograph Injuries

A blurry photo is useless. To get “vet-ready” documentation:

Scale: Place a common object (like a coin or a syringe or a banana) next to the injury so the viewer can tell the size.

Lighting: Use a bright, indirect light. Flash often “washes out” the detail of a wound or a pale gum line.

Multiple Angles: Take one “context” shot (the whole squirrel) and three “detail” shots (close-up of the injury).

The “Clear Bag” Trick: If a squirrel is too wiggly or aggressive to hold, put them in a clear Ziploc bag (with air holes\!) for 30 seconds to get a clear photo of their belly or feet through the plastic.

2. Fish and Game or Wildlife Reporting

As a permitted rehabber, you are a steward of your state’s wildlife.

The Logbook: Keep a running log of:

Date of intake.

Location found (as specific as possible—cross streets or GPS).

Species and age.

Final Outcome (Released, Died, Euthanized, Transferred).

Reporting Deadlines: Most Idaho permits require a Seasonal or Annual Report. Mark your calendar for December—missing this deadline can result in your permit being pulled.

Immediate Calls: Certain species or suspicious “mass die-offs” require an immediate call to your regional F\&G officer.

3. Tracking Outcomes for Your Own Learning

Don’t just record the “What,” record the “How.”

The “Why”: If a squirrel died, try to pinpoint why. Was it aspiration? Was it the refeeding syndrome?

The Success Folder: Keep a spreadsheet of your “Win Rate.” It’s incredibly grounding to see that even though you lost three this week, your overall success rate for the year is 85%.

Medication Logs: Keep a dedicated sheet for each animal to track doses. Never rely on your memory at 3:00 AM.

4. Seasonal Statistics

At the end of every year, look at your numbers:

The “Hot Spots”: Are most of your squirrels coming from one specific neighborhood? (Could indicate a local poisoning issue or a tree-service company that isn’t checking for nests).

Peak Dates: Tracking when your first spring babies arrive helps you prep your “911 Kit” and order formula ahead of the rush.
