heading: APPENDIX — SQUIRREL FACTS (The Victory Lap)
text:
# **APPENDIX — SQUIRREL FACTS (The Victory Lap)**

You made it. You’ve mastered the “Sugar Cure,” you’ve survived the “Spring Crunch,” and you’ve balanced the calcium. Now, here is the cool stuff to tell finders (or use to win bar bets).

1. The Brain Power

Master Gardeners: Gray squirrels are responsible for planting billions of trees every year. They “scatter-hoard” thousands of nuts and forget about 25% of them. You aren’t just raising a squirrel; you’re raising a forest.

Spatial Memory: They don’t find their nuts by smell; they find them using a highly developed spatial map in their brain. Their hippocampus actually grows in size during the caching season.

2. Physical Marvels

The “360-Degree” Ankles: Squirrels are one of the few mammals that can rotate their hind ankles 180 degrees. This allows them to descend a tree head-first while still maintaining a grip.

Sweaty Paws: Squirrels don’t sweat through their skin like humans. They sweat through the pads of their paws. If you see damp little footprints on a hot day, you’ve found a sweaty squirrel.

The “Swiss Army” Tail: Their tail is a parasol (shade), a blanket (warmth), a rudder (balance), and a communication flag. It also acts as a “decoy”—if a hawk grabs the tail, the fur pulls away (tail-slip), allowing the squirrel to escape.

3. The “Super-Sonic” Communicators

Infrared Defense: California Ground Squirrels can heat up their tails with blood flow to “harass” rattlesnakes. The snake, which sees in infrared, perceives a much larger, more threatening animal.

The “Peep” and the “Quack”: Squirrels have a complex vocabulary. A “Kuk” is a general warning, a “Qua” is a higher-intensity threat, and the “Seet” is the ultimate ‘Hawk\! Run for your life\!’ signal.

4. Squirrel “Math”

The Fall Velocity: A squirrel’s “terminal velocity” (the fastest they can fall) is about 13–15 mph. Because they are so light and can “parachute” with their limbs, a squirrel can theoretically survive a fall from almost any height—including a skyscraper—provided they don’t hit a mid-air obstacle.

The Teeth: A squirrel’s incisors grow between 6 and 8 inches per year. This is why the “Move-It” pumpkin and sticks are so important—they are biological chainsaws that never turn off.

5. The Idaho Special

Flyers Among Us: Most Idahoans don’t realize that Northern Flying Squirrels are everywhere in our forests. They aren’t rare; they’re just strictly nocturnal. If you hear a “chirp” in the woods at 2:00 AM, it’s not a bird—it’s a flyer “gliding” up to 150 feet in a single leap.

The Final Word

“The squirrel that you kill in jest, dies in earnest.” — Henr

heading: Quick Reference — Medical Abbreviations and Terms
text:
## **Quick Reference — Medical Abbreviations and Terms**

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond, p. 210*

---

### **Treatment Frequencies**

| Abbreviation | Latin | Plain English |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **SID** | semel in die | Once daily — give one dose every 24 hours |
| **BID** | bis in die | Twice daily — give one dose every 12 hours (morning and evening) |
| **TID** | ter in die | Three times daily — give one dose every 8 hours |
| **QID** | quater in die | Four times daily — give one dose every 6 hours |
| **PRN** | pro re nata | As needed — give only when the symptom is present |
| **q48h** | — | Every 48 hours (every other day) |

**Important note on BID dosing and dosing charts:** Many drug charts express the **total daily dose**, not the per-dose amount. When a drug is given BID, give **half the chart volume** at each of the two doses — morning and evening, approximately 12 hours apart. The entries in this formulary that use BID dosing (Baytril, Doxycycline, Clavamox) include explicit SID/BID columns or notes to make this clear.

---

### **Administration Routes**

| Abbreviation | Full Term | What It Means |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **PO** | per os | By mouth — swallowed orally |
| **SQ** or **SC** | subcutaneous | Injected just under the skin (not into muscle) |
| **IM** | intramuscular | Injected directly into a muscle |
| **IV** | intravenous | Injected directly into a vein — requires trained hands; vet only |
| **OTM** | oral transmucosal | Absorbed through the gum or inner lip tissue (not swallowed) |
| **Topical** | — | Applied directly to the skin or wound surface |
| **Nebulized** | — | Converted to fine mist and inhaled in an enclosed space |

---

### **Medical Terms Defined**

**Strength** — The concentration of the drug: how much active ingredient is in each milliliter (or gram, for creams). Written as mg/mL, %, or mg/tablet. *Example: “22.7 mg/mL” means every 1 mL of liquid contains 22.7 mg of drug.*

**Form** — The physical presentation of the drug: suspension (liquid you shake), tablet, injectable solution, topical cream, ophthalmic ointment, etc. *Example: “oral suspension” means a liquid you give by mouth.*

**Dosage** — The amount of drug calculated for a specific animal. Calculated as: \> mg/kg dose × animal weight in kg \= total mg needed \> total mg needed ÷ concentration (mg/mL) \= mL to give

*Example: 10 mg/kg × 0.100 kg \= 1 mg needed. 1 mg ÷ 22.7 mg/mL \= 0.044 mL.*

**Frequency** — How often the dose is repeated. See the Treatment Frequencies table above.

**Duration** — The total number of days treatment continues. *Example: “5 days” means give the dose at the prescribed frequency for 5 consecutive days, then stop.*

---

### **Table of Comparative Measures**

| Measure | Equivalents |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 kilogram (kg) | 1,000 grams · 2.2 pounds |
| 1 pound (lb) | 16 ounces · 454 grams |
| 1 ounce (oz) | 28.35 grams |
| 1 milliliter (mL) | 1 cc · approximately 20 drops |
| 1 teaspoon (tsp) | 5 mL |
| 1 tablespoon (tbsp) | 15 mL · 3 teaspoons |

**Squirrel weight context:** A Pinky-stage animal weighs \~25 g (0.025 kg). A fully grown Teenager weighs \~400 g (0.4 kg). Most rehabbers weigh animals in grams on a kitchen scale; divide by 1,000 to get kilograms for dosage math.

---

### **Weight Stages Reference**

| Weight | Stage Name |
| :---- | :---- |
| 25 g or less | Pinky |
| 26–50 g | Gray |
| 51–100 g | Infant |
| 101–150 g | Baby |
| 151–200 g | Toddler |
| 201–250 g | Explorer |
| 251–300 g | Juvenile |
| 301–350 g | Pre-Teen |
| 351–400 g | Teenager |
| 400 g+ | Adult / Release Candidate |

---

### **How to Calculate Your Own Dose**

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond, pp. 212–214*

Before you can dose any medication, you need three pieces of information. All three are either on the drug label or in this formulary:

| What You Need | Where to Find It |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Weight of the animal** | Weigh on a kitchen scale — in grams, then divide by 1,000 to get kilograms |
| **Strength of the medicine** | On the label as mg/mL (liquids) or mg/tablet (solids) |
| **Recommended dosage** | In this formulary as mg/kg |

**The Formula:**

**Dose (mL) \= Animal’s weight in kg × Dosage (mg/kg) ÷ Strength of drug (mg/mL)**

**Worked example from the book** *(1 kg animal, 30 mg/kg dose, 100 mg/mL drug):*

| Weight | × | Dosage | × | Strength | \= | Amount to Give |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1,000 g / 1 kg | × | 1/30 mg | × | 1 mL / 100 mg | \= | **0.3 mL** |

Or in plain math: 1.0 kg × 30 mg/kg ÷ 100 mg/mL \= 0.3 mL

**Important:** If you receive medication from your veterinarian in an unlabeled vial, ask them to label it with the drug name, strength (mg/mL), your prescribed dosage (mg/kg), and the date. You cannot safely dose from an unlabeled container.

---

### **Dilutions — Making Small Doses Measurable**

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond, pp. 213–214*

For very small animals, the correct dose at full drug concentration may be too small to measure accurately with any syringe. In those cases, dilute the drug to a lower concentration so the measurable volume is larger.

**10% Dilution (1:9 ratio):** \> Mix 1 part medicine with 9 parts of a veterinarian- or pharmacist-approved compatible diluent. Do not assume water, saline, syrup, or flavoring is compatible with every drug; stability, pH, palatability, sterility, and route of administration matter. \> The resulting solution is 10% of the original concentration. \> **To find the dose from a 10% dilution:** look up the full-concentration dose in the formulary, then move the decimal point **one place to the right**. \> *Example: full-strength dose is 0.03 mL → 10% dilution dose is 0.3 mL*

**1% Dilution (1:99 ratio):** \> Mix **1 part medicine** with **99 parts diluent** — OR — take your already-made 10% dilution and mix **1 part of that** with **9 more parts diluent**. \> The resulting solution is 1% of the original concentration. \> **To find the dose from a 1% dilution:** move the decimal point **two places to the right** from the original formulary dose. \> *Example: full-strength dose is 0.003 mL → 1% dilution dose is 0.3 mL*

**Diluting tablets and capsules:** \- Crush the tablet finely with a pill crusher or mortar and pestle \- Add a measured amount of liquid diluent (e.g., 1 mL liquid per 1 tablet \= the resulting solution has the same mg/mL as 1 tablet per mL) \- Half a tablet dissolved in 1 mL \= half the tablet’s strength per mL \- This math works the same way as liquid dilutions — know your resulting concentration before dosing

**Mixing two liquids in a syringe:** 1\. Draw up the measured amount of medicine 2\. Draw up a small amount of air (this makes room to mix) 3\. Draw up the measured amount of diluent 4\. Block the tip and rock the syringe up and down to mix 5\. Expel the air before dosing

⚠️ **Stomach capacity:** For very small animals, 1 mL may be greater than their entire stomach volume. When calculating a diluted dose, make sure the final volume is one the animal can actually receive in a single administration without overloading the stomach.

Quick Reference — Medical Abbreviations and Terms

## Quick Reference — Medical Abbreviations and Terms

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond, p. 210*

---

### Treatment Frequencies

| Abbreviation | Latin | Plain English |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| SID | semel in die | Once daily — give one dose every 24 hours |
| BID | bis in die | Twice daily — give one dose every 12 hours (morning and evening) |
| TID | ter in die | Three times daily — give one dose every 8 hours |
| QID | quater in die | Four times daily — give one dose every 6 hours |
| PRN | pro re nata | As needed — give only when the symptom is present |
| q48h | — | Every 48 hours (every other day) |

Important note on BID dosing and dosing charts: Many drug charts express the total daily dose, not the per-dose amount. When a drug is given BID, give half the chart volume at each of the two doses — morning and evening, approximately 12 hours apart. The entries in this formulary that use BID dosing (Baytril, Doxycycline, Clavamox) include explicit SID/BID columns or notes to make this clear.

---

### Administration Routes

| Abbreviation | Full Term | What It Means |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| PO | per os | By mouth — swallowed orally |
| SQ or SC | subcutaneous | Injected just under the skin (not into muscle) |
| IM | intramuscular | Injected directly into a muscle |
| IV | intravenous | Injected directly into a vein — requires trained hands; vet only |
| OTM | oral transmucosal | Absorbed through the gum or inner lip tissue (not swallowed) |
| Topical | — | Applied directly to the skin or wound surface |
| Nebulized | — | Converted to fine mist and inhaled in an enclosed space |

---

### Medical Terms Defined

Strength — The concentration of the drug: how much active ingredient is in each milliliter (or gram, for creams). Written as mg/mL, %, or mg/tablet. *Example: “22.7 mg/mL” means every 1 mL of liquid contains 22.7 mg of drug.*

Form — The physical presentation of the drug: suspension (liquid you shake), tablet, injectable solution, topical cream, ophthalmic ointment, etc. *Example: “oral suspension” means a liquid you give by mouth.*

Dosage — The amount of drug calculated for a specific animal. Calculated as: > mg/kg dose × animal weight in kg = total mg needed > total mg needed ÷ concentration (mg/mL) = mL to give

*Example: 10 mg/kg × 0.100 kg = 1 mg needed. 1 mg ÷ 22.7 mg/mL = 0.044 mL.*

Frequency — How often the dose is repeated. See the Treatment Frequencies table above.

Duration — The total number of days treatment continues. *Example: “5 days” means give the dose at the prescribed frequency for 5 consecutive days, then stop.*

---

### Table of Comparative Measures

| Measure | Equivalents |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 kilogram (kg) | 1,000 grams · 2.2 pounds |
| 1 pound (lb) | 16 ounces · 454 grams |
| 1 ounce (oz) | 28.35 grams |
| 1 milliliter (mL) | 1 cc · approximately 20 drops |
| 1 teaspoon (tsp) | 5 mL |
| 1 tablespoon (tbsp) | 15 mL · 3 teaspoons |

Squirrel weight context: A Pinky-stage animal weighs ~25 g (0.025 kg). A fully grown Teenager weighs ~400 g (0.4 kg). Most rehabbers weigh animals in grams on a kitchen scale; divide by 1,000 to get kilograms for dosage math.

---

### Weight Stages Reference

| Weight | Stage Name |
| :---- | :---- |
| 25 g or less | Pinky |
| 26–50 g | Gray |
| 51–100 g | Infant |
| 101–150 g | Baby |
| 151–200 g | Toddler |
| 201–250 g | Explorer |
| 251–300 g | Juvenile |
| 301–350 g | Pre-Teen |
| 351–400 g | Teenager |
| 400 g+ | Adult / Release Candidate |

---

### How to Calculate Your Own Dose

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond, pp. 212–214*

Before you can dose any medication, you need three pieces of information. All three are either on the drug label or in this formulary:

| What You Need | Where to Find It |
| :---- | :---- |
| Weight of the animal | Weigh on a kitchen scale — in grams, then divide by 1,000 to get kilograms |
| Strength of the medicine | On the label as mg/mL (liquids) or mg/tablet (solids) |
| Recommended dosage | In this formulary as mg/kg |

The Formula:

Dose (mL) = Animal’s weight in kg × Dosage (mg/kg) ÷ Strength of drug (mg/mL)

Worked example from the book *(1 kg animal, 30 mg/kg dose, 100 mg/mL drug):*

| Weight | × | Dosage | × | Strength | = | Amount to Give |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1,000 g / 1 kg | × | 1/30 mg | × | 1 mL / 100 mg | = | 0.3 mL |

Or in plain math: 1.0 kg × 30 mg/kg ÷ 100 mg/mL = 0.3 mL

Important: If you receive medication from your veterinarian in an unlabeled vial, ask them to label it with the drug name, strength (mg/mL), your prescribed dosage (mg/kg), and the date. You cannot safely dose from an unlabeled container.

---

### Dilutions — Making Small Doses Measurable

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond, pp. 213–214*

For very small animals, the correct dose at full drug concentration may be too small to measure accurately with any syringe. In those cases, dilute the drug to a lower concentration so the measurable volume is larger.

10% Dilution (1:9 ratio): > Mix 1 part medicine with 9 parts of a veterinarian- or pharmacist-approved compatible diluent. Do not assume water, saline, syrup, or flavoring is compatible with every drug; stability, pH, palatability, sterility, and route of administration matter. > The resulting solution is 10% of the original concentration. > To find the dose from a 10% dilution: look up the full-concentration dose in the formulary, then move the decimal point one place to the right. > *Example: full-strength dose is 0.03 mL → 10% dilution dose is 0.3 mL*

1% Dilution (1:99 ratio): > Mix 1 part medicine with 99 parts diluent — OR — take your already-made 10% dilution and mix 1 part of that with 9 more parts diluent. > The resulting solution is 1% of the original concentration. > To find the dose from a 1% dilution: move the decimal point two places to the right from the original formulary dose. > *Example: full-strength dose is 0.003 mL → 1% dilution dose is 0.3 mL*

Diluting tablets and capsules: - Crush the tablet finely with a pill crusher or mortar and pestle - Add a measured amount of liquid diluent (e.g., 1 mL liquid per 1 tablet = the resulting solution has the same mg/mL as 1 tablet per mL) - Half a tablet dissolved in 1 mL = half the tablet’s strength per mL - This math works the same way as liquid dilutions — know your resulting concentration before dosing

Mixing two liquids in a syringe: 1. Draw up the measured amount of medicine 2. Draw up a small amount of air (this makes room to mix) 3. Draw up the measured amount of diluent 4. Block the tip and rock the syringe up and down to mix 5. Expel the air before dosing

⚠️ Stomach capacity: For very small animals, 1 mL may be greater than their entire stomach volume. When calculating a diluted dose, make sure the final volume is one the animal can actually receive in a single administration without overloading the stomach.

Labeling, storage, and discard rules *(from book, p. 214):* - Label every diluted preparation with: drug name, original concentration, dilution ratio, resulting concentration, and the date prepared - Use adhesive tape on the vial and write clearly - Refrigerate all diluted solutions - Discard diluted solutions after one week — degradation and contamination risk increase beyond that point - To minimize waste, make only as much as you expect to need in one week - Shake diluted solutions thoroughly before each use — some medicines settle out of suspension

heading: ALBON (Sulfadimethoxine)
text:
## **ALBON (Sulfadimethoxine)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Sulfonamide antibiotic / Anti-Parasitic **Indications:** Coccidiosis (intestinal parasitic infection); off-label use for susceptible bacterial infections of the respiratory, urinary, and digestive tracts

⚠️ **USE ONLY IF PONAZURIL IS UNAVAILABLE.** Ponazuril (Marquis) is the preferred first-line coccidiostat because it is coccidiocidal — it kills coccidia at multiple life stages. Albon is only coccidiostatic — it prevents coccidia from reproducing but does not kill existing parasites. The animal’s own immune system must clear the surviving population, making treatment longer and recovery slower.

**Form:** Albon 5% oral suspension — 50 mg/mL (250 mg per 5 mL teaspoon). Requires veterinary prescription. **Route:** Oral (PO) **Frequency:** Once daily (q24h) **Mechanism:** Bacteriostatic sulfonamide; competitively inhibits the enzyme dihydropteroate synthase, blocking the synthesis of folic acid. Bacteria and protozoa cannot use dietary folic acid and must synthesize their own — this blocks that pathway. Mammalian cells are unaffected because they use dietary folate.

**Dosing Protocol — Two-Phase (50 mg/mL suspension)**

**Day 1 — Loading Dose: 55 mg/kg**

| Animal Weight | Stage | Volume |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.055 mL |
| 75 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.083 mL |
| 100 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.110 mL |
| 125 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.138 mL |
| 150 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.165 mL |
| 175 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.193 mL |
| 200 g (Explorer) | Explorer | 0.220 mL |
| 250 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.275 mL |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.330 mL |
| 350 g (Pre-Teen) | Pre-Teen | 0.385 mL |
| 400 g (Teenager) | Teenager | 0.440 mL |

**Days 2 onward — Maintenance Dose: 27.5 mg/kg once daily**

| Animal Weight | Stage | Volume |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.028 mL |
| 75 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.041 mL |
| 100 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.055 mL |
| 125 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.069 mL |
| 150 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.083 mL |
| 175 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.096 mL |
| 200 g (Explorer) | Explorer | 0.110 mL |
| 250 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.138 mL |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.165 mL |
| 350 g (Pre-Teen) | Pre-Teen | 0.193 mL |
| 400 g (Teenager) | Teenager | 0.220 mL |

**Treatment Duration:** Continue until the animal has been asymptomatic (formed stools, good energy, eating well) for at least 48 hours — typically 10–21 days total depending on severity. Do not stop early just because the animal looks better.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Common side effects: soft or loose stools, decreased appetite, occasional vomiting — these are expected and manageable \- Albon can cause crystalluria (crystal formation in urine) if the animal is dehydrated; ensure the animal is well-hydrated throughout treatment \- Sulfonamides may cause rare sensitivity reactions; discontinue and contact your vet if the animal develops skin rash, extreme lethargy, or facial swelling \- **Do not use in Pinky or Gray-stage animals** (under \~50 g) without veterinary guidance — sulfonamides can interfere with neonatal development \- Calcium binds to sulfonamides similarly to tetracyclines; separate any calcium supplementation by at least 2 hours \- Requires prescription from a licensed veterinarian

heading: AMOXICILLIN / CLAVAMOX (Amoxicillin/Clavulanate)
text:
## **AMOXICILLIN / CLAVAMOX (Amoxicillin/Clavulanate)**

**Evidence: \[A\] DIRECT SQUIRREL / SCIURIDAE**

**Drug Class / Type:** Potentiated penicillin antibiotic **Brand Names:** Clavamox (veterinary); Augmentin (human equivalent) **Indications:** Pneumonia; cat bite wounds (eliminates *Pasteurella multocida*); wound infections; skin and soft tissue infections; abscesses; bladder and urinary tract infections; bone and oral infections. Clavamox is often the first-choice antibiotic for cat attack survivors. **Mechanism:** Amoxicillin disrupts bacterial cell wall synthesis, causing the bacteria to rupture. Clavulanic acid inhibits beta-lactamase enzymes — the enzymes bacteria use to break down penicillin-type antibiotics — making the combination effective against a broader range of resistant organisms than amoxicillin alone. **Form:** Oral suspension (standard rehabber concentration: 62.5 mg/ml); also available as tablets (62.5 mg, 125 mg, 250 mg, 375 mg). The oral suspension is strongly preferred for squirrels — it allows precise dosing and is easier to administer. **Dosage:** 20 mg/kg **Route:** PO (oral) **Frequency:** BID (twice daily — morning and evening, approximately 12 hours apart) **Treatment Duration:** 7–10 days. Complete the full course even if the animal appears to improve early.

**Weight-Based Dosing Reference** *(62.5 mg/ml suspension · 20 mg/kg)*

| Animal Weight | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- |
| 25 g (Pinky/Gray) | 0.008 ml — requires dilution; see note below |
| 50 g (Infant) | 0.016 ml |
| 75 g (Infant) | 0.024 ml |
| 100 g (Baby) | 0.032 ml |
| 125 g (Baby) | 0.040 ml |
| 150 g (Toddler) | 0.048 ml |
| 175 g (Toddler) | 0.056 ml |
| 200 g (Explorer) | 0.064 ml |
| 250 g (Explorer/Juvenile) | 0.080 ml |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | 0.096 ml |
| 350 g (Pre-Teen) | 0.112 ml |
| 400 g (Pre-Teen/Teenager) | 0.128 ml |

**Dilution note for small animals (under 50 g):** At these weights the volumes are too small to draw accurately with a standard syringe. Mix 0.1 ml of the 62.5 mg/ml suspension with 0.9 ml of sterile water to create a 6.25 mg/ml diluted solution. At that concentration, dose at 0.32 ml per 100 g of body weight. Consult your vet for the specific dilution protocol they prefer.

**Storage:** \- Refrigerate after mixing. Discard mixed suspension after 10 days. \- Unmixed powder may be stored refrigerated for up to 3 months. \- Never freeze the mixed suspension.

**Warnings / Cautions:** \- ⚠️ **Do NOT use on lagomorphs** (rabbits, hares, pikas). Penicillin-class antibiotics can cause fatal GI dysbiosis in lagomorphs. \- All penicillins carry a significant risk of GI upset in rodents, including diarrhea and disruption of gut flora. This is manageable but must be monitored. \- **Probiotics:** Give a probiotic (such as Bene-Bac or plain, unsweetened yogurt with live cultures) at least 2 hours before OR after each Clavamox dose. Never give probiotics at the same time as the antibiotic — the antibiotic will kill the probiotic organisms. \- Watch for loose or watery stool during treatment. If diarrhea becomes severe or bloody, contact your vet — the antibiotic may need to be discontinued or changed. \- Do not use if the animal has a known penicillin allergy.

heading: FISH MOX (Amoxicillin — OTC, without Clavulanate)
text:
## **FISH MOX (Amoxicillin — OTC, without Clavulanate)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Penicillin antibiotic — over-the-counter option **Also known as:** Fish Mox, Fish Mox Forte (available at most pet stores and online without a prescription) **Indications:** Upper respiratory infections; secondary infections (eye infections, wound infections, urinary tract infections); mild to moderate soft tissue infections. **Not appropriate as sole treatment for severe infections or cat bites** — use prescription Clavamox for those. **Route:** Oral (PO) **Frequency:** BID (twice daily — every 12 hours) **Treatment Duration:** 3–4 weeks. Do not stop when symptoms resolve — the infection is not gone just because the animal looks better. Completing the full course prevents relapse and antibiotic resistance.

---

### **Fish Mox vs. Clavamox — Understanding the Difference**

This is the debate worth having before you reach for the pet store shelf.

Fish Mox is **amoxicillin alone**. Clavamox is **amoxicillin \+ clavulanate**. That difference matters clinically:

|  | Fish Mox (amoxicillin) | Clavamox (amoxicillin/clavulanate) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Prescription required | No — OTC at pet stores | Yes — veterinary prescription |
| Coverage | Susceptible bacteria only | Broader — includes beta-lactamase-producing strains |
| Cost | Low | Higher |
| Availability | Widely available | Requires vet access |
| Best for | Mild/moderate infections, easy access situations | Cat bites, wound infections, treatment failures |
| Works against resistant bacteria | No | Yes |

**Clavulanate is a beta-lactamase inhibitor.** Many bacteria — including *Staphylococcus*, *Pasteurella*, and some strains of *E. coli* — produce beta-lactamase enzymes that break down amoxicillin and render it useless. Clavulanate blocks those enzymes and restores the amoxicillin’s effectiveness. Fish Mox has no such protection.

**When Fish Mox is appropriate:** Mild upper respiratory infections, early wound infections, UTIs in otherwise stable animals, situations where vet access is genuinely limited and treatment cannot wait.

**When to use Clavamox instead:** Cat attack survivors (non-negotiable — *Pasteurella* is beta-lactamase producing and can be rapidly fatal), severe or spreading infections, any infection that has not responded to Fish Mox within 3–5 days.

**Fish Mox works best in combination:** The notes on this entry are clear — amoxicillin pairs well with Baytril (enrofloxacin). Together they provide broader coverage than either drug alone. If the animal is sick enough to need antibiotics, strongly consider running both.

---

### **Home Suspension Recipe**

**One 250 mg Fish Mox capsule makes a 7.5 mL suspension at 33.33 mg/mL.**

**Ingredients:** \- 1 × 250 mg amoxicillin capsule (Fish Mox) \- 5 mL hot water \- 2.5 mL flavoring (strawberry syrup, coffee flavoring, or Ensure all work — squirrels need to find it palatable)

**Instructions:** 1\. Open the capsule carefully over a small container — the powder is fine and will scatter; open slowly 2\. Add 5 mL hot water to the powder and stir 3\. Add 2.5 mL of your flavoring 4\. Stir or shake to combine — **the powder will not fully dissolve; visible particles are normal and expected** 5\. Total volume \= 7.5 mL at **33.33 mg/mL** 6\. Label with the date; **refrigerate; discard after 14 days**

⚠️ **Volume matters for concentration.** The 33.33 mg/mL concentration assumes exactly 7.5 mL total (5 mL water \+ 2.5 mL flavoring). If you change the amounts of water or flavoring, the concentration changes and the dose table below is no longer valid. Measure carefully.

---

### **Weight Table — 33.33 mg/mL Suspension at 30 mg/kg BID**

*Math verified: every value back-calculated at 30 mg/kg. Formula: weight\_g × 0.0009 \= dose in mL.*

| Weight | Stage | Dose per Administration |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 30 g | Pinky | 0.02 mL |
| 60 g | Gray | 0.05 mL |

| 125 g | Baby | 0.11 mL |

| 330 g | Juvenile | 0.30 mL |

| 440 g | Adult | 0.40 mL |

| 530 g | Adult | 0.48 mL |

---

| Availability | Widely available | Requires vet access |
| Best for | Mild/moderate infections, easy access situations | Cat bites, wound infections, treatment failures |
| Works against resistant bacteria | No | Yes |

Clavulanate is a beta-lactamase inhibitor. Many bacteria — including *Staphylococcus*, *Pasteurella*, and some strains of *E. coli* — produce beta-lactamase enzymes that break down amoxicillin and render it useless. Clavulanate blocks those enzymes and restores the amoxicillin’s effectiveness. Fish Mox has no such protection.

When Fish Mox is appropriate: Mild upper respiratory infections, early wound infections, UTIs in otherwise stable animals, situations where vet access is genuinely limited and treatment cannot wait.

When to use Clavamox instead: Cat attack survivors (non-negotiable — *Pasteurella* is beta-lactamase producing and can be rapidly fatal), severe or spreading infections, any infection that has not responded to Fish Mox within 3–5 days.

Fish Mox works best in combination: The notes on this entry are clear — amoxicillin pairs well with Baytril (enrofloxacin). Together they provide broader coverage than either drug alone. If the animal is sick enough to need antibiotics, strongly consider running both.

---

### Home Suspension Recipe

One 250 mg Fish Mox capsule makes a 7.5 mL suspension at 33.33 mg/mL.

Ingredients: - 1 × 250 mg amoxicillin capsule (Fish Mox) - 5 mL hot water - 2.5 mL flavoring (strawberry syrup, coffee flavoring, or Ensure all work — squirrels need to find it palatable)

Instructions: 1. Open the capsule carefully over a small container — the powder is fine and will scatter; open slowly 2. Add 5 mL hot water to the powder and stir 3. Add 2.5 mL of your flavoring 4. Stir or shake to combine — the powder will not fully dissolve; visible particles are normal and expected 5. Total volume = 7.5 mL at 33.33 mg/mL 6. Label with the date; refrigerate; discard after 14 days

⚠️ Volume matters for concentration. The 33.33 mg/mL concentration assumes exactly 7.5 mL total (5 mL water + 2.5 mL flavoring). If you change the amounts of water or flavoring, the concentration changes and the dose table below is no longer valid. Measure carefully.

---

*Math verified: every value back-calculated at 30 mg/kg. Formula: weight_g × 0.0009 = dose in mL.*

*Give BID (twice daily, every 12 hours) for 3–4 weeks.*

Warnings / Notes: - ⚠️ Do NOT use on lagomorphs (rabbits, hares, pikas) — penicillin-class antibiotics cause fatal GI dysbiosis in lagomorphs - GI upset (loose stool, diarrhea) is possible with any penicillin; give a probiotic (Bene-Bac or plain unsweetened yogurt with live cultures) at least 2 hours before or after each dose — never simultaneously - If diarrhea becomes severe or bloody, discontinue and contact your vet - Fish Mox is sold as a fish medication to bypass prescription requirements; the amoxicillin molecule is the same, but manufacturing quality control may not match pharmaceutical-grade veterinary products — for severely ill animals, prescription Clavamox is the stronger choice - Amoxicillin requires a prescription when obtained through a veterinarian; Fish Mox is an OTC workaround for situations where vet access is limited — consult your supervising vet whenever possible - See also: AMOXICILLIN / CLAVAMOX entry for the prescription potentiated version with broader coverage; BAYTRIL entry for combination antibiotic therapy

heading: BAYTRIL (Enrofloxacin)
text:
## **BAYTRIL (Enrofloxacin)**

**Evidence: \[A\] DIRECT SQUIRREL / SCIURIDAE**

**Drug Class / Type:** Fluoroquinolone antibiotic **Indications:** Cat attack wounds (Pasteurella and polymicrobial infection coverage); aspiration pneumonia and severe respiratory infections; urinary tract infections; bone infections; soft tissue, skin, and external ear infections. Often a first-line choice after cat attack and a go-to for infections unresponsive to penicillin-class antibiotics. **Form:** Injectable solution (22.7 mg/mL) — this is the standard rehabber formulation, given orally despite being labeled as injectable. Also available as oral suspension, and flavored tablets (5.7, 22.7, 68, 136 mg). **Strength:** 22.7 mg/mL **Dosage Range:** 2.5–15 mg/kg total daily dose **Route:** PO (oral) or SQ injection. The injectable solution may be given by mouth; this is standard rehabber practice. The first dose may be given by SQ injection for faster therapeutic levels, with subsequent doses by mouth. **Frequency:** SID (once daily) *or* BID (twice daily — preferred). The chart below gives the **total daily dose**. For BID dosing, give **half the chart volume** twice daily, approximately 12 hours apart. BID produces a better therapeutic effect by maintaining more consistent drug levels throughout the day; SID is used when handling stress is a concern.

**Weight-Based Dosing Reference** *(22.7 mg/mL · 10 mg/kg total daily dose)*

| Weight | Stage | SID — give once daily | BID — give twice daily |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 25 g (Pinky/Gray) | Pinky | 0.011 mL — see dilution note | 0.006 mL — see dilution note |
| 50 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.022 mL | 0.011 mL |
| 75 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.033 mL | 0.017 mL |
| 100 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.044 mL | 0.022 mL |
| 125 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.055 mL | 0.028 mL |
| 150 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.066 mL | 0.033 mL |
| 175 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.077 mL | 0.039 mL |
| 200 g (Explorer) | Explorer | 0.088 mL | 0.044 mL |
| 250 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.110 mL | 0.055 mL |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.132 mL | 0.066 mL |
| 350 g (Pre-Teen) | Pre-Teen | 0.154 mL | 0.077 mL |
| 400 g (Teenager) | Teenager | 0.176 mL | 0.088 mL |

**Dilution note for animals under 25 g (Pinky stage):** Volumes at Pinky weights are too small to measure accurately. Consult your vet for a dilution protocol using sterile water or saline to bring the concentration down to a measurable range before dosing animals this small.

**Dose adjustment:** The table uses 10 mg/kg (mid-range). For milder infections, 5 mg/kg may be sufficient. For severe aspiration pneumonia or deep tissue infections, 15 mg/kg is appropriate. Adjust the volume proportionally.

**Treatment Duration:** \- Cat attack (suspected): 3–5 days \- Confirmed wounds, bite injuries, other infections: 5–7 days \- If a longer course is needed, switch to a different antibiotic class rather than extending Baytril beyond 7–10 days

**Mechanism:** Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV enzymes, preventing DNA replication and transcription. Bactericidal — kills bacteria rather than just inhibiting growth.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- ⚠️ **Do not administer with calcium-containing formula, dairy, or calcium supplements** — divalent cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺) chelate fluoroquinolones and dramatically reduce absorption. Separate dosing by at least 2 hours. \- **Seizure threshold:** Fluoroquinolones can lower the seizure threshold. Use with caution in any animal with known head trauma or neurological injury; discuss with your vet before using in these cases. \- **Bone and cartilage caution:** There is theoretical concern about cartilage effects in rapidly growing neonates. The clinical evidence suggests this risk requires either significant overdose or prolonged use at therapeutic doses — “It is certainly safe to use” at correct doses for standard course lengths (*Wild Mammal Babies*, p. 235). The benefit in treating a serious infection far outweighs this theoretical risk, especially in Pinkies with life-threatening illness. \- Baytril has a distinctly bitter, unpleasant taste. Animals often resist it. Mix with a small amount of formula or a flavored carrier immediately before dosing to improve compliance — but do not pre-mix large batches, as this affects stability.

heading: BENADRYL (Diphenhydramine)
text:
## **BENADRYL (Diphenhydramine)**

**Evidence: \[B\] RODENT ANALOG \+ \[C\] REHAB / CLINICAL PRECEDENT**

**Drug Class / Type:** Antihistamine / Allergy and Inflammatory Reduction **Indications:** Insect stings (bees/wasps), ant bites, and severe localized allergic swelling; may serve as a mild sedative for highly stressed animals **Dosage:** \- Adults: 0.35 ml \- Teenagers (12–18 weeks): 0.25 ml \- Babies (4–12 weeks): 0.15 ml \- Babies (3 weeks and younger): 0.05 ml **Route:** Oral (liquid) or topical (cream applied to affected area) **Frequency:** Every 8–12 hours as needed (q8–12h PRN). For an acute sting or allergic reaction, one to two doses given 8–12 hours apart are typically sufficient — most reactions resolve within 24 hours. Do not exceed 3 doses per day. Stop once swelling and symptoms resolve. **Warnings / Notes:** \- Blocks H1 receptors, preventing histamine from binding and causing swelling, itching, and redness \- Available as children’s liquid (cherry flavored) or compounded liquid, or topical cream \- DO NOT USE ADULT STRENGTH \- Causes drowsiness; overdosing risks include extreme lethargy or respiratory depression \- Monitor for “Floppy Squirrel Syndrome” if combined with Trazodone or Gabapentin, as excessive sedation increases aspiration pneumonia risk

heading: BETADINE (Povidone-Iodine)
text:
## **BETADINE (Povidone-Iodine)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Topical Antiseptic **Indications:** Cleaning superficial wounds, cuts, and site preparation for lancing abscesses; preferred for contaminated wounds **Dosage:** No specific mg/kg dosage; see dilution protocol **Route:** Topical **Frequency:** Apply at each wound-cleaning session — typically BID (twice daily — morning and evening) for the first 2–3 days on a fresh wound, then SID (once daily) as the wound begins to close. Discontinue topical antiseptics once healthy granulation tissue forms and infection risk is controlled; continued use past that point delays healing by irritating new tissue. **Dilution Protocol:** Never use full-strength on open tissue. Mix with sterile saline or clean water until it reaches the “color of weak tea” (approx. 1:10 dilution) **Warnings / Notes:** \- Effective against bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa \- Iodine is inactivated by organic matter (blood or pus) — do NOT use Betadine on wounds that are actively bleeding or oozing pus; switch to Chlorhexidine for those \- If the solution is too dark (dark brown), it is cytotoxic and will delay wound healing rather than help it \- Contraindicated in individuals with iodine sensitivities

heading: BUPRENORPHINE
text:
## **BUPRENORPHINE**

**Drug Class / Type:** Opioid Analgesic — CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE – High-Level Pain Management **Indications:** Acute trauma (electrocution, crushing injuries, fractures); surgical recovery (first 24–48 hours post-amputation); severe burns with pain uncontrolled by NSAIDs; end-of-life/hospice care **Dosage:** **Requires veterinary prescription and individualized dosing.** Published reference ranges for small rodents: **0.05–0.1 mg/kg** given OTM or SQ (ExoticDVM; veterinary pharmacology references). Your prescribing vet will specify the exact dose based on the animal’s condition and the concentration of your buprenorphine formulation (commonly 0.3 mg/mL injectable). Do not dose from the reference range without direct vet guidance — the therapeutic window is narrow and respiratory depression is a real risk. **Route:** OTM (Oral Transmucosal) — applied inside the cheek or lower lip where it is absorbed through the mucous membrane; or SQ (subcutaneous injection). OTM is preferred in conscious squirrels as it avoids the stress of injection and achieves good bioavailability. **Frequency:** Every **6–12 hours** depending on the dose and the animal’s pain level — your vet will specify. The half-life of buprenorphine is 4–8 hours in most small mammals, making q8h a common interval. Reassess pain regularly and consult your vet before each dose extension. **Warnings / Notes:** \- Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist providing superior pain relief for severe injuries \- OTM described as the “secret weapon” for squirrels \- Respiratory Depression: Can slow breathing; monitor respiratory rate closely \- GI Effects: Opioids can cause ileus (gut shutdown); requiring probiotics if used beyond 48 hours \- Drug Interactions: \- Gabapentin: Red Alert — Severe respiratory depression and extreme sedation \- Benadryl: Yellow Alert — Additive sedation effects \- Meloxicam/Ibuprofen: Safe — “Gold Standard for pain” combination \- Antibiotics: Monitor — GI stasis risk; requires probiotics \- Must be kept in a double-locked, secure location in original amber glass or dark container, protected from light and extreme temperatures

---

text:
## **BUTORPHANOL**

**Drug Class / Type:** Opioid Analgesic — CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE – Moderate-to-High Pain Management **Indications:** Moderate to moderately severe pain; acute trauma; post-procedural pain in situations where buprenorphine is unavailable. Butorphanol is a mixed opioid agonist-antagonist, making it useful as an intermediate analgesic but less potent than buprenorphine for severe pain. **Dosage:** **0.2–2 mg/kg** SQ or IM — wide therapeutic range; dose to effect under vet guidance.

heading: CALCIUM (Calcium Carbonate / Calcium Gluconate / Calcium Glubionate)
drug: CALCIUM (Calcium Carbonate / Calcium Gluconate / Calcium Glubionate)
text:
## **CALCIUM (Calcium Carbonate / Calcium Gluconate / Calcium Glubionate)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Mineral Supplement / Antacid **Indications:** Emergency treatment for MBD (Metabolic Bone Disease) calcium crashes — muscle tremors, tetany, or full seizures caused by hypocalcemia; bone health support during growth; long-term MBD recovery; occasionally as a mild antacid during GI irritation.

**What an MBD crash looks like:** Muscle tremors starting in the hind limbs, progressing to the whole body; extreme lethargy; inability to grip; weakness of the jaw; aggression or disorientation; hypersensitivity to touch or sound; and in severe cases, full convulsive seizures, coma, and death. **In very severe crashes, the animal may also develop hyperthermia (overheating)** from sustained muscle activity — keep the environment cool and do not add external heat during an active crash. This is a medical emergency — begin calcium supplementation immediately and contact your vet or wildlife emergency line. Improvement is typically seen within **1–5 days** of consistent treatment.

---

### **Understanding Elemental Calcium vs. Calcium Carbonate**

⚠️ **Critical distinction:** Protocols dose in *elemental calcium* — the biologically available fraction. Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) is only **40% elemental calcium** by weight. When reading any calcium protocol, confirm which unit is being used.

| Product | Calcium Carbonate | Elemental Calcium |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Tums Regular Strength (1 tablet) | 500 mg CaCO₃ | **200 mg elemental Ca** |
| Tums Extra Strength (1 tablet) | 750 mg CaCO₃ | **300 mg elemental Ca** |
| Tums Ultra Strength (1 tablet) | \~1,000 mg CaCO₃ | **\~400 mg elemental Ca** |
| Calcium carbonate powder (1 g) | 1,000 mg CaCO₃ | **400 mg elemental Ca** |

---

### **Forms Available**

**Oral (home/rehab use):** \- **Tums (calcium carbonate tablets)** — most accessible; crush and dissolve in warm water \- **Calcium carbonate powder** (health food store, compounding pharmacy) — most precise for small doses \- **Calcium glubionate syrup** (Calcionate, Neo-Calglucon) — liquid form, easier for very small animals; available at some pharmacies and veterinary suppliers

**Veterinary-administered only:** \- **Calcium gluconate 10% injectable** — IV (slow push over 10 minutes) or IM/IP for acute crashes. **Never administer IV calcium without veterinary supervision** — cardiac arrhythmia risk.

---

### **Route**

**Oral (PO):** Dropper or syringe at the corner of the mouth. Mix with almond butter, plain yogurt, or formula to improve palatability and absorption — calcium carbonate requires stomach acid and food for proper dissolution.

**IV/IM/IP (veterinary only):** Calcium gluconate 10% injectable — see vet protocol below.

---

### **Dosing Protocols**

#### *Protocol 1 — Oral Crash Protocol (Henry’s Pets / Rehab Standard)*

*Source: Henry’s Pets MBD emergency treatment protocol, validated across wildlife rehabilitation community*

**Phase 1 — Active crash (tremors present):**

| Animal Size | Elemental Calcium | Tums Equivalent | Frequency |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Adult / Juvenile (\>12 weeks) | **100 mg elemental Ca** | ½ Regular Tums tablet | Every **4 hours** |
| Baby / Small (\<12 weeks, \<150g) | **50 mg elemental Ca** | ¼ Regular Tums tablet | Every **4 hours** |

Continue Phase 1 dosing until tremors resolve and the animal regains grip and voluntary muscle control. Do not extend the interval while tremors are still present.

**Phase 2 — Long-term recovery (tremors resolved):**

Total daily dose: **500 mg elemental calcium/day**, divided into **5 doses** (approximately every 4–5 hours). This is equivalent to 2½ Regular Tums tablets per day.

| Animal Size | Per-Dose Elemental Ca | Tums Equivalent | Doses/Day |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Adult / Juvenile (\>12 weeks) | **100 mg** | ½ Regular Tums | 5× daily |
| Baby / Small (\<12 weeks) | **50 mg** | ¼ Regular Tums | 5× daily |

**Phase 3 — Taper (stable animal eating well):** Once the animal is eating a balanced diet and shows no relapse signs, reduce total daily calcium by **50 mg every 2 weeks** until discontinued. Abrupt discontinuation risks rebound hypocalcemia.

**Important:** If you are also feeding Henry’s Blocks (a commercial wildlife rehab supplement that contains calcium), **cut the supplemental calcium dose in half** from the start — the blocks provide significant calcium and double-dosing can cause hypercalcemia.

---

#### *Protocol 2 — Veterinary IV/IM Protocol (acute crash, vet-administered only)*

*Sources: squirrelrehabilitation.com (veterinary-level reference) \+ MSD Veterinary Manual (eclampsia/acute hypocalcemia protocol, small animals)*

**Acute crash with severe seizures — IV (vet only):** \- Calcium gluconate 10%: **0.5–1.5 mL/kg IV**, administered slowly over **10–30 minutes** \- Equivalent elemental calcium: 5–15 mg/kg IV slowly \- Expected response: improvement within **15 minutes** of starting infusion \- ⚠️ **Cardiac monitoring is mandatory during infusion** — listen with a stethoscope or use ECG throughout \- ⚠️ **If bradycardia or arrhythmia develops:** Stop the infusion immediately. Wait for cardiac rhythm to normalize, then resume at **half the original rate** \- Once stabilized: continue calcium support via SQ route (see below) or transition to oral

**Post-IV SQ continuation (vet-administered, hospital setting):** \- Dilute calcium gluconate 10% **1:1 in sterile saline** → gives 5% solution \- Administer SQ every **8 hours** until stable enough to transition to oral supplementation \- This bridge option allows continued calcium support after IV without requiring IV access

**Acute crash — IM or IP alternative (vet only):** \- Calcium gluconate: **100 mg/kg** IM or IP

**Vitamin D companion therapy (acute, vet-prescribed):** \- Calcitriol (active Vitamin D₃, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol): **0.03–0.06 mcg/kg** once daily \- *Note: calcitriol is the pre-activated form of Vitamin D₃ — it bypasses liver/kidney conversion and works faster than the cholecalciferol in our VITAMIN D₃ entry. Used in acute settings or when kidney function is impaired. Vet prescription required.* \- Source: MSD Veterinary Manual eclampsia protocol

**Oral maintenance (vet prescription preferred):** \- Calcium glubionate (Calcionate syrup): **1 mL/kg PO q12h** (twice daily) \- Calcium glubionate is better tolerated than calcium carbonate in very small or debilitated animals and is easier to dose precisely in liquid form

---

#### *A Note on mg/kg Oral Maintenance Dosing: Two Protocols, Different Goals*

| Protocol | Dose | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| MSD Vet Manual (eclampsia) | **25–50 mg elemental Ca/kg/day** in 3–4 divided doses | Post-acute maintenance in animals with otherwise adequate calcium stores |
| Henry’s Pets (MBD) | **\~1,250 mg/kg/day** (500 mg for 400g adult) in 5 divided doses | Chronic repletion — rebuilding severely depleted bone calcium over weeks |

These are not contradictory — they serve different clinical situations. **Eclampsia** is an acute serum calcium drop in an animal whose bones still contain normal calcium stores; the goal is rapid serum correction and modest maintenance. **MBD** represents months of inadequate calcium intake with severe skeletal depletion; the goal is sustained repletion at much higher doses over weeks. Squirrel MBD patients generally follow the Henry’s Pets higher-dose protocol for this reason.

---

### **Practical Preparation — Emergency Oral Suspension**

**Quick single dose:** Crush **½ Regular Tums tablet** and dissolve in **1–2 mL warm water** by stirring until fully dissolved. Give by dropper at the corner of the mouth.

**Batch suspension for 24-hour supply:** Dissolve **2½ Regular Tums tablets** (= 500 mg elemental Ca) in **10 mL warm water** → gives a **50 mg/mL elemental calcium** suspension. Store refrigerated, discard after 24 hours. Give 2 mL per dose (= 100 mg elemental Ca) for adults; 1 mL per dose (= 50 mg) for babies.

---

### **Monitoring Response**

* Tremors should begin to reduce within **30–60 minutes** of the first dose

* The animal should begin to grip and hold itself up within **2–4 hours**

* Full stabilization: expect **1–5 days** of consistent treatment

* ⚠️ **White feces or a milky film on urine** \= over-supplementation → reduce the dose immediately

* If no improvement after 3 oral doses, escalate to veterinary care — severe hypocalcemia may require IV calcium gluconate

---

### **Warnings / Notes**

* ⚠️ **Calcium binds to Doxycycline and Baytril (Enrofloxacin)**, dramatically reducing their absorption. Separate all calcium doses (including calcium-containing formula) from these antibiotics by at least **2 hours** — dose antibiotics first, wait 2 hours, then give formula/calcium.

* ⚠️ **IV calcium without cardiac monitoring is dangerous** — cardiac arrhythmia and arrest are possible. IV administration is strictly veterinary. If arrhythmia develops during IV infusion, stop immediately, wait for rhythm to normalize, then resume at half the original rate.

* ⚠️ **Corticosteroids (Prednisone, Dexamethasone) lower serum calcium** — giving steroids to an animal that is already hypocalcemic, or during MBD recovery, can worsen or precipitate a crash. If steroids are medically necessary, calcium supplementation and monitoring must be intensified. Do not use steroids and assume calcium levels will hold.

* ⚠️ **Over-supplementation** causes calcification of soft tissues (kidneys, blood vessels) and urinary stones — white feces and milky urine are early warning signs. Taper and stop once dietary calcium is adequate.

* ⚠️ **Do not add external heat during an active crash** — muscle activity during seizures already generates excess body heat. Hyperthermia in severe crashes can compound organ damage. Keep the environment cool and well-ventilated.

* Calcium carbonate requires adequate stomach acid to dissolve and absorb — always give with food (formula or solid food) when possible

* Calcium glubionate (liquid) absorbs more readily and is the preferred form for very small or debilitated animals

* Vitamin D₃ is required for calcium absorption — an animal with MBD may be deficient in both. See VITAMIN D₃ entry. Without adequate D₃, calcium supplementation is less effective.

* Transitioning a recovering MBD animal to rodent blocks (Mazuri Rodent, Oxbow Essentials) provides the correct calcium-to-phosphorus ratio that prevents MBD recurrence — this is the long-term fix

* See also: LRS (Lactated Ringer’s Solution) entry — severely crashed animals may require subcutaneous fluid support alongside oral calcium

* See also: VITAMIN D₃ entry — calcium absorption depends on adequate D₃

What an MBD crash looks like: Muscle tremors starting in the hind limbs, progressing to the whole body; extreme lethargy; inability to grip; weakness of the jaw; aggression or disorientation; hypersensitivity to touch or sound; and in severe cases, full convulsive seizures, coma, and death. In very severe crashes, the animal may also develop hyperthermia (overheating) from sustained muscle activity — keep the environment cool and do not add external heat during an active crash. | Tums Extra Strength (1 tablet) | 750 mg CaCO₃ | 300 mg elemental Ca |

heading: CAPSTAR (Nitenpyram)
text:
## **CAPSTAR (Nitenpyram)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Insecticide / Anti-Fly Strike **Indications:** Adult flea elimination; fly maggot (fly strike) treatment **Dosage:** \- Oral: 1/4 tablet dissolved in 1 ml water given orally once a day for 2 days \- Topical: 1/2 tablet dissolved in 2 ml water and applied topically externally as a flush for ears, nose, eyes, or anus **Route:** Oral or topical **Frequency:** Once daily for 2 days (oral); as needed (topical flush) **Warnings / Notes:** \- Form: Small unflavored tablets (11.4 mg) — cat strength recommended \- Interferes with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in insect nervous systems, causing rapid paralysis and death \- Begins working within 30 minutes \- Leaves system within 24–48 hours; no long-term residual effect \- Described as extremely safe with a wide margin of safety, even in very small neonates \- Does not eliminate eggs or unhatched larvae; manual removal remains necessary \- For fly strike cases, aggressive wound flushing and systemic antibiotics (such as Baytril) are essential alongside Capstar treatment to address toxins and bacteria from larval damage

heading: CARPROFEN (Rimadyl)
text:
## **CARPROFEN (Rimadyl)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) / Analgesic **Indications:** Pain management for musculoskeletal injuries, post-operative recovery, and inflammatory conditions when meloxicam is unavailable or when a vet recommends an alternative NSAID. Carprofen is one of the most widely used veterinary NSAIDs and is familiar to many vets and rehabbers.

*Source: BSAVA Exotic Pets Formulary (Sciurus vulgaris — red squirrel)*

**Dosage:** **5 mg/kg** SQ once daily

| Weight | Stage | Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | Gray | 0.25 mg |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.50 mg |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.75 mg |
| 200 g | Explorer | 1.00 mg |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 1.50 mg |
| 400 g | Adult | 2.00 mg |

*Carprofen injectable (50 mg/mL) is vet-administered; 25 mg chewable tablets can be compounded or cut, but tablets are difficult to dose accurately for small animals. A compounded oral suspension is the most practical route for outpatient rehab use — your vet can prescribe this.*

**Route:** SQ (subcutaneous injection) per BSAVA; oral via compounded suspension in rehab settings **Frequency:** SID — once daily

**Warnings / Notes:** \- All NSAID warnings apply: do not use in dehydrated animals (renal blood flow risk), do not combine with steroids (GI ulceration risk), do not use in animals with GI bleeding or known kidney/liver disease \- ⚠️ **NEVER combine with Meloxicam or other NSAIDs** — simultaneous use multiplies GI and kidney risk dramatically. Use one NSAID at a time only. \- Standard NSAID duration: 3–5 days for acute injury; reassess with vet before extending beyond 7 days \- Available as Rimadyl (brand); generic carprofen is also available through veterinary suppliers \- See also: MELOXICAM entry — meloxicam is the first-choice NSAID for squirrels where available

heading: CHLORHEXIDINE (Nolvasan / Hibiclens)
text:
## **CHLORHEXIDINE (Nolvasan / Hibiclens)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Topical Antiseptic **Indications:** Visible infections, abscesses, and surgical site preparation; functions effectively in presence of blood or pus **Dosage:** No specific mg/kg; see dilution protocol **Route:** Topical **Frequency:** Apply at each wound-cleaning session — BID (twice daily — morning and evening) for active infections or new wounds. SID (once daily) for maintenance and as the wound improves. Chlorhexidine retains antimicrobial residual activity on the skin surface for 4–6 hours, making BID appropriate for infected wounds. **Dilution Protocol:** \- General cleaning of intact or minimally broken skin: 1 ounce per gallon water (\~0.05% solution) \- Open wound flushing: 0.05% solution (approximately 1 part 2% chlorhexidine to 40 parts sterile saline) **Warnings / Notes:** \- Potent antimicrobial with rapid bactericidal action and residual antimicrobial effect after application \- Never use in or near eyes or ears \- Ototoxic — causes permanent deafness if reaching middle ear through ruptured eardrum \- Risk of corneal ulcers if splashed in eyes \- Use solution form only, not scrub; the scrub contains detergents toxic to open tissue; scrub should be limited to intact skin only

heading: DECONGESTANT SPRAY / AFRIN (Oxymetazoline)
text:
## **DECONGESTANT SPRAY / AFRIN (Oxymetazoline)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Nasal Decongestant / Nasal Swelling Reduction **Indications:** Used for animals with upper respiratory infections that make breathing difficult **Dosage:** \- Adults: 3 drops mixed with 5 ml saline \- Squirrels 12 weeks and younger: 2 drops mixed with 5 ml saline **Route:** Nebulizer (inhaled via enclosed space nebulization) **Frequency:** BID (twice daily — morning and evening). For severe congestion, TID (three times daily) may be used. Each session: allow the animal to sit in the nebulized mist for 15–20 minutes in an enclosed space, then return to open housing. **Maximum duration: Do not use for more than 3 consecutive days.** After 3 days, oxymetazoline causes rebound congestion — the nasal vessels compensate for the drug’s vasoconstriction by becoming *more* dilated when the drug wears off, worsening the congestion it was treating. If congestion persists past 3 days, switch to saline-only nebulization and address the underlying respiratory infection with systemic antibiotics. **Warnings / Notes:** \- Causes vasoconstriction in nasal blood vessels, diminishing swelling and secretion production \- Delivered via nebulizer: allow to nebulize in an enclosed space \- Use with caution; the 3-day limit is strict — see Frequency note above

heading: GABAPENTIN
text:
## **GABAPENTIN**

**Drug Class / Type:** Pain Relief / Anti-Convulsant / Neurological Distress Alleviation **Indications:** Neuropathic and nerve pain from spinal injuries; head trauma pain management; severe limb fracture pain; phantom pain following amputation; seizure management in post-traumatic or neurologically compromised animals. *Secondary consideration under veterinary guidance:* neuropathic itch associated with skin trauma or nerve involvement — gabapentin has been used for neuropathic pruritus in some species; confirm with your vet before using for this indication specifically.

**Route:** Oral (PO) — home-prepared suspension from capsules (see protocol below) **Frequency:** BID (twice daily — every 12 hours)

---

### **Expert Rehabber Protocol — Home Suspension from 300 mg Capsules**

This protocol was provided by an experienced squirrel rehabber with an established track record in the field. It has been mathematically verified to deliver **exactly 12.5 mg/kg BID** regardless of the animal’s weight, using a dose formula derived from a 50 mg/mL suspension.

**Step 1 — Make the suspension:** \- Open **one 300 mg gabapentin capsule** and empty the powder into a small container \- Add **6 mL of water** and stir until fully dissolved \- This yields a **50 mg/mL suspension** \- Label the container with the date; **refrigerate; discard after 14 days**

**Step 2 — Calculate the dose:**

**Dose formula: weight in grams × 0.00025 \= dose volume in mL (BID)**

This formula always delivers **12.5 mg/kg**, verified:

dose\_mg \= weight\_g × 0.00025 mL × 50 mg/mL  
mg/kg   \= dose\_mg ÷ (weight\_g ÷ 1000\)  
        \= 12.5 mg/kg — always, at any weight

**Step 3 — Administer:** \- Give the calculated volume orally BID (every 12 hours) \- Use a 1 mL syringe with 0.01 mL markings for accuracy

---

### **Weight Table — 50 mg/mL Suspension (Standard Protocol)**

| Weight | Stage | Formula | Dose Volume | mg Delivered | mg/kg |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 25 g | Pinky | 25 × 0.00025 | **0.006 mL** | 0.31 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 50 g | Gray | 50 × 0.00025 | **0.013 mL** | 0.63 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 100 g | Baby | 100 × 0.00025 | **0.025 mL** | 1.25 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 150 g | Toddler | 150 × 0.00025 | **0.038 mL** | 1.88 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 189 g | Explorer | 189 × 0.00025 | **0.047 mL** | 2.36 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 200 g | Explorer | 200 × 0.00025 | **0.050 mL** | 2.50 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 300 × 0.00025 | **0.075 mL** | 3.75 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 400 g | Adult | 400 × 0.00025 | **0.100 mL** | 5.00 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 500 g | Adult | 500 × 0.00025 | **0.125 mL** | 6.25 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |
| 752 g | Adult | 752 × 0.00025 | **0.188 mL** | 9.40 mg | 12.5 mg/kg |

*The rehabber’s example animals: 189g → dose 0.047 mL; 752g → dose 0.188 mL (may round to 0.19 or 0.20 mL). Both confirmed correct.*

---

### **Alternate Dilution — For Larger Animals or Easier Measurement**

If 0.00025 mL volumes feel too small to measure accurately on your syringe, use a **more concentrated** suspension:

* Open **one 300 mg capsule** into **3 mL of water** (half the water)

* Yields **100 mg/mL**

* New dose formula: **weight\_g × 0.000125 mL**

* Delivers the same 12.5 mg/kg BID

*Alternatively, at the original 50 mg/mL, a 752g squirrel doses 0.188 mL — round to 0.19 or 0.20 mL. The formula already produces manageable volumes for larger animals.*

---

### **Evidence Basis — Informed Extrapolation**

A squirrel-specific pharmacokinetic dose has not been established in the published literature located to date. The 12.5 mg/kg BID starting protocol below is an informed, conservative extrapolation from published small-mammal and laboratory-rodent dosing and requires veterinary authorization:

| Source | Species | Dose | Frequency | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Expert rehabber protocol (this entry) | Squirrel | **12.5 mg/kg** | BID (q12h) | Mathematically verified |
| Rat Guide (veterinary reference) | Rat | 10–30 mg/kg | q8h | Primary rat dose: 30 mg/kg |
| Merck Veterinary Manual | Small mammals | 10–15 mg/kg, titrate to 20–30 mg/kg | q8h | Dose can be increased |
| Guinea Pig Forum (vet-sourced) | Guinea pig | 5 mg/kg starting, adjust to response | BID | Conservative start |

**Evidence basis:** A squirrel-specific pharmacokinetic dose for gabapentin has not been established in the published literature located to date. A 12.5 mg/kg BID starting protocol falls within published gabapentin dosing ranges used in other small mammals and laboratory rodents (Merck: 10–15 mg/kg titrating to 20–30 mg/kg; Rat Guide: 10–30 mg/kg q8h in rats) and should be used only under veterinary authorization. Published rat and other small-mammal dosing provides useful comparative context when squirrel-specific data is unavailable, but it does not establish a squirrel dose. The convergence of available small-mammal references supports 12.5 mg/kg as a conservative starting point under veterinary authorization; this remains informed extrapolation, not a confirmed squirrel-specific dose.

---

### **A Note on the Original Source Error**

The original source (thesquirrelbible.com) listed **0.1–0.2 mg/kg** as the gabapentin dose. This figure is inconsistent with published veterinary and laboratory-rodent gabapentin ranges and is believed to represent a documentation or transcription error — the exact source of the error is unknown. The source of the original error has not been definitively established.

**What is established:** at 50 mg/mL, a 25–50g squirrel’s BID dose is **0.006–0.013 mL** — a value that is plausibly consistent with the kind of number that could become garbled in transcription. Regardless of origin, 0.1–0.2 mg/kg falls 50–300× below the published therapeutic range for comparable species and is not supported as an effective squirrel dose by the evidence reviewed for this edition. **It should not be used.**

---

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Mimics the neurotransmitter GABA, stabilizing electrical activity in the brain and peripheral nerves; effective for neuropathic pain and active seizure management under veterinary direction \- Can cause significant sedation and ataxia — monitor for stumbling, falling, or difficulty gripping within the first 2–4 hours after first dose; if profound, reduce dose by half \- **Do not stop abruptly** — taper gradually (reduce dose by 25% every 3–5 days) to avoid rebound seizures or pain flares \- ⚠️ **Monitor for “Floppy Squirrel Syndrome”** if combined with Trazodone, Benadryl, or Buprenorphine — additive sedation increases risk of aspiration pneumonia due to impaired swallowing reflex \- **Avoid xylitol-containing formulations** unless specifically cleared by a wildlife veterinarian — commercial human liquid gabapentin formulations sometimes contain xylitol, which is documented as acutely toxic in dogs and is a concern in small mammals; squirrel-specific toxicity thresholds have not been established, but the risk is not worth taking. The home-prepared suspension from pure capsule powder dissolved in plain water contains no xylitol and is the safest option. \- Gabapentin requires a prescription — a supervising veterinarian must authorize and confirm the dose for the specific animal and indication \- **Refrigerate the suspension; discard after 14 days** — stability data for room-temperature storage is unreliable; cold storage is required

heading: ALBUTEROL SULFATE (Salbutamol) — NEBULIZED
text:
## **ALBUTEROL SULFATE (Salbutamol) — NEBULIZED**

**Evidence: \[B\] RODENT ANALOG \+ \[C\] REHAB / CLINICAL PRECEDENT \+ \[PROVISIONAL\]**

**Drug Class / Type: Short-acting beta-2 agonist bronchodilator**

**Primary Uses: Acute bronchospasm, wheezing, and lower-airway constriction; adjunctive respiratory support when bronchoconstriction is contributing to pneumonia or aspiration-associated respiratory distress. Do NOT use simply because respiratory rate is elevated.**

**What It Does: Relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and improves airflow. It does NOT treat bacterial pneumonia, aspirated material, mucus plugs, pulmonary edema, or the underlying infection.**

**Clinical Selection Note — PROVISIONAL: Rapid breathing/tachypnea alone is not an indication for albuterol and may reflect pneumonia, hypoxia, pain, fever, shock, or other non-bronchospastic causes. Because albuterol can increase heart rate and cardiovascular workload, avoid or use extreme caution when tachypnea is the primary sign without evidence of bronchoconstriction. Consider albuterol when labored breathing or gasping appears consistent with lower-airway constriction/bronchospasm, especially when accompanied by wheezing, prolonged expiration, or obvious difficulty moving air. Gasping alone is not diagnostic of bronchospasm; continue to assess for hypoxia, severe pneumonia, pulmonary edema, airway obstruction, and neurologic causes. This distinction is awaiting veterinarian validation.**

**Common Form: Albuterol sulfate inhalation solution 0.083% \= 2.5 mg/3 mL \= approximately 0.833 mg/mL.**

**PROVISIONAL RODENT-DERIVED NEBULIZATION PROTOCOL: Published/exotic-mammal and rat protocols include 0.083% albuterol diluted with approximately 3 mL sterile 0.9% saline and nebulized for about 15 minutes q8–12h. A separate rat respiratory protocol uses 0.5 mL of 0.083% albuterol in a total nebulizer mixture of approximately 9 mL, with 10–15 minute chamber exposure 2–3 times daily. Device output, chamber volume, ventilation, and exposure time substantially affect delivered dose; these are not interchangeable with a fixed mg/kg dose.**

**Supportive Humidity: Sterile saline in the nebulizer provides useful airway humidification and may help loosen secretions. The chamber must remain ventilated; avoid condensation buildup, overheating, or hypercapnia.**

**Monitoring / Stop Criteria: Observe continuously. Stop treatment for panic, marked agitation, tremor, pronounced tachycardia, weakness, worsening respiratory effort, or collapse. Excessive beta-agonist exposure can cause tachycardia, tremor/agitation, and hypokalemia.**

**⚠️ VALIDATION STATUS: No validated squirrel-specific inhaled mg/kg dose has been located. This entry is intentionally retained as a rodent-derived emergency reference because rat protocols are commonly used as squirrel analogs when direct Sciuridae literature is absent. Awaiting veterinarian validation of concentration, dilution, session duration, and frequency for squirrel use. Once veterinary guidance is received, replace this provisional block with the veterinarian-approved squirrel protocol.**

**Sources / Evidence Basis: Sciuridae / Squirrel / Prairie Dog Veterinary & Rehabilitation Formulary Landscape; exotic-mammal respiratory proceedings; rat respiratory protocols; squirrel rehabilitation precedent.**

heading: GENTAMYCIN (Gentamicin / Gentocin)
text:
## **GENTAMYCIN (Gentamicin / Gentocin)**

**Evidence: \[B\] RODENT ANALOG \+ \[C\] REHAB / CLINICAL PRECEDENT**

**Drug Class / Type:** Aminoglycoside antibiotic **Indications:** Reserved for high-risk aspiration pneumonia or chronic respiratory infections unresponsive to first-line oral antibiotics like Baytril and Doxycycline. **Not a first-line drug.** Use only after Baytril ± Doxycycline have failed or are contraindicated. **Mechanism:** Bactericidal aminoglycoside; binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and causes misreading of bacterial mRNA, producing nonfunctional proteins that disrupt the bacterial cell membrane. **Route:** Nebulized — the nebulizer converts the liquid solution into a fine mist (aerosol) that the squirrel breathes in while enclosed in a small nebulization chamber. Nebulization delivers drug directly to lung tissue while minimizing systemic absorption, which substantially reduces kidney and inner-ear toxicity compared to systemic (injectable) gentamicin. **Frequency:** BID to TID (2–3 times daily). Each session: 15–20 minutes in the nebulization chamber. **Treatment Duration:** 7–14 days, depending on response.

⚠️ **DILUTION: Obtain specific dilution ratio from your prescribing veterinarian.**

Gentamicin injectable solution is available at 50 mg/mL and 100 mg/mL — two very different concentrations. Standard nebulization protocols dilute the injectable with sterile saline, but the exact ratio depends on your nebulizer type, chamber volume, and the concentration of your specific vial. Using the wrong ratio can result in underdosing (ineffective) or overdosing (systemic absorption and kidney/ear toxicity). **Ask your vet for the dilution ratio prescribed for your vial.** A common starting point in small mammal rehabilitation is 50 mg/mL diluted 1:9 with sterile saline → final concentration 5 mg/mL, using 0.5–1 mL of working solution per nebulization session — but this must be confirmed with your vet before use.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Nebulized gentamicin is an adjunct to systemic treatment, not a replacement — the squirrel typically also needs oral Baytril or Doxycycline for bacteria beyond the lung airways \- ⚠️ **Bronchoconstriction risk** — gentamicin can trigger airway spasm in some animals; your vet may include a bronchodilator (Albuterol/Terbutaline) in the nebulization solution to prevent this \- ⚠️ **Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity** — aminoglycosides cause irreversible kidney damage and permanent inner-ear hearing loss if absorbed systemically at high levels; nebulization is used specifically to minimize this, but the risk is not zero — monitor hydration and urine output during the course \- Nebulizer equipment must be cleaned thoroughly after every use to prevent bacterial contamination of the reservoir \- Requires veterinary prescription and guidance

Warnings / Notes: - Nebulized gentamicin is an adjunct to systemic treatment, not a replacement — the squirrel typically also needs oral Baytril or Doxycycline for bacteria beyond the lung airways - ⚠️ Bronchoconstriction risk — gentamicin can trigger airway spasm in some animals; your vet may include a bronchodilator (Albuterol/Terbutaline) in the nebulization solution to prevent this - ⚠️ Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity — aminoglycosides cause irreversible kidney damage and permanent inner-ear hearing loss if absorbed systemically at high levels; nebulization is used specifically to minimize this, but the risk is not zero — monitor hydration and urine output during the course - Nebulizer equipment must be cleaned thoroughly after every use to prevent bacterial contamination of the reservoir - Requires veterinary prescription and guidance

heading: IBUPROFEN
text:
## **IBUPROFEN**

**Drug Class / Type:** Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) / Pain relief / Fever reducer / Inflammation Reducer **Indications:** Minor pain and fever reduction — **last resort only when Meloxicam is unavailable.** Meloxicam is strongly preferred. **Form:** **Infant Concentrated Drops only** (50 mg per 1.25 mL \= **40 mg/mL**). Do NOT use Children’s suspension (20 mg/mL) — if you give the same volume of Children’s formula as Infant Drops, you give half the dose; if you mistakenly use the Children’s formula volume for Infant Drops, you double the dose. Confirm your bottle’s concentration before every use. **Dosage:**

| Age Group | Volume | Concentration | mg dose | Approx mg/kg |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Adults (≈ 400 g) | 0.1 mL | 40 mg/mL Infant Drops | 4.0 mg | ≈ 10 mg/kg |
| Teenagers (12–18 weeks, ≈ 300 g) | 0.05 mL | 40 mg/mL Infant Drops | 2.0 mg | ≈ 6.7 mg/kg |

**Route:** Oral (Infant Concentrated Drops — 40 mg/mL formulation only) **Frequency:** Every 4–6 hours as needed; **maximum 4 days total** **Warnings / Notes:** \- ONLY IF THERE ARE NO OTHER PAIN RELIEVERS AVAILABLE — LAST RESORT MEDICATION \- DO NOT USE ON SQUIRRELS 12 WEEKS AND YOUNGER \- Inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes to block the production of prostaglandins \- Very narrow safety margin in squirrels; overdose or use in dehydrated animals risks rapid gastric ulcers and kidney failure \- Never mix with steroids \- Many rehabilitators now prefer Meloxicam due to superior safety profile

heading: IVERMECTIN
text:
## **IVERMECTIN**

**Drug Class / Type:** Anti-Parasitic **Indications:** \- Sarcoptic mange, notoedric mange, ear mites (*Otodectes*), demodectic mange \- Larval heartworms (NOT adult heartworms); some lice and fleas \- Fly strike: kills maggots that have entered a wound \- Some internal nematodes (NOT tapeworms or whipworms — use Panacur for those)

**Form:** 1% injectable solution (10 mg/mL) is the preferred formulation for squirrels. Available without prescription from farm and ranch supply stores (Ivomec, Noromectin, etc.). Paste formulations (0.27%, 1.87%) are available but difficult to dose accurately at squirrel weights — see paste note below.

**Route:** \- If diluted with **propylene glycol**: **Oral (PO) only** — propylene glycol is harmful by injection \- If diluted with **sterile water**: May be given PO, IM, or SQ \- For fly strike: a drop of working solution may be applied directly into the wound

---

### **Protocol A — Mange (sarcoptic, notoedric) and Ear Mites**

⚠️ **Rodent-specific dosing:** The standard chart dose for general mammals is 0.25 mg/kg. However, rodents (including squirrels) and rabbits require the **higher range: 0.4–0.5 mg/kg** (*Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond*, p. 264). Use the rodent-specific table below, not the general mammal chart.

**Dilution (1:9 — makes 1 mg/mL working solution):** Mix **1 part 1% ivermectin injectable** with **9 parts propylene glycol** *or* **9 parts sterile water**. Shake well before each use. Label with the date; discard after **2 weeks**.

**Dose:** 0.4–0.5 mg/kg — use 0.4 mg/kg as a conservative starting point; 0.5 mg/kg is appropriate for confirmed mange.

**Weight-Based Dosing Reference** *(1 mg/mL working solution)*

| Weight | Stage | 0.4 mg/kg | 0.5 mg/kg |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | Infant | 0.020 mL | 0.025 mL |
| 75 g | Infant | 0.030 mL | 0.037 mL |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.040 mL | 0.050 mL |
| 125 g | Baby | 0.050 mL | 0.062 mL |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.060 mL | 0.075 mL |
| 175 g | Toddler | 0.070 mL | 0.087 mL |
| 200 g | Explorer | 0.080 mL | 0.100 mL |
| 250 g | Juvenile | 0.100 mL | 0.125 mL |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 0.120 mL | 0.150 mL |
| 350 g | Pre-Teen | 0.140 mL | 0.175 mL |
| 400 g | Teenager | 0.160 mL | 0.200 mL |

**Frequency / Schedule:** Single dose, repeated every **10–14 days** — typically 2–3 total doses. Change bedding and clean the enclosure thoroughly after each treatment to eliminate re-exposure from shed mites and eggs.

---

### **Protocol B — Demodectic Mange**

Demodectic mange requires a longer, more intensive protocol than sarcoptic or notoedric mange.

**Dose:** 0.6 mg/kg (600 µg/kg) — higher than Protocol A **Formulation:** Use the 1 mg/mL working solution (same 1:9 dilution as above) **Frequency:** Once daily **Duration:** At minimum 2 months, continued until a skin scraping confirms negative results

**Weight-Based Dosing Reference** *(1 mg/mL working solution · 0.6 mg/kg)*

| Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | Infant | 0.030 mL |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.060 mL |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.090 mL |
| 200 g | Explorer | 0.120 mL |
| 250 g | Juvenile | 0.150 mL |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 0.180 mL |
| 350 g | Pre-Teen | 0.210 mL |
| 400 g | Teenager | 0.240 mL |

This is a long-term protocol. Consult your supervising vet before beginning and confirm a skin scraping before discontinuing.

---

### **Notes on Pinkies / Grays (under 50 g)**

Ivermectin is generally not used in animals under 50 g. Mange and mite infestations in very young animals should be managed with manual removal and topical approaches; discuss with your vet before using ivermectin below Infant stage.

### **Note on Equine Paste**

Apple-flavored equine paste (1.87%) is sometimes seen in older protocols (“grain of rice” dosing). At squirrel weights the required amount is literally invisible — a 200 g squirrel needs approximately 2 mg, which is a fraction of a milligram of paste. Paste is not recommended. The diluted injectable method is the only approach that allows accurate dosing.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Causes paralysis and death of parasites by potentiating GABA-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle cells; mammalian CNS is protected by the blood-brain barrier at therapeutic doses \- ⚠️ **Do NOT use simultaneously with Revolution (Selamectin)** — additive toxicity risk \- **Neurotoxicity if overdosed:** Signs include tremors, stargazing, ataxia, profound lethargy. Measure carefully every time. \- Ineffective against tapeworms and adult heartworms; does not treat whipworms. Use Panacur for GI parasites. \- Ineffective against ticks

---
