heading: L-GLUTAMINE
text:
## **L-GLUTAMINE**

**Drug Class / Type:** Amino acid supplement / GI mucosal support **Form:** Capsules (500 mg); open and use the powder — mix directly into formula batch **Route:** Oral (PO) — delivered through formula at every feeding **Indications:** Supporting GI tract integrity during the transition from mother’s milk to rehabilitation formula; gut lining repair after the stress of orphaning; improving formula absorption and weight gain in formula-fed baby squirrels

---

### **What It Is and Why It Works**

L-Glutamine is an amino acid — not a drug, not a supplement in the marketing sense, but a fundamental building block that the body uses specifically to fuel and maintain the intestinal lining. The cells that line the gut wall (intestinal epithelial cells) use glutamine as their primary energy source. When those cells are healthy and well-fed, formula gets absorbed properly. When they’re damaged or depleted — as they often are after the stress of losing a mother, handling, temperature fluctuation, and the abrupt switch from species-appropriate milk to formula — absorption suffers, gut motility gets dysregulated, and babies fail to thrive even when fed correctly.

L-Glutamine rebuilds the absorption surface. It reduces intestinal permeability (the “leaky gut” that lets undigested proteins and pathogens through), supports the mucus layer that protects the gut wall, and helps restore normal motility. The result: formula actually gets absorbed instead of passing through a compromised gut.

**This protocol came to us from the opossum rescue community** — rehabbers who work with animals that are, if anything, even more GI-fragile than squirrels at intake. The results speak for themselves: babies on L-Glutamine are noticeably fatter, eat more consistently, and make the formula transition more smoothly than those without it.

---

### **The Protocol — Mixed Into Formula Batch**

This protocol is elegant because it is self-correcting: feeding volume scales with body weight (the 5% rule), so every baby at every weight automatically gets the same proportional dose per feeding without any individual calculation.

**Batch preparation:** \- Mix your standard formula batch: **⅔ cup (approximately 158 mL)** \- Open **one 500 mg L-Glutamine capsule**, use **half the powder (250 mg)**; store the other half sealed for the next batch \- Add the powder directly to the formula batch and stir to dissolve — it mixes cleanly with no taste or texture issue \- The resulting concentration: **\~1.58 mg/mL** throughout the batch \- Feed normally — every baby gets L-Glutamine with every feeding from that batch

**Scaling for different batch sizes:** \- ⅓ cup batch (\~79 mL): use ¼ capsule (125 mg) \- 1 cup batch (\~237 mL): use ¾ capsule (375 mg) \- The ratio is always approximately **1.6 mg per mL of formula**

---

### **Dose Delivered — Verified Math**

*At 1.58 mg/mL concentration, feeding at 5% body weight:*

| Weight | Stage | Feed Volume | Glutamine/Feeding | Daily (5 feeds) | mg/kg/day |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | Gray | 2.5 mL | 4.0 mg | 19.8 mg | \~396 mg/kg |
| 75 g | Infant | 3.8 mL | 5.9 mg | 29.7 mg | \~396 mg/kg |
| 100 g | Baby | 5.0 mL | 7.9 mg | 39.6 mg | \~396 mg/kg |
| 150 g | Toddler | 7.5 mL | 11.9 mg | 59.3 mg | \~396 mg/kg |
| 200 g | Explorer | 10.0 mL | 15.8 mg | 79.1 mg | \~396 mg/kg |

Every baby receives **\~79 mg/kg per feeding, \~396 mg/kg/day** — regardless of size, because the dose scales automatically with feeding volume. This falls within the veterinary critical care range of \~500 mg/kg/day used for gut repair in intensive care patients, confirming the protocol is therapeutically meaningful, not just trace supplementation.

---

### **When to Use It**

* **Start at intake** — the moment a baby comes in and is stable enough to begin formula, add L-Glutamine to the first batch

* **Continue through the formula-feeding period** — until the squirrel is fully transitioned to solid foods and no longer receiving formula

* **Use during and after antibiotic courses** — antibiotics damage gut flora and the epithelial cells themselves; L-Glutamine helps repair the lining while probiotics restore the bacteria. Give both.

* **Use during recovery from diarrhea or GI illness** — gut lining takes a beating during illness; this speeds recovery of absorption capacity

---

### **Safety Profile**

L-Glutamine is one of the safest supplements in this formulary. It is a naturally occurring amino acid present in virtually every food. It is water-soluble — excess is excreted, not stored. There is no meaningful toxicity ceiling at these doses. It has no drug interactions. It does not require a prescription.

The only caution: **do not use a product that contains added sweeteners or flavorings** — check the capsule ingredients and confirm the only ingredient is L-Glutamine (or L-Glutamine and a vegetable capsule shell). Some supplement brands add fillers. Pure powder or pure capsules only.

**Storage:** Store the capsules in a cool, dry place per the product label. Once mixed into formula, treat the batch as you would any formula — refrigerate and use within the normal formula freshness window.

*Source: Field protocol from the opossum rehabilitation community, adopted into squirrel rehab practice. Mathematically verified: dose scales proportionally with feeding volume under the 5% body weight feeding rule, delivering a consistent therapeutic mg/kg/day across all weight classes.*

---

heading: LACTATED RINGER’S SOLUTION (LRS)
text:
## **LACTATED RINGER’S SOLUTION (LRS)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Rehydration / Electrolyte Support **Indications:** Correcting dehydration; treating shock; flushing system during toxin/poison ingestion or fly strike **Dosage:** Weight-based administration, typically 5%–10% of body weight **Route:** Subcutaneous (Sub-Q) injection (sterile fluid bag) **Frequency:** Split into multiple sessions over 24 hours; continue until skin tenting resolves **Warnings / Notes:** \- Unlike plain saline, LRS contains sodium lactate, potassium, and calcium, which helps buffer the blood and replace essential electrolytes lost during illness or trauma \- Must be warmed to body temperature before administration; cold fluids can put a compromised baby squirrel into fatal cardiac arrest

heading: MARBOFLOXACIN (Zeniquin) — Oral Suspension
text:
## **MARBOFLOXACIN (Zeniquin) — Oral Suspension**

**Evidence: \[VET\] VETERINARIAN-PRESCRIBED**

**Drug Class / Type:** Fluoroquinolone antibiotic (same family as Baytril) **Indications:** Bacterial infections including *E. coli* — e.g., infected post-surgical wounds **Form:** Compounded aqueous oral suspension, **10 mg/mL** (prescription) **Route:** Oral (PO) **Frequency:** Once daily (SID) **Duration:** 14 days, or as your vet directs **Dose:** ≈ **4.76 mg/kg** (0.25 mL for a 525 g squirrel; veterinarian prescription, October 2026)

**Weight-Based Dosing Reference** *(10 mg/mL · 4.76 mg/kg once daily)*

| Weight | Dose (mg) | Volume |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | 0.24 mg | 0.024 mL |
| 75 g | 0.36 mg | 0.036 mL |
| 100 g | 0.48 mg | 0.048 mL |
| 150 g | 0.71 mg | 0.071 mL |
| 200 g | 0.95 mg | 0.095 mL |
| 250 g | 1.19 mg | 0.119 mL |
| 300 g | 1.43 mg | 0.143 mL |
| 350 g | 1.67 mg | 0.167 mL |
| 400 g | 1.90 mg | 0.190 mL |
| 450 g | 2.14 mg | 0.214 mL |
| 525 g | 2.50 mg | 0.250 mL |

**Warnings / Notes:** \- **Never combine with Baytril** — same drug class. \- **Growing babies:** fluoroquinolones carry a cartilage caution in young, growing animals; use in unweaned or growing babies only when your vet directs (see the "Pinky Exception," Ch. 80). \- **Compounded:** confirm the mg/mL on your bottle — if it isn't 10 mg/mL, this table doesn't apply. \- Finish the full course, even when the wound looks better.

text:
## **MELOXICAM (Metacam)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) / Pain Relief, Fever, Inflammation Reduction **Indications:** Management of pain, fever, and inflammation resulting from trauma or surgical procedures — fractures, cat attacks, head trauma, post-surgical recovery, or any significant injury. The preferred NSAID for squirrels when available. **Mechanism:** Selectively inhibits COX-2 enzymes, blocking prostaglandin synthesis at the site of injury. Preferential COX-2 selectivity gives meloxicam a better GI safety profile than older NSAIDs like ibuprofen.

⚠️ **CONCENTRATION WARNING — READ BEFORE DOSING**

Metacam is available in **two concentrations: 0.5 mg/mL** (cat formulation) **and 1.5 mg/mL** (dog formulation). A rehabber who uses the wrong table will dose at 3× too much or 3× too little. **Check your vial before every use and use only the table that matches your concentration.** If you are unsure which concentration you have, contact your vet before dosing.

The original source doses were calculated for **0.5 mg/mL at 0.125 mg/kg** — verified by back-calculation. A rehabber using 1.5 mg/mL with those same volumes would inadvertently give 0.375 mg/kg, which is still within the safe range for small rodents but is 3× the intended dose. **Always use the table below that matches your concentration.**

---

### **A Note on Dosage: Two Sources, Very Different Numbers**

⚠️ **Important clinical context — read before dosing**

Two authoritative sources give significantly different meloxicam doses for squirrels:

| Source | Dose | Species |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| thesquirrelbible.com (back-calculated) | **0.125 mg/kg** PO SID | Eastern gray squirrel |
| BSAVA Exotic Pets Formulary | **1–2 mg/kg** SC or PO SID | Red squirrel (*S. vulgaris*) |

This is an **8–16× difference**, and it is clinically significant. The explanation is almost certainly that thesquirrelbible.com applied cat or dog dosing (cats: 0.05 mg/kg; dogs: 0.1 mg/kg) to squirrels. This is a common but pharmacologically incorrect approach — small mammals metabolize NSAIDs considerably faster than dogs and cats and require proportionally higher doses. Published rabbit meloxicam doses are 0.5–1.5 mg/kg; the BSAVA squirrel dose of 1–2 mg/kg is entirely consistent with that pattern.

**The BSAVA dose is more likely to provide adequate analgesia.** A squirrel dosed at 0.125 mg/kg may be receiving sub-therapeutic meloxicam and inadequate pain control.

**Recommendation:** Consult your supervising veterinarian about which dose to use. The tables below show **both doses** so you can use whichever your vet confirms. The lower dose (0.125–0.2 mg/kg) carries less GI and renal risk; the higher dose (1 mg/kg) provides better analgesia in line with species-appropriate pharmacology.

---

**Route:** Oral (PO) — honey-flavored suspension; most animals accept it readily. SQ injection is an option for hospitalized animals under vet supervision (BSAVA protocol uses SC route). **Frequency:** SID — once daily. Duration: 3–5 days for acute injury; up to 7 days max without vet reassessment.

---

### **Table Set A — Conservative Dose (0.125–0.2 mg/kg) · Source-Based**

**0.5 mg/mL · 0.2 mg/kg** *(cat Metacam)*

| Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 25 g | Pinky | 0.010 mL — dilution needed; see note below |
| 50 g | Gray | 0.020 mL |
| 75 g | Infant | 0.030 mL |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.040 mL |
| 125 g | Baby | 0.050 mL |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.060 mL |
| 175 g | Toddler | 0.070 mL |
| 200 g | Explorer | 0.080 mL |
| 250 g | Juvenile | 0.100 mL |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 0.120 mL |
| 350 g | Pre-Teen | 0.140 mL |
| 400 g | Teenager | 0.160 mL |

**1.5 mg/mL · 0.2 mg/kg** *(dog Metacam)*

| Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | Gray | 0.007 mL — dilute to 0.5 mg/mL for accuracy |
| 75 g | Infant | 0.010 mL |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.013 mL |
| 125 g | Baby | 0.017 mL |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.020 mL |
| 175 g | Toddler | 0.023 mL |
| 200 g | Explorer | 0.027 mL |
| 250 g | Juvenile | 0.033 mL |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 0.040 mL |
| 350 g | Pre-Teen | 0.047 mL |
| 400 g | Teenager | 0.053 mL |

---

### **Table Set B — BSAVA Squirrel Dose (1 mg/kg) · Species-Appropriate**

*Source: BSAVA Exotic Pets Formulary, Red Squirrel (Sciurus vulgaris). Use this dose when your vet confirms 1 mg/kg is appropriate for your animal.*

**0.5 mg/mL · 1 mg/kg** *(cat Metacam)*

| Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 25 g | Pinky | 0.050 mL |
| 50 g | Gray | 0.100 mL |
| 75 g | Infant | 0.150 mL |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.200 mL |
| 125 g | Baby | 0.250 mL |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.300 mL |
| 175 g | Toddler | 0.350 mL |
| 200 g | Explorer | 0.400 mL |
| 250 g | Juvenile | 0.500 mL |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 0.600 mL |
| 350 g | Pre-Teen | 0.700 mL |
| 400 g | Teenager | 0.800 mL |

**1.5 mg/mL · 1 mg/kg** *(dog Metacam)*

| Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 25 g | Pinky | 0.017 mL — consider diluting |
| 50 g | Gray | 0.033 mL |
| 75 g | Infant | 0.050 mL |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.067 mL |
| 125 g | Baby | 0.083 mL |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.100 mL |
| 175 g | Toddler | 0.117 mL |
| 200 g | Explorer | 0.133 mL |
| 250 g | Juvenile | 0.167 mL |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 0.200 mL |
| 350 g | Pre-Teen | 0.233 mL |
| 400 g | Teenager | 0.267 mL |

---

**Dilution note for 1.5 mg/mL with small animals (under 100g):** Draw 0.1 mL of 1.5 mg/mL into a syringe and add 0.2 mL of sterile water → 0.3 mL of 0.5 mg/mL. Use the 0.5 mg/mL table. Discard unused diluted solution after 24 hours.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Inhibits COX-2 enzymes, reducing prostaglandin production that drives pain and swelling; COX-2 selectivity preserves stomach-protective prostaglandins better than older NSAIDs \- ⚠️ **NEVER use with steroids (Prednisone, Dexamethasone)** — combined NSAID \+ steroid use causes life-threatening GI ulceration and bleeding. This is a hard stop. \- ⚠️ **Use only in well-hydrated animals.** NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow through prostaglandin inhibition — in a dehydrated animal, this can trigger acute kidney failure. Rehydrate with LRS before giving Meloxicam if the animal is dehydrated. \- Do not use in animals with active GI bleeding, known kidney disease, or severe liver disease \- Do not exceed recommended dose — higher doses do not increase benefit but dramatically increase GI and kidney risk \- ⚠️ **FATAL TO CATS** — even a single drop of dog-concentration Metacam can kill a cat. Keep clearly labeled and separate from any cat medications in your facility.

heading: MYLICON (Simethicone)
text:
## **MYLICON (Simethicone)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Anti-gas (anti-foaming agent) **Indications:** Treat bloat and gas in formula-fed baby squirrels, which can be life-threatening if the abdomen becomes hard and distended **Dosage:** **1–2 drops of infant simethicone drops (20 mg/0.3 mL concentration)** per feeding. For severe bloat with a visibly distended, hard abdomen, give before the feeding and again after, then again at the next feeding if not resolved. Simethicone has no systemic absorption and essentially no toxicity ceiling — a few extra drops will not harm the animal. **Route:** Oral (pediatric/infant drops — the unflavored or berry formula; use the infant drops, not tablets or adult-strength products) **Frequency:** PRN (as needed) — given at feedings where bloat is present or as a preventive measure during formula changes, overfeeding recovery, or when stools are off. Give at the beginning of the feeding. Can be used at every feeding if bloat is persistent until the cause is resolved. **Warnings / Notes:** \- Breaks down the surface tension of gas bubbles in the GI tract, allowing the squirrel to pass gas more easily \- Extremely safe with virtually no side effects, as it acts mechanically rather than chemically \- Does not treat the cause of the bloat (like overfeeding), only the symptom \- Not absorbed into the bloodstream

heading: METRONIDAZOLE (Flagyl)
text:
## **METRONIDAZOLE (Flagyl)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Antibiotic / Antiprotozoal — Nitroimidazole **Indications:** GI infections including Giardia and other protozoan parasites; anaerobic bacterial infections; dental/oral infections; wound infections where anaerobic coverage is needed alongside aerobic antibiotics (e.g., Baytril for aerobic \+ Metronidazole for anaerobic). Commonly used in squirrel rehab for soft or bloody stools, diarrhea with a protozoal cause, or wounds with a foul odor indicating anaerobic contamination.

*Source: BSAVA Exotic Pets Formulary (Sciurus vulgaris — red squirrel)*

**Dosage:** \- **Oral (PO):** 10–20 mg/kg q12h (twice daily) \- **Subcutaneous (SQ, vet-administered):** 20 mg/kg once daily

**Route:** Oral preferred for outpatient rehab use; SQ for hospitalized animals

**Frequency:** \- Oral: BID (every 12 hours) \- SQ: SID (once daily)

**Duration:** 5–10 days for most GI infections; 7–14 days for Giardia; follow vet guidance

**Practical Preparation — Oral Suspension:** Metronidazole 250 mg tablets are widely available. For a 5 mg/mL suspension: crush one 250 mg tablet and dissolve completely in 50 mL of warm water with stirring. Store refrigerated, discard after 5 days. Shake before each use.

**Weight-Based Dosing Reference — Oral — 10 mg/kg · 5 mg/mL suspension**

| Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose (BID) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 25 g | Pinky | 0.050 mL |
| 50 g | Gray | 0.100 mL |
| 75 g | Infant | 0.150 mL |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.200 mL |
| 125 g | Baby | 0.250 mL |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.300 mL |
| 175 g | Toddler | 0.350 mL |
| 200 g | Explorer | 0.400 mL |
| 250 g | Juvenile | 0.500 mL |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 0.600 mL |
| 350 g | Pre-Teen | 0.700 mL |
| 400 g | Adult | 0.800 mL |

*For 20 mg/kg dosing, double the above volumes.*

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Metronidazole is bitter — some animals resist oral dosing. Mix into formula, almond butter, or yogurt to improve acceptance \- Neurological side effects (ataxia, head tilt, seizures) are possible at high doses or with prolonged use — if any neurological signs appear, discontinue immediately and contact your vet \- Do not use in pregnant animals during the first trimester — teratogenic risk (though rarely relevant in wildlife rehab) \- GI upset (nausea, reduced appetite) is common; give with food when possible \- Metronidazole covers anaerobic bacteria but NOT aerobic bacteria — pair with Baytril or Doxycycline when broad-spectrum coverage is needed for mixed infections \- ⚠️ **Do not use alcohol-based products** in animals on metronidazole — theoretical disulfiram-like reaction (not well-characterized in small mammals, but avoid as a precaution)

heading: NEOSPORIN (Triple Antibiotic)
text:
## **NEOSPORIN (Triple Antibiotic)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Topical Antibiotic **Active Ingredients:** Bacitracin, neomycin, and polymyxin B **Indications:** Minor cuts, scrapes, and superficial wounds to prevent bacterial infection **Dosage:** Not specified in mg/kg; topical ointment or cream **Route:** Topical **Frequency:** Applied 1 to 3 times daily until the skin has healed **Warnings / Notes:** \- Creates a physical barrier while the three antibiotics kill various strains of bacteria on the skin’s surface \- Use sparingly; squirrels are groomers; if they lick off large amounts, the neomycin can cause GI upset \- Ensure it is rubbed in well or used in areas they cannot easily reach \- Do not use in deep puncture wounds (like cat bites), which require systemic antibiotics

heading: NUFLOR (Florfenicol)
text:
## **NUFLOR (Florfenicol)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Advanced broad-spectrum antibiotic **Indications:** Last-resort antibiotic for respiratory infections that are not responding to Baytril or Doxycycline — specifically *Bordetella bronchiseptica*, *Pasteurella*, and *Mycoplasma*. Also used for refractory wound infections. **Not for routine use.** **Form:** Injectable (300 mg/mL) — must be diluted before oral administration. **The raw 300 mg/mL solution is far too concentrated to dose accurately at squirrel weights and is caustic to oral tissue. Always dilute.** **Dilution:** Mix **1 part Nuflor injectable (300 mg/mL)** with **9 parts sterile water** → working solution of **30 mg/mL**. Give only orally once diluted. Discard unused working solution after **2 weeks**. **Strength (working solution):** 30 mg/mL **Dosage:** 20 mg/kg **Route:** PO (oral), after dilution **Frequency:** Two doses total — give once, then repeat **48 hours later**. **DO NOT GIVE A THIRD DOSE.**

**Weight-Based Dosing Reference** *(30 mg/mL working solution · 20 mg/kg)*

| Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 25 g (Pinky) | Pinky | 0.017 mL |
| 50 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.033 mL |
| 75 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.050 mL |
| 100 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.067 mL |
| 125 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.083 mL |
| 150 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.100 mL |
| 175 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.117 mL |
| 200 g (Explorer) | Explorer | 0.133 mL |
| 250 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.167 mL |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.200 mL |
| 350 g (Pre-Teen) | Pre-Teen | 0.233 mL |
| 400 g (Teenager) | Teenager | 0.267 mL |

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Bacteriostatic; inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit. High lipid solubility allows effective penetration into lung tissue — its primary advantage over Baytril when respiratory infections are refractory. \- ⚠️ **Not to be used routinely** — reserve for confirmed treatment failures. Overuse contributes to resistance. \- This medicine **tastes extremely bitter** and can cause foaming at the mouth. Animals often resist it strongly. Mix with a small flavored carrier immediately before dosing; do not pre-mix batches. \- Can significantly disrupt gut flora; monitor for bloating and diarrhea; pair with probiotics separated from dose timing. \- Use in Pinkies is **strongly discouraged** due to potential growth and developmental effects. \- **Storage:** Raw 300 mg/mL stock vial — room temperature, do not refrigerate. Discard 30 days after first puncture. Diluted 30 mg/mL working solution — refrigerate and discard after 2 weeks.

Overuse contributes to resistance. - This medicine tastes extremely bitter and can cause foaming at the mouth. Animals often resist it strongly. Mix with a small flavored carrier immediately before dosing; do not pre-mix batches. - Can significantly disrupt gut flora; monitor for bloating and diarrhea; pair with probiotics separated from dose timing. - Use in Pinkies is strongly discouraged due to potential growth and developmental effects. - Storage: Raw 300 mg/mL stock vial — room temperature, do not refrigerate. Discard 30 days after first puncture. Diluted 30 mg/mL working solution — refrigerate and discard after 2 weeks.

heading: PANACUR (Fenbendazole)
text:
## **PANACUR (Fenbendazole)**

**Evidence: \[A\] DIRECT SQUIRREL / SCIURIDAE**

**Drug Class / Type:** Anti-parasitic / Anthelmintic (dewormer) **Indications:** Roundworms (nematodes); hookworms; whipworms; Giardia and other susceptible protozoa **Form:** Panacur 10% oral suspension (100 mg/mL) — preferred formulation for squirrels. Also available as granules (22.2%) and equine paste (10%), both of which require dilution before use at squirrel weights. **Route:** Oral (PO) **Frequency:** Once daily (q24h)

**Standard Dosing (roundworms, hookworms, whipworms): 20 mg/kg/day × 5 consecutive days**

*Using Panacur 10% suspension (100 mg/mL):*

| Animal Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.010 mL |
| 75 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.015 mL |
| 100 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.020 mL |
| 125 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.025 mL |
| 150 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.030 mL |
| 175 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.035 mL |
| 200 g (Explorer) | Explorer | 0.040 mL |
| 250 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.050 mL |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.060 mL |
| 350 g (Pre-Teen) | Pre-Teen | 0.070 mL |
| 400 g (Teenager) | Teenager | 0.080 mL |

**Giardia Dosing: 50 mg/kg/day × 5 consecutive days**

*Using Panacur 10% suspension (100 mg/mL):*

| Animal Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.025 mL |
| 75 g (Infant) | Infant | 0.037 mL |
| 100 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.050 mL |
| 125 g (Baby) | Baby | 0.062 mL |
| 150 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.075 mL |
| 175 g (Toddler) | Toddler | 0.087 mL |
| 200 g (Explorer) | Explorer | 0.100 mL |
| 250 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.125 mL |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | Juvenile | 0.150 mL |
| 350 g (Pre-Teen) | Pre-Teen | 0.175 mL |
| 400 g (Teenager) | Teenager | 0.200 mL |

**Don't under-dose.** Panacur has a very wide safety margin, so being a little over 20 mg/kg is not a concern. The bigger risk is under-treating, which breeds resistant parasites. Giardia takes the higher dose: 50 mg/kg/day × 5 days.

**Repeat Dosing:** A second 5-day course is often administered 2–3 weeks after the first to catch parasites that were in egg form and unaffected by the first treatment. Confirm repeat dosing schedule with your vet.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Interferes with parasite energy metabolism by binding to tubulin, preventing cellular uptake of glucose — kills the parasite by starvation; does not affect mammalian cells at therapeutic doses \- Generally considered to have a very high safety margin; one of the safest anthelmintics available for small mammals \- **Do not administer to animals under 5 weeks old** (Pinky stage) or to animals that are visibly sick or severely malnourished — wait until the animal is stable \- Potential side effects: mild loose stools or vomiting, particularly with heavy parasite loads (die-off reaction); this is expected and not a reason to discontinue unless severe

heading: PONAZURIL (Marquis)
text:
## **PONAZURIL (Marquis)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Anti-parasitic / Antiprotozoal **Indications:** First-line treatment for coccidiosis (preferred over Albon). Ponazuril is **coccidiocidal** — it kills coccidia at multiple life stages rather than just slowing reproduction. Treatment is rapid (2 doses, 48 hours apart) compared to Albon’s 10–21 day course. **Mechanism:** Targets the apicoplast organelle found in apicomplexan parasites (coccidia, Toxoplasma); disrupts mitochondrial electron transport, killing the parasite at multiple life stages. **Route:** Oral — compounded liquid (preferred) or thick equine paste (requires dilution before use; consult vet for dilution protocol). **Frequency:** Once every 48 hours — **two total doses**, given 48 hours apart. Repeat in 2–4 weeks if clinical signs recur or fecal float remains positive.

⚠️ **CONCENTRATION WARNING:** Ponazuril is compounded at different concentrations. The volumes below are concentration-specific. **Confirm the mg/mL of your specific bottle before dosing.** The underlying dose is **20 mg/kg** for each administration — if you know your concentration, you can calculate your own volume: (weight in kg × 20\) ÷ concentration (mg/mL) \= mL per dose.

**Dosing by concentration (20 mg/kg dose):**

| Concentration | Formula | Example volume for 200 g animal |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 30 mg/mL | 0.2 mL × (weight in kg ÷ 0.2 kg) | 0.2 mL per dose |
| 50 mg/mL | 0.1 mL × (weight in kg ÷ 0.2 kg) | 0.1 mL per dose |
| 100 mg/mL | 0.05 mL × (weight in kg ÷ 0.2 kg) | 0.05 mL per dose |

**Quick weight-based table — 50 mg/mL · 20 mg/kg** *(the most common rehabber formulation)*

| Weight | Stage | Volume per Dose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | Gray/Infant | 0.020 mL |
| 100 g | Baby | 0.040 mL |
| 150 g | Toddler | 0.060 mL |
| 200 g | Explorer | 0.080 mL |
| 250 g | Juvenile | 0.100 mL |
| 300 g | Juvenile | 0.120 mL |
| 350 g | Pre-Teen | 0.140 mL |
| 400 g | Teenager | 0.160 mL |

**Warnings / Notes:** \- ⚠️ **Confirm your mg/mL before every dose** — Ponazuril comes in multiple concentrations from different compounding pharmacies \- Ensure the animal is well-hydrated before treatment — give LRS or ensure adequate fluid intake \- Generally well-tolerated; safer for young or debilitated animals than Albon \- Acts much faster than Albon (2 doses over 48 hours vs. 10–21 days) — this speed is its primary advantage

heading: PERMETHRIN — DO NOT USE
text:
## **PERMETHRIN — DO NOT USE**

**We no longer use permethrin on squirrels.** Safer options do the same job:

- **Fleas:** Capstar (Nitenpyram) or Revolution (Selamectin)
- **Mites and mange:** Revolution, or the measured Ivermectin protocols

**Why it was pulled:**

- **Too risky for squirrels in care:** contraindicated under 16 weeks because young livers can't process it, which covers most of the squirrels we raise.
- **Fatal to cats** at even small exposures (see "Other Animals in Your Home," Ch. 1).
- **Toxic to fish:** rinsing treated bedding or bowls near an aquarium or pond can kill fish.

If a squirrel has been exposed (for example, from a dog's flea treatment) and shows drooling, tremors, or wobbling: bathe it with mild dish soap, rinse well, keep it warm, and call your vet.

heading: PREDNISONE (Prednisolone)
text:
## **PREDNISONE (Prednisolone)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Synthetic corticosteroid / Immune Suppressant / Inflammation Reduction **Indications:** Emergency cases of head trauma, spinal cord injuries, or severe allergic shock **Dosage:** **Requires veterinary prescription — do not dose without explicit vet guidance.** Published reference ranges for small mammals: anti-inflammatory dosing typically begins at **0.5–1 mg/kg/day**; shock/acute trauma protocols may use **1–2 mg/kg** as an initial dose. Your vet will determine the specific dose and taper schedule for your animal and situation. **Route:** Oral (oral syrup; Prednisolone is the active form and is absorbed without hepatic conversion — preferred over Prednisone in small mammals) **Frequency:** **Requires veterinary guidance — do not dose without a vet’s specific protocol.** Typical small mammal protocols begin with a higher anti-inflammatory or shock dose (often 1–2 mg/kg/day) for 2–3 days, then taper by halving the dose every 2–3 days down to zero. Abrupt discontinuation after more than 2–3 days of use can cause adrenal insufficiency. Your vet will prescribe the specific dose, frequency, and taper schedule. **Warnings / Notes:** \- Inhibits inflammatory pathways and suppresses the immune response to reduce tissue swelling \- Should not be given alongside NSAIDs (Meloxicam/Ibuprofen) \- Long-term use can suppress the immune system \- Typically requires tapering off slowly; abrupt discontinuation should be avoided

heading: REVOLUTION (Selamectin)
text:
## **REVOLUTION (Selamectin)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Anti-Parasitic **Indications:** Fleas, ear mites, sarcoptic mange. Described as potentially safer for neonates than some other antiparasiticides due to a wide safety margin in cats. **Mechanism:** Enters the bloodstream through the skin and redistributes into skin and sebaceous glands, where it acts on parasite nervous systems (GABA agonism in invertebrates). Provides \~30 days of residual protection.

⚠️ **DOSAGE: NOT AVAILABLE FROM COMMERCIAL TUBES AT SQUIRREL WEIGHTS**

The standard human-accessible formulation of Revolution — the kitten/puppy spot-on tube (15 mg) — **cannot be dosed accurately for squirrels.** Even a 400 g Teenager needs only 2.4 mg (16% of one tube) at the standard 6 mg/kg dose. A 50 g Infant would need 0.3 mg — 2% of a tube. These are fractions of a droplet, not measurable with any practical field method.

**The practical answer: use Ivermectin instead.** The diluted injectable ivermectin protocol (Protocol A in this formulary) handles the same indications — mange, ear mites — at squirrel weights with accurate, measurable volumes. It is the preferred first-line choice for the same parasites.

**If your vet specifically prescribes Revolution for your animals:** Ask for a custom-compounded preparation at a concentration appropriate for squirrel weights (typically 1–3 mg/mL, dispensed in a syringe for topical application at the back of the neck). Do not use a standard commercial tube without a vet’s explicit dosing instructions for that specific animal’s weight.

**Route:** Topical — applied to the skin at the back of the neck where the animal cannot lick it. **Frequency:** Single application, with residual protection lasting approximately 30 days. Repeat only on veterinary guidance.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- ⚠️ **Do NOT use simultaneously with Ivermectin** — additive toxicity risk from two macrocyclic lactone antiparasiticides \- Apply only where the animal cannot reach with its mouth; accidental oral ingestion increases toxicity risk \- Monitor for signs of toxicity for 24 hours post-application: tremors, ataxia, excessive salivation

## **SMZ-TMP (Sulfamethoxazole + Trimethoprim)**

**Evidence: \[VET\] VETERINARIAN-PRESCRIBED**

**Drug Class / Type:** Potentiated sulfonamide antibiotic (also known as TMS, Bactrim, Septra) **Indications:** Bacterial infections as your vet directs — commonly urinary, GI, respiratory, and skin/wound infections **Form:** Oral suspension, **240 mg/5 mL = 48 mg/mL** combined (200 mg sulfamethoxazole + 40 mg trimethoprim per 5 mL) (prescription) **Route:** Oral (PO) **Frequency:** Every 12 hours (BID) **Duration:** 10 days, or as your vet directs **Dose:** ≈ **27.4 mg/kg** combined, twice daily (0.3 mL for a ~525 g squirrel; prescribed independently by two veterinarians, October 2026)

**Weight-Based Dosing Reference** *(48 mg/mL · 27.4 mg/kg twice daily)*

| Weight | Dose (mg) | Volume |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | 1.37 mg | 0.029 mL |
| 75 g | 2.06 mg | 0.043 mL |
| 100 g | 2.74 mg | 0.057 mL |
| 150 g | 4.11 mg | 0.086 mL |
| 200 g | 5.49 mg | 0.114 mL |
| 250 g | 6.86 mg | 0.143 mL |
| 300 g | 8.23 mg | 0.171 mL |
| 350 g | 9.60 mg | 0.200 mL |
| 400 g | 10.97 mg | 0.229 mL |
| 450 g | 12.34 mg | 0.257 mL |
| 525 g | 14.40 mg | 0.300 mL |

heading: SSD CREAM / SILVADENE (Silver Sulfadiazine)
text:
## **SSD CREAM / SILVADENE (Silver Sulfadiazine)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Topical Antimicrobial / Burn Treatment **Indications:** Thermal burns from heating pads; electrical burns from chewing wires; severe abrasions or degloving injuries **Dosage:** No specific mg/kg dosage; topical application **Route:** Topical (1% white cream applied in a thick layer — “buttering” the wound) **Frequency:** Cleaned and reapplied every 12–24 hours **Treatment Duration:** Applied daily until a healthy bed of granulation tissue (new pink skin) forms **Warnings / Notes:** \- Releases silver ions that are lethal to a wide range of bacteria and fungi, while the sulfonamide component provides an additional layer of antibiotic protection \- Contraindicated in squirrels with sulfa allergies \- Must prevent hardening into a crust through regular cleaning and reapplication

heading: TERRAMYCIN (Oxytetracycline)
text:
## **TERRAMYCIN (Oxytetracycline)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Tetracycline antibiotic (ophthalmic) **Indications:** Eye infections (conjunctivitis); inflamed eyelids; “sticky eye” in weanling squirrels; effective against Mycoplasma and Chlamydia **Dosage:** Ophthalmic ointment — applied as a thin ribbon (\~1–2 mm) along the inner lower eyelid (the conjunctival sac). No mg/kg calculation needed; the dose is determined by the size of the ribbon applied to the eye, not by body weight. **Route:** Topical ophthalmic — gently pull the lower eyelid down and apply a small ribbon of ointment inside. The animal will blink to distribute it across the eye surface. **Frequency:** BID to QID (2–4 times daily) depending on severity of infection. For mild conjunctivitis, BID is usually sufficient. For significant discharge or swelling, TID or QID until the discharge resolves, then taper to BID to finish the course. **Warnings / Notes:** \- Interferes with the ability of bacteria to produce essential proteins, effectively stopping the infection at the site of the eye \- Very safe for topical use \- Ensure the tip of the tube never touches the squirrel’s eye to prevent contaminating the remaining medication

heading: TRAZODONE
text:
## **TRAZODONE**

**Drug Class / Type:** Anti-anxiety / Sedative — Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI) **Indications:** Enforced cage rest for high-stress animals; management of spinal injuries, fractures, or post-surgical cases requiring immobility; reduction of self-mutilation behaviors from capture stress or neurological trauma **Dosage:** **Requires veterinary prescription and test dose under vet supervision.** Published reference ranges for small exotic mammals: **5–10 mg/kg** once or twice daily, with significant individual variation in response — some animals require adjustment up or down. Always begin with the lower end of the range or a partial dose (test dose), with a vet present for the first administration. Your vet will determine the appropriate dose for your specific animal. **Route:** Oral (tablets — human generic; or compounded flavored oral liquids) **Frequency:** Usually administered 1 to 2 times daily depending on the level of sedation required **Warnings / Notes:** \- Individual squirrel’s metabolism affects efficacy significantly \- Test dose recommended with veterinarian present to monitor \- Risk of excessive sedation leading to aspiration pneumonia \- Caution with concurrent serotonergic medications \- Overdosage risks include severe lethargy, “floppy squirrel syndrome,” or serotonin syndrome; respiratory depression possible

heading: VITAMIN C (Ascorbic Acid)
text:
## **VITAMIN C (Ascorbic Acid)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Water-Soluble Vitamin / Antioxidant **Indications:** Supportive care for stressed, injured, or ill squirrels; immune support; wound healing; antioxidant support during antibiotic therapy or oxidative stress. Squirrels, unlike guinea pigs, can synthesize their own Vitamin C — but synthesis may be insufficient during severe stress, illness, trauma, or recovery from injury.

**Note:** Routine Vitamin C supplementation is NOT necessary for healthy squirrels eating a varied diet. Reserve supplementation for animals that are ill, injured, immunocompromised, or recovering from surgery or infection.

**Form:** \- **Ascorbic acid tablets or powder** — plain ascorbic acid; avoid chewable formulations with sweeteners \- **Pediatric liquid Vitamin C drops** — convenient for small volumes; check label for artificial additives \- **Fresh foods** — preferred source for animals eating solid food: broccoli, kale, red bell pepper, strawberries, kiwi, parsley

⚠️ **Do NOT add Vitamin C to drinking water** — ascorbic acid oxidizes rapidly in water and loses potency within hours. Mix into food or formula instead.

**Route:** Oral (PO) — mixed into formula, soft food, or almond butter for palatability

**Dosage:** *No squirrel-specific published dose is available. The following is extrapolated from guinea pig clinical data (closest small-rodent analog with published Vitamin C requirements):*

| Indication | Dose (elemental ascorbic acid) |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Maintenance / preventive** (ill or stressed animal) | 10–30 mg/kg/day PO |
| **Treatment** (active deficiency, wound healing, post-surgery) | 50 mg/kg/day PO |
| Pregnant / nursing females | 30 mg/kg/day minimum |

**Frequency:** Divide total daily dose into 2 doses (BID) — Vitamin C is eliminated quickly and divided dosing maintains more consistent blood levels than a single daily dose.

**Practical Dosing — Reference Weights:**

| Weight | Maintenance (20 mg/kg) | Treatment (50 mg/kg) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g (Infant) | 1.0 mg/day | 2.5 mg/day |
| 100 g (Baby) | 2.0 mg/day | 5.0 mg/day |
| 150 g (Toddler) | 3.0 mg/day | 7.5 mg/day |
| 200 g (Explorer) | 4.0 mg/day | 10.0 mg/day |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | 6.0 mg/day | 15.0 mg/day |
| 400 g (Adult) | 8.0 mg/day | 20.0 mg/day |

*These are very small doses — most standard Vitamin C supplements are 250–500 mg tablets. A 400g adult on treatment dosing needs only 20 mg/day. Use powder for precision: measure with a milligram-accurate scale, or dissolve one 100 mg tablet in 100 mL water → 1 mg/mL solution → dose by the mL.*

**Monitoring:** Water-soluble; excess is excreted in urine. Toxicity at these doses is not a concern. Discontinue supplementation when the animal resumes eating a varied, fresh diet that includes Vitamin C-rich vegetables.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- Vitamin C is water-soluble and has a wide safety margin — excess is excreted, not stored. This contrasts with fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), which can accumulate to toxic levels. \- Squirrels synthesize their own ascorbic acid in the liver — supplementation during health is unnecessary and redundant \- Avoid multivitamin products; they often contain fat-soluble vitamins (especially A and D) that can reach toxic levels if over-supplemented \- Fresh vegetables are always preferable to supplements when the animal is eating solid food \- Ascorbic acid is sensitive to heat, light, and air — store supplements in a cool, dark, sealed container

heading: VITAMIN D₃ (Cholecalciferol)
text:
## **VITAMIN D₃ (Cholecalciferol)**

**Drug Class / Type:** Fat-Soluble Vitamin / Calcium Metabolism Regulator **Indications:** Prevention and treatment of Vitamin D₃ deficiency, which impairs calcium absorption and causes or perpetuates MBD (Metabolic Bone Disease); essential companion to calcium supplementation in MBD recovery. **Without adequate Vitamin D₃, supplemental calcium cannot be properly absorbed** — an animal receiving calcium for MBD who is also D₃-deficient will not fully respond to calcium treatment alone.

**Preferred source:** Natural, **unfiltered** sunlight — 20–30 minutes of direct sun exposure daily, without glass or plastic between the animal and the sun (these filter UVB). This is always superior to supplementation.

**Alternative if sunlight is unavailable:** A reptile-grade **UVB bulb** (5.0 or 10.0 UVB fluorescent/T5 HO tube), positioned 12–18 inches from the animal, 10–12 hours per day, with a shaded area available. Replace bulbs every 6 months — UVB output declines before the visible light dies.

**Form:** \- **Vitamin D₃ drops or liquid** (cholecalciferol) — most practical for precise small-animal dosing \- **Combined calcium \+ D₃ products** — convenient but use with caution: watch for over-supplementation of calcium if separate calcium supplementation is also being given

⚠️ **Never use Vitamin D₂ (ergocalciferol)** — this plant-derived form is less effective in mammals and may not correct deficiency adequately. Confirm product is **D₃ (cholecalciferol).**

**Route:** Oral (PO) — mixed into formula or food. A fat-containing vehicle (formula, yogurt, almond butter) improves absorption of this fat-soluble vitamin.

**Dosage:** *Squirrel-specific published data is limited. The following dose is the established reference for all rodent species:*

| Indication | Dose |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Supplementation in rodents** | **200–400 IU/kg/day** PO |

*Source: squirrelrehabilitation.com (veterinary-level reference for rodent species)*

**Practical Dosing — Reference Weights:**

| Weight | Low end (200 IU/kg) | High end (400 IU/kg) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g (Infant) | 10 IU/day | 20 IU/day |
| 100 g (Baby) | 20 IU/day | 40 IU/day |
| 200 g (Explorer) | 40 IU/day | 80 IU/day |
| 300 g (Juvenile) | 60 IU/day | 120 IU/day |
| 400 g (Adult) | 80 IU/day | 160 IU/day |

*Standard human Vitamin D₃ drops are typically 400 IU/drop or 1,000 IU/drop — these concentrations are far too high for direct use in small squirrels. Dilute appropriately: 1 drop of 400 IU/drop product diluted into 4 mL of formula or oil gives approximately 100 IU/mL; then dose by the mL.*

**Duration:** Supplement only until adequate diet and/or sunlight exposure is established. Reassess at 4–6 weeks.

⚠️ **FAT-SOLUBLE — TOXICITY RISK:** Unlike Vitamin C, Vitamin D₃ accumulates in body fat and the liver. **Overdose causes hypercalcemia** (too much calcium in the blood), leading to soft tissue calcification, kidney damage, and cardiac arrhythmias — the same complications as calcium over-supplementation. **Do not supplement above 400 IU/kg/day without veterinary guidance.**

**Signs of Vitamin D₃ toxicity:** \- Loss of appetite \- Vomiting, lethargy \- Increased thirst and urination (polyuria/polydipsia) \- White deposits in soft tissues (visible on necropsy) \- Progresses to kidney failure

**Monitoring:** When supplementing both calcium and Vitamin D₃, watch for signs of hypercalcemia (white feces, milky urine, loss of appetite). If these appear, reduce or discontinue both.

**Warnings / Notes:** \- ⚠️ **Do not give both supplemental D₃ AND unrestricted sunlight access** simultaneously — combined sources can cause toxicity \- Vitamin D₃ interacts synergistically with calcium — monitor both when supplementing either \- Most commercial wildlife rehabilitation diets (Mazuri Rodent, Oxbow Essentials) contain adequate D₃ — supplementation is only needed in animals not yet eating formulated food \- Natural sunlight exposure is always the safest and most physiologically appropriate source of Vitamin D₃ for squirrels \- See also: CALCIUM entry — Vitamin D₃ is required for calcium absorption; MBD recovery requires adequate levels of both

heading: ZINC TOXICITY
text:
## **ZINC TOXICITY**

⚠️ **THIS IS NOT A DRUG ENTRY. THIS IS A HAZARD WARNING.** Zinc is not a medication used in squirrel rehabilitation — it is an environmental poison that kills. This entry exists because zinc exposure from common rehabilitation equipment is preventable, and because there is **no reliable treatment** once toxicity develops. Read this before you buy anything your squirrel will eat from, drink from, or live inside.

---

### **What Is Zinc Toxicity?**

Zinc is a heavy metal. In trace amounts it is an essential nutrient. In excess — particularly from chronic low-level contact with galvanized metal surfaces — it accumulates in the body and causes progressive, irreversible organ damage. Squirrels and ferrets are among the most susceptible small mammals to zinc toxicity, and symptoms can develop from nothing more than eating and drinking from the wrong bowl.

Galvanized metal is steel coated with zinc to prevent rust. It is widely sold in feed stores and farm supply retailers as a durable, “natural” material for small animal equipment. It looks appropriate for a wildlife setting. It is not safe.

---

### **Sources of Zinc Exposure in Rehab Settings**

**The most common and most dangerous:** \- **Galvanized metal food and water bowls** — the animal’s tongue and saliva make direct contact with the zinc coating at every meal and every drink; acidic foods and liquids accelerate zinc leaching \- **Galvanized wire hardware cloth** — used in enclosure construction; squirrels chew on wire constantly and ingest zinc with every gnaw; **newer galvanized wire with white rust or loose solder is especially hazardous** — the surface oxidation increases zinc availability \- **Galvanized hardware** — zinc-plated screws, washers, bolts, nuts, staples, quick-links, and zippers anywhere the animal can access or chew

**Topical products:** \- **Zinc oxide cream** (Desitin, most diaper rash creams, many barrier ointments) — applied to skin wounds and then groomed off by the animal or nestmates; **never apply zinc oxide to a squirrel of any age** \- **Calamine lotion** — contains zinc oxide; same hazard

**Other sources:** \- **Post-1982 US pennies** — 97.5% zinc; if a squirrel chews or ingests a penny, this is an acute toxicity emergency \- **Zinc-containing supplements overdosed** — zinc is present in some wildlife rehab diet supplements; follow dosing guidelines exactly

---

### **How Zinc Damages the Body**

**Critical fact: squirrels cannot vomit.** Unlike dogs or cats, rodents lack the physiological mechanism to expel stomach contents. When a squirrel chews and ingests a zinc-containing object — a piece of galvanized wire, a penny, a zinc-plated washer — that object stays in the acidic stomach environment and continuously leaches free zinc ions into the bloodstream. The longer it sits, the more zinc is released. There is no natural mechanism to stop it.

Zinc ions in the bloodstream attack red blood cells directly — disrupting cell membranes and causing **intravascular hemolysis** (the red blood cells rupture inside the blood vessels). The debris from ruptured cells turns the urine red or orange (**hemoglobinuria**) — one of the most distinctive and alarming signs of zinc toxicity. Simultaneously, zinc accumulates in the liver and kidneys, causing direct organ toxicity. Bone marrow suppression compounds the anemia by reducing the body’s ability to produce replacement red blood cells.

**For chronic low-level exposure** (galvanized bowl, galvanized wire enclosure): damage is cumulative. The squirrel absorbs small amounts of zinc daily. By the time symptoms are visible, significant internal damage has already occurred over weeks or months.

**For acute ingestion** (penny, hardware, large zinc object): progression can be rapid — hours, not days. The inability to vomit means the source stays active in the stomach until a veterinarian removes it.

---

### **Symptoms — What Zinc Toxicity Looks Like**

**Early signs** (often missed or attributed to other causes): \- Lethargy, reduced activity \- Anorexia (loss of appetite) \- Pale or white mucous membranes (gums, inner eyelids) — this is anemia \- Weakness, reluctance to move

**Progressive signs:** \- Pronounced hind limb weakness — squirrel drags or cannot use back legs normally \- Rapid or labored breathing (anemia means less oxygen delivery to tissues) \- Pale or yellow gums and mucous membranes (jaundice/icterus) \- **Red or orange urine** (hemoglobinuria) — ruptured red blood cells releasing hemoglobin into the urine; one of the most distinctive signs of zinc toxicity

⚠️ **Before you panic — stop and think about what they’ve been eating.** Squirrels eating an abundance of acorns can also produce red or orange urine from the high tannin content — this is dietary pigmentation and is not an emergency. The difference is the whole clinical picture:

|  | Tannin urine (dietary) | Hemoglobinuria (zinc toxicity) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Appetite | Normal — eating well | Reduced or absent |
| Activity | Normal — alert, moving | Lethargic, weak |
| Gum color | Pink and moist | Pale, white, or yellow |
| Other symptoms | None | Hind limb weakness, labored breathing |
| Acorn/tannin exposure | Yes | Not necessarily |
| Zinc exposure | Not necessarily | Galvanized bowl, wire, hardware |

If the squirrel is eating, active, and otherwise behaving normally — check the diet first. If the squirrel is lethargic, not eating, and has pale or yellow gums — this is an emergency regardless of what they’ve been eating.

**Advanced toxicity:** \- Gastric hemorrhage (bloody or tarry stool) — zinc is directly corrosive to stomach lining \- Bone marrow depression → severe, non-regenerative anemia \- Nephrosis (kidney damage) → increased thirst and urination, then shutdown \- Liver failure \- Uraemia (waste product buildup from kidney failure) \- Seizures \- Coma \- Death

---

### **Treatment — This Is a Veterinary Emergency**

⚠️ **Zinc toxicity requires immediate veterinary intervention. Prognosis worsens with every hour of delay. Do not wait to see if the animal improves — call your vet the moment you suspect exposure.**

Treatment exists and can be effective — particularly for acute ingestion of a zinc object — but it requires a veterinarian. This is not a home treatment situation.

**Step 1 — Remove the source and get to a vet:** \- Identify and eliminate all zinc contact immediately (bowl, wire, hardware) \- Transport to your supervising veterinarian or an emergency exotic vet now \- Tell them you suspect zinc toxicity and describe the likely source

**What your vet will do:**

**Radiographs (X-rays) — first step for acute ingestion:** Zinc-containing objects (pennies, hardware, wire fragments) are radiopaque — visible on X-ray. Your vet needs to know if there is a physical object in the stomach that must be removed. This is the most urgent diagnostic step for suspected acute ingestion.

**Source removal:** Because squirrels cannot vomit, the object cannot be expelled naturally. If found on X-ray, it must be removed via **endoscopy** (a scope inserted into the stomach) or **emergency gastrotomy** (surgical opening of the stomach) once the animal is stable enough for anesthesia. Every minute the object remains in the stomach, more zinc is leaching.

**Aggressive fluid therapy:** Balanced crystalloid IV fluids at twice maintenance rates — to protect the kidneys from zinc damage and flush systemic toxins. This begins immediately.

**Gastroprotectants:** Zinc is directly corrosive to stomach lining. Your vet will use: \- **Omeprazole** (proton pump inhibitor) to reduce stomach acid and protect the mucosa — see Omeprazole entry for dose \- **Famotidine** (H2 blocker) at **0.5–1.0 mg/kg** as an alternative; reduces acid production and provides gastroprotection

**Blood transfusion:** If hemolytic anemia is severe (packed cell volume critically low), a whole-blood transfusion from a compatible donor animal may be necessary to keep the patient alive while treatment proceeds.

**Chelation therapy:** After the physical zinc source has been removed, **Calcium EDTA** is the standard veterinary chelating agent — it binds residual zinc ions in the bloodstream and allows excretion through the kidneys. Chelation is used after source removal, not as a substitute for it.

**Prognosis:** \- **Acute ingestion caught early, source removed:** Guarded to fair with aggressive treatment \- **Chronic exposure (galvanized bowl/wire), symptomatic on presentation:** Poor — organ damage is cumulative and may be irreversible \- **Any case showing hemoglobinuria, jaundice, or hind limb collapse:** Grave — these indicate significant hemolysis and organ involvement already underway

**The only truly effective intervention is prevention.** Once a squirrel is symptomatic, you are racing organ failure. Stop it before it starts.

---

### **Prevention — What to Use Instead**

**For food and water bowls:** \- ✅ **Stainless steel** — the gold standard; durable, non-reactive, easy to sanitize \- ✅ **Glass** — safe; heavy and breakable but chemically inert \- ✅ **Food-safe ceramic** (unglazed interior, or glazed with food-safe glaze) — confirm glaze does not contain lead or zinc \- ✅ **Hard BPA-free plastic** — acceptable for temporary use; check for cracks where bacteria can harbor \- ❌ **Galvanized metal** — never, under any circumstances \- ❌ **Unknown metal bowls from feed stores** — if you cannot confirm it is stainless steel, do not use it

**For enclosure construction:** \- ✅ **Powder-coated wire** — zinc-free when coating is intact; inspect regularly for chips or rust \- ✅ **Stainless steel hardware cloth** — expensive but the safest option \- ✅ **PVC-coated wire** — safe if coating is fully intact \- ❌ **Galvanized hardware cloth** — the most common enclosure material sold at hardware stores; do not use for animals that will chew on it (squirrels always chew on it) \- ❌ **Galvanized nails, bolts, washers, or staples** inside the animal’s reach

## ZINC TOXICITY

⚠️ THIS IS NOT A DRUG ENTRY. THIS IS A HAZARD WARNING. Zinc is not a medication used in squirrel rehabilitation — it is an environmental poison that kills. This entry exists because zinc exposure from common rehabilitation equipment is preventable, and because there is no reliable treatment once toxicity develops. Read this before you buy anything your squirrel will eat from, drink from, or live inside.

---

### What Is Zinc Toxicity?

Zinc is a heavy metal. In trace amounts it is an essential nutrient. In excess — particularly from chronic low-level contact with galvanized metal surfaces — it accumulates in the body and causes progressive, irreversible organ damage. Squirrels and ferrets are among the most susceptible small mammals to zinc toxicity, and symptoms can develop from nothing more than eating and drinking from the wrong bowl.

Galvanized metal is steel coated with zinc to prevent rust. It is widely sold in feed stores and farm supply retailers as a durable, “natural” material for small animal equipment. It looks appropriate for a wildlife setting. It is not safe.

---

### Sources of Zinc Exposure in Rehab Settings

The most common and most dangerous: - Galvanized metal food and water bowls — the animal’s tongue and saliva make direct contact with the zinc coating at every meal and every drink; acidic foods and liquids accelerate zinc leaching - Galvanized wire hardware cloth — used in enclosure construction; squirrels chew on wire constantly and ingest zinc with every gnaw; newer galvanized wire with white rust or loose solder is especially hazardous — the surface oxidation increases zinc availability - Galvanized hardware — zinc-plated screws, washers, bolts, nuts, staples, quick-links, and zippers anywhere the animal can access or chew

Topical products: - Zinc oxide cream (Desitin, most diaper rash creams, many barrier ointments) — applied to skin wounds and then groomed off by the animal or nestmates; never apply zinc oxide to a squirrel of any age - Calamine lotion — contains zinc oxide; same hazard

Other sources: - Post-1982 US pennies — 97.5% zinc; if a squirrel chews or ingests a penny, this is an acute toxicity emergency - Zinc-containing supplements overdosed — zinc is present in some wildlife rehab diet supplements; follow dosing guidelines exactly

---

### How Zinc Damages the Body

Critical fact: squirrels cannot vomit. Unlike dogs or cats, rodents lack the physiological mechanism to expel stomach contents. When a squirrel chews and ingests a zinc-containing object — a piece of galvanized wire, a penny, a zinc-plated washer — that object stays in the acidic stomach environment and continuously leaches free zinc ions into the bloodstream. The longer it sits, the more zinc is released. There is no natural mechanism to stop it.

Zinc ions in the bloodstream attack red blood cells directly — disrupting cell membranes and causing intravascular hemolysis (the red blood cells rupture inside the blood vessels). The debris from ruptured cells turns the urine red or orange (hemoglobinuria) — one of the most distinctive and alarming signs of zinc toxicity. Simultaneously, zinc accumulates in the liver and kidneys, causing direct organ toxicity. Bone marrow suppression compounds the anemia by reducing the body’s ability to produce replacement red blood cells.

For chronic low-level exposure (galvanized bowl, galvanized wire enclosure): damage is cumulative. The squirrel absorbs small amounts of zinc daily. By the time symptoms are visible, significant internal damage has already occurred over weeks or months.

For acute ingestion (penny, hardware, large zinc object): progression can be rapid — hours, not days. The inability to vomit means the source stays active in the stomach until a veterinarian removes it.

---

### Symptoms — What Zinc Toxicity Looks Like

Early signs (often missed or attributed to other causes): - Lethargy, reduced activity - Anorexia (loss of appetite) - Pale or white mucous membranes (gums, inner eyelids) — this is anemia - Weakness, reluctance to move

Progressive signs: - Pronounced hind limb weakness — squirrel drags or cannot use back legs normally - Rapid or labored breathing (anemia means less oxygen delivery to tissues) - Pale or yellow gums and mucous membranes (jaundice/icterus) - Red or orange urine (hemoglobinuria) — ruptured red blood cells releasing hemoglobin into the urine; one of the most distinctive signs of zinc toxicity

⚠️ Before you panic — stop and think about what they’ve been eating. Squirrels eating an abundance of acorns can also produce red or orange urine from the high tannin content — this is dietary pigmentation and is not an emergency. The difference is the whole clinical picture:

|  | Tannin urine (dietary) | Hemoglobinuria (zinc toxicity) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Appetite | Normal — eating well | Reduced or absent |
| Activity | Normal — alert, moving | Lethargic, weak |
| Gum color | Pink and moist | Pale, white, or yellow |
| Other symptoms | None | Hind limb weakness, labored breathing |
| Acorn/tannin exposure | Yes | Not necessarily |
| Zinc exposure | Not necessarily | Galvanized bowl, wire, hardware |

If the squirrel is eating, active, and otherwise behaving normally — check the diet first. If the squirrel is lethargic, not eating, and has pale or yellow gums — this is an emergency regardless of what they’ve been eating.

Advanced toxicity: - Gastric hemorrhage (bloody or tarry stool) — zinc is directly corrosive to stomach lining - Bone marrow depression → severe, non-regenerative anemia - Nephrosis (kidney damage) → increased thirst and urination, then shutdown - Liver failure - Uraemia (waste product buildup from kidney failure) - Seizures - Coma - Death

---

### Treatment — This Is a Veterinary Emergency

⚠️ Zinc toxicity requires immediate veterinary intervention. Prognosis worsens with every hour of delay. Do not wait to see if the animal improves — call your vet the moment you suspect exposure.

Treatment exists and can be effective — particularly for acute ingestion of a zinc object — but it requires a veterinarian. This is not a home treatment situation.

Step 1 — Remove the source and get to a vet: - Identify and eliminate all zinc contact immediately (bowl, wire, hardware) - Transport to your supervising veterinarian or an emergency exotic vet now - Tell them you suspect zinc toxicity and describe the likely source

What your vet will do:

Radiographs (X-rays) — first step for acute ingestion: Zinc-containing objects (pennies, hardware, wire fragments) are radiopaque — visible on X-ray. Your vet needs to know if there is a physical object in the stomach that must be removed. This is the most urgent diagnostic step for suspected acute ingestion.

Source removal: Because squirrels cannot vomit, the object cannot be expelled naturally. If found on X-ray, it must be removed via endoscopy (a scope inserted into the stomach) or emergency gastrotomy (surgical opening of the stomach) once the animal is stable enough for anesthesia. Every minute the object remains in the stomach, more zinc is leaching.

Aggressive fluid therapy: Balanced crystalloid IV fluids at twice maintenance rates — to protect the kidneys from zinc damage and flush systemic toxins. This begins immediately.

Gastroprotectants: Zinc is directly corrosive to stomach lining. Your vet will use: - Omeprazole (proton pump inhibitor) to reduce stomach acid and protect the mucosa — see Omeprazole entry for dose - Famotidine (H2 blocker) at 0.5–1.0 mg/kg as an alternative; reduces acid production and provides gastroprotection

Blood transfusion: If hemolytic anemia is severe (packed cell volume critically low), a whole-blood transfusion from a compatible donor animal may be necessary to keep the patient alive while treatment proceeds.

Chelation therapy: After the physical zinc source has been removed, Calcium EDTA is the standard veterinary chelating agent — it binds residual zinc ions in the bloodstream and allows excretion through the kidneys. Chelation is used after source removal, not as a substitute for it.

Prognosis: - Acute ingestion caught early, source removed: Guarded to fair with aggressive treatment - Chronic exposure (galvanized bowl/wire), symptomatic on presentation: Poor — organ damage is cumulative and may be irreversible - Any case showing hemoglobinuria, jaundice, or hind limb collapse: Grave — these indicate significant hemolysis and organ involvement already underway

The only truly effective intervention is prevention. Once a squirrel is symptomatic, you are racing organ failure. Stop it before it starts.

---

heading: XYLITOL
text:
## **XYLITOL**

⚠️ **THIS IS NOT A DRUG ENTRY. THIS IS A POISON WARNING.** Xylitol is a sugar alcohol sweetener that is acutely toxic to small mammals. It is found in hundreds of everyday products — many of which look completely appropriate to use in a rehab setting. **Before giving any oral liquid, syrup, chewable tablet, or flavored medication to a squirrel, read the inactive ingredients label and confirm xylitol is absent.**

---

### **What Is Xylitol?**

Xylitol is a sugar substitute derived from plant fibers. It tastes like sugar, has fewer calories than sugar, and is marketed as “natural” and “tooth-friendly.” It is safe for humans. It is not safe for squirrels, dogs, ferrets, or most small mammals.

It does not take much. In small mammals, xylitol triggers a rapid, massive release of insulin — causing life-threatening hypoglycemia (dangerously low blood sugar) within 30 minutes to an hour of ingestion. At higher doses it also causes acute liver failure. The two effects can happen simultaneously.

---

### **Where Xylitol Hides — Read This Carefully**

Xylitol is not only in sugar-free gum. It is in a wide range of products that a rehabber might reach for without thinking twice:

**Medications and supplements (the most dangerous category for rehab):** \- **Liquid medications and oral syrups** — including some children’s cough syrups, liquid vitamins, and flavored medications. Pharmacies sometimes add xylitol as a sweetener to compounded medications and flavored suspensions. \- **Chewable tablets and gummies** — vitamins, supplements, and some OTC medications in gummy or chewable form \- **Oral suspensions** — liquid gabapentin, some liquid antibiotics, some liquid pain relievers \- **Nasal sprays** — some brands include xylitol as a humectant \- **Flavored oral syringes** — some are pre-sweetened

**Food products used in rehab (flavoring agents, supplements):** \- **Peanut butter** — several brands now use xylitol as a sweetener; Jif and Skippy regular formulas do not, but always check store brands and “natural” varieties \- **Yogurt** — some flavored yogurts contain xylitol; plain unsweetened yogurt does not \- **Flavoring syrups** — some coffee syrups and flavoring agents used to improve palatability of medications

**Other products that may enter a rehab space:** \- Mouthwash and toothpaste (don’t use these on squirrels regardless) \- Sugar-free baked goods or treats \- Some protein powders and meal replacements

---

### **Other Names for Xylitol on Labels**

Manufacturers are not always straightforward. Xylitol may also appear as: \- **Birch sugar** (xylitol made from birch wood) \- **Birch bark extract** \- **Wood sugar** \- **E967** (the EU food additive code for xylitol)

If you see any of these on a label for something you are giving a squirrel — stop. Find an alternative product without them.

---

### **What Xylitol Does to the Body**

In humans, xylitol does not trigger insulin release — the body processes it slowly without a glycemic spike. In dogs, squirrels, and most small mammals, the pancreas mistakes xylitol for sugar and releases a massive surge of insulin in response — far more than the small amount of xylitol warrants. Blood glucose crashes within 30–60 minutes.

**Phase 1 — Hypoglycemia (30–60 minutes after ingestion):** \- Sudden weakness or collapse \- Tremors, seizures \- Loss of coordination (stumbling, falling) \- Disorientation, unresponsiveness \- Pale or white gums

**Phase 2 — Liver failure (12–24 hours, at higher doses):** \- Jaundice (yellow gums, skin, eyes) \- Vomiting \- Bloody stool \- Severe lethargy \- Clotting failure (bleeding that won’t stop) \- Death

The hypoglycemia phase can kill before liver failure even develops. Both phases are potentially fatal.

---

### **Treatment**

⚠️ **Xylitol ingestion is a veterinary emergency. Call your vet or animal poison control immediately — do not wait for symptoms.**

* There is no antidote

* If ingestion was very recent (within 30 minutes), a vet may attempt to induce vomiting — but squirrels cannot vomit, so this is not an option

* Treatment is supportive: IV dextrose to correct hypoglycemia, liver protectants, monitoring

* **Early intervention dramatically improves survival.** By the time symptoms appear, blood sugar has already crashed.

**Animal Poison Control:** \- ASPCA Animal Poison Control: **(888) 426-4435** (consultation fee applies) \- Pet Poison Helpline: **(855) 764-7661** (consultation fee applies) \- Call your supervising veterinarian first if reachable

---

### **The Rule**

**Before giving any oral liquid, syrup, flavored suspension, chewable tablet, or gummy supplement to a squirrel — read the full inactive ingredients list. If you see xylitol, birch sugar, birch bark extract, wood sugar, or E967 — do not use it.**

When you prepare a home suspension (like the Gabapentin or Fish Mox recipes in this formulary), use plain water and a safe flavoring. Strawberry syrup, Ensure, or plain formula are safe choices. Do not use sugar-free products of any kind as flavoring agents.

When your compounding pharmacy prepares a flavored medication — ask them explicitly to confirm no xylitol is used in the flavoring. Most will accommodate this without issue if you ask.

*See also: GABAPENTIN entry — xylitol warning in commercial oral solutions; FISH MOX entry — home suspension avoids xylitol risk by using pure capsule powder.*

heading: FRONTLINE (Fipronil)
text:
## **FRONTLINE (Fipronil)**

⚠️ **DO NOT USE ON SQUIRRELS. DO NOT USE ON ANY SMALL RODENT.** Frontline (fipronil) is a widely available, effective flea and tick treatment for dogs and cats. It is acutely toxic to squirrels and small rodents. This entry exists solely as a warning. If your squirrel has fleas or ticks, see CAPSTAR, IVERMECTIN, and REVOLUTION entries for safe alternatives.

---

### **Why People Reach for It**

Frontline is at every pet store. It works. It’s what people know. When a squirrel comes in covered in fleas, a well-meaning rehabber who has used Frontline on their cats and dogs for years may reach for it without hesitation — because it has never hurt any animal they’ve used it on before.

The problem is that fipronil’s safety profile in cats and dogs does not extend to rodents. The pharmacology is different. The body weight is dramatically lower. And the margin between “effective dose” and “toxic dose” in a small rodent is essentially nonexistent.

---

### **What Fipronil Does**

Fipronil is a phenylpyrazole insecticide that works by blocking GABA-gated chloride channels in insects — disrupting their nervous system. In mammals, the same channels exist, but fipronil is selective enough that dogs and cats tolerate it at label doses.

In small rodents — rats, mice, squirrels — fipronil causes **central nervous system toxicity** at doses that are safe for larger animals. The blood-brain barrier in small rodents appears less effective at excluding fipronil, and the dose per unit body weight from even a small topical application can push a squirrel into the toxic range.

**Signs of fipronil toxicity in small rodents:** \- Tremors and seizures \- Hypersalivation \- Muscle weakness and incoordination \- Respiratory distress \- Death

---

### **Safe Alternatives for Flea and Parasite Treatment**

| Indication | Safe Alternative |
| :---- | :---- |
| Fleas (any age over 4 weeks) | **Capstar (Nitenpyram)** — oral, fast-acting, safe for squirrels |
| Fleas \+ mange \+ ear mites | **Ivermectin** — see Ivermectin entry for protocols |
| Fleas \+ broader coverage | **Revolution (Selamectin)** — requires precise dosing from vet; see Revolution entry for limitations |
| Ectoparasites in animals over 16 weeks | **Revolution (Selamectin)** — vet prescription; or **Capstar** for fleas |

⚠️ **Never use Frontline, Advantage (imidacloprid), or any other dog/cat flea product on a squirrel without explicit veterinary confirmation that the specific product and dose are safe for small rodents.** The fact that a product is safe for cats does not mean it is safe for squirrels.

heading: LOPERAMIDE (Imodium)
text:
## **LOPERAMIDE (Imodium)**

⚠️ **USE WITH EXTREME CAUTION — DANGEROUS IN SQUIRRELS WITHOUT VETERINARY GUIDANCE.** Loperamide (Imodium) is a common OTC antidiarrheal that works by slowing gut motility. This same mechanism that stops diarrhea in humans can cause **life-threatening GI stasis** in small mammals. Do not give Loperamide to a squirrel without direct veterinary instruction.

---

### **The Problem**

Loperamide works by binding opioid receptors in the gut wall, dramatically reducing intestinal contractions and slowing the movement of contents through the GI tract. In humans, this is helpful for diarrhea. In squirrels, whose GI systems are already sensitive and who are prone to life-threatening stasis (complete gut shutdown), artificially slowing gut motility can:

* Convert a manageable case of diarrhea into complete GI stasis

* Cause painful gas accumulation and bloat

* Lead to intestinal rupture in severe cases

* Mask the underlying cause of the diarrhea, which may require antibiotic treatment

**Diarrhea in a squirrel is almost always a symptom of something that needs to be addressed — not suppressed.** Stopping the symptom while the cause continues is not treatment.

---

### **When Diarrhea Occurs — What to Do Instead**

* **Identify the cause:** Dietary (wrong formula, overfeeding, formula change), bacterial (Metronidazole may be indicated), parasitic (treat the parasite)

* **Support the GI system:** Probiotics (Lactobacillus/Bene-Bac), dietary adjustment, hydration

* **Consult your vet:** If diarrhea is bloody, persistent, or accompanied by lethargy — this is not an OTC situation

Loperamide is not a safe substitute for diagnosis and appropriate treatment. If a veterinarian specifically prescribes it for a squirrel at a carefully calculated dose, follow their instructions. Do not reach for the human Imodium in your medicine cabinet.

*See also: METRONIDAZOLE entry for bacterial diarrhea treatment; MYLICON/SIMETHICONE entry for gas and bloat management.*

In squirrels, whose GI systems are already sensitive and who are prone to life-threatening stasis (complete gut shutdown), artificially slowing gut motility can:

* Convert a manageable case of diarrhea into complete GI stasis

* Cause painful gas accumulation and bloat

* Lead to intestinal rupture in severe cases

* Mask the underlying cause of the diarrhea, which may require antibiotic treatment

Diarrhea in a squirrel is almost always a symptom of something that needs to be addressed — not suppressed. Stopping the symptom while the cause continues is not treatment.

---

### When Diarrhea Occurs — What to Do Instead

* Identify the cause: Dietary (wrong formula, overfeeding, formula change), bacterial (Metronidazole may be indicated), parasitic (treat the parasite)

* Support the GI system: Probiotics (Lactobacillus/Bene-Bac), dietary adjustment, hydration

* Consult your vet: If diarrhea is bloody, persistent, or accompanied by lethargy — this is not an OTC situation

Loperamide is not a safe substitute for diagnosis and appropriate treatment. If a veterinarian specifically prescribes it for a squirrel at a carefully calculated dose, follow their instructions. Do not reach for the human Imodium in your medicine cabinet.

*See also: METRONIDAZOLE entry for bacterial diarrhea treatment; MYLICON/SIMETHICONE entry for gas and bloat management.*

heading: TRAMADOL
text:
## **TRAMADOL**

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond (Caslick), p. 222*

**What it is:** An opioid-class analgesic (pain reliever) used in wildlife rehab for moderate to severe pain — post-surgical, traumatic injury, fracture pain. Works differently from NSAIDs like Metacam: instead of reducing inflammation at the injury site, Tramadol acts centrally, changing how the brain processes pain signals. That’s why they work well together.

**Form:** 50 mg tablets (human prescription medication)

**Dilution:** Crush 1 tablet (50 mg) and dissolve in 10 mL sterile water → **5 mg/mL**

Store refrigerated in a labeled syringe. Discard after 14 days. If solution becomes cloudy or discolored, discard immediately.

---

### **Dose**

**2 mg/kg BID to TID (every 8–12 hours), by mouth**

**Formula: weight in grams × 0.0004 \= dose in mL**

*(This delivers exactly 2 mg/kg at every weight when prepared at 5 mg/mL)*

| Animal Weight | Dose Volume (5 mg/mL) | mg Delivered | Dose Check |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | 0.02 mL | 0.1 mg | 2.0 mg/kg ✓ |
| 75 g | 0.03 mL | 0.15 mg | 2.0 mg/kg ✓ |
| 100 g | 0.04 mL | 0.2 mg | 2.0 mg/kg ✓ |
| 125 g | 0.05 mL | 0.25 mg | 2.0 mg/kg ✓ |
| 250 g | 0.10 mL | 0.5 mg | 2.0 mg/kg ✓ |
| 500 g | 0.20 mL | 1.0 mg | 2.0 mg/kg ✓ |
| 750 g | 0.30 mL | 1.5 mg | 2.0 mg/kg ✓ |
| 1000 g | 0.40 mL | 2.0 mg | 2.0 mg/kg ✓ |

---

### **Important Notes**

**Works well with Metacam.** Tramadol and Meloxicam (Metacam) are synergistic — together they provide better pain control than either drug alone, because they target different parts of the pain pathway. If your vet has prescribed both, this is intentional and correct.

**Watch for over-sedation.** Signs include extreme lethargy, loss of balance, or unresponsiveness. If you see this, reduce the dose or increase the interval. Contact your vet.

**Bizarre behavior is a signal.** Some animals react with dysphoria (distress, agitation, unusual vocalizations) rather than sedation. This is also a signal to reduce the dose or stop. Not every animal responds the same way to opioids.

**Frequency matters.** Tramadol has a short half-life in small mammals — dosing every 8 hours (TID) maintains better steady-state pain control than every 12 hours (BID). For animals in significant pain, TID is preferred. For mild-to-moderate maintenance, BID may be adequate. Follow your vet’s guidance.

⚠️ **DO NOT USE ULTRACET.** Ultracet is a combination product that contains Tramadol \+ **acetaminophen (Tylenol)**. Acetaminophen is **toxic to squirrels and many small mammals** at standard doses. Always verify that you have plain Tramadol — not a combination product.

*See also: MELOXICAM entry for synergistic NSAID pain management; BUTORPHANOL entry for short-term injectable analgesia*
