heading: ACTIVATED CHARCOAL (Toxiban)
text:
## **ACTIVATED CHARCOAL (Toxiban)**

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond (Caslick), p. 260*

**What it is:** An emergency toxin-adsorbing agent used when a squirrel has ingested a poison that can bind to charcoal. Activated charcoal works like a sponge — it has an enormous surface area and physically traps toxins in the GI tract before they can be absorbed into the bloodstream. The Toxiban formulation also contains **sorbitol**, which acts as a cathartic (stimulates gut movement), helping to move the bound toxins out of the body faster.

This is an emergency tool. If you suspect poisoning, call your vet or a poison hotline immediately. Activated charcoal is most effective when given as soon as possible after ingestion — ideally within 1–2 hours.

**Poison hotlines:** \- ASPCA Poison Control: **(888) 426-4435** (consultation fee may apply) \- Pet Poison Helpline: **(855) 764-7661**

**Form:** Toxiban oral suspension, **0.2 g/mL** (200 mg/mL)

**Route:** By mouth, or via stomach tube for unresponsive or unwilling animals. Can be repeated every 4–8 hours for up to 2 days for toxins with enterohepatic recirculation.

---

### **Dose**

**10 mL/kg (delivers 2 g/kg — the lower end of the therapeutic 2–8 g/kg range)**

**Formula: weight in grams × 0.01 \= dose in mL**

| Animal Weight | Dose Volume | Charcoal Delivered |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 10 g | 0.1 mL | 0.02 g |
| 25 g | 0.25 mL | 0.05 g |
| 50 g | 0.5 mL | 0.1 g |
| 100 g | 1.0 mL | 0.2 g |
| 200 g | 2.0 mL | 0.4 g |
| 300 g | 3.0 mL | 0.6 g |
| 500 g | 5.0 mL | 1.0 g |
| 1000 g | 10.0 mL | 2.0 g |

For severe or rapidly progressing poisoning, the dose range extends to 20 mL/kg (4 g/kg). Follow your vet’s guidance on whether to increase.

---

### **⚠️ What Activated Charcoal DOES NOT Work On**

This is the critical part. Giving activated charcoal when it won’t help wastes precious time you could spend on effective treatment. Activated charcoal **does not bind** the following — do not use it as the primary response to these:

| Toxin Type | Examples | Why Charcoal Fails |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Heavy metals** | Zinc, lead, iron, mercury | Metal ions don’t bind to carbon surface |
| **Inorganic toxins** | Salt, sodium, potassium salts | Ionic compounds pass through |
| **Petroleum products** | Gasoline, mineral oil, motor oil | Non-polar hydrocarbons don’t bind |
| **Corrosive acids/alkalies** | Bleach, drain cleaners | Already reacting with tissue; binding too slow |
| **Camphor** | Moth balls, some topicals | Poor binding; too rapidly absorbed |
| **Cationic detergents** | Some fabric softeners, disinfectants | Ionic structure limits binding |
| **Xylitol** | Sugar-free gum, some medications | Partially absorbed (8–23%); not reliable |

**Zinc toxicity in particular:** Activated charcoal will NOT help a squirrel who has ingested a galvanized bowl screw, piece of hardware cloth, or zinc oxide cream. See the ZINC TOXICITY entry for the correct emergency protocol.

---

### **Medication Interaction — 3-Hour Rule**

**Wait at least 3 hours before giving any other oral medications after a dose of activated charcoal.** The charcoal will bind to the medications just as aggressively as it binds to toxins — rendering antibiotics, GI protectants, and other drugs useless if given too close together. If oral medication timing is critical, discuss with your vet whether to give the medication before the charcoal, or switch to injectable routes temporarily.

**One reassurance from the book:** Giving activated charcoal when it turns out not to be necessary (diagnostic error) has no significant adverse effects. In an emergency where you aren’t certain what was ingested, charcoal is a reasonable first response — just keep that 3-hour window in mind for all other meds.

*See also: ZINC TOXICITY entry for heavy metal ingestion; XYLITOL entry for sugar substitute poisoning; LOPERAMIDE entry for GI motility caution*

---

heading: SUCRALFATE (Carafate)
text:
## **SUCRALFATE (Carafate)**

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond (Caslick), p. 252*

**What it is:** A GI protectant that works mechanically, not chemically. When sucralfate hits the acidic environment of the stomach, it forms a thick, paste-like barrier over ulcers, erosions, and irritated stomach lining — physically shielding damaged tissue from further acid exposure while it heals. Think of it as a bandage you swallow that sticks to the wound inside.

This makes sucralfate different from acid-reducers like Famotidine and Omeprazole, which reduce acid production. Sucralfate doesn’t change acid levels — it protects tissue directly. The two are often used together for comprehensive GI protection.

**Use it for:** GI ulcers, gastric hemorrhage risk (including zinc toxicity cases), esophageal irritation, stress-induced gastritis, any case where the stomach lining is at risk.

**Form:** Oral suspension, **200 mg/mL** (also available as 1 g tablets, but the suspension is far easier to dose accurately in small mammals)

---

### **Dose**

**75 mg/kg every 4–6 hours, by mouth**

**Formula: weight in grams × 0.000375 \= dose in mL**

*(This delivers exactly 75 mg/kg at every weight when using 200 mg/mL suspension)*

| Animal Weight | Dose Volume | mg Delivered | Dose Check |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | 0.019 mL | 3.8 mg | 75 mg/kg ✓ |
| 100 g | 0.038 mL | 7.5 mg | 75 mg/kg ✓ |
| 150 g | 0.056 mL | 11.3 mg | 75 mg/kg ✓ |
| 200 g | 0.075 mL | 15.0 mg | 75 mg/kg ✓ |
| 300 g | 0.113 mL | 22.5 mg | 75 mg/kg ✓ |
| 500 g | 0.188 mL | 37.5 mg | 75 mg/kg ✓ |
| 750 g | 0.281 mL | 56.3 mg | 75 mg/kg ✓ |
| 1000 g | 0.375 mL | 75.0 mg | 75 mg/kg ✓ |

---

### **⚠️ Timing Is Everything — Give BEFORE Feeding**

**Give sucralfate 10 minutes before feeding, not after.**

Sucralfate needs an empty stomach to work. When food is present, the sucralfate can’t reach the stomach wall — it binds to food particles instead of damaged tissue. Ten minutes before feeding is enough time for the sucralfate to coat the stomach before formula arrives.

**Keep it away from other medications by at least 2 hours.** Sucralfate actively binds to drugs the same way it binds to toxins and food — it will significantly reduce the absorption of antibiotics (Baytril, Doxycycline, Clavamox, Fish Mox), vitamins, and other oral medications if given too close together. The standard recommendation is:

* Give sucralfate → wait 2 hours → give other oral medications

* Or give other oral medications → wait 2 hours → give sucralfate

This is not optional. Sucralfate given with Baytril, for example, can reduce the antibiotic’s blood levels enough that it becomes therapeutically ineffective — you’d be medicating without actually treating.

*See also: OMEPRAZOLE and FAMOTIDINE entries for complementary acid-reduction therapy; ZINC TOXICITY entry — sucralfate is part of the acute zinc toxicity treatment protocol*

heading: FAMOTIDINE (Pepcid)
text:
## **FAMOTIDINE (Pepcid)**

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond (Caslick), p. 252*

**What it is:** An H₂-receptor blocker (acid reducer). Famotidine tells the stomach to produce less acid — it blocks histamine receptors on the acid-producing cells of the stomach lining, reducing the total acid output. Less acid means less damage to an already-stressed or ulcerated GI tract, and a better environment for healing.

Famotidine is in the same class as Cimetidine (Tagamet), but with a longer duration of action, fewer drug interactions, and better tolerability — it’s the preferred H₂ blocker in most wildlife rehab settings.

**Use it for:** GI ulcers, stress gastritis, cases involving GI bleeding or suspected erosion, zinc toxicity (as part of the gastroprotection protocol), any animal on long-term NSAIDs where stomach protection is warranted.

**Form available:** \- **10 mg tablets** (OTC, human Pepcid — widely available) \- 10 mg/mL injectable (veterinary, requires prescription)

For rehab purposes, the tablet is the practical choice. Crush and dissolve for accurate small-volume dosing.

**Tablet dilution:** Crush 1 tablet (10 mg) into 10 mL sterile water → **1 mg/mL**

Prepare fresh; famotidine solutions degrade. Use within 24 hours or refrigerate and use within 48 hours.

---

### **Dose**

**0.5 mg/kg every 12–24 hours, by mouth**

**Formula: weight in grams × 0.0005 \= dose in mL (at 1 mg/mL)**

| Animal Weight | Dose Volume (1 mg/mL) | mg Delivered | Dose Check |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g | 0.025 mL | 0.025 mg | 0.5 mg/kg ✓ |
| 100 g | 0.050 mL | 0.050 mg | 0.5 mg/kg ✓ |
| 150 g | 0.075 mL | 0.075 mg | 0.5 mg/kg ✓ |
| 200 g | 0.100 mL | 0.100 mg | 0.5 mg/kg ✓ |
| 300 g | 0.150 mL | 0.150 mg | 0.5 mg/kg ✓ |
| 500 g | 0.250 mL | 0.250 mg | 0.5 mg/kg ✓ |
| 750 g | 0.375 mL | 0.375 mg | 0.5 mg/kg ✓ |
| 1000 g | 0.500 mL | 0.500 mg | 0.5 mg/kg ✓ |

---

### **Famotidine vs. Omeprazole — Which One?**

Both reduce stomach acid, but they work differently and have different strengths:

|  | Famotidine (Pepcid) | Omeprazole (Prilosec) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Class** | H₂-receptor blocker | Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) |
| **Onset** | 30–60 minutes | 1–4 hours (needs to be activated in body) |
| **Duration** | 12–24 hours | 24 hours |
| **Acid reduction** | Moderate | More complete |
| **Availability** | OTC, widely available | OTC, widely available |
| **Drug interactions** | Fewer | More (affects CYP450 enzymes) |
| **Best for** | Acute stress, short-term GI protection | Chronic ulcers, severe acid-related disease |

In practice: Famotidine is the go-to for short-term gastroprotection and acute situations (including zinc toxicity cases where you’re hospitalizing overnight). Omeprazole is better for animals with confirmed, persistent ulceration who need deep, sustained acid suppression.

**Using both together** is not harmful and is sometimes done for severe cases — they block different parts of the acid-producing pathway, so the effect is additive.

*See also: OMEPRAZOLE entry for the proton pump inhibitor alternative; SUCRALFATE entry for the complementary physical barrier protectant; ZINC TOXICITY entry — famotidine is part of the acute gastroprotection protocol*

heading: BB WOUNDS / PROJECTILE INJURIES
text:
## **BB WOUNDS / PROJECTILE INJURIES**

*Source: Wildlife rehabilitation clinical practice; cross-reference Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond (Caslick), p. 184*

**The situation:** A squirrel comes in with a BB embedded in its body — visible entry wound, confirmed or suspected on palpation or radiograph. Maybe you found it, maybe the person who brought it in saw it happen. The question every rehabber faces: do we leave it, or do we try to get it out?

The standard answer in wildlife rehabilitation has long been: **leave it.** The reasoning is sound. A BB sitting quietly in muscle or subcutaneous tissue, getting walled off by the body, has often been genuinely less dangerous than the operation to remove it.

That answer hasn’t changed. But there is a layer to this situation that changes how seriously you take everything that comes after.

---

### **The Problem You Cannot Solve From the Outside**

**You cannot identify what the BB is made of without removing it — and removing it to find out defeats the argument for leaving it.**

This matters because the materials involved are not inert:

**Zinc-coated steel BBs** are not a specialty product or an edge case. Standard steel BBs are almost universally zinc-plated as a corrosion treatment — it is the default manufacturing process. When you are looking at a BB wound, you are almost certainly looking at a zinc-coated object. You are not trying to identify a subset; you are looking at the standard product and simply lack a label to confirm what you already probably have.

**Lead shot** is also in circulation — older ammunition, certain BB guns, pellet guns — and lead is also a heavy metal toxin with a well-documented leaching profile. On a radiograph, you cannot tell zinc-plated steel from lead from bismuth from plain steel. Density appears different between materials, but distinguishing lead from zinc-coated steel reliably requires more than a standard radiograph read in a rehab setting.

Because both zinc and lead toxicity are possible, and because the leaching from embedded tissue (pH \~7.4) is slower than from an object in stomach acid (pH 1.5–3.5), toxicity signs may not appear immediately. The body will begin forming a fibrous capsule around the object, which reduces — but does not eliminate — ongoing metal contact with surrounding tissue.

**Monitor daily during active rehab care:**

| Sign | What It May Indicate |
| :---- | :---- |
| Pale or white mucous membranes | Anemia from intravascular hemolysis (zinc) or bone marrow suppression (lead) |
| Hind limb weakness or paralysis | Zinc or lead toxicity affecting neuromuscular function |
| Red or orange urine | Hemoglobinuria — red blood cell destruction (zinc) |
| Lethargy, loss of interest in food | General toxicity; any heavy metal exposure |
| Tremors, seizures | Lead toxicity, CNS involvement |
| Abdominal pain or bloating | GI involvement |
| Progressive weight loss despite eating | Chronic heavy metal exposure |

**Urine color note:** Red or orange urine in a squirrel eating a lot of acorns can be tannin-related and not an emergency. A squirrel who is symptomatic — weak, pale, lethargic — with red or orange urine is a different situation entirely. Context matters. See the ZINC TOXICITY entry for the full differential.

**Blood work:** If your vet can run a CBC and serum zinc levels, do it at intake and again at 2 weeks. Falling hematocrit (red blood cell percentage) with elevated zinc is confirmatory. Lead levels can also be tested and should be if zinc comes back normal but the animal is still declining.

---

### **If Toxicity Signs Appear — The Calculus Changes**

This is where the guidance shifts.

When the animal was asymptomatic, you were comparing **surgical risk** against **theoretical toxicity risk**. The surgery risk was real and concrete. The toxicity was possible but unconfirmed.

Once toxicity signs appear, you are comparing **surgical risk** against **ongoing heavy metal poisoning that will kill this animal.** The surgery that was previously hard to justify is now potentially the only path to survival. The BB that was tolerable as a “leave it” when the animal was stable is now actively poisoning it.

**Call your vet immediately.** At this point the conversation is: \- Confirm the toxicity (bloodwork if not already done) \- Assess surgical feasibility — location of the BB on radiograph, depth, proximity to vasculature or organs, anesthetic risk given the animal’s current condition \- Begin supportive care: IV fluids at 2× maintenance, GI protectants (Famotidine 0.5 mg/kg q12h, Sucralfate 75 mg/kg q4-6h), gastroprotection \- For confirmed zinc toxicity: Ca EDTA chelation therapy (vet-administered) \- For confirmed lead toxicity: DMSA (succimer) or CaEDTA chelation (vet-administered) \- Removal decision made with full picture in hand

There is no home treatment for active heavy metal toxicity in a squirrel. This is a vet emergency.

---

### **The Honest Conversation About Prognosis**

A squirrel who has been shot with a BB and presents to rehab has already survived something significant. If the BB is leaving them alone — no toxicity signs, eating well, healing — the odds of a good outcome are reasonable, and the “leave it” position holds.

If toxicity develops, the prognosis depends on how quickly it’s caught, how much metal has leached, and what the surgical options are. **Early detection is everything.** This is why the monitoring protocol isn’t optional even when the animal looks fine.

Document everything. Date of intake, BB location on radiograph, monitoring notes, any symptom onset with the date it first appeared. If this animal ends up at a vet in a deteriorating state, that documentation is the difference between an informed treatment decision and starting from scratch.

*See also: ZINC TOXICITY entry for full toxicity mechanism, symptom progression, and treatment protocol; FAMOTIDINE and SUCRALFATE entries for GI protection; BAYTRIL and CLAVAMOX entries for wound infection management*

drug: PREBIOTICS AND PROBIOTICS (Bene-Bac, Primal Defense, LA-200, FortiFlora, Proviable-DC, VSL#3)
text:
## **PREBIOTICS AND PROBIOTICS (Bene-Bac, Primal Defense, LA-200, FortiFlora, Proviable-DC, VSL\#3)**

*Source: Wild Mammal Babies: The First 48 Hours and Beyond (Caslick), pp. 255–257*

---

### **Understanding the Difference**

**Prebiotics** are not live organisms — they’re the food that feeds beneficial bacteria. They’re nondigestible fiber carbohydrates, specifically inulin and fructooligosaccharide (FOS), that pass through the upper GI tract undigested and arrive in the lower intestine where they feed the good bacteria that live there. Natural prebiotic sources include breast milk, soybeans, oats, beets, dandelion greens, chicory root, and bananas. Many commercial probiotic products include prebiotics as well, which is why you’ll sometimes see “synbiotics” on the label — that’s a product that combines both.

**Probiotics** are the live bacteria themselves. Millions of beneficial bacteria live in the small and large intestine of healthy animals. They digest food, crowd out harmful bacteria, and actively stimulate the local and systemic immune system. When that microbial balance gets disrupted — by illness, stress, capture, dietary changes, antibiotic therapy — harmful bacteria get the opening they’ve been waiting for, and diarrhea, gut dysfunction, and immune compromise can follow.

**When to use probiotics:** \- Antibiotic therapy (absolutely — this is non-negotiable) \- NSAIDs such as Meloxicam (gut flora takes a hit) \- At weaning (a major biological stressor) \- Dietary changes or poor nutritional intake \- Stress-related diarrhea \- Food intolerance or maldigestion \- At intake — any animal that has been through the stress of capture and transport

---

### **⚠️ The Timing Rule — Read This First**

**Do not give probiotics at the same time as antibiotics.**

The antibiotic doesn’t distinguish between the harmful bacteria it’s targeting and the live beneficial bacteria in the probiotic — it kills both. A probiotic given at the same time as Baytril is just expensive dead bacteria.

**Give the probiotic dose several hours before or after the antibiotic dose.** For BID antibiotics (morning and evening), give the probiotic at midday and bedtime, or find a window that keeps them separated. Keep giving the probiotic after the antibiotic course completes — the gut flora doesn’t bounce back the moment the last antibiotic dose is gone. Continue through recovery.

---

### **Products and Dosing**

#### *Bene-Bac® / Probiocin® (Lactobacillus)*

The most commonly used and most widely available probiotic in wildlife rehabilitation. Bene-Bac provides a concentrated live culture of intestinal flora microorganisms and is helpful for very young animals, emaciated animals, those on antibiotic therapy, and any animal in a stressful situation.

**Form:** Powder (packets) or gel (tube)  
**Dose:** 1 gram per 10 pounds body weight  
**Route:** PO — mix into formula or give directly  
**Frequency — standard protocol:** On admission, then day 3, day 5, day 7, and at weaning  
**Frequency — stress protocol:** 1 gram per 10 lbs; repeat in 3 days

| Animal Weight | Dose (at 1g/10 lbs) | Practical Guidance |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 50 g (0.11 lbs) | \~11 mg | Tiny smear of gel, or a barely-there pinch of powder into formula batch |
| 100 g (0.22 lbs) | \~22 mg | Small pinch of powder; small smear of gel |
| 200 g (0.44 lbs) | \~44 mg | Slightly larger pinch; a small pea-sized smear of gel |
| 454 g (1 lb) | \~100 mg (0.1g) | About 1/10th of a 1g packet |
| 908 g (2 lbs) | \~200 mg (0.2g) | About 1/5th of a 1g packet |

**Practical note for tiny babies:** At these doses, the powder form is nearly unmeasurable individually. The most practical approach for neonates is to mix a small amount into a formula batch — a pinch into ⅔ cup of formula distributes across all the feedings in that batch. The gel form (Bene-Bac Pet Gel, which comes in a syringe tube) is easier to control for individual tiny doses. Both work; use whatever you have.

---

#### *Primal Defense®*

A vegetarian probiotic made from barley grass and oat grass. What makes it different from most probiotics is that it contains Homeostatic Soil Organisms (HSOs) — beneficial bacteria found naturally in healthy soil that are vital for maintaining a balanced intestinal environment. It also contains a wide spectrum from 12 bacterial species including Lactobacilli, Bifidobacteria, and soil organisms, plus fermented ingredients with naturally occurring beneficial bacteria. Primal Defense® can survive stomach acid and bile acid, making it particularly hardy.

**Best for:** Herbivores (this one was specifically designed for herbivore gut biology)  
**Dose:** 1 gram per 10 lbs (same as Bene-Bac); baby herbivores: 1/8 tsp of powder mixed into formula

---

#### *LA-200 (Fox Valley)*

A probiotic powder produced by Fox Valley that provides naturally occurring viable Lactobacillus Acidophilus to help balance intestinal microflora during stress.

⚠️ **Do not confuse with the injectable antibiotic also called LA-200.** The injectable is Liquimycin (oxytetracycline) — also labeled LA-200 on some packaging. One is a probiotic supplement you mix into formula. The other is an antibiotic you inject. Read the label. Confirm the form before you use it.

---

#### *FortiFlora® by Purina*

Formulated for dogs and cats but used in wildlife rehab. Provides a guaranteed amount of live active cultures plus antioxidant Vitamins A, E, and C to support immune function. When choosing a probiotic, the manufacturer should guarantee viability of live microorganisms throughout the product’s shelf life — FortiFlora does this. Beneficial bacteria strains include Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Enterococcus.

---

#### *Proviable-DC® by Nutramax*

A multi-strain probiotic containing seven key strains for restoring intestinal microfloral balance after disruption. Comes in sprinkle capsules — easy to open and mix a partial capsule into formula. Good option when you want multi-strain coverage without the veterinary prescription barrier.

---

#### *VSL\#3®*

A high-potency probiotic containing 8 bacterial strains, considered a medical food. Regulates the intestinal barrier function. Studies on puppies recovering from parvovirus enteritis showed 20% more improvement in VSL\#3-treated animals versus controls — which tells you something about how seriously this one is taken clinically. For animals with severe gut compromise (post-parvovirus, post-severe illness, major surgery), this is a step up in power from standard probiotics.

---

### **The Gut Flora Timeline**

| Event | What Happens | Probiotic Response |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Intake / Capture stress | Stress hormones spike, gut flora disrupted | Give on admission |
| Starting antibiotics | Antibiotic kills beneficial bacteria alongside harmful | Give several hours offset from each dose |
| Weaning | Major dietary transition, gut environment shifts | Give at weaning; anticipate loose stool |
| End of antibiotic course | Gut flora depleted, takes time to recover | Continue probiotic through recovery |
| Diarrhea onset | Flora imbalance allowing harmful bacteria overgrowth | Give immediately; also investigate cause |

**One more thing:** Probiotics are not a substitute for identifying what’s causing diarrhea. They support the gut environment while you find and treat the underlying problem — dietary, bacterial, parasitic, or otherwise. A squirrel with persistent diarrhea who isn’t responding to probiotics and dietary adjustment needs a vet conversation, not more probiotic.

*See also: METRONIDAZOLE entry for bacterial diarrhea treatment; MYLICON/SIMETHICONE entry for gas management; L-GLUTAMINE entry for formula transition support; LOPERAMIDE hazard entry — never suppress diarrhea with Imodium*

---

*EVIDENCE CROSSWALK — SCIURIDAE / RODENT FORMULARY LANDSCAPE*

*This crosswalk records the strongest evidence tier identified in the Sciuridae / Squirrel / Prairie Dog Veterinary & Rehabilitation Formulary Landscape. It is intended to sit beside the individual entries until every formulary entry has been individually tagged and source-audited.*

*\[A\] DIRECT SQUIRREL / SCIURIDAE: Amoxicillin/clavulanate (Clavamox); Enrofloxacin (Baytril); Meloxicam; Carprofen; Butorphanol; Metronidazole; Fenbendazole (Panacur); Ivermectin; Atropine; Cimetidine; Metoclopramide; Furosemide; Dexamethasone; Ketamine; Midazolam; Buprenorphine; Toltrazuril; Doxapram; Medetomidine; Dexmedetomidine; Atipamezole; Fipronil; Interferon omega.*

*\[A/B\] DIRECT SCIURIDAE \+ RODENT SUPPORT: Doxycycline (direct prairie-dog \+ broader rodent respiratory data); Gabapentin (dedicated prairie-dog pharmacokinetic study \+ rat data); Lactated Ringer's Solution; Ketoprofen; Flunixin; Naloxone; Diazepam; Tramadol; Oxytetracycline.*

*\[B/C\] RODENT ANALOG / REHAB PRECEDENT: Albuterol; Gentamicin nebulization; Diphenhydramine; N-acetylcysteine; Simethicone (direct squirrel rehab use but weak dose standardization); normal saline nebulization/supportive use.*

*\[C\] DOCUMENTED USE / LIMITED SCIURIDAE DOSE VALIDATION: Prednisone/prednisolone; Ponazuril; Nystatin; Selamectin; Azithromycin; Ciprofloxacin; Levetiracetam; Triple antibiotic ointment; Silver sulfadiazine.*

*\[D\] SPECIALIST / HIGH-CAUTION OR INSUFFICIENT SCIURIDAE DOSING: Phenobarbital; clindamycin; penicillin G/procaine penicillin; activated charcoal; calcium disodium EDTA; cholestyramine; other entries where only experimental rodent exposure or specialist extrapolation is available.*

*Interpretation rule: When a direct squirrel/Sciuridae regimen exists, prefer that over generic rodent dosing unless a veterinarian selects otherwise. When no direct Sciuridae regimen exists, rat/rodent protocols may be used as an analog under veterinary direction and should remain explicitly labeled as extrapolated. Device-dependent inhaled therapies such as albuterol are especially dependent on concentration, nebulizer output, chamber volume, ventilation, and exposure time rather than simple mg/kg conversion.*

*Landscape source added 2026-09-10: Sciuridae / Squirrel / Prairie Dog Veterinary & Rehabilitation Formulary Landscape. This crosswalk should be revised whenever stronger direct Sciuridae evidence or veterinarian-validated squirrel protocols become available.*

*\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_*

*End of Formulary — 44 drug/supplement entries \+ 3 hazard/warning entries \+ 1 clinical situation entry · All entries reviewed and updated for clinical accuracy*

*See also: METRONIDAZOLE entry for bacterial diarrhea treatment; MYLICON/SIMETHICONE entry for gas management; L-GLUTAMINE entry for formula transition support; LOPERAMIDE hazard entry — never suppress diarrhea with Imodium*
